This study examines the generalization error of two-layer neural networks used to compute the ground state of the Schr\"odinger operator within a $d$-dimensional hypercube. We demonstrate that the convergence rate of this error remains independent of the dimension $d$, provided a suitable integral operator is employed as the network's target. To achieve this, we introduce methods to bound the Lipschitz constant of the integral operator with respect to various norms, as well as bounds on the covering numbers of finite rational approximations to these networks. Furthermore, we establish bounds for the Lipschitz constants of the network components. These technical advancements are applicable beyond this specific context, offering utility for broader machine learning challenges. Finally, we present numerical results for the first few eigenvalues of the Schr\"odinger operator in one, two, and three dimensions, utilizing networks trained via Unsupervised Dirac Training. Trained in approximately 20 minutes, the Dirac Training approach yields highly accurate results. Additionally, we show how to derive explicit error bounds for the generalization error, which can be optimized regarding the number of training samples and network size. The computational cost for training the proposed networks remains low. Trained in less than an hour, the resulting networks require minimal time for evaluation. For instance, the three-dimensional network necessitates only 1,000 training samples and comprises roughly 1.5 million parameters. With these parameters, calculating the network at a single point takes approximately 0.0001 seconds. Consequently, the proposed method is highly efficient for both training and computation. Overall, our findings indicate broad applicability for solving high-dimensional partial differential equations. For example, the three-dimensional network was trained in less than an hour and achieved an accuracy of approximately 10% relative to the true solution. This corresponds to a required training time of approximately 2 hours to achieve the same error margin in higher dimensions. In summary, the results presented in this paper are both accurate and highly efficient for solving high-dimensional Schr\"odinger eigenvalue problems. Achieving comparable results with finite difference or finite element methods would require either significantly longer training times or the use of much larger networks. For context, the three-dimensional network analyzed here was trained in under one hour using 1,000 samples with 1.5 million parameters, whereas the 1,000-sample, 1.5-million-parameter grid used in standard finite difference or finite element approaches would require approximately 200 hours of computation. This approach enables the estimation of conditional activity, given the states of other neurons, and reveals distinct activity patterns in unsampled neurons by extrapolating from available data. Furthermore, the method allows for the learning of activity patterns over extended time scales beyond the original dataset. We demonstrate that these models can be trained efficiently within a few minutes on a single GPU, even across populations of dozens of worms. The framework is validated through a single-neuron case study and an analysis involving up to 20 neurons. Additionally, the paper explores how this method can generate synthetic data, facilitate the design of genetic interventions to alter activity patterns, and predict activity in worms with altered synaptic connectivity. This paper extends the work of Cheong, Galashin, and Panova by demonstrating that the local limit of the fixed point forest is an infinite tree featuring dwarf nodes, thereby confirming their conjecture. Furthermore, this result offers a new perspective on the work of Gao, Li, and Panova, as it validates a conjecture proposed within that study. Additionally, we confirm another conjecture from the same reference regarding the limit shape of the fixed point forest. Specifically, we demonstrate that the rescaled forest converges in distribution to an infinite forest of random trees, where each tree possesses either zero or one node, with a probability of being single-node equal to $1 - e^{-\pi/2}$. This conclusion is derived from an expansion of a hypergeometric function that emerges in the generating function for fixed points. Our proof adapts the method employed by Galashin and Panova, which builds upon the approach established by Abulimit Tursunov and Tikhomirov. We conclude by addressing an open question posed by Cheong, Galashin, and Panova. To achieve this, we utilized an implementation of the fixed point forest by Chen, Galashin, and Pylyavskyy, originally released as computer algebra code. Finally, we validate the resulting conjecture through Monte Carlo simulations. A strong Gelfand pair (G,H) consists of a group G and a subgroup H where every irreducible character of H induces a multiplicity-free character on G. This paper classifies the strong Gelfand pairs for the special linear groups SL(2, p), where p denotes a prime number. Furthermore, we examine the associated spaces of double coset functions for these pairs, presenting a classification of irreducible characters that are not induced with multiplicity within this context. Finally, we apply these findings to classify subgroups of SL(2, p) that possess the strong Gelfand property. To facilitate these results, we also developed a computational implementation in GAP and provided a dataset of strong Gelfand pairs for SL(2, p), where p ranges from 5 to 17, in the form of a text file. This file includes information on the double coset spaces, the number of non-vanishing, unitary, and non-negative (a) characters, and the strong Gelfand property status of these pairs. Users can cross-reference specific strong Gelfand pairs by referencing their respective groups. Additionally, we offer a gap package containing functions to facilitate the computation of these pairs. This package can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/omar-ayad/StrongGelfandPairs. The package also includes a text file with pre-computed strong Gelfand pairs for SL(2, p) with p between 5 and 17, alongside a function designed to compute these pairs. The authors intend to release both the package and the text file through JAM in the near future. The data within the text file is also available at: https://omar-ayad.github.io/strongGelfandPairs/. This study investigates the electromagnetic characteristics of hidden-charm molecular pentaquarks containing strange quarks. We examine the magnetic dipole moments and electromagnetic form factors for the states $P_s(4430)(3924)$, $P_s(4380)(2600)$, and $P_s(4360)(3600)$, which correspond to $D_{s}^{*}D_{s}^{*}J/\psi$, $D_{s}^{*}D_{s}J/\psi$, and $D_{s}^{*}D_{s}J/\psi$ bound states, respectively. Furthermore, we analyze the helicity amplitudes associated with the reaction $J/\psi\phi \to PP$, where $P$ represents any of these three pentaquark states. Our results indicate that the magnetic dipole amplitudes $A_{1/2}$ and $B_{1/2}$ for the $P_s(4430)$ state are significantly larger than its electric dipole counterpart, $C_{1/2}$. Additionally, the magnetic dipole amplitudes for $P_s(4380)$ and $P_s(4430)$ are notably greater than those of $P_s(4360)$. These distinct electromagnetic signatures provide valuable insights for analyzing experimental data from the LHCb collaboration. Finally, our predictions for transition rates and decay widths of relevant particles offer new avenues for understanding hidden-charm molecular pentaquark properties. This research holds significant promise for advancing the field of multi-quark physics. Our methodology is fully applicable to exploring the electromagnetic attributes of other multiquark states. This work deepens our understanding of pentaquark states and their underlying physical mechanisms, potentially paving the way for future experimental investigations. We anticipate that the LHCb collaboration will soon confirm the existence of these three pentaquark states, thereby enriching our understanding of the physical nature of pentaquarks. This investigation represents a crucial step toward unraveling the complex nature of pentaquark matter. The LHCb collaboration is expected to soon reveal the electromagnetic properties of these three pentaquark states, which will provide new insights into the physical mechanisms of pentaquark formation. Our findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of the physical mechanisms underlying pentaquark formation. This paper demonstrates that all finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras over any field are nilpotent, thereby extending earlier findings that established their solvability. Additionally, we examine specific subclasses of Zinbiel algebras, proving the nilpotency or solvability of several through direct computation. To support these proofs, we present methods for identifying non-nilpotent Zinbiel algebras by utilizing bases with almost all identical elements. Furthermore, we establish the general theorem by constructing a family of identities characterized by the same property. Finally, the paper concludes with an analysis of the equivalence between these two approaches. This paper investigates the scattering theory for the inhomogeneous cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring an inverse square potential in three dimensions:
$$ i\partial_t u + (-\Delta + \frac{\mu}{|x|^2})u = |x|^\alpha |u|^2 u, \quad (t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^3, $$
where $\mu\in (-1, \frac{1}{4})$ and $\alpha\in (-1, 0)$. We establish local well-posedness within the critical homogeneous Sobolev space $\dot{H}^{\frac{3-\alpha}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^3)$. Leveraging the specific structure of the critical space relative to the nonlinear term, we demonstrate global well-posedness and scattering for solutions whose initial data fall below the ground state threshold. Specifically, by utilizing the sharp profile decomposition applicable to this critical space, we provide a direct proof of multilevel concentration-compactness without relying on the variational characterization of the threshold solution. This approach circumvents the need to analyze the stability of a second solution arising from a modified equation with constant coefficients. Furthermore, we establish global well-posedness for data below the threshold in the case where $\alpha\in [-1, -\frac{1}{2}]$. Finally, we demonstrate scattering for initial data in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ when $\alpha = -1$. These findings are optimal as they encompass all previously studied cubic inhomogeneous Schrödinger equations. The methodology employed extends the recent direct proof of scattering for the focusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with an inverse square potential by Genkai Zhang. Additionally, our results offer a novel perspective on the scattering phenomenon by providing a direct argument that avoids sharp variational characterizations. We anticipate these findings will facilitate the development of new techniques for analyzing scattering phenomena. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance where scattering theory for inhomogeneous nonlinear Schrödinger equations has been applied in this specific manner. The study concludes with an outline of the techniques employed and an examination of related works.
Keywords: Inhomogeneous nonlinear Schrödinger equation; cubic nonlinearity; inverse square potential; scattering; concentration-compactness; threshold solutions.

We introduce a migration infection (MI) process defined as the union of two independent mechanisms: a simple random walk (SRW) and a basic contagion (BC) process, where the SRW represents the migration component. Within this framework, the system begins with a single infected agent at time $t=0$, who undergoes a SRW. The complete MI process is terminated the moment a second agent is infected. Consequently, the total duration of any specific MI process equals the time instant of the second infection event. By examining two variants of this process—where the container holds either a fixed $N$ agents or allows for $N$ agent births over $t$ time steps—we determine the average lifetime of the MI process for both scenarios. In the first variant, the mean lifetime approximates $t^*$, calculated as the average number of steps a SRW requires to infect a second agent. In the second variant, the average lifetime is derived from the intersection of the SRW and BC components, yielding an approximation of $t^{**}$. For the fixed-$N$ agent variant, we further demonstrate that the SRW approximation holds true for any $N$ when applied to a one-dimensional system. Finally, we establish that the contagion component of the MI process can be approximated by the average of the SRW and BC results. Overall, the findings indicate that migration significantly extends the average lifetime of the MI process, particularly within a one-dimensional environment. These results are supported by both analytical methods and computer simulations. Keywords: Random walks, basic contagion processes, migration infection processes. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 60J10, 60K35, 60K37.

K2-138 stands out as a key exoplanetary system for investigating the frequency of 3:2 resonant chains in planetary populations. This study employs a novel method to validate the existence of a 3:2 resonant chain within the K2-138 system. We analyze the orbital period ratios of the five planets, revealing a distinct pattern characterized by five consecutive period ratios consistently below unity and five consecutively above unity, which indicates the presence of a resonant chain. To confirm this, we conduct a dynamical analysis using real data, demonstrating that the system possesses a stable 3:2 resonant chain. Our findings indicate that planet c occupies the 3:2 resonance with planet b, while planets d, e, and f form a 3:1 resonant chain. Furthermore, we examine the eccentricity evolution of the system and establish the order of resonant angles. We also explore the formation and migration mechanisms of K2-138, suggesting that its resonant configuration may have arisen through simultaneous planet formation and migration. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for understanding the frequency of 3:2 resonant chains in exoplanetary systems. This work is significant for determining resonance formation mechanisms and assessing the impact of resonant formations on system stability and evolution. Our analysis of the K2-138 system will aid in comprehending the dynamics of exoplanetary systems and the migration processes of exoplanets. Additionally, this study will assist in selecting optimal targets for future observations and investigations. We believe this work will be valuable for advancing our understanding of exoplanetary systems and their evolution. The SiD Detector represents one of two proposed designs for the future International Linear Collider (ILC), a configuration currently led by the experimental SiD collaboration comprising approximately 200 physicists and technical experts. Conceived in 2003, the detector was originally engineered for a 500 GeV electron-positron collider. Since then, advancements in particle accelerator technology and significant gains in simulation and data analysis capabilities have informed updates to its design. The discussion will highlight key detector systems, analyze their performance under current design specifications, and outline proposed technical upgrades. Furthermore, the presentation will address ongoing R&D initiatives, software developments, simulation studies, and simulation-driven design enhancements. Finally, the talk will explore a scenario for integrating SiD into an Higgs Factory environment. The SiD collaboration warmly invites the community to participate in these discussions. Amorphous ice exhibits two distinct local structures: a high-density amorphous (HDA) phase and a low-density amorphous (LDA) phase. Although HDA ice is generated under high pressure, theoretical models propose it may possess a hexagonal close-packed hexagonal long-range order, contrasting with the locally tetrahedrally coordinated LDA. While HDA ice can form in astronomical settings, LDA is believed to dominate the interstellar medium. Our prior research identified tetrahedral ice clusters in both HDA and LDA amorphous ices, which we termed the "tetrahedral ice phase." In this study, we expand upon our earlier findings by constructing a complete network of tetrahedral clusters across two amorphous ice models, revealing a novel structure: the tetrahedral ice phase with long-range order, or the crystal-ice domain. This newly identified crystal-ice domain displays local structures characteristic of both ice and carbon. Furthermore, we successfully constructed the carbon-ice phase, a previously unreported structure, by substituting tetrahedral clusters within the crystal-ice domain with benzene rings. This study demonstrates that the density of ice models significantly influences their structural properties, thereby expanding the design of theoretical ice models. These findings offer valuable insights for interpreting the chemical signatures of amorphous ices in the interstellar medium. Additionally, the crystal-ice domain and carbon-ice phase identified here may serve as theoretical foundations for future research into astrochemical ice phases. Finally, the crystal-ice domain is expected to exhibit unique physical and chemical properties, making it a prime candidate for further investigation into its formation and occurrence in the universe. This report outlines my second-year project conducted at the Centre for Nano Science and Technology at IIT Roorkee, utilizing a variable temperature Scanning Tunneling Microscope (STM). The primary objective was to employ STM and Scanning Tunneling Spectroscopy (STS) for the atomic-scale imaging and measurement of a material's Local Density of Spectra (LDOS). The study included the fabrication of graphite, silicon, and gold samples, followed by imaging LDOS at room temperature and varying vertical temperatures (5 K, 300 K, 323 K) for silicon. Additionally, STS data was gathered to observe how the LDOS gap in n-type silicon varies with temperature. The results successfully demonstrated LDOS measurement in graphite and gold at atomic resolution, whereas silicon proved challenging due to complications arising from both tunneling and scanning. Furthermore, the temperature-dependent LDOS of n-type silicon was analyzed to understand the impact of thermal excitation on the density of states. The report also examines potential limitations of the experimental setup and the sample preparation process. Overall, this work serves as an introduction to the capabilities of LDOS measurement. To achieve atomic resolution, the experiment utilized a Si tip for graphite and a W tip for gold and silicon samples. The STM was a variable-temperature, ultra-high-vacision (10^-10 mbar) instrument featuring a piezo-electric scanner, a feedback loop, a bias supply, and a current amplifier. LDOS was determined by applying a small bias voltage between the sample and tip, adjusting the tip height to maintain a constant tunneling current, and analyzing the resulting spatial variations in electron density. The tunneling current is governed by the bias voltage, tip-sample separation, LDOS, and tip shape. By applying a small bias between a conductive tip and a sample, electrons tunnel between them, with the tunneling current proportional to the bias voltage. The LDOS at a specific point reflects the local electron density, which can be visualized by adjusting the tip position relative to the sample surface. By setting a constant tunneling current, the tip height is inversely related to the LDOS; thus, by scanning a tip with a fixed current across a sample, the local electron density at each point can be measured. To maintain a constant current, the tip must be positioned closer to regions of high electron density and farther from regions of low density. The tip-sample separation is adjusted using a piezo-electric stage, which moves the tip in response to applied voltages.

This growth has resulted in numerous cross-library dependencies, creating a complex web of obligations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applying our previously proposed algorithms for simplifying dependency graphs can produce more accessible ISAF libraries, particularly for initiatives like the Mathematics in Computer Science initiative. Ultimately, this article aims to establish a foundation for assessing library complexity to facilitate more effective library organization. Finally, we outline several promising future research directions concerning the application of our tools and metrics to enhance libraries within ISAF. Specifically, we propose using these tools to analyze recent simplification efforts, including the Computer Mathematics initiative and the recently launched Mathematics in Computer Science initiative. Heliospheric observations utilize various instruments to record ultralow-frequency (ULF) magnetospheric plasma waves, which are critical for analyzing energy and momentum transfer between the solar wind and Earth. This study examines the impact of instrument noise on data quality across different missions. By applying various filtering techniques to OGO-5 data, we compare the effects of band-pass, high-pass, and wavelet filters, subsequently assessing how noise influences the determination of ULF wave polarization. The analysis reveals that band-pass and high-pass filters alter magnetic variance in specific directions, whereas the wavelet filter preserves these characteristics. Additionally, we demonstrate the application of Hilbert transforms with wavelet filters to extract magnetospheric phase information. Ultimately, we evaluate the utility of making ULF waves audible through spectrogram and sonogram visualizations. These methods are particularly effective for detecting the most intense waves, such as those occurring during magnetic substorms, and for identifying the relative phases of magnetic fluctuations across multiple directions. Furthermore, they facilitate rapid visual inspection of the data. Overall, this work provides the foundation for visualizing and listening to ULF plasma waves to facilitate more intuitive analysis. Specifically, we have made various audio files from OGO-5 available for public access. Furthermore, the observational data and analysis methods presented here are applicable to any mission recording ULF magnetospheric plasma waves. Consequently, this research is especially relevant to current missions like the Van Allen Probes, Cluster, and MMS. Finally, this work offers a preliminary overview of ULF waves, complementing our earlier publication on magnetospheric plasma wave analysis. We investigate the thermodynamic properties of charged rotating dilaton black branes coupled to logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics, focusing on their phase structure. For simplicity, we assume constant electromagnetic coupling. Our findings indicate that the phase transition is of first order, and the critical parameter values depend directly on the electromagnetic coupling function. Additionally, we examine the effects of the dilaton field, observing a significant impact on the system's thermodynamics, which suggests a potential link to dilaton-electromagnetism. Finally, we analyze the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, revealing a notable dependence on both the dilaton field and the electromagnetic coupling function. These results suggest that the electromagnetic field and the dilaton scalar field are essential for the existence of matter and energy in the universe. All of these effects are substantially influenced by the specific form of the nonlinear electrodynamics. Our results could be relevant to astrophysics, particularly in the study of active galactic nuclei and magnetars. Furthermore, these findings may contribute to theoretical physics, offering potential insights into quantum gravity, superstring theory, supergravity, black holes, AdS/CFT correspondence, quark-gluon plasma, and the early universe. This study also offers a new perspective on understanding various astrophysical phenomena. Finally, we anticipate that these results will encourage further research and exploration in both theoretical and astrophysical contexts. This paper is part of a comprehensive effort to explore the charged rotating dilaton black brane system coupled to nonlinear electrodynamics, building upon a series of related works that examine different electromagnetic models, including power-law, exponential, sine-Gordon, tanh-modified, logarithmic, sinh-modified, and tanh nonlinear electrodynamics, as well as non-minimally coupled scenarios. These related studies are detailed in references [1-16]. Natural language is a complex and ambiguous human communication method that encapsles both explicit and implicit information. Representing text data in a format that machines can easily comprehend is a critical challenge in text mining. This study proposes a new memory-based structure for modeling text, drawing inspiration from the fact memory component of large-scale neural network architectures. The primary advantage of this approach is its ability to retain the original text data in its initial format while simultaneously extracting and storing metadata in a structured manner. This enables a more comprehensive interpretation of text compared to conventional methods. The paper outlines the principles behind this model and details two experimental text mining tasks solved using it: detecting the relative positions of entities within local contexts and identifying negative relationships between entities. These solutions operate without any pre-training and involve no human intervention. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the model can be enhanced through the application of standard machine learning techniques for feature selection and classification. Ultimately, the paper argues that the effectiveness of the solved tasks validates the utility of the proposed structure. The results achieved without pre-training or human input are competitive with state-of-the-art solutions relying on the same data. Additionally, the solved tasks are among the most fundamental in text mining, providing the foundation for the development of more advanced models. The paper concludes by identifying directions for future research. All code and data referenced in this study are publicly available. Specifically, the code required to replicate the experiments is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/rafal-mazur/desmem, and the evaluation data for the tasks is accessible via Conda at https://anaconda.org/rafal-mazur/nlpcorpus. We present a family of unital C* algebras defined by a continuous parameter, linking Cuntz-Alogluu (CAR) and Cuntz-Toeplitz (CCR) generalized canonical commutation relation algebras. Specifically, the CAR algebra corresponds to the zero-parameter limit, while the CCR algebra emerges from the co-induced subalgebra within the Cuntz-Toeplitz algebra generated by an isometry that vanishes at the zero-parameter limit. The Gogol language family was created to offer fixed-point semantics for the evaluation of algorithms. To our knowledge, this study presents the first small-step operational semantics for any Gogol language. Consequently, this work aims to demonstrate the expressiveness of small-step operational semantics and introduce novel formal techniques. Specifically, we focus on the GP 2 language, the most sophisticated variant in the Gogol family, which incorporates support for exceptions. The developed semantics employs an expression-based small-step approach. Our analysis emphasizes several key aspects: abstract machines, handling expressions, the management of the computation stack and continuation, and the modeling of exceptions. Furthermore, we prove fundamental properties such as determinism, preservation of values and stacks, and progress. Notably, the proof of the last property necessitates a significant modification to the standard last property definition to accurately reflect the behavior of exceptions. Finally, we establish a head-reduction semantics tailored for normal forms and provide a third, independent formalization of exceptions. This demonstrates that the last property can be proven without modification when utilizing an alternative semantics for the same language. The ongoing debate regarding the origin of molecular gas in protoplanetary disks centers on whether photoevaporation, MHD winds, or both processes contribute. To address this, we developed models to predict free-free emission from these mechanisms and compared them with current and future observations of TW Hydrae using the VLA, EHT, and VLT/ALMA. Our results indicate that free-free emission from MHD disk wind models is extremely weak, making it undetectable with current facilities. Consequently, we propose a future observational strategy for TW Hydrae that targets ionized gas potentially sourced from photoevaporation. We conclude that the free-free emission from the TW Hydrae disk will be detectable by ALMA within approximately 100 hours using a 1 GHz bandwidth at 1.3 GHz, with sensitivity improving with longer integration times. This emission would be significantly stronger if the disk's ionization fraction were elevated by cosmic rays or X-rays. Ultimately, observing TW Hydrae serves as a critical test for photoevaporation models, offering a pathway to understand the history of gas in disks and the subsequent formation of gas giant planets. A future ALMA observation of TW Hydrae at 1.3 GHz with a 1 GHz bandwidth and a sensitivity of roughly 100 $\mu$Jy/beam would be sufficient to constrain photoevaporation models. Furthermore, we outline a future strategy for studying photoevaporation in the MHD context, including the development of a model for ionized gas produced by MHD winds. Finally, we outline future research directions to better constrain the physical conditions of the disk atmosphere and ionization sources, as these factors directly influence the free-free emission from photoevaporation. This research will be conducted using MURAM, a global hydrodynamic model capable of simulating photoevaporation and cosmic ray and X-ray induced ionization. Ultimately, the free-free emission from the disk will provide a unique tool for testing models of gas accretion onto young stars. The paper concludes with a discussion of the challenges associated with this approach. Alvaro B. M. P. Intelligent protection strategies utilizing current and voltage data from the primary and secondary circuits of two-core symmetric phase-angle regulators (also known as phase shifting transformers) have been investigated. The study establishes a mathematical framework for calculating current and voltage transformation ratios, as well as phase shifts for each core. Furthermore, the paper introduces a method to classify transient incidents—specifically internal faults, short-term losses, and long-term losses—based on measured current and voltage values. This approach incorporates the analysis of both no-load and loaded transient characteristics. Results from computer simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. A prototype was subsequently constructed and tested using real-world transient data, with outcomes aligning perfectly with simulated predictions. The proposed intelligent protection technique is applicable to various transient types, including internal faults, short-term losses, and long-term losses, as well as switching events. Additionally, the study extends to classifying overvoltage events within the classified system. The proposed solution offers the advantages of simplicity, reliability, and cost-effectiveness. A prototype implementation is currently under development for deployment in the power sector. Future work will expand this approach to three-core symmetric phase-shifting transformers. To achieve this, a new classification algorithm is being designed to incorporate current and voltage data from transformer terminals alongside measurements from the power grid. This proposed solution provides the benefit of simplicity. The authors anticipate that this solution will prove beneficial, and they invite researchers in power systems to utilize these findings to their advantage. Multicasting, where a base station (BS) transmits to multiple groups of users via a hybrid analog-digital precoder, holds significant promise for millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems by balancing performance and computational complexity. This paper investigates optimal hybrid multicasting precoding strategies, specifically examining the impact of restricting analog precoders to the maximum number of path directions per group. The study demonstrates that this limitation can substantially degrade multicasting gains. To mitigate this degradation, a digital precoder distribution method is proposed that ensures all group paths remain distinct. Furthermore, a path-direction quantization metric is introduced to effectively reduce the count of path directions. Simulation outcomes confirm the efficacy of the proposed path direction selection and distribution techniques. Finally, the influence of multicasting on achievable rates and outage probability across various group configurations is analyzed. These results indicate that multicasting is particularly advantageous when users in different groups exhibit distinct channel path directions. Out of the two key factors—group size and path direction diversity—path direction diversity proves to be the more critical factor. Outage analysis reveals that multicasting benefits small groups of users with diverse path directions but offers negligible benefit to large groups. In contrast, achievable rate analysis suggests that multicasting is more beneficial for large groups. Ultimately, multicasting strategies are viable when user groups are small and heterogeneous in terms of path directions. To achieve optimal multicasting, the proposed path direction selection and distribution techniques should be implemented. Specifically, when user groups are small and diverse, digital precoders must be assigned to all possible path directions. Conversely, if groups are large and similar, path directions should be selected based on their most frequent occurrences. Additionally, the potential multicasting gain is significantly higher when groups are small and heterogeneous compared to when groups are large and homogeneous. Finally, the paper outlines multicasting applications within non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) networks. It confirms that multicasting can substantially improve NOMA's achievable rate and outage performance, particularly when users in different groups have varying path directions. However, multicasting offers minimal benefit to NOMA when path directions are homogeneous. Furthermore, NOMA's multicasting strategy is feasible when user groups are small and heterogeneous, whereas it is not feasible when groups are large and homogeneous. In terms of selection criteria, group size exerts a greater influence than path direction diversity. The analysis concludes that multicasting improves NOMA's performance by enabling the use of different power allocation and codebook distribution patterns for different groups. Additionally, we outline a general approach for constructing groups with near exponential residual finiteness growth, a method we apply to the Sanov group $\langle a,b,c,d\mid (ab)^2=(cd)^2=1\rangle$. This work investigates the stretched Euler–Bernoulli beam on a metric graph composed of an interval and a star-shaped component featuring $N$ edges, with the system governed by four-order differential operators. By employing a change of variables, we transform the problem into a system of second-order differential operators, solving the Cauchy problem for the resulting hyperbolic equations to derive a stability estimate. Furthermore, we establish that normal modes grow no faster than a geometric progression. These findings are applied to prove the asymptotic stability of the Cauchy problem when the graph consists of a finite countable union of intervals, subject to boundary conditions at the origin and boundary dissipation solely at one endpoint of each interval. Additionally, asymptotic stability is demonstrated for a graph formed by a finite union of intervals under specific boundary conditions at the origin, provided the intervals are not isospectral. Finally, it is shown that if the intervals are isospectral, the associated boundary conditions can be selected to induce oscillatory behavior. These results build upon and extend previous studies by M. M. Masmoudi, L. Marini, and the third author. Notably, unlike many existing works, this paper avoids reliance on small eigenvalue asymptotics. Instead, it utilizes a hyperbolic approach grounded in energy methods, thereby ensuring a direct proof of stability. The methodology developed offers a viable alternative to spectral analysis for proving stability in stretched graphs with periodic structures. The paper concludes with an outline of future research directions aimed at extending these findings to more general stretched graphs. Sapphire serves as a fundamental substrate for numerous superconducting quantum technologies, including transmon qubits, kinetic inductance detectors, and parametric amplifiers. However, variations in dielectric loss tangent ($\tan \delta$) measurements across different groups and frequencies have hindered its precise quantification as a material parameter. By employing high-precision microwave dielectric spectroscopy, we have directly measured the $\tan \delta$ of high-quality sapphire up to 100 GHz, achieving a sensitivity of 1 ppb. Our findings indicate that the intrinsic microwave loss of sapphire, represented by the $\tan \delta$, exhibits a frequency dependence of $\nu^{0.01 \pm 0.01}$. Furthermore, we identified that as-grown sapphire plates possess a higher $\tan \delta$ compared to sapphire synthesized via heat treatment. These results offer the first quantitative analysis of the microwave dielectric loss properties of sapphire, establishing a new standard for the reliability and reproducibility of dielectric loss measurements in quantum devices fabricated with this material. Additionally, the intrinsic loss of sapphire plates is approximately one order of magnitude lower than that of other common dielectrics used in superconducting quantum systems. Finally, we present a model correlating $\tan \delta$ with the loss tangent angle, a property measurable via optical ellipsometry. This model aligns with prior studies demonstrating that oxygen vacancies are the primary source of dielectric loss in sapphire. Consequently, the intrinsic dielectric loss of sapphire arises from its high crystal purity, and the overall dielectric loss of sapphire-based devices is primarily determined by the quality of the grown sapphire plates. These insights provide a valuable foundation for the development of high-performance dielectric-based devices. This work was conducted in collaboration with the Center for High-Precision Measurement at the University of Science and Technology of China. Y.C. and J.W. contributed equally to this research.

A moving dielectric interface can induce a non-conservative force that drags light through a dielectric medium, a phenomenon termed "optical drag." In this work, we identify an anomalous form of optical drag occurring at dielectric boundaries, which significantly enhances the conventional effect, particularly in regimes involving strong dispersion and absorption. This mechanism arises fundamentally from the condition that the electric field must vanish at any dielectric airgap, thereby eliminating any phase-matched photon propagation through air within the gap. Consequently, all photon propagation across the entire gap becomes dependent on the material's refractive index and dielectric permittivity. This dependence generates a substantial optical drag force whenever the interface moves, provided the transverse wave vector remains below the cutoff for any phase-matched propagating mode in the gap. This phenomenon is termed "anomalous optical drag." We demonstrate such a force in a photonic crystal slab waveguide, where it arises from airgaps situated both above and below the structure. Furthermore, we show that another source of absorption-induced momentum transfer can amplify this force by several orders of magnitude. This effect is most pronounced when light propagates in a photonic crystal slab waveguide situated near a guided resonance of the underlying periodic structure, which creates an extremely narrow and deep pole in the photonic band structure specifically for guided light. This guided resonance photonic pole constitutes a photonic equivalent to the Feshbach resonance atom-molecule bound state in atomic physics. We illustrate this phenomenon using a photonic crystal slab waveguide coupled to a photonic crystal slab grating, where the anomalous optical drag force increases by approximately four orders of magnitude near the resonance frequency of the grating. This phenomenon is termed "resonant optical drag." We also observe resonant optical drag in a photonic crystal slab waveguide by exploiting the momentum transfer associated with enhanced absorption at any frequency near the waveguide's photonic band edge. This waveguide's photonic band edge is fundamentally linked to the photonic pole of the refractive index of silicon, which is not directly observable in standard optics. We refer to this as "photonic index pole momentum transfer." The existence of resonant optical drag and photonic index pole momentum transfer underscores a profound connection between photonic pole physics and photonic momentum transfer. This connection is particularly evident when considering the optical forces experienced by photonic structures during grating illumination. We further explore the potential applications of these novel optical forces in controlling and manipulating the motion of photonic structures. The investigation into socioeconomic conditions has gained significant traction within the fields of computer science and data science. However, existing research often suffers from data limitations, including a lack of diversity, multi-distribution, multi-resolution, and multi-modal characteristics. This paper introduces the H4M Dataset, designed for advanced socioeconomic analytics in Beijing. Comprising 100 heterogeneous, multi-source, multi-modal, multi-resolution, and multi-distributional datasets, the H4M Dataset includes 14 spatially distributed datasets aligned with Beijing's 10 municipal districts and 86 subdistricts. These datasets span various analytical dimensions: (1) spatial distribution across administrative areas, (2) temporal granularity ranging from minutes to years, (3) data types including spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal, (4) pixel resolutions from 10 meters to 1 kilometer, and (5) semantic categories encompassing 21 dimensions such as air quality, social, and economic data. This work demonstrates how the H4M Dataset can be utilized for socioeconomic analysis and serves as a foundational resource for developing intelligent city management systems. Furthermore, it provides a multi-distributional, multi-modal, and multi-resolution training foundation for deep learning applications in socioeconomic analysis. Pattern extraction and exploration represent fundamental challenges in both computer science and mathematics. While recent advancements in image processing and pattern-driven exploration have significantly transformed these fields through the application of patterns to various real-world images and services, these methods have primarily focused on natural images. In contrast, scientific and engineering datasets often exhibit distinct, interpretable visual patterns that can be leveraged to enhance data analysis. These patterns are frequently embedded within complex visual representations and span diverse applications, including gene expression analysis, particle simulation, fluid dynamics, and material science. This paper introduces a unified framework for pattern extraction and exploration specifically tailored for scientific and engineering data. By integrating high-performance deep learning models for image processing with state-of-the-art convolutional neural networks for pattern matching, we demonstrate that visual patterns can serve as a powerful signal to improve data analysis. Furthermore, we emphasize the role of human users in interpreting these patterns, which facilitates data discovery and interpretation, particularly for large-scale datasets. We validate the effectiveness of this framework across three real-world big data applications and demonstrate its utility for rapid data exploration. Ultimately, our findings suggest that visual patterns can act as a vital signal for data analysis and support human interpretation, thereby contributing to the exploration and understanding of big data. This approach offers a significant opportunity for data analysis and human-computer interaction researchers to develop novel visual methods for data exploration. Additionally, our framework is designed to be easily adaptable for future extensions to handle other exploration tasks and additional datasets. To foster further research, we have made the code and datasets publicly available. This paper is intended to be paired with another that details our data exploration system. Together, these works illustrate how visual patterns can function as a critical signal for data analysis and how interactive exploration can address the specific requirements of data analysis and discovery tasks. Ultimately, visual patterns and their interactions with users provide novel insights for data analysis and exploration, enhancing both analytical outcomes and the human experience. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become essential for numerous graph-based applications. However, acquiring sufficient task-specific data to train these models effectively is often difficult. Consequently, leveraging knowledge from large general datasets to address specific tasks through transfer learning is a promising solution. This study investigates transfer learning within the domain of graph classification, examining the impact of task similarity, source dataset size, and network hyperparameters. The results indicate that transfer learning can enhance performance, particularly when applied to small datasets with tasks similar to those in the source data. Additionally, a model utilizing pre-edges demonstrates superior performance, highlighting the value of structural information in GNNs. The study further reveals that GNNs are more sensitive to transfer learning than MLPs, and it offers insights into selecting appropriate architectures for both novel transfer learning scenarios and established graph classification benchmarks. The experimental findings are consistent across the MNIST, FMNIST, and FEMNIST datasets. Furthermore, this research represents the first comprehensive examination of transfer learning specifically for GNNs. Current collaborative filtering methods typically model users and items using latent features, but these features often lack direct interpretability for end-users. To address this limitation, we propose a "double feature allocation" model for a recommender system, ensuring that while latent features drive the actual recommendations, a second set of dictionary features remains interpretable. Although this enhanced transparency does not necessarily boost the actual recommendation accuracy, it enables the evaluation of how transparent the system is to human observers and fosters trust. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of a recommender system utilizing a double feature allocation structure. To verify the transparency of the generated human interpretations of user and item features, we conducted an experiment involving questionnaires and open-ended interviews. The experimental results confirmed our hypothesis, demonstrating the value of the double feature allocation model for human comprehension of users and items. Furthermore, the paper outlines potential future applications of this double representation approach in e-commerce and marketing. Set disjointness is a foundational problem in data streams that has garnered significant interest due to its relevance to graph coloring. While numerous studies have tackled this problem, a recent breakthrough by Boning et al. established the first non-trivial lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ on the space complexity of a $(2-\epsilon)$-approximation algorithm for $(1+\epsilon)$-coloring, thereby resolving an open question posed by Boning and Bonucci. However, their technique is intricate and relies heavily on the specific choice of "bad" graphs. In this work, we provide a straightforward proof of a new set disjointness algorithm that achieves a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1/3})$, matching the result of the previous study. Our approach is more straightforward and more readily applicable to other set disjointness problems. Furthermore, our method introduces a novel and practical perspective on resolving lower bounds in data streams. We also examine the data-intensiveness of graph coloring, demonstrating that our algorithm can achieve a $(1+\epsilon)$-coloring for $(n^{2/3}-\delta)$-colorable graphs within $(O(n^{2/3}/\epsilon)/\delta)$ space. Additionally, we present a new algorithm for $(1+\epsilon)$-coloring $(\Delta-k)$-colorable graphs that utilizes $O(n/(k\epsilon)^2)$ space. To our knowledge, this represents the first algorithm to provide non-trivial space complexity for this class of graphs. The simplicity of our approach also yields the first $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithm for 3-colorable graphs utilizing $O(1/\epsilon^2)$ space. Finally, we introduce the first $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithm for $(\Delta-2)$-colorable graphs operating within $(n^{1/2}-\delta)$ space for any $\delta>0$. This result is derived by extending our algorithm for 3-colorable graphs, which employs $O(n^{1/2}/\delta)$ space to deliver a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation. Our findings also yield a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithm for 4-colorable graphs with a space complexity of $O(n^{1/2}/\epsilon^2)$. We demonstrate that our algorithm for 3-colorable graphs is optimal in terms of space complexity. Moreover, we show that our algorithm for $(\Delta-2)$-colorable graphs is optimal in space complexity

This study investigates the momentum dependence of the static transverse spin susceptibility in the paramagnetic phase of the 3D classical O(3) model, which serves as a continuum representation of the 3D Heisenberg (TN=1) antiferromagnet. Utilizing the standard momentum cutoff regularization for tensor integrals derived from theTN=1 Lagrangian, the susceptibility $\chi_{+}(\mathbf{q})$ is demonstrated to deviate from simple analyticity in low momentum $\mathbf{q}$, exhibiting a unique non-analytic term proportional to $|\mathbf{q}|$. This contrasts with the analytical momentum dependence found in Nematic (TN=-1) and TN=2 magnets. Consequently, this non-analyticity in $\chi_{+}(\mathbf{q})$ results in a distinct correction to the $k$-space correlation function near the critical point, thereby influencing critical exponents. Specifically, re-evaluating the $k$-space correlation function with this non-analytic contribution and re-assessing the associated critical exponents reveals that the static susceptibility exponent $\gamma_{+}$ is enhanced by 0.01, while the dynamic exponent $\theta$ is reduced by 0.02 compared to the standard TN=2 values. These adjustments bring the calculated exponents into better alignment with available experimental data. Furthermore, the specific heat exponent $\alpha_{+}$ is predicted to undergo a sign change from negative to positive due to this non-analytic momentum dependence. Finally, the paper examines the implications of these revised exponents for the specific heat of the 3D Heisenberg magnet. Finally, the non-analyticity of $\chi_{+}(\mathbf{q})$ is linked to the momentum dependence of the self-energy in the $\mathbf{q} \rightarrow 0$ limit, a feature also present in other quantum field theories. These findings underscore the necessity of re-evaluating the specific heat of the 3D classical O(3) model, as well as the specific heat and critical exponents of the 3D Heisenberg magnet. The current research is the initial step toward this re-evaluation. The paper concludes by outlining the required next steps to rigorously prove the shift in $\alpha_{+}$ from negative to positive. This study introduces an on-chip multi-grating architecture designed for the controlled trapping and readout of ultracold single atoms within an optical tweezer chip using evanescent fields above a waveguide. By leveraging near-field coupling, our proposed multi-grating system enables the integration of multiple optical traps, controls, and sensing functionalities onto a single circuit. Furthermore, this multi-grating architecture facilitates multi-dimensional single-atom trapping, addressing a critical challenge for large-scale quantum information processing. As a demonstration of single-atom multi-dimensional trapping and manipulation, we successfully captured a cold Rubidium-87 atom ($^{87}$Rb) in an atom-cavity system within a three-dimensional atomic cavity formed by four evanescent-field optical tweezers, while maintaining an evanescent field near the atom-core waveguide. Our multi-grating design holds significant promise for developing functional photonic circuits capable of long-term single-atom trapping. Additionally, we demonstrate an evanescent-field grating coupler that reads out the single-atom fluorescence state within the atom-cavity system, achieving an average coupling efficiency of approximately 40%. This design is expected to serve as a pivotal component for large-scale quantum information processing using single atoms. Ultimately, our multi-grating approach provides a practical pathway for creating functional photonic circuits capable of single-atom trapping. Furthermore, our demonstrated single-atom coupling efficiency of around 40% establishes a foundation for large-scale single-atom photonic circuits. The nonlinear Hall effect was previously formulated as a geometric property of real-k space curvature in velocity. This study demonstrates that the nonlinear Hall effect retains the definition of a geometric property, governed by the curvature of the velocity distribution function in real-k space, even when disorder and interactions are present. Specifically, the nonlinear Hall conductivities under time-reversal breaking disorder are defined by the integrated real-k space velocity distribution function's curvature. Furthermore, we incorporate interaction effects through the random-phase approximation, which modifies the geometric character of the nonlinear Hall effect by adjusting the form factor of the curvature without eliminating it. Consequently, both real and momentum space descriptions illustrate how the nonlinear Hall effect persists in systems with interacting electrons and disorder. These findings are substantiated by explicit calculations of the nonlinear Hall conductivity for tight-binding models, including the Chern-Simons Hamiltonian and the Hubbard model, which are solved using the self-consistent self-energy method. Additionally, we address issues regarding current conservation and the definition of nonlinear Hall current. Finally, we generalize the nonlinear Hall effect to itinerant ferromagnets by substituting real space with real magnetic space. Finally, we demonstrate the robustness of this phenomenon against internal noise and temperature effects. Our results indicate that the nonlinear Hall effect serves as a valuable tool for extracting information from novel quantum materials. Notably, it can be observed in systems exhibiting trivial Hall responses, such as those with vanishing Chern numbers or zero Berry curvature. This capability is demonstrated through calculations of nonlinear Hall current noise and conductivity in various models. Our findings underscore the utility of the nonlinear Hall effect as a probe for investigating fundamental electronic properties in quantum materials. Ultimately, our findings suggest the potential for developing novel devices capable of converting nonlinear electric fields into detectable Hall voltages. For instance, in Hubbard model itinerant ferromagnets, the real-space velocity distribution function curvature is governed by the spin-polarization vector, which can be tuned by external magnetic fields. This suggests a pathway to achieve tunable nonlinear Hall responses in magnetic materials. Finally, our findings may contribute to the design of efficient spintronic devices that leverage the nonlinear Hall effect. In conclusion, our findings may contribute to the design of spintronic devices that exploit the nonlinear Hall effect. Many challenges in science and engineering involve science and engineering tasks that are both scientific and technical in nature. This specific chemical engineering case study within the broader context of dynamic optimization serves as an introduction to direct transcription methods. These techniques are now considered a standard tool across diverse applications, supported by robust, user-friendly solvers that have become essential for scientists and engineers. The goal of this tutorial is to provide a practical and accessible introduction to one of the most widely used direct transcription approaches: Chebyshev direct transcription. This method is particularly popular in engineering for its ability to handle problems with unknown final times and to efficiently solve multiple parametric versions of a problem simultaneously. The tutorial begins with a concise overview of the theoretical foundations, including the core ideas, equivalent problem formulations, and a high-level description of standard solution algorithms. It then applies Chebyshev direct transcription to a case study on duality patient control for COVID-19 pneumonia, designed to be accessible to undergraduate students and early-career researchers. This involves implementing the method within a general-purpose dynamic optimization solver. The tutorial concludes with an overview of the solution algorithms employed by the solver. This hands-on approach is intended to help students and researchers develop a deep understanding of both the theoretical and practical aspects of direct transcriptions. Additionally, it provides a practical introduction to general-purpose dynamic optimization solvers, which are crucial for addressing real-world problems in science and engineering. The Chebyshev direct transcription method is applicable to a broad spectrum of scientific and engineering challenges. Furthermore, the solver developed in this tutorial can be utilized for various other problems beyond the specific case study presented. This report is structured to guide readers from basic principles to advanced applications, making it suitable for both educational purposes and research initiatives. Each section builds upon the previous one, offering a comprehensive learning experience. The material is intended to be accessible to undergraduate students and early-career researchers, while also providing a solid foundation for those with more advanced backgrounds. The tutorial is designed to be self-contained, with all necessary code and data available online. This allows readers to replicate the results and explore additional features without external resources. The authors hope this tutorial will inspire further research and innovation in the field of dynamic optimization. By providing a practical introduction to direct transcriptions and general-purpose solvers, the tutorial aims to equip readers with the knowledge and skills needed to tackle a wide range of problems. The hope is that this work will inspire future developments in scientific and engineering disciplines. The authors believe that the practical experience gained from this tutorial will be invaluable to researchers

A rational map $f:\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ defined on the Riemann sphere is termed {\em bicritical} if it possesses precisely two critical points. This note provides a comprehensive classification of the groups (up to isomorphism) that arise as deck transformation groups for iterates of such bicritical rational maps, covering all possible cases. Notably, this methodology also establishes the classification for iterates of quasi-bicritical maps, which differ from bicritical maps by having only one critical point of multiplicity 2. As a corollary, we fully classify the deck groups for the iterates of rational maps possessing multiplicity at most 1 at every point other than two. Furthermore, for each iterate $f^n$, we identify the specific subset of the dynamical parameter space where the deck group is non-abelian. This research is motivated by the iterative construction of holomorphic dynamical systems featuring exceptional sets, including the construction of non-abelian deck groups for iterates of quasi-bicritical maps, which relies on solving a system of equations with a single solution. We conjecture that the sets parameterizing rational maps with non-abelian deck group iterates are always discrete. Additionally, we present a novel construction of a non-abelian deck group iterate for a quasi-bicritical map, relying on a solution with exactly three distinct values, thereby validating our conjecture in this specific instance. Finally, we propose a conjecture regarding the potential abundance of quasi-bicritical maps exhibiting non-abelian deck group iterates. To support this proposal, we construct a one-parameter family of such maps, where two members are identified within the post-critically finite rational maps of degree 4. One of these maps is closely related to the sum of two cubics, while the other arises from the symmetric product of a hyper-elliptic map. The paper concludes with an extensive list of questions inspired by these findings. For context, we also examine meromorphic functions, offering examples of bicritical functions with non-abelian deck group iterates, and list the available literature on this subject. We further compile a table of known bicritical rational maps with non-abelian deck group iterates, including those with algebraic parameter values, and propose a conjecture concerning the parameter values for two of these examples. Finally, we present a list of questions regarding the parameters of rational maps with non-abelian deck group iterates

Molybdenum and tungsten dichalcogenides (MDM) serve as effective two-dimensional (2D) materials for both fundamental and practical applications. This study investigates the work function, ionization energy, and electron affinity of MDM in both bulk and 2D limits using density functional theory (DFT) and the GW method. These parameters are critical for understanding charge transport and Schottky barrier heights. The research examines four specific MDM compounds: MoS$_2$, WS$_2$, MoSe$_2$, and WSe$_2$. By applying the DFT-MGGA approach, we observe that the thickness-dependent variations in these parameters are minimal. Specifically, the 2D-to-bulk changes in work function, ionization energy, and electron affinity for these materials do not exceed 0.1 eV. These findings are corroborated by GW calculations. Consequently, the results indicate that MDM parameters remain nearly constant regarding thickness. This suggests that any single parameter obtained from either bulk or 2D configurations can be reliably utilized in Schottky contact simulations. Furthermore, the study confirms that the thickness-dependent behavior of MDM is weak, a conclusion supported by prior experimental data. Finally, the computed work functions and energy band gaps for MDM are compared against existing literature values. These outcomes demonstrate that the proposed combined DFT-GW methodology is a robust and efficient tool for accurately calculating bulk and 2D electronic properties. Additionally, the work functions and energy band gaps for four specific MDM materials are predicted for the first time. A key advantage of this combined DFT-GW approach is its computational efficiency compared to standalone GW calculations. Delta lenses provide a mature mathematical framework for representing and managing bidirectional, dependent data transformations. Building on this, we introduce a component called "change propagation," which serves as a category within delta lenses and, when equipped with side effects, forms a monad. This paper demonstrates that the underlying data structure of any supervised learning model can be represented using this change propagation framework. Specifically, a trained model functions as a change propagation that diffences the model output from the input, while a new prediction acts as a forward/backward pair. Through this representation, the traditional operation of supervised learning—applying a model to new data—is reinterpreted as a change propagation (diffing input/output) that eliminates conflicts (putting model output to zero), with side effects directing residual changes (model output differences) back to the original input data. This perspective offers a promising avenue for creating new, general-purpose model optimization and management tools. Furthermore, it extends to applications beyond standard supervised learning, encompassing tasks like image denoising, inpainting, and upscaling, all of which rely on the propagation of constraints. Consequently, this paper aims to broaden the application domain of change propagation and suggest potential future research directions. As an initial step, we present a tool that implements change propagation for convolutional neural networks (CNNs) written in the deep learning framework PyTorch. Using this tool, we illustrate that a CNN can be trained to perform image deoiling, followed by manual user adjustments to the input image, demonstrating automatic image inpainting. These examples confirm that the change propagation of this work is not restricted to the YOLO object detection model, which was used only for demonstration purposes. Ultimately, this research paves the way for developing new, general-purpose tools for the analysis, management, and maintenance of deep learning models. Additionally, it offers a novel approach to data-driven design, where models are developed by iteratively applying change propagation to data, thereby defining the model as the set of transformations eliminating conflicts across a specific set of data pairs. Finally, this work provides a foundation for applying well-established human-centered design techniques to the automatic design of machine learning models. To our knowledge, this interpretation of change propagation and its application to deep learning models are original contributions. Furthermore, this approach to change propagation and its potential for human-machine collaborative design represent a promising new direction for research. This paper examines estimates for oscillatory integrals featuring a stationary phase. While prior research has achieved uniform stationarity estimates under conditions of high smoothness and nondegeneracy within the phase function, we demonstrate that uniform estimates remain valid for phase functions with low smoothness by eliminating the necessity for phase nondegeneracy. Specifically, we derive $L^p$ bounds for oscillatory integrals where the derivative of the phase satisfies a weak side condition characterized by a parameter $\sigma > 0$. When $\sigma=1$, the phase phase is assumed to be Lipschitz continuous. Our methodology relies on establishing oscillation inequalities for potentials with low smoothness and the application of oscillatory maximal functions. Furthermore, we provide proofs for the oscillation inequalities of axially symmetric potentials previously stated in [10] and employ these results to analyze oscillatory maximal operators associated with low-smoothness Sobolevel potentials. We outline the necessary conditions on the phase and the measure to ensure uniform stationarity estimates. Additionally, we introduce novel uniform oscillatory estimates for a broad class of oscillatory maximal operators. Notably, we demonstrate that uniform estimates hold for the spherical maximal function even when the phase dimension is low and the phase is not necessarily phase flat. Finally, we extend our findings to oscillatory maximal operators derived from convolutions with radial, piecewise constant functions.

Keywords: Oscillatory integrals, Oscillatory maximal functions, Oscillation inequality, Piecewise constant convolution.

A primary challenge in rarefied gas dynamics research is obtaining steady-state solutions to the Boltzmann equation efficiently. While the Lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) offers an effective iteration approach for this purpose, it often requires numerous iterations to achieve steady-state accuracy in multiscale environments. This study introduces an iteratively improved iteration (II) method grounded in the LBM, designed to accelerate convergence. By applying a correction term to the iteration equation derived from the difference between the exact and linearized Boltzmann equations, the proposed method enhances convergence speed. Validation across various multiscale test cases—including slip, transition, and shock waves—demonstrates that the new method achieves steady-state accuracy within dozens of iterations, exhibiting stable performance across a broad range of parameters. Furthermore, a preliminary analysis indicates that the iteration process is essentially linear. These findings provide a valuable reference for accelerating the computation of rarefied gas flows. **Keywords:** Lattice Boltzmann method, rarefied gas, Boltzmann equation, iteration method, high Reynolds number. **AMS Subject Classification:** 76P05, 76L05, 76N15. **DOI:** 10.3934/DCDSDD.2021010. **Corresponding authors:** Qiang Song (qiang.song@pku.edu.cn), Shijie Li (lijsh@pku.edu.cn). **Affiliation:** Computational Fluid and Solid Mechanics, Department of Engineering Mechanics, PKU-HKU Joint Laboratory for Computational Dynamics, State Key Laboratory for Mechanical Behavior of Materials, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, Anhui, 230026, China; and Peking University. **Received:** 2020-12-11 **Accepted:** 2021-02-01 **Published:** 2021-02-01. **Suggested Citation:** Qiang Song, Shijie Li, Can we find steady-state solutions to multiscale rarefied gas flows within dozens of iterations?, *Discrete and Continuous Dynamical Systems - Series: D*, 2021, 6(1): 121-136. doi: 10.3934/DCDSDD.2021010. https://doi.org/10.3934/DCDSDD.20

The Horizon-10T collaboration is developing a specialized camera designed to detect sub-millimeter to millimeter scale "fireballs" generated by particle collisions in snow. Building on the discovery that single-frame Horizon-10T images exhibit significant correlations, this study investigates a potential cluster phenomenon. We initially demonstrate the feasibility of a multi-modal clustering algorithm utilizing both image data and reconstructed cluster features, followed by an analysis of the probability distribution of the Axion Quark Nugget (AQN) cluster size. This research paves the way for AQN cluster analysis, offering algorithmic support to enhance the sensitivity of the multi-modal clustering method. Ultimately, our findings indicate that AQN clusters do not show significant correlation with the spatial distribution of the collision point. Furthermore, we confirm that the proposed clustering algorithm is effective for AQN analysis, successfully identifying the most probable cluster size. Consequently, this work provides foundational support for AQN analysis and aims to improve the sensitivity of the Horizon-10T camera. Keywords: Multi-Modal Clustering, Axion Quark Nuggets, Horizon-10T. This paper presents the most recent CMS inclusive analysis of the Higgs-like boson observed in the two-photon decay channel, combining results from 2012 through 2016. The study utilizes data from 36.3 fb$^{-1}$ collected in 2015 and 5.0 fb$^{-1}$ from 2012, alongside findings from 2013 and 2014. Inclusive signal strengths for individual channels are reported, along with inclusive and combined cross-sections within specific kinematic regions. Additionally, inclusive signal strengths across various models are detailed, incorporating up to four additional jets. All derived inclusive signals show consistency with a Standard Model Higgs boson having a mass of 125 GeV. The combined significance reaches 6.0 standard deviations, corresponding to a Higgs-like signal with a mass of 124.9 GeV. Ultimately, the inclusive signal strengths for the ATLAS+CMS collaboration achieve a significance of 9.9 standard deviations. Furthermore, this study investigates the Higgs-like signal in a more restricted dataset containing 26.3 fb$^{-1}$ that includes isolated, tag-and-probe selected, jetless, muonless events with a di-photon mass between 118 and 128 GeV. This specific analysis yields a significance of 5.2 standard deviations and an excess of signal events over the background-only hypothesis of 4.2 standard deviations. Using a background model derived from sidebands, the cross-section times production mode times branching ratio is measured as 0.17 $\pm$ 0.02 fb, which aligns with Standard Model expectations. Additionally, the di-photon mass spectrum is fitted with a narrow Gaussian alongside broader shapes representing background, yielding a signal strength of 1.08 $\pm$ 0.14 relative to the Standard Model. Finally, the paper examines the cross-section scaling of the Higgs-like signal with jet multiplicity, observing that the inclusive signal strength is approximately 2.5 times that predicted by the Standard Model. This observation persists even when restricting the analysis to Higgs production modes with well-understood jet radiation patterns, such as gluon fusion and boson fusion. These results indicate that the inclusive Higgs-like signal exhibits a stronger coupling to gluons and electroweak bosons than anticipated. We outline the $p$-divisibility transference theorems regarding the Fourier coefficients of Siegel modular forms, originally established by Dongho Ha and Sungho Kim for those of Siegel cusp forms. Additionally, we introduce novel findings concerning the $p$-divisibility of the Fourier coefficients of Siegel modular forms that are not necessarily cuspidal. Specifically, under the assumption that $p$ does not divide $n(n-1)$, we enhance the existing transference result by Ha and Kim to yield new findings in the case where $n=3$. However, when $p$ divides $n(n-1)$$, no meaningful result can be achieved. In an appendix, we also address the longstanding issue of determining the $p$-adic valuation of the product of even numbers from $1$ to $2n$. We propose a conjecture for the $p$-divisibility of $2 \cdot 4 \cdots 2n$ and provide a proof for the $p$-divisibility of $2 \cdot 4 \cdots 2n (2n+1) \cdots 4n$ in a subsequent paper. The results by Ha and Kim follow as corollaries from our primary theorem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that their Theorem 1.1 is equivalent to a specific identity involving $p$-adic valuations. Finally, the paper concludes with an outline of the proof strategy. Keywords: Siegel modular forms, $p$-divisibility, Fourier coefficients. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 11F71, 11B39. In 2002, Biss examined a sequence of Rigid Fibrations linked to homotopy groups of spheres, proposing a method to calculate the fibers of these structures. This paper offers a negative response to one of the questions he raised. Additionally, we provide a proof for Theorem A presented in Reference [5]. By doing so, we establish the exactness of the related sequence involving rational E-invariants and rigid fibrations. Furthermore, we have extended Biss's results by constructing a new type of spectral sequence and addressing several existing problems. Specifically, we have tackled two of the three questions he posed, with the remaining question being addressed in our forthcoming publication. Finally, we suggest that the newly introduced spectral sequence can be utilized to resolve some of the open problems he identified. To achieve this exact sequence, we required the development of a novel approach to rigid towers. We demonstrate that this new framework not only yields the desired exact sequence of rigid fibrations but also enables the calculation of higher homotopy groups of spheres using rational E-invariants. To address Biss's third question, we present a counterexample to his conjecture. We believe this paper will be instrumental in advancing research on "New Approaches to Rigid Fibrations." The zeroing neural network (ZNN) is a neural dynamical system designed to solve time-varying matrix problems by utilizing the error vector function. This approach offers superior real-time performance and lower computational complexity compared to other neural network solvers. The ZNN architecture is built upon a linear error-driven framework, which can be extended to a nonlinear error-driven model, allowing for the customization of system dynamics to address various types of matrix problems. This tutorial provides a non-rigorous overview of ZNNs, focusing on their application to time-varying matrix problems. It begins with a concise introduction to ZNN fundamentals, followed by a survey of recent advancements in solving these problems. The text demonstrates the versatility of ZNNs across multiple domains, including matrix inversion, rank, singular value, eigenvalue, Riccati, and Lyapunov equations. Additionally, the tutorial explores their potential for matrix completion and other tasks. ZNNs are also effective for controlling time-varying systems, such as robotic manipulators and autonomous vehicles.
