Deep neural networks have achieved significant advancements in image recognition, yet they often fail to capture low-level features, such as the receptive fields of biological neurons. This paper introduces a deep network architecture equipped with tunable low-level receptive fields that are trained directly from data. Our approach utilizes an unsupervised pre-training stage that incorporates an additional component into the deep sparse coding objective function. This extra term encourages neurons to develop an on-off structure, creating center-surround receptive fields where either the center or the surround is activated depending on the input. Following the application of the objective function, the network transitions into a supervised phase where an Asymmetric Convolutional Block (ACB) is applied to the convolutional layers. The ACB's bias term is derived from the receptive fields established during pre-training. Experimental results demonstrate that our network outperforms state-of-art models in both accuracy and robustness. For image classification on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, we achieve accuracy levels of 99.6% and 97.9%, respectively, while attaining 50% and 13% higher robust accuracy against adversarial attacks compared to state-of-the-art models. The code and models are accessible at https://github.com/zhongtao-pan/ON-SF-Net. \footnote{The robust models can be found at: https://github.com/zhongtao-pan/ON-SF-Net/tree/master/Pytorch_models.ckpt.} \footnote{Additional code is available at: https://github.com/zhongtao-pan/ON-SF-Net/tree/master/Pytorch_code.} to facilitate replication. Furthermore, we release our trained models and trained weights for low-level receptive fields at: https://github.com/zhongtao-pan/ON-SF-Net/tree/master/Pytorch_pretrained. We hope these resources will be beneficial to the community. Developing and optimizing ray-traced X-ray optical systems is a complex and time-intensive process. This difficulty is exacerbated by the lack of straightforward, general-purpose analytical formulas that can rapidly and reliably screen the vast array of possible spatial and spectral response functions. Optimizing X-ray optics for wide-field missions is particularly demanding because of the numerous degrees of freedom involved in achieving wide fields of view with high sensitivity. This paper presents an overview of current X-ray optical design optimization methods, including both traditional techniques and those utilizing optimization algorithms. It provides a general introduction to these approaches, supported by specific examples and wide-field design case studies. Additionally, we introduce a newly developed, open-source Python package named PyXOP, which implements these algorithms and is demonstrated using several example cases. Finally, we offer a perspective on the future of X-ray design optimization. This paper is intended for readers with a background in geometric optics and ray tracing. This work introduces a novel class of twisted bilayer graphene systems featuring magnetic Reentrant Graphene Bands (RGBs), characterized by an average $2\pi$ flux per moiré unit cell. The study provides an analytical and numerical examination of the Reentrant Metallic phase, which emerges from the nonmagnetic Reentrant Graphene Band (RGB) state. Notably, this metallic state exhibits perfect Bloch oscillations and a linear dispersion. Additionally, several configurations display Chern numbers of $\pm1$, signaling a quantized Hall effect, and support a local Berry curvature gauge form of $\pm\pi\delta(k_y)$. These systems are constructed by combining classical honeycomb and hexagonal lattices with graphene-like sites, utilizing two distinct types of gauge interactions: classical Aharonov-Bohm interactions and Ising Pseudospin interactions. The research offers a comprehensive list of RGB models, each accompanied by rigorous proofs. Furthermore, numerical simulations are employed to illustrate the reemergence of metallicity, the restoration of Bloch and Berry phases, and the associated quantized Hall effect. These findings provide a robust framework for modeling the reemergence of graphene-like systems under strong magnetic fields. This approach holds significant potential for advancing quantum simulation research, particularly in creating Chern insulators and investigating strongly correlated systems. Ultimately, these models may serve as a foundation for understanding graphene systems subjected to large fluxes, such as those found in Kagome lattices and twisted bilayer graphene. Finally, the paper proposes a specific model for $\pi$ flux twisted bilayer graphene and outlines a path toward its experimental realization. This model demonstrates an RGB with real, linear dispersion, and its reentrant metallic state exhibits perfect Bloch oscillations and a quantized Hall effect. Furthermore, the Berry curvature gauge in real space exhibits two sharp peaks of $\pm\pi$ at $k_y=0$ and $k_y=\pi$, respectively. The proposed twisted bilayer graphene model is experimentally viable and can be realized by applying a $\pi$ flux per bilayer unit cell through two methods: (1) employing a magnetic field of approximately $100$ Tesla, or (2) utilizing electrically induced twisted boundary conditions. In this scenario, the Kagome lattice can be engineered by twisting two honeycomb lattices, with each twisted unit cell containing one Kagome site. The resulting Kagome model exhibits an RGB with real, linear dispersion, and its reentrant metallic state shows perfect Bloch oscillations and a quantized Hall effect.

Driven by privacy concerns, we developed a stegosystem allowing two users to share encrypted messages without revealing the communication to an adversary. Our solution introduces a novel linguistic stegosystem utilizing a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network. Evaluated on Twitter and Enron email datasets, our method produces high-quality steganographic text and substantially increases capacity compared to prior work, even on privacy-sensitive data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a steganographic channel can facilitate the transmission of encrypted messages and prove that our approach successfully enables this specific use case. Finally, we show that both LSTM-based and information-theoretic steganographic channels can reliably transmit messages with any distribution, provided the receiver possesses knowledge of the sender's channel. However, our findings indicate that an LSTM channel outperforms a Berlekamp-Wagner (BW) channel in generating high-quality steganographic messages, particularly when the BW rate approaches the channel's capacity. Unit commitment (UC) represents a critical challenge in the economic scheduling of power systems, where the unit commitment constraint alone constitutes a significant hurdle. Current research typically relies on mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulations, which are computationally demanding and often require screening techniques to make UC tractable. Existing screening methods, such as those utilizing convex relaxation, offer substantial speedups for specific UC forms but struggle to generalize across diverse generator data and operating conditions. To address this, we propose a machine learning-based screening method that identifies incommitable units by analyzing historical units and their cost structures. Our approach leverages a novel deep learning architecture capable of processing multidimensional cost models. This model learns the cost landscape and predicts the commitment status of new units based on their cost characteristics. By evaluating the predicted incommitability of units, the method can skip the solution of UC constraints for those deemed incommitable. We validate our approach's effectiveness and robustness through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that our method achieves substantial speedups in solving UC problems while maintaining high accuracy. Furthermore, our approach exhibits strong robustness, performing effectively across a wide range of generator cost characteristics and load conditions. The source code is available at: https://github.com/zhongyuanli12347/DeepUnitCommitment. Finally, we introduce CostMap, a new benchmark dataset for evaluating the performance of UC constraint screening. The dataset and detailed information can be accessed at: https://github.com/zhongyuanli12347/DeepUnitCommitment/tree/master/scripts/generator_cost_generation. Additionally, the associated paper has been submitted to the KDD 2021 Datasets and Applications track. This study examines the pressure-induced dimerization and the suppression of antiferromagnetism in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$, a material known for hosting Kitaev interactions. Zero-field-cooled magnetization measurements reveal a sharp diamagnetic response at 1.7 kbar, indicating field-induced ferromagnetic ordering on dimers, which aligns with the Neel temperature observed in the zero-pressure field-dependent data. X-ray diffraction analysis confirms that this phase transition occurs at 1.4(1) kbar, coinciding with a structural transition from the P2$_1$2$_1$2$_1$ to the P2$_1$/m space group. The resulting dimerization of the Ir sites causes the collapse of long-range antiferromagnetic order. Furthermore, a significant increase in diamagnetism is observed at 2.5 kbar, marking another structural shift from P2$_1$/m to P-2/m. This final dimerization, characterized by an inter-dimer distance of 3.38(2) Å, further diminishes antiferromagnetic order while enhancing ferromagnetic ordering on the dimers. Additionally, resistivity data indicate that the formation of the P-2/m phase coincides with a jump in the metallic character of the material. Finally, the potential for detecting Kitaev physics in this system is explored. These findings are interpreted as consequences of pressure-induced modifications to the single-ion anisotropy and Kitaev exchange interactions. Overall, this work demonstrates that manipulating the Kitaev exchange interaction offers a viable pathway to observe and study the Kitaev quantum spin liquid state. Notably, the P-2/m structure of Li$_2$IrO$_3$ represents one of the few experimentally realized lattices capable of hosting a quantum spin liquid. Furthermore, the observed dimerization and magnetic field response in Li$_2$IrO$_3$ support the validity of a non-Kitaev mechanism for establishing Kitaev physics, as previously proposed. Finally, the ability to tune the Kitaev exchange interaction in this material may facilitate the study of quantum criticality and novel emergent phenomena. Synthetic control methods are widely used to estimate treatment effects on single units by constructing a weighted combination of control units designed to match the treated unit's pre-treatment characteristics and outcome trajectory. However, this approach relies on the assumption of sufficient overlap between the variation of the treated unit's pre-treatment outcome and the composite unit's outcome after treatment. We propose a theory of identification and inference for synthetic controls that retains the same assumptions as prior literature while explicitly allowing for the absence of overlap in pre-treatment variables. Under sufficient overlap, we provide a straightforward identification guarantee; otherwise, we demonstrate that synthetic control still enables valid causal inference if the data exhibits pre-treatment mean square predictability from the control units. Furthermore, we develop an inferential framework that leverages the inherent dimensionality of synthetic control problems to derive asymptotic inference for the treatment effect. This approach involves reweighting the synthetic control objective function using an estimated weight, under the condition that the pre-treatment mean and mean square are accurately predicted by the control units' units. We also present an asymptotic bias-corrected treatment effect estimator that achieves first-order accuracy in both bias and variance. Finally, we apply our theoretical findings to the 1996 National Educational Longitudinal Study (NELS:96) to identify the causal impact of a Florida school intervention. Monte Carlo simulations indicate that our estimator achieves significant power gains compared to standard synthetic control in scenarios with sufficient overlap, while scenarios with insufficient overlap yield no significant differences in performance. Simulations using data similar to NELs:96 demonstrate that our estimator can accurately recover the causal effect of a school intervention, achieving up to a 30% reduction in root mean square error compared to synthetic control. To facilitate practical implementation, we have released an R package named \texttt{synthctl}. This package includes an implementation of \texttt{synthctl}, which calculates an optimal weight by reweighting the synthetic control objective function to account for differences in pre-treatment outcome and pre-treatment mean square predictability between the treated and control units. Additionally, \texttt{synthctl} offers an implementation of \texttt{synthctl}_bc, which applies our proposed bias correction to achieve first-order accuracy in both bias and variance. Identifying differences between two graphs is a fundamental challenge in both theoretical and applied contexts. While prior research has primarily concentrated on Euclidean graphs, this study addresses the critical issue of measuring the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy for non-metric graphs containing diverse attribute types. By ensuring local differential privacy for sensitive node attributes, we prevent sensitive information from being revealed during graph matching. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that the Gromov-Wasserstein distance between two structural graphs can be approximated with an error bound of $O(m/n)$, where $m$ represents the count of non-self edges and $n$ denotes the total number of nodes. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of Graph Gromov-Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks (GAWGANs) in a privacy-preserving setting and validate our approach through numerical experiments comparing privacy guarantees and structural similarities. These results confirm that the proposed method effectively maintains both privacy and graph structure. Notably, the GAWGAN algorithm outperforms baseline methods in terms of both privacy and structural fidelity. For instance, when applied to Twitter data under a local differential privacy budget of $\epsilon=0.1$, the GAWANs approach yields an AUC improvement of 1.2% over DNGAN and 2.6% over SAN, while also providing a significantly higher privacy guarantee. This indicates that the GAWGAN framework is highly effective for privacy-sensitive graph generation tasks. Additionally, we demonstrate the method's utility in detecting communities within social networks. The associated Python code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuanliu/GAWGAN.

We introduce a novel particle-in-cell simulation model designed to simulate a specific laser-plasma interaction regime driven by self-steepening effects in intense ultrashort pulses. This study examines the propagation of circularly polarized (CP) laser pulses through underdense plasma, demonstrating that this process generates a train of self-steepened pulses. This pulse train facilitates the creation of a series of plasma wakefield structures, each containing an electron injector capable of producing multiple electron bunches. These bunches are injected at the rear of every driven wake and accelerated by the resulting field. By adjusting pulse-propagation parameters, the spacing between successive bunches can be controlled. Furthermore, we analyze how varying CP parameters influences the injection and acceleration of these electron bunches. Finally, we explore potential applications of this new laser-plasma interaction regime. In conclusion, our research indicates that polarization control of electron injection and acceleration within plasma wakefields is achievable through the self-steepening of intense CP laser pulses. This method offers a means to manipulate the injection of electron bunches and represents a significant advancement toward high-energy, high-contrast accelerators. Additionally, it may serve as a dual mechanism to achieve complete inversion in nuclear systems. These findings are expected to stimulate further research in laser-plasma interaction physics. Additionally, the proposed scheme could be valuable for free-electron lasers, space-based laser communications, and nuclear physics. Finally, this scheme may aid in achieving inversion in nuclear systems. We conducted a $10^{45}$ atom-yr exposure study of natural platinum to examine neutrinoless double beta decay, thereby establishing the most stringent constraints on effective mass and couplings of neutral scalars and dark matter particles to nucleons. Additionally, we analyzed experimental data for potential dark matter signatures, yielding the first ever limits on light dark matter ($<1$ GeV$/c^2$) interacting with nucleons through vector, axial-vector, tensor, or pseudo-scalar forces. Our dark matter constraints cover coupling strengths down to approximately $10^{-4}$ in scalar and tensor modes, and somewhat weaker bounds for vector and axial-vector interactions. Notably, our upper mass mass limits for tensor and vector dark matter scenarios extend the sensitivity of nucleon scattering experiments by nearly two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, this is the inaugural investigation into novel neutral scalar interactions mediated by light particles ($\sim 10$ MeV$/c^2$), where we derived significant constraints on the couplings between light scalars and nucleons. Finally, we conducted a thorough examination of systematic errors, demonstrating that the study is robust against variations in the platinum isotopic composition. This paper investigates a colorization challenge involving a color database. Our goal is to learn a colorizer that accepts a grayscale image of a camera, time, and attitude as input and generates a corresponding colorized image. The underlying premise is that an image's appearance is largely determined by the camera, time, and attitude, allowing a colorizer to focus on the correlation between these appearance factors and color, thereby reducing dependency on the image content itself. To address the issue of color inconsistency in the traditional deep colorizer, we introduce the concept of a color database. However, real-world color databases are scarce, so we synthesize one by creating a color, time, attitude, and grayscale dataset from real images. This approach enables the development of a deep colorizer that accepts only grayscale images as input, significantly lowering the requirements for camera, time, and attitude. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of our proposed deep colorizer. Finally, we examine the limitations of the method and explore potential solutions. The code and colorized images are available at: https://github.com/chenchen1998/Cross-CameraDeep-Colorization. The paper can be found here: https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.03017. We update recent findings regarding the classification of the generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov system, extending its validity to include discrete time cases. Our analysis reveals that the previously cited criteria for integrability are insufficient. By leveraging the connection between this system and the Euler top, we establish a criterion based on the existence of first integrals that ensures integrability in generalized coordinates and time. Furthermore, utilizing the Cartan-Karlhede algorithm, we demonstrate that the curvature properties of the underlying time manifold are independent of the potential; these properties alone determine the number of first integrals in general cases and enable the integration of the generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov system. As a practical application, we employ the algorithm to verify the integrability of a system recently proposed to model certain astrophysical phenomena. Finally, we illustrate how the rank of the Cartan-Karlhede invariants can be utilized to construct a non-integrable chaotic Hamiltonian model featuring time-dependent masses. Finally, it is important to note that the $n$-dimensional Ermakov system, which generalizes the well-known 1D variant, is a fundamental model in theoretical physics. Defined as a second-order nonlinear differential equation of the form $\ddot{r}=\omega^2 r+f(r)$, it serves as the foundational component for constructing various physically significant two-component models. These include the Chandrasekhar-Ermakov-Aronson system, the Ermakov-Pinney system, the Chini system, and the recently introduced generalized $2$D Ermakov system, the latter of which has been applied to describe the evolution of elliptical orbits and ellipsoids. While the $2$D case has been extensively explored, the $n$-dimensional scenario has received less attention. This work aims to advance the understanding of the $n$-dimensional problem by employing the Cartan-Karlhede algorithm. Our findings indicate that the degree of the generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov system can be determined by examining the rank of the Cartan-Karlhedi invariants. Specifically, we show that when the rank is 0, the system admits a first integral; when the rank is 1, it is non-integrable. These conclusions are derived from the formulation of the problem and the specific choice of the function $f(r)$. Obtaining a public transport network's description from its Public Transport Information Format (PTIF) feed is a common method for researchers to analyze systems. However, this process often fails without access to the specific Transit Feed Specification (TFS) governing that system. This paper introduces a novel machine learning approach that bypasses the need for the TFS by training a neural network to replicate the TFS using only PTIF data. Utilizing data from the Paris metropolitan network, the study demonstrates how a recurrent neural network can be retrained on PTIF data collected over a year to accurately reproduce the corresponding TFS. This capability enables researchers to estimate a TFS for a system of interest; if available, they can fine-tune the model, whereas researchers on new systems can proceed directly to run the model. Ultimately, this facilitates the automatic extraction of system descriptions, such as the number of stations and lines, aiding research on new systems. Additionally, the paper offers a novel perspective on existing machine learning applications in public transport, proposing a method to estimate network characteristics for systems with limited data. To support reproducibility, the Python source code is accessible at https://github.com/romainboulanger/TFSReproduction. The results are also available through Replicator.io, where users can execute the tool online and view outputs without installing the code. Specifically, researchers can upload one year of PTIF data, and the platform will automatically generate the corresponding TFS. Access to these results is provided at https://replicator.io/experiments/1020/TFS-REPRODUCTION. Furthermore, researchers may upload up to 50 MB of data to test how well the model reproduces the network's characteristics. While PTIF data is generally easy to obtain, typically from the authority managing public transport services, the model is specifically trained on a year of data from the RATP organization in Paris. Consequently, estimates for other cities or regions may not be as precise as those generated for the Paris network. It is important to note that this model does not replicate the network's geometry. Finally, TFS data is not required to execute the model, as all necessary information is contained within the code available on Replicator.io. To utilize the model, simply upload a PTIF data file. For detailed usage instructions, please refer to the README file on Replicator.io. If you have any questions, do not hesitate to contact the authors. Few-shot learning aims to classify novel categories based on a limited number of labeled examples. A widely used method involves calculating class-level prototypes from support sets and computing similarity scores against query data. However, since the quantity of support examples is extremely small in few-shot scenarios, these prototypes often fail to accurately represent their respective categories. To address this limitation, we introduce an unsupervised few-shot learning technique that leverages class-level prototypes to guide neural network training. Our approach consists of two main phases: first, we extract class-level prototypes from pre-trained models and utilize them to generate augmented training samples; second, we utilize these augmented samples to retrain the neural network. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing few-shot learning algorithms. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhengyuanwang2017/Class-level-prototype. Furthermore, the method achieved top performance in the first challenge of the 2020 International Conference on Image Processing (ICIP) on Non-Parametric Few-Shot Classification. The challenge can be accessed here: https://www.kaggle.com/c/icip-2020-np-fsl. The competition rankings are available at: https://www.kaggle.com/s/icip-2020-np-fsl. Additionally, our method secured the top rank in the "No Class Specific Training" category of the challenge. We investigate systems featuring an infrared non-invertible symmetry. In the non-Abelian scenario, the symmetries characterized by continuous parameters form a non-invertible group that cannot be expressed as the product of an invertible symmetry and an anomalous global symmetry, distinguishing it from systems with redundant non-invertible symmetries. We demonstrate an enhanced Goldstone theorem within these systems, noting that the additional continuous symmetry generates an extra Noether current and an extra conserved charge. A key implication of this finding is the presence of an extra charge that anti-commutes with the invertible symmetry in the non-Abelian case. Furthermore, we offer an alternative derivation of this result by reducing the non-Abelian system to one possessing only discrete non-invertible symmetries. Additionally, we determine the anomalies of this non-invertible symmetry through an effective theory constructed via T-duality from a system with an invertible non-invertible symmetry. Finally, we propose a method for constructing an effective action for the system in terms of the non-invertible symmetry's order parameter. This action incorporates an extra term derived from the anomalous term in the effective action of the related system with an invertible non-invertible symmetry. Finally, we suggest a field-theoretic argument supporting the existence of such an effective action. This study introduces a novel algorithm designed to distinguish tau leptons from jets produced by quarks and gluons, utilizing the hadronic final states of decaying taus. The approach employs a deep neural network, specifically a Graph Attention Network (GAT), which operates without dependence on event pileup. We apply this method to simulated proton-proton collision data, assuming the detection capabilities of the future High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) detector. The analysis demonstrates that GAT-based discrimination outperforms both quark- and gluon-jet discriminators, achieving a 10% improvement in signal efficiency at a fixed background rejection rate. Furthermore, the tau discriminator exhibits greater sensitivity to hadronic tau decays with three prongs. These findings suggest that GAT networks are highly effective tools for identifying hadronic tau decays. Additionally, we illustrate that combining our pileup-independent algorithm with traditional tau identification techniques using a simple neural network further enhances performance. This leads to an 11% increase in signal efficiency and a corresponding 10% increase in background rejection at a fixed signal efficiency level. These results indicate that such a combined approach is suitable for application across all tau physics sectors within the HL-LHC data sample. Finally, this method holds significant potential for various physics investigations, including the search for rare Higgs boson decays into taus and the identification of third-generation quark and lepton pair production. Future surveys from the next-generation Rubin telescope are expected to generate up to 20 TB of scientific data daily, with a significant portion classified as astronomical. Although Neural Networks (NNs) offer a highly efficient automated classification method for such big data, they face notable challenges, including the risk of overfitting and outputs lacking confidence metrics. To address these issues, we propose utilizing Bayesian Neural Networks, which incorporate uncertainty estimation alongside traditional NNs. This approach employs the Monte-Carlo Markov Chain algorithm to sample from the posterior distribution of network weights, providing a robust solution for large-scale binary image classification tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Bayesian Neural Networks through an example large-scale image classification problem. Furthermore, we explore strategies to enhance Bayesian Neural Networks, such as implementing a novel dropout technique and selecting appropriate architectures to optimize their performance. Our experimental results indicate that Bayesian Neural Networks can match the accuracy of their deterministic counterparts while simultaneously providing uncertainty estimates. Additionally, we find that strategic choices regarding dropout application and network architecture can significantly improve their performance. These advancements suggest that Bayesian Neural Networks will be instrumental in classifying big data during the era of Rubin and similar telescopes. The Orbit Algebra of a finite reflection group serves as the endomorphism algebra of the trivial module within the finite group representation algebra. This algebra is isomorphic to a specific quotient of a polynomial algebra, where the ideal used for quotienting is generated by a regular sequence of homogeneous elements with degree matching the degree of each basic invariant. These polynomials constitute the algebra of degrees, which is generated by a regular sequence known as the Chevalley basis within the orbit algebra. For finite reflection groups of B-type, this foundational theorem has been extended to the finite Heisenberg supergroup representation algebra. This extension relies on key elements specific to B-type groups: odd elements within the Weyl group and a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form defined on the root lattice. This paper provides a proof of that basis theorem for B-type groups. Additionally, we examine the case where the odd Weyl group elements are excluded from the supergroup definition, presenting a similar but distinct proof for the resulting algebra. Finally, we outline a basic connection between these two related algebras. In this context, we acknowledge the work of K. I. Oginuma, who previously established this same result for B-type groups. We also present a corresponding theorem for D-type groups. For both B and D types, the proofs are derived from an earlier version of this theory for A-type groups, which was developed in our 2019 paper. The foundation of this theory lies in the original findings by K. Brown and J. Hillar regarding A-type groups. This research contributes to the broader understanding of the relationship between the orbit algebra of a finite reflection group and the representation algebra of the finite group. Specifically, for A and D types, the orbit algebra is isomorphic to a quotient of a polynomial algebra, whereas in B and D types, this equivalence holds only up to a rank difference of one. This distinction arises from the odd elements present in the Weyl group for B-type and D-type groups, as well as the presence of a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form on the root lattice. We also address a related question concerning the relationship between the orbit algebra and the representation algebra of the finite Heisenberg supergroup, which is expected to yield a different outcome. To address this, we examine a variant of the basis theorem where the algebra of degrees is replaced by an algebra of quasi-invariants, which we refer to as the 'extended basis theorem.' We demonstrate that this extended basis theorem applies to both A and D type groups

The Set-Union Knapsack Problem (SUKP) and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem (BMCP) are both NP-hard combinatorial optimization challenges. In the SUKP, one must select a subset of items that does not exceed a weight limit while maximizing the union of their associated elements. The BMCP operates similarly but imposes a budget constraint on the number of items. While existing solutions for both problems rely on local search, they often struggle with inefficiency or lack adaptability. This paper introduces a novel, versatile local search algorithm designed for both problems. To enhance efficiency, the algorithm utilizes a specialized data structure for set union operations and adopts a hybrid strategy that integrates strengths from multiple conventional local search methods. To improve adaptability, it incorporates a dynamic mechanism for adjusting the weights of elements within the objective function. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in both efficiency and effectiveness. Specifically, it achieves optimal or near-optimal solutions for 90.5% of SUKP instances and 95.7% of BMCP instances. Notably, it attains the same objective value as the best-known algorithms for all previously solved instances. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits superior performance on large-scale instances, reaching optimality for 90.0% of SUKP instances and 100.0% of BMCP instances. These findings confirm the algorithm's robustness and highlight its potential for future research. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenChunwei1993/EFFESUC. Online gambling operators aim to attract new customers while retaining existing ones, as acquiring new users is significantly more costly than preserving them. This paper investigates methods for predicting and preventing customer churn. We developed a machine learning model using a dataset of nearly 100,000 players, tracking their activity and financial transactions over five years. By analyzing time-series data across various time scales (daily, weekly, monthly), we identified patterns that effectively distinguish between active/active and churned/active players. Furthermore, we developed and evaluated a dynamic, personalized churn prevention system, which was shown to be feasible and capable of increasing operator revenue. Our approach surpasses the performance of all baseline models, achieving a 1.5-fold improvement in accuracy over the best baseline. These findings offer promising implications for both gambling operators and financial institutions. Finally, we outline several directions for future research. This study represents an initial step in that field, demonstrating the potential of machine learning in both identifying and implementing interventions to prevent churn. Given that online gambling is a major consumer activity, we anticipate that subsequent research in this area will yield further valuable insights for the industry. Additionally, our proposed methodology is applicable to other sectors involving player or customer retention. Beyond online gambling, we have applied this approach to other activities, and we intend to share the results of those applications in future work. Finally, we address the complex ethical challenges associated with preventing churn in online gambling. Although gambling operators generate substantial revenue, the industry is heavily regulated, and governments aim to reduce the number of gamblers. We argue that preventing churn is more effective than other measures for this objective. Furthermore, we consider it unethical to target at-risk individuals with aggressive marketing campaigns, as this could encourage them to continue gambling despite the associated risks. Instead, we propose that these customers should be offered resources to quit. This aligns with the view that ethical machine learning should be a joint effort between data scientists and domain experts. When these particles approach a nucleus with sufficiently small transverse momentum, they can interact electromagnetically with it. This study examines such interactions within ultra-peripheral collisions of lead nuclei at the Large Hadron Collider. We analyze electromagnetic probe-nucleus interactions, specifically electron and positron nuclear scattering, along with their associated photon-nucleus interactions, including electron and positron pair production. We also investigate electron and positron emission and their nuclear interactions in association with a forward neutron. Our findings indicate that the observed rates of electron-positron pair production via electromagnetic probe-nucleus interactions are approximately two orders of magnitude lower than those arising from photon-photon interactions. However, the measured transverse momentum distributions of electrons and positrons may exhibit a noticeable distortion resulting from these electromagnetic nuclear interactions. Additionally, we predict that the total number of emitted electrons and positrons could be observable in experiments, with the primary background stemming from photon-photon interactions where one of the photons interacts with the nucleus. These predictions can be validated during a dedicated data-taking period with the lead lead beam, independent of the proton-proton or lead-lead collision program. For cyclists, traffic accidents often result in fatalities or severe injuries. While bicycle helmet technology has advanced significantly in recent years, the appropriate speed for cyclists remains a contentious issue globally. Adopting an effective strategy to encourage cyclists to reduce their speed requires understanding the factors influencing accident risks and their associated costs. This study introduces the first step toward a strategy by developing an intelligent, context-aware risk descriptor (RD) for cyclists. The RD is inferred by analyzing the correlation between cycling contexts and the likelihood of accidents. Utilizing video-based cyclist tracking, the system monitors context variables such as road type, cyclist density, cyclist speed, and helmet usage. The costs of accidents are quantified in terms of human suffering, financial loss, and societal impact. Empirical analysis of accident data reveals thatRDs exhibit a strong correlation with these costs, accounting for approximately 80% of accident severity. Consequently, the RD is defined as an indicator of accident severity rather than probability. This paper presents a novel, intelligent, context-aware risk descriptor designed to assist cyclists in managing accident severity within their specific contexts. The study also offers guidance on adopting appropriate speeds based on context conditions to minimize accident severity and provides recommendations for improving cycling infrastructure. Additionally, the paper proposes a generic, intelligent, context-aware risk management approach applicable to various domains, including manufacturing, aviation, and automotive sectors. The validity of this approach is supported by its successful application in multiple domains, as detailed in our previous work. Ultimately, RD serves as a critical metric for cyclists to evaluate accident severity in their contexts, enabling them to adopt suitable speeds to mitigate potential accidents. The paper concludes with an analysis of RD's effectiveness and an overview of the associated challenges. The proposed RD is intended to assist cyclists in navigating cycling contexts and may inspire further research into context-aware risk descriptors. A cover of an associative ring $R$ (which may lack unity or commutativity) is defined as a set of subrings whose union encompasses the entire set $R$. Analogous to the chromatic number of a graph, the covering number $\operatorname{ch}(R)$ represents the minimum cardinality of such a cover. We present a novel construction that extends Golod's famous infinite family of rings exhibiting zero covering number. Our results demonstrate that for certain families of rings, the covering number is directly influenced by the vector space dimension of their additive group. Additionally, we examine rings possessing a covering number equal to that of a field and explore the maximal possible covering number for rings of specific orders and dimensions. Throughout the study, the influence of symmetry on covering numbers emerges as a significant factor. We conclude by posing several open questions. Notably, our findings indicate that unlike graphs, non-commutative rings admit covers of zero cardinality. Furthermore, we identify classes of rings for which any cover must consist of subrings of equal size. Our analysis also extends to modules, yielding several novel results. Deep learning models face adversarial examples, which are subtle perturbations applied to images that cause these model-dependent classifiers to misclassify them. This study re-examines adversarial examples through the lens of data augmentation. We introduce a novel method that enhances adversarial robustness by integrating adversarial samples into training sets. Specifically, we utilize data augmentation techniques, such as horizontal flipping, to generate transformed versions of adversarial examples. These generated samples, along with the original adversarial examples and clean data, are incorporated during training. Furthermore, we examine two optimization strategies for creating these perturbed adversarial examples. Experiments conducted on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves a significant improvement in adversarial robustness compared to current methods. Additionally, we explore an alternative strategy for creating personalized adversarial examples, drawing inspiration from malware detection. This demonstrates that adversarial examples can be generated based on specific model characteristics, making them more natural and distinct from standard image perturbations. Nonlocal traffic models, defined as convolution-type partial differential equations where flux relies on the density profile $rho$ instead of a single point, offer a more realistic depiction of driver behavior by incorporating a look-ahead kernel. These kernels weight nearby drivers more heavily than distant ones, a property typically modeled as exponential decay. However, this study examines kernels with a more general decay rate. While these models are generally Hamiltonian and admit entropy solutions, an entropy-based singular limit as the kernel size $\varepsilon$ approaches zero remains a significant open challenge. This work addresses these issues by applying the theory of singular perturbations in conservation laws. We demonstrate that for a broad class of kernels, the singular limit $\varepsilon\to 0$ occurs within a specific time scale that depends on both the kernel size and the model parameters. Furthermore, we establish the entropy admissibility of this singular limit, derive an $L^1$ convergence rate for these entropy solutions, and provide a stable numerical scheme to approximate them. Finally, these findings are applied to the singular limits of the Lighthill-Whithem Richards and Aw-Medina traffic models. Additionally, the paper concludes with numerical experiments that validate the entropy solutions of these singular models. These computations not only confirm the entropy admissibility but also illustrate how kernel choice influences the relaxation time required to reach the local model. Notably, a power-law decay in the kernel correlates with a significantly longer relaxation time. These insights are then utilized to propose a novel kernel for the AWR model that better aligns with empirical evidence. Finally, a comprehensive discussion of these kernels is provided, along with numerical evidence regarding the entropy solutions of the associated singular problems. Dilation surfaces extend the concept of translation surfaces by allowing atlas transition maps to include translations and homotheties with positive ratios. Unlike translation surfaces, the directional flow on dilation surfaces can contain trajectories that accumulate on limit cycles; these are closed geodesics termed hyperbolic due to the nontrivial homothety they induce. A longstanding conjecture posits that a dilation surface lacking any hyperbolic closed geodesics is essentially a translation surface. We present a counterexample to this conjector and subsequently demonstrate that the conjector holds true for dilation surfaces exhibiting Morse-Smale dynamics, specifically examining the projections of translation surfaces featuring at most one singular orbit. Furthermore, we analyze the topology of dilation surfaces characterized by a specific combinatorial structure regarding their singular orbits and explore the relationship between Rauzy-Villani dynamics and cylinder decompositions within these structures. The proof primarily relies on combinatorial analysis of singular orbits, utilizing cylinder diagrams and braid permutations. Additionally, we offer an alternative proof of the translation surface classification theorem, which categorizes these surfaces based on the combinatorial data of their cylinder at the boundary. This approach utilizes a novel perspective on this classification, grounded in translation surface geometry rather than abstract combinatorial methods. Finally, we conclude by discussing the topology of dilation surfaces through the lens of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we investigate the topology of the dilation surface moduli space associated with a fixed translation surface $\Sigma$, demonstrating that it is homeomorphic to a non-trivial manifold whenever $\Sigma$ possesses a specific combinatorial property. This property is defined by the existence of a saddle connection from every singular orbit to itself. The proof of this result depends on an algorithm that generates a cylinder decomposition from data derived from a generic path in the moduli space. Consequently, our findings yield a new algorithm for constructing cylinder decompositions within dilation surface moduli. Moreover, our methodology establishes a translation surface version of the decomposition of the moduli of curves into strata based on monodromy. To achieve this, we construct a group representation of the fundamental group of the moduli space, which classifies monodromy up to conjugation. We also provide a translation surface interpretation of the results by Kontsevich and Zorich regarding the description of dilation surface moduli via closure properties. Finally, we address the challenge of characterizing translation surfaces within dilation surface moduli using combinatorial data. This study introduces a total correlation (TC) based functional connectome, utilizing a multivariate total correlation coefficient (mTCC) derived from the neural network as a metric for multivariate dependence. Unlike conventional connectomes that rely on pairwise correlations, this approach employs multivariate information theory to capture both linear and nonlinear dependencies among brain regions, thereby generating a more comprehensive and detailed connectome. Validation across multiple datasets confirms the efficacy and superiority of the TC-based connectome, demonstrating that it reveals richer topological structures and better distinguishes between healthy controls and schizophrenia patients. Furthermore, the application of a graph cut algorithm to partition the TC-based connectome yields brain partitions that produce more biologically meaningful networks and generate more distinct groups. These findings suggest that the TC-based connectome holds significant potential for advancing brain research. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang1990/TC-connectome. We develop a unified approach for extending the Segal-Bargmann transform to Clifford algebras with even dimension $N$. This extension incorporates both a Clifford algebra extension of $\mathbb{R}^N$ and a Z$_2$-grading of the target algebra. We demonstrate that this extended transform constitutes a natural extension of the Taylor isomorphism for Whitney jets. Furthermore, we establish an extension of the Poincaré-Lefschetz theorem within Clifford analysis. A primary application of this research involves representing functions defined on Clifford analysis in terms of generalized Dirac eigenvalues. Finally, key results are illustrated through examples in Clifford analysis for $N=2$ and $N=3$. Notably, these findings provide a foundation for analyzing the spectral properties of the Dirac operator on manifolds using Clifford analysis. Additionally, we examine applications in modeling the dynamics of spin-1/2 particles. The text concludes with an appendix detailing the dynamics of a particle subject to a time-dependent magnetic field. The work utilizes notations and methods from our prior publications. We acknowledge that other authors have also explored related topics; for instance, [13] offers an alternative method for extending the Segal-Bargmann transform to Clifford analysis. However, their work focuses on functions defined on a manifold rather than within a Clifford algebra. Consequently, their results do not provide a comprehensive description of spectral properties in a Clifford analysis framework. In contrast, this paper offers a detailed examination of such properties. This study introduces a conditional Gaussian process model designed to simulate the sample paths of a process y, given specific realizations of another process x. By approximating the Gaussian process posterior using a Gaussian approximation derived from the gradient of the log-density relative to the mean, the required kernel cross-kernels can be computed without exact analytical forms, provided they are evaluated along the paths x and y. This approach enables the construction of Gaussian process generators where trajectories of one process are strictly determined by those of a second process. We apply this framework to generate galaxy light curves within an observational framework, utilizing one color time series and temporal covariates rooted in stellar evolution theory to synthesize theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we present additional experiments demonstrating the method's versatility and accuracy in generating Gaussian process sample paths. Our findings indicate that the proposed model can effectively generate sample paths constrained by a limited number of observations from a secondary process, making it valuable for generating synthetic observational data for future space missions. This paper investigates a ground-based wireless sensor system augmented by a fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that function as mobile relays. We demonstrate that for any specified $\epsilon > 0$, achieving $\epsilon$-optimality with respect to both transmission power and network connectivity requires a UAV fleet size that scales as $O(1/\epsilon^{2/3})$. Furthermore, we establish an lower bound of $\Omega(1/\epsilon^{3/5})$ for this required number of vehicles, indicating that the proposed upper bound nearly matches the theoretical lower limit. Additionally, we find that the power consumption of both static ground sensors and the mobile UAVs scales with $\epsilon$ at a rate of $O(1/\epsilon^{4/3})$. Our findings regarding ground sensing networks apply more broadly to any power-based connectivity metric, encompassing concepts such as connectivity capacity, power efficiency, and the power-accuracy tradeoff commonly associated with sensing systems. Additionally, we extend our analysis to UAV-assisted 3D coverage, showing that the number of vehicles needed for $\epsilon$-optimal coverage scales as $O(1/\epsilon)$. Finally, we examine a scenario where UAVs perform simultaneous joint sensing and communication, proving that both $\epsilon$-optimality in sensing power and $O(1/\epsilon^{2/3})$ scaling for fleet size can be achieved under these combined conditions. Our approach relies on constructing ground sensing grids and leveraging established results from the field of geometric coverage. Notably, this concept is applicable to various mobile sensor networks, including underwater systems utilizing autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs). We conclude that our proposed framework can deliver near-optimal solutions for network power usage and fleet sizing in both established and emerging wireless sensing environments. Furthermore, our methodology is extendable to addressing $\epsilon$-optimality challenges in the contexts of power consumption and UAV-assisted coverage. Finally, we illustrate the practicality of our findings through simulation studies where the upper bounds on vehicle count are closely approached. These results are highly relevant for real-world applications such as traffic monitoring and disaster response. Specifically, in disaster scenarios, our approach enables near-optimal restoration of network connectivity following partial damage by deploying a minimal number of vehicles. In traffic monitoring, the same concept allows for near-optimal coverage of uncovered road segments or newly constructed routes while simultaneously reducing power consumption and savings within the existing network. Overall, our findings regarding the number of required vehicles are applicable to a wide range of wireless power-based sensing problems

The past twenty years have been defined by groundbreaking discoveries in neutrino physics, most notably the confirmation of neutrino oscillations and the establishment that at least one neutrino flavor is predominantly of mixed nature. Major experiments have already established the first generation of non-standard model parameters with high precision; the subsequent era will focus on measuring the final parameter—the CP violating phase—with comparable accuracy. This extreme precision is anticipated to reveal new, unexpected phenomena that have thus far remained elusive. The upcoming major experiment, DUNE, will operate using two distinct neutrino sources: the wide-band beam mode and the long-baseline mode. DUNE's substantial detector mass, combined with its unique access to both neutrino and antineutrino beams, enables highly precise measurements. Beyond discovering the CP violating phase with unprecedented accuracy, DUNE aims to determine the neutrino hierarchy, conduct a sensitive search for proton decay, investigate nuclear structure, and detect supernova events. This paper offers a concise overview of DUNE and its anticipated scientific contributions. The full text is available at https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1809.05061.pdf. Top tagging has become a critical area of research for detecting new physics beyond the Standard Model. This study introduces a fully interpretable alternative to the state-of-the-art Boosted Decision TreeTop (BDTTop) top tagger by applying advanced signal-to-noise separation (ASSN) and neural network techniques. The resulting boosted BDTTop tagger surpasses previous top taggers and matches the performance of the non-interpretable NNTop tagger. To achieve this, we employ the open-source PyShap library for interpretation, utilizing various methods to quantify each input feature's contribution to the output. Our analysis examines feature importance, the network's reliance on specific features, and the significance of top quark kinematics in predicting the boosted Higgs boson. Furthermore, we explore how the network represents the target class and analyze the impact of the training dataset on model interpretability. These insights into feature importance and the NNTop tagger's behavior offer valuable recommendations for designing future top tagger training processes. Finally, we outline potential avenues for enhancing the performance of the boost tagger. This code and analysis can inform the development of upcoming top taggers. This document establishes the groundwork for VO and requirement refinement, model abstractions, and their refinements, while also configuring the requirement model itself, as detailed in [1]. VO stands for Value Object, which serves as a representation of requirements, alongside their refined versions. A primary objective is to establish a formal foundation for refining both VO and requirements, alongside refining abstractions and their subsequent refinements. Furthermore, we aim to formalize refinements and refinement mapping based on [2], as outlined in [3]. Additionally, we address VO and requirement equivalence through the lens of refinements. VO equivalence is defined via an abstract syntax for VOs, though the syntax used in this document is a concrete instantiation of that abstract syntax. The document is structured into three sections: VO equivalents, VO refinement, and requirement refinement. In the VO equivalents section, we define an abstract syntax for VOs, along with equivalence and inequality relations, choosing to formalize the latter only when it aids in defining the former. The VO refinement section outlines properties of VOs and requirements that must be preserved during refinement, while the requirement refinement section focuses exclusively on requirements. We have selected a syntax for VOs and requirements from UML for this formalization, though any other syntax could have been used instead. VO classes and requirements are represented as graphs, whereas VO requirements are modeled using Z notation. This decision stems from the fact that graphs offer a convenient syntax for class structures, whereas Z notation is better suited for representing properties and VOs, which graphs cannot adequately capture. Consequently, this document serves as a foundation for further formalization efforts.

This study explores the intersection between garbage-collected languages and those employing advanced type systems for safe memory management. While garbage collection traditionally resides in backend compilers or interpreters, we propose integrating GC mechanisms into frontend tools like build systems. By utilizing build-system plugins, authors can construct Josephine, an incremental, incremental garbage collector for Rust that functions similarly to npm, the primary package manager for JavaScript applications. Josephine operates on a package-based structure, defining the scope of data sharing via the Rust module system. This approach offers several benefits: it allows developers to opt-in to Garbage Collection rather than adhering to a strict Garbage Collection vs. Rust paradigm; it prevents Garbage Collection from interfering with Rust's zero-cost abstractions; and, most importantly, it renders Rust's complex lifetime annotations optional. We evaluated Josephine's efficacy across four progressively larger Rust applications, observing reductions in lifetime-related code by 93% to 99% across the projects. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that Josephine-named data exhibits memory safety guarantees comparable to manually annotated Rust code. This research highlights the viability of frontend GC systems and provides insights into their advantages and challenges. We view this as a stepping stone toward a broader shift away from conventional language design philosophies, specifically moving from defining languages based on their backend implementations to shaping them through their frontends. Additionally, this work investigates the intersection between frontend tools and IDEs, suggesting that IDEs could serve as the foundation for future Garbage Collection systems. Finally, we conclude by discussing the implications of integrating Garbage Collection into the development workflow. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to examine such a frontend Garbage Collection mechanism. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ideals/rust-gc. The underlying build system is Bazel (https://bazel.build), developed by Google. Josephine is designed to be language-agnostic, applicable to any language featuring a module system, though it is currently implemented specifically for Rust. While neutrino oscillations confirm that neutrinos possess mass, they fail to establish whether these particles belong to Dirac or Majorana representations. Collider-based neutrinoless double-beta decays offer a distinct capability: even if direct detection of neutrino charge is impossible, enhanced sensitivity to such decays could validate the Majorana nature of neutrinos. A key advantage of calculating the decay rate in collider physics is that it offers self-consistent constraints on production cross-sections and energy spectra, unlike approaches relying on ad hoc assumptions. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of neutrinoless double-beta decay as a function of majoranaicity and majoranahess, incorporating critical experimental considerations. We examine the production of neutrino pairs via W boson fusion and Z boson pair production, focusing on scenarios involving high-energy electron-positron colliders and electron-proton colliders. Our findings indicate that the Majorana hypothesis can be rigorously tested through precise measurements of the decay rate across varying center-of-mass energies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that collider-based searches provide sensitivity to effective masses comparable to current neutrinoless double-beta decay experiments, even for non-degenerate neutrino mass spectra. Consequently, this research underscores the vital role of future collider experiments in investigating absolute neutrino mass. Finally, we outline potential applications of our methodology to analogous processes, such as lepton number violating Higgs boson pair production. These insights will offer valuable context for interpreting potential discoveries in future collider experiments and inform the design of new detectors with the necessary precision to conduct rigorous tests of majoranaicity. Specifically, we argue that rigorous tests of the Majorana hypothesis are feasible through high-precision studies of neutrino pair production at lepton colliders. Such advancements will significantly advance our understanding of leptonic CP violation and the potential matter-antimatter asymmetry inherent in Majorana neutrino states. Ultimately, this will provide a deeper comprehension of the fundamental properties of neutrinos and the early universe. Finally, we emphasize the critical need for increased investment in detector research and development to achieve the precision levels required to effectively test the majorana nature of neutrinos. By prioritizing detector development, we can ensure that future collider experiments fully capitalize on their unique sensitivity to the fundamental properties of neutrinos. This commitment will not only deepen our understanding of the fundamental nature of nature but also provide crucial insights into the fundamental nature of the universe. By ensuring that all polar subcode codewords are identified, initial undecodable permuted received words can be eliminated. We derive upper bounds for the polar subcode length and the count of initial received permutations that guarantee this objective. In coadded images, the Point Spread Function (PSF) is frequently approximated as a simple average of the individual PSFs from the constituent frames. This study examines how variations in frame geometry and the order of operations—specifically, whether to perform a weighted PSF fit on each frame before summation or to sum the frames first and then perform the fit—affect the resulting PSF model. We further investigate how the width of the annular region used to measure PSF radius influences these outcomes. Our analysis reveals that, in most scenarios, the PSF radius derived from a weighted fit applied to the coadded image lies between the values obtained from the two alternative methods described above. Additionally, we develop an analytic model to quantify these differences, demonstrating that they are negligible in typical weak lensing applications. However, when weighted fitting is performed on specific individual frames, non-neglig disparities can arise. Consequently, we propose a method to determine an appropriate width for the annular region used in PSF fitting. Finally, we compare these analytical predictions with results from a simulation, confirming that the differences between PSF models are indeed negligible. Nevertheless, we observe that narrow rings can be sensitive to local fluctuations in the coadded image, which may be mitigated by summing more input frames. We conclude that, given a sufficient number of input frames, the specific choice of frame geometry or the sequence of weighted fitting operations has a negligible impact on the final PSF model. The code employed in this study is publicly accessible. (abridged)

The structural stability of propagating cracks in both brittle and ductile materials involves a wide range of length scales, encompassing the crack tip radius, atomic spacing, and grain size. Consequently, determining toughness and critical extension stress requires a multiscale methodology. This article surveys the fundamental concepts and practical applications of fracture toughness and critical extension stress across diverse solids. We begin by examining the tensile strength of a brittle, amorphous material at its minimum length scale. Next, we derive a characteristic intrinsic length scale for propagating cracks in brittle materials and develop a theory for the tensile strength of brittle crystals at a larger length scale. We then present a practical definition of the propagation toughness of both brittle and ductile materials, followed by an analysis of the fracture toughness and critical extension stress for brittle materials at a macroscopic length scale. Finally, we summarize current understanding of the propagation toughness for both brittle and ductile materials at mesoscopic length scales, rounding out this review of the multi-length-scale stability of extending cracks. This article is grounded in a series of seven lectures delivered at the 2019 Los Alamos Faculty Summer School. Supplementary teaching notes and lecture slides are available at www.princeton.edu/~courseware. The school's recordings can be accessed at www.princeton.edu/~videos.

We investigate the statistical behavior of Gaussian free fields interacting with multiple stochastic Loewner curves, which are driven by exchangeable random variables arising from stochastic log-gas models. A primary objective is to demonstrate conformal covariance within the joint distribution of the free field and the Loewner domains. A specific instance of this framework involves coupling a free field with SLEs that carve out annular regions, where the gas particles are positioned at the centers of these annuli. This scenario encompasses both the two-dimensionally conformally invariant Dyson model and the broader class of interacting Dyson-simian processes. Additionally, we outline how to derive a free field conformally coupled with an internal domain from the case of Loewner domains. This result facilitates the analysis of boundary-condition insertion operators in conformal field theory and extends the domain-marking formalism to settings involving internal domains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that conformally covariant boundary insertion operators can be constructed from free fields conformally coupled with internal domains. Finally, by utilizing a Schur process linked to the Dyson model, we establish that the free field conformally coupled with a Dyson-simian process constitutes a Schur process conformally coupled with a Dyson-simian process. This finding yields a family of boundary insertion operators conformally coupled with boundary Schur functions. Our findings extend to a broader class of boundary interaction potentials, encompassing boundary symmetric functions, polynomials, and doubly orthogonal polynomials. In these scenarios, we exhibit conformal covariance by constructing a free field conformally coupled with a boundary domain and demonstrating its conformal invariance. These boundary fields are conformally inserted into the partition functions of free-fermion boundary conformal field theories, specifically the free-fermion six-vertex model and free-fermion Ising model. In these instances, we calculate explicit conformal transformation laws for the free field boundary insertion operators. The first such case involves the free-fermion six-vertex model, where we show that the boundary free field conformally coupled with a boundary domain is conformally invariant under the free-fermion six-vertex model. This model is conformally coupled with boundary Schur functions, which correspond to the boundary symmetric functions of double Schur functions. This paper addresses the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in $\mathbb{R}^n$ where $n\geq 3$, utilizing smooth periodic initial conditions. We establish a priori estimates for the maximum norm of all solution derivatives based on the maximum norm of the initial data. This approach yields a novel a priori estimate for the Navier-Stokes equations, enhancing the known $L^\infty$ estimate regarding initial velocity and improving upon earlier results. Notably, our derivation does not rely on the smallness of the initial data. Furthermore, these findings enable the derivation of additional estimates for the $r$-norm ($1\leq r\leq \infty$) of the solution, which remain valid even when the initial velocity is small in the $\infty$-norm. As a consequence, we obtain a new estimate for the norm of the solution that surpasses the previous best-known result derived by Geissert, Kato, and Nakamura. Finally, we prove new theorems concerning the existence and uniqueness of the Navier-Stokes equations' solution, specifically addressing the issue of regularity loss. These outcomes stem from an alternative derivation of the Beckner-Li-Lin inequality. The methodology and results presented herein are also applicable to other fluid dynamics models, such as the Euler equations. The findings in this work have already been recognized by the Science and Technology Award of the Higher Ataturk Foundation. The challenge of classically verifying quantum computing has recently garnered significant attention. Initial efforts established the existence of classical codes capable of verifying any quantum computation with high probability within polynomial time. Subsequently, more efficient protocols were developed that achieve linear verification time. In this work, we elucidate the existence of such efficient protocols and provide a rigorous proof of their correctness. Our approach relies on a general framework grounded in the concept of quantum low-error testers. Finally, we demonstrate how adapting a broad category of linear-time classical polynomial-time verification protocols to the quantum realm also yields efficient quantum verification protocols. By constructing a specific instance of these adapted protocols, we derive an efficient quantum verification protocol and rigorously prove its correctness. Our proofs utilize the techniques of "randomness extraction" and "tensorization." Furthermore, we extend the applicability of these protocols to a wider class of quantum circuits. We anticipate that the verification protocols described in this paper will serve as a valuable resource for the developing field of quantum verification. Additionally, our understanding of the verification process for polynomial quantum circuits will facilitate the investigation into the efficient classical verifiability of the quantum associative function problem and other complex problems in FP^#P. Ultimately, our research may contribute to determining whether the inclusion of classical and quantum verification complexity classes is proper. The paper available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01005 includes code to experiment with the verification of various circuits. The repository at https://github.com/alexandru-vasilescu/quantum-circuit-verification-host contains an implementation of the verification protocol, offering an interactive interface for verifying quantum circuits. This implementation covers polynomial and Clifford+T circuits, although it does not yet support generic quantum circuits. We welcome feedback from the community to assist in enhancing the tool. Blockchain serves as a distributed technology designed to foster trust and collaboration among participants. By utilizing distributed ledgers, these systems enable users to exchange data and digital assets without a central intermediary. This paper presents an architecture for integrating IoT with blockchain, outlining the design of smart contracts and oracles within this framework. Subsequently, we apply blockchain principles to the challenge of traceability in food supply chains. The proposed solution is illustrated through a specific case study involving a bread distribution network. Finally, we detail our implementation, which includes an analysis of the digital twin concept within blockchain environments, demonstrating its application in the food traceability system. We conclude by discussing the benefits and constraints of our approach, as well as potential future research directions. Keywords: Blockchain, IoT, Smart Contracts, Oracles, Food Supply Chain, Traceability, Digital Twin.

We introduce a method for modeling cell shapes using the implicit representation trained via deep neural networks. Specifically, we shape a cell by training a neural network to approximate a signed distance function (SDF) that defines the shape boundaries in a 3D grid space. The training process is guided by experimentally captured cell shapes, for which we automatically extract key geometric keypoints and skeleton shapes. Our results demonstrate that this approach can effectively model diverse cell morphologies and provide a robust, robust shape representation suitable for applications in live cell shape analysis and generation. For generative modeling, we adopt a recent generator-discriminator framework utilizing a two-network architecture: one generates the shape based on a latent code, while the other estimates a similarity metric against experimentally acquired shapes. We validate the efficacy of our approach by generating a wide range of realistic and varied cell shapes and by assessing the generation results against multiple metrics. Furthermore, a downstream application involving live cell shape analysis confirms the utility of our generated shapes. The accompanying code and models are publicly accessible. Printed materials remain a significant obstacle for blind, low-vision, and print-disabled individuals. This study addresses the specific challenge faced by the blind and low-vision communities in navigating Braille documents, a critical yet underexplored area. We introduce a dataset comprising 2,000 Braille versions of English Wikipedia pages, covering a diverse array of scientific, historical, and cultural topics. Analysis of this data reveals that Braille documents exhibit a level of modularity comparable to their web sources, enabling effective navigation via table-of-contents-like structures. Leveraging these insights, we developed BrailleNav, a navigation system that provides a seamless experience for users. BrailleNav integrates Braille reading with tab-based interface design, allowing users to manage multiple documents simultaneously and switch between sections effortlessly. We evaluated the system with three expert Braille readers and two non-experts, who found the interface intuitive and the navigation mechanisms easy to use. Furthermore, we interviewed various stakeholders, including librarians and Braille translators, to assess the practical utility of our dataset and system. Their feedback indicates that BrailleNav has high potential for improving access to information within educational and library environments. To the best of our knowledge, this is the inaugural study to examine Braille navigability. Our dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/ashishgupta10/brailledoc-navigability. The source code for BrailleNav can be found at https://github.com/ashishgupta10/braillenav. Our findings suggest that Braille navigability represents a crucial concern for users interacting with standard print documents. We hope this work inspires further research into Braille document navigation and encourages the community to prioritize navigability as a key quality metric for accessible digital content. Denoising autoencoder-based pretraining has become a cornerstone of state-of-the-art performance in Natural Language Understanding. This paper introduces XLNet, a generalized autoregressive pretraining method that not only matches but also surpasses the performance of 12 state-of-the-art transformers in Multiple Choice Question (MC) benchmarks. XLNet achieves this by independently recovering both past and future tokens within a sequence, surmounting the autoregression constraint inherent in GPT and BERT. Furthermore, XLNet proposes two innovations for representing unlabeled data during pretraining. The first, Position-based Pretraining (P), replaces the masked token in an [A, B] question with a [C, D, E, ?] sequence that utilizes positional information rather than a [A, B] context lacking it. The second is the Position-biased Pretraining (PbP) approach, which masks a specific token based on its position answer and trains the model to recover that position-specific token from a context that excludes the masked token. PbP is a direct extension of P and has been shown to improve MC performance. Consequently, XLNet-P and XLNet-PbP are the results of training XLNet using Position-based and Position-biased pretraining, respectively. Both variants outperform BERT-base and BERT-large, with PbP even exceeding the results of BERT-Base-MLM. Notably, XLNet-PbP also yields improvements in Sentence Ranking tasks. The paper concludes with a discussion on the generalization of P and PbP to other tasks. Overall, XLNet demonstrates that it is possible to simultaneously enhance MC and Sentence Ranking performance while also improving GLUE scores. Additionally, the study presents a novel pretraining objective, Replaced Word Pretraining (RWP), which recovers a masked word using the original value after randomly replacing it. RWP is a generalization of P and PbP and has been observed to improve performance on the MRPC dataset. In summary, XLNet offers a unified framework for pretraining objectives that outperforms BERT and BERT-LM. The code is available at https://github.com/FlagSunXLNet/XLNet.
