Exoplanet atmospheres are typically investigated through transit spectroscopy, a method inherently susceptible to stellar activity. While existing literature has examined this interference, the impact of active regions on short-wavelength transmission spectra at low resolutions remains inadequately quantified. This study utilizes a Monte Carlo framework to simulate transit spectra, modeling both exoplanets and active regions. Our findings indicate that at low resolutions, stellar activity introduces transmission variations of approximately 10^-3 across wavelengths, a level of noise comparable to or exceeding potential planetary signals. Consequently, we demonstrate that employing higher spectral resolutions can effectively mitigate these low-level fluctuations caused by exoplanetary atmospheric absorption. This approach offers a pathway to reduce uncertainties in spectroscopic measurements of exoplanet atmospheres. Furthermore, we provide a Python-based mitigation tool, HARP-STAR, accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi/HARP-STAR, which incorporates a model for active region effects on exoplanetary spectra. This tool can be integrated into the standard spectral extraction pipeline for exoplanet transit spectroscopy. We applied HARP-STAR to Kepler-16b, a well-studied planet, to analyze activity-induced spectral features and confirm the effectiveness of using high-resolution data to remove them. Our results show that high-resolution observations can reduce activity-related errors by about 50% compared to low-resolution ones. Additionally, we demonstrate that combining high-resolution data with the HARP-STAR model enables the detection of CO absorption features in Kepler-16b's atmosphere. Finally, we outline a strategy for designing future transit spectroscopy missions aimed at characterizing exoplanet atmospheres. We propose that carrying multiple spectrographs with different resolutions could serve as an effective mitigation strategy against stellar activity. Specifically, we suggest that space-based missions equipped with a 0.3 R spectrograph to observe the 1.1–1.7 $\mu$m range would be capable of observing H$_2$O, CO, and CH$_4$ features for small planets. This recommendation is based on the observation that active region effects are significantly lower at 0.3 R than at 0.05 R. We conclude that developing future missions with multi-resolution capabilities is essential for accurately characterizing exoplanet atmospheres. Our analysis indicates that the 0.3 R spectrograph should cover a spectral range of 1.1–1.7 $\mu$m, as active region effects are substantially reduced in this band compared to 0.8–1.3 $\mu$m

By formulating an ordinary differential equation derived from a specific type of meromorphic 1-form, we present an explicit method for constructing certain constants curvature metrics on a Riemann surface equipped with a set of singular points. This approach extends the classical S. Poincaré uniformization theorem for constant curvature metrics on smooth Riemann surfaces to the case where a set of singular points is present. Furthermore, we establish the smooth equivalence or the topological smooth equivalence of Riemann surfaces derived from distinct curvature forms that yield the same signature. Finally, we apply this framework to the analysis of elastic curves and closed elastic bands on a sphere. Notably, our research demonstrates the non-existence of periodic solutions for the elastic bands case when the singularity pole count is odd, and confirms the topological distinctness of the elastic bands case for even counts. These findings align with, or expand upon, the conclusions reached by J. C. Zhang, X. L. Li, and X. P. Xu. Additionally, X. L. Li's work indicates the existence of periodic solutions when $k \neq -2$, a detail not explicitly elaborated upon. We have integrated this existence conclusion into our paper and will explore it within the context of the existence and uniqueness of constant curvature metrics on singular Riemann surfaces. Finally, our methodology offers a straightforward proof of the Weierstrass representation of constant curvature surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$ featuring ends of screw type, and our theory of curvature forms can be applied to derive the Wirtinger representation for minimal surfaces and the Weierstrass formula for isometric immersion of surfaces with mean curvature $H$ possessing planar ends. These applications will be addressed in a forthcoming publication. The content of this paper serves as a preliminary exploration in this research direction. Research into the air-water interface locomotion of the centipede *L. forficatus* shows that its 14 leg pairs coordinate similarly to biological hydrofoils, propelling the organism against the wind. However, because these creatures are lightweight, they are significantly influenced by air drag, and their elongated bodies result in substantial aerodynamic and hydrodynamic mechanical coupling. This paper examines the coupled dynamics of *L. forficatus* and establishes a theoretical framework for its locomotion, accounting for both mechanical and kinematic body coupling. The model demonstrates the presence of various passive and active self-organization modes, including the generation of traveling waves during locomotion. Furthermore, the study identifies a critical Froude number at which these waves emerge, aligning with experimental observations. Finally, the study explores the impact of flow direction on locomotion, confirming that *L. forficatus* moves more efficiently in the direction of the flow. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the swimming dynamics of lightweight, water-surface dwellers. The proposed theoretical model and its predictions are expected to advance the broader field of biomechanics. Notably, the identified self-organization modes in *L. forficatus* may also apply to other surface swimmers, such as insects and small fish. We present the first JWST Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) deep field observations of the COSMOS-Web Early Lensed Field (COSMOS-ELF), a region selected via weak gravitational lensing from the Hubble COSMOS field. Our analysis identifies 18 galaxies with redshifts exceeding 4 and surface brightnesses below AB 24 mag arcsec$^{-2}$ at 4.4 $\mu$m, with redshifts confirmed through spectroscopy in five cases. Notably, we detected no galaxies meeting these criteria at the same redshifts but at higher surface brightness levels. The average stellar mass for the 13 most massive of these ultra-faint, far-infrared bright (fIRB) galaxies is approximately $10^{10.5\pm0.2}$ M$_\odot$, roughly a thousand times less massive than their brighter counterparts. These faint fIRB galaxies exhibit stellar mass specific star formation rates (SsFR) roughly an order of magnitude higher than typical star-forming galaxies at this redshift, suggesting they are undergoing intense, short-lived starbursts. Their physical properties resemble those of galaxies with significant dust extinction at lower stellar masses and similar redshifts, implying that these obscured, highly star-forming systems are a common phenomenon. Furthermore, these galaxies are likely progenitors of the bright, dust-obscured galaxies found in the local universe. The COSMOS-ELF field is uniquely suited for studying such faint fIRB galaxies due to its ability to isolate them from brighter neighbors and its capacity to isolate their mid- and far-infrared emission from the near-infrared stellar light. This capability allows for a cleaner investigation of their star formation rates, dust properties, and kinematics. The COSMOS-Web Deep and Large programs will offer even greater sensitivity to these sources, while COSMOS-ELF's unique lensing environment will facilitate the study of their clustering properties. This research was conducted using JWST public data, including NIRCam imaging at 2.0, 2.3, 3.3, 4.4, and 4.8 $\mu$m, NIRSpec spectroscopy, and MIRI imaging at 10 and 12 $\mu$m. This study examines two-dimensional granular packings of disks with varying sizes and weights into a container. While prior research established that jammed states exist for packs of identical disks as well as for packs with multiple disk sizes, it was noted that the latter are accessible only through quasi-one-dimensional methods, such as slow sedimentation in a vertical channel or compression within a channel before expansion in 2D. The current work focuses on packs created via sedimentation in a vertical channel. We present a configuration consisting of 100 disks with 1.5 times the radius of the dominant species that defies the pattern of alternating layers. This pack was generated by inserting disks into the channel in an order that randomizes the resulting structure. We contend that this pack, along with others in the literature, can be interpreted as a pack of monodisperse disks if the interpretation of contact lines between disks of different sizes is appropriately adjusted. We contend that the construction rules for jammed packs of disks with multiple species are more comprehensive than previously acknowledged. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for packs formed through sedimentation in a channel, the sequence of diameters within a single channel, when read from bottom to top, must adhere to the single-species rule of no more than two species appearing consecutively. This observation holds true for packs composed of disks with a range of radii. Additionally, we show that this observation remains valid for packs of weighted disks with 1.25 times the radius of the dominant species, provided that lighter disks are not significantly heavier than the dominant species. However, this observation does not apply to packs of monodisperse disks or to jammed packs of non-monodisperse disks constructed using non-sedimentation methods. Finally, we propose that this observation will also hold for packs of non-monodisperse disks where each radius appears no more than three times consecutively. These findings contribute to the conjecture that a conjectured set of rules for jammed packs of non-monodisperse disks is complete. This conjecture extends the conjecture by Cohn and Kumar, which posits that the only complete set of rules is the Fibonacci sequence. This study investigates how distinct flavors of El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) affect global seasonal precipitation extremes. By analyzing 32 years of Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) Core Lightning Imaging and Precipitation (GPMIP) satellite data, we identified significant variations between the two primary ENSO flavors, Eastern (El Niño) and Modoki (MP), regarding the frequency of very low and high precipitation events. The MP regime is characterized by a zonal dipole of very low precipitation (VP) and high precipitation (HP) extremes, whereas the ENSO regime displays a zonal pattern of HP and VP, respectively. While both regimes exhibit a substantial zonal asymmetry in very low precipitation, the Imprints of very high precipitation (HP) events differ markedly: a strong dipole asymmetry is observed under the ENSO regime, whereas the Modoki regime produces a weaker, yet distinct, response. These divergent patterns of extreme precipitation are primarily driven by contrasting diabatic heating responses of the two regimes, which in turn generate distinct tropical and extratropical cloud feedbacks. These findings highlight the critical need to account for the specific flavor of ENSO when assessing the impacts of tropical variability on hydrological extremes. Furthermore, our results indicate that the Modoki regime may leave a detectable signature on global seasonal precipitation extremes, a signal that could be valuable for climate model evaluation and the assessment of climate change impacts. Finally, we emphasize the necessity of accurately simulating ENSO flavors in climate models to achieve a more reliable understanding of the water cycle's response to climate change. This is achieved by incorporating a robust representation of the observed zonal asymmetry in tropical cloud feedbacks. We conclude by demonstrating that a recently developed parameterization, which captures this zonal asymmetry, successfully reproduces the observed ENSO and Modoki impacts on VP and HP extremes. This underscores the vital role of zonal asymmetry in tropical cloud feedbacks for accurately representing the impacts of tropical variability on the global hydrological cycle. Our approach offers a promising avenue for enhancing the accuracy of climate model projections of seasonal precipitation extremes. This study examines a single-population model incorporating age structure and psychological impacts within a polluted setting. The population is segmented into juvenile and adult cohorts, with psychological effects influencing only the juvenile phase. The environmental pollutant diminishes population carrying capacity and introduces a mortality risk specifically for juveniles. Purposefully decoupled from prior literature, the analysis focuses on the stability of the trivial solution and the emergence of periodic solutions. Furthermore, global stability for the trivial solution and steady-state populations is established, alongside the derivation of a Hopf bifurcation. Numerical simulations are provided to validate these theoretical findings. Ultimately, the model demonstrates that psychological effects and juvenile exposure to pollution significantly affect population survival. These insights may inform strategies for mitigating the adverse effects of psychological stress and environmental pollution on living organisms. Additionally, the modeling approach and associated methodologies could be applicable to developing models for multispecies communities with age structure. The model's framework is also extendable to other contexts, such as multispecies systems or populations in pristine environments. This single-population model serves as a foundational step toward constructing more complex, realistic representations. This paper introduces a series of weak substructural logics within the hypersequent framework, characterized by specific structural rules and a semantics based on ordered sets of worlds with relations for truth-value assignment. We demonstrate that these systems support a Gentzen-style cut-elimination theorem and possess the decision problem property with an exponential upper bound on complexity. Furthermore, we examine an intermediate logic incorporating the monotonicity rule, noting that while it admits a similar cut elimination theorem, its cut-free proof height is unbounded, thereby lacking computability regarding the decision problem. Finally, we analyze the impact of incorporating the weakening rule, observing that for one specific system, it yields a linear bound on the decision problem's complexity, whereas in another system, such computability is entirely lost. These findings underscore the significance of monotonicity in hypersequent-based substructural frameworks, particularly when utilizing ordered-world semantics. Additionally, we provide an overview of related work and conclude by outlining promising avenues for future research. Our primary contributions are twofold: first, we define a family of weak substructural logics in the hypersequent setting via ordered-world semantics and prove the cut-elimination theorem for these systems; second, we establish upper bounds on complexity for the decision problems of these logics. To our knowledge, this represents the initial development of an ordered-world semantics for (weak) substructural logics and the first results concerning cut elimination and decision problem complexity for this specific semantic approach. These findings hold significant interest for the broader study of non-classical logics. Specifically, they offer a novel perspective on understanding the influence of monotonicity on hypersequent substructural logics by providing a comparison between a non-monotonic and an monotonic system. This contrasts with existing literature, such as [10], which focuses on various forms of negation rather than monotonicity. Consequently, our work serves as a foundation for further investigating the role of monotonicity through the lens of ordered-world semantics. Finally, the derived weak substructural logics may facilitate the investigation of non-monotonic reasoning, an area currently lacking in research within the hypersequent framework. We have previously addressed this gap in [11] by developing an alternative semantics for non-monotonic substructural logics.

This study investigates how intermolecular forces within weakly interacting molecular dimers respond to external electric fields. We utilized the S66 dataset, which comprises 165 molecular dimers (including water) and covers a broad spectrum of non-covalent interactions essential for modeling supramolecular and biomolecular systems, previously validated for high-accuracy quantum chemistry methods. To assess the impact of field-induced changes in the electronic structure of individual molecules on these interactions, we employed the coupled-pair many-electron approximation (CPM) and its second-order variant (second-order Møller-Plesset perturbation theory, MP2). Our findings indicate that electric fields up to 0.05 a.u. (approximately 0.08 V/Å) trigger significant and non-linear alterations in the interaction energy of most dimers, with relative variations reaching approximately 100% in extreme cases. These substantial effects stem from an increased population of high-energy electronic states, which amplifies both electrostatic and polarization contributions to the interaction energy. Additionally, we examined the sensitivity of these interactions to the relative alignment of the molecules under an applied field. Finally, we demonstrated that simple geometric models, which rely on the classical response of nuclei, provide a qualitatively accurate description of how external electric fields influence dimer interactions. Collectively, these results suggest that applying external electric fields can significantly modify supramolecular interactions, a factor that must be accounted for in future investigations of molecular systems. This becomes particularly critical in emerging technologies such as electrostatic force microscopy and field-induced chemistry, where precise understanding of intermolecular forces is essential. Furthermore, our research underscores the necessity of including external field effects in computational models, such as those employed in molecular dynamics simulations. We conclude by proposing a molecular force probe technique that quantifies the influence of external fields on dimer interactions. This approach involves measuring forces between two molecules at varying field strengths and relative orientations, thereby generating an external-field-dependent force field. Such an approach could facilitate the identification of molecular pairs exhibiting exceptionally strong interaction modifications, a property valuable for applications like force spectroscopy and molecular switches. To enable this, we provide the complete S66 dimer interaction energy and polarization energy surfaces as functions of intermolecular distance and external field strength and direction, along with the associated Python code. These data and tools offer a comprehensive resource for investigating and quantifying how external electric fields affect intermolecular forces. Access to the S66 interaction energy and polarization surfaces is available at https://www.s6

The fourth industrial revolution has significantly enhanced our ability to handle non-deterministic factors in scheduling, notably through the increased availability of real-time data via Industry 4.0 technologies. This study investigates how incorporating additional real-time information influences the performance uncertainty of job shop schedules, specifically examining two key aspects: the timing of machine setup completions and the real-time completion of jobs. To address this, we developed and enhanced a polynomial-time exact strong dual-based algorithm capable of generating competitive stochastic scenarios to assess uncertainty. Using a commonly applied metric, we analyzed the impact of delayed data acquisition on uncertainty measures and identified the optimal data acquisition strategy to minimize these uncertainties. The results demonstrate that accessing real-time setup completion data and monitoring the completion of up to 50% of jobs can reduce uncertainty measures by 20%. Consequently, these findings offer valuable insights for strategically managing real-time data acquisition to optimize the benefits derived from uncertainty modeling in advanced industrial environments. Finally, the algorithm's computational efficiency was validated through extensive numerical tests. A comprehensive supplementary document provides further details on the algorithmic design and performance analysis. This work is especially relevant to researchers utilizing our recent algorithm, which is detailed in our associated paper. The document includes an extended version of the algorithm for easier implementation and additional tests that explore further completion volume variations. Our algorithm is also featured in our related paper, where we present further details on uncertainty analysis and explore various uncertainty measures. We invite readers to consult that paper for more in-depth information. In this version, we focus on introducing the algorithm, its functionality, and the methodology for analyzing the impact of data acquisition timing on uncertainty measures. The algorithm was developed to be highly competitive, and we have made every effort to ensure its efficiency. We have also included a detailed explanation of the algorithm's operations within the code, which is available for download. We hope this contributes meaningfully to your research. Resilience is a crucial concept for addressing challenges in diverse domains, ranging from resource allocation to network design. This paper introduces an explicit STL-based framework for modeling and analyzing the resilience of cyber-physical systems against cyber-physical attacks. We establish a syntax and corresponding semantics for a resilience formula, which utilizes temporal logic expressions to define a system's resilience against such attacks. We demonstrate that the model checking problem for this formula is decidable and prove that its computational complexity is non-primitive recursive. Furthermore, we provide a procedure to compute the robustness of resilience for a given system, alongside an analysis of its computational complexity. Finally, we validate the applicability of our approach through a numerical example involving a power grid subjected to a cyber-physical attack. Additionally, we extend the resilience formula to accommodate multi-objective scenarios involving multiple stakeholders, and we establish the complexity for both the model checking of the extended formula and the computation of the robustness of this extended version. In both contexts, the complexities are demonstrated to be non-primitive recursive. Our results indicate that computing the resilience of a cyber-physical system is generally more demanding than standard robustness analysis. All proofs for the proposed definitions and analyses can be found in the full version of this paper available at arXiv:2102.01019v2 [cs.CR]. Dark matter remains one of physics' most significant unresolved mysteries. Since it is established that dark matter interacts gravitationally with visible matter, searches utilizing accelerometers are particularly promising. This article outlines recent and prospective investigations into dark matter candidates—including feebly interacting particles trapped within the Earth, scalar-matter domain walls, and axion quark nuggets—by employing accelerometer networks. Furthermore, it provides an outlook on how emerging ultra-sensitive atomic-interference gravimeters will expand the sensitivity ranges of these searches in the coming years. Finally, the discussion highlights the critical importance of conducting cross-comparison studies involving gravimeter-based dark matter searches. These efforts must involve both theoretical and experimental collaborations to fully leverage the unique potential of accelerometer networks. To initiate such collaborations, a prototype search for self-interacting dark matter using accelerometers is currently being prepared. This proof-of-concept experiment will demonstrate that accelerometer networks can contribute to dark matter research and may offer insights into fundamental properties of these elusive particles. Additionally, it will establish a framework for integrating future accelerometer-based dark matter searches into the broader fundamental dark matter research community. To facilitate this, we propose and define the concept of the "accelerometer network sensitivity curve." Finally, we outline several fundamental open questions and challenges that must be addressed to fully realize the potential of these networks. We conclude by offering recommendations for advancing this field. Overall, we believe that accelerometers offer a largely unexplored avenue for dark matter research and that these devices could identify new types of dark matter particles. This conclusion is supported by the fact that multiple distinct dark matter models involving novel particles interacting with normal matter solely through gravity are already well-motivated by theory and remain subject to rigorous experimental scrutiny. Consequently, accelerometer-based searches could address some of the most challenging and intriguing aspects of the dark matter problem. This conclusion also underscores the need for further research into whether purely gravitational interactions can be detected using gravimeters and whether such interactions can be distinguished from background gravitational signals. Thus, accelerometers could play a pivotal role in solving the dark matter puzzle. This conclusion also emphasizes the necessity for further development of gravitational sensors, as well as the creation of innovative experimental and data analysis techniques to extract the full potential of gravimeter-based dark matter searches. This conclusion also stresses the importance of funding and implementing such research. This article was written by members of the fundamental dark matter community who are deeply committed to advancing accelerometers as a viable tool for dark matter research. We hope that this work will inspire further interest in this promising and largely unexplored research direction

The origin of compact, faint radio sources (CFRSs) remains a significant enigma in source physics. This study investigates the nature of CFRSs by analyzing their morphology, source sizes, and flux density distributions. We examined 12 CFRSs located in the 3CRR bright sources Cygnus A, Perseus A, and Coma Berenices, characterized by flux densities ranging from 0.01 to 0.03 mJy and angular sizes between 0.01 and 0.1 arcsec. Our analysis revealed that the flux density distributions of these sources are highly skewed toward low values, with a mean of 0.023 mJy and a standard deviation of 0.002 mJy. Furthermore, the flux density and size distributions are strongly skewed toward low values, with means of 0.023 mJy and 0.015 arcsec², respectively. The observed flux densities align with theoretical predictions for sources emitting synchrotron radiation. The CFRSs within the Coma cluster exhibit a mean size of 0.015 arcsec², while those in the Cygnus and Perseus clusters average 0.010 and 0.020 arcsec², respectively. The flux density distributions of the Coma and Cygnus CFRSs closely resemble the overall sample, whereas the Perseus CFRSs display flux densities approximately double that of the sample mean. Finally, we determined the upper limits for the mean sizes of unresolved CFRSs to be 0.001 arcsec², 0.002 arcsec², and 0.003 arcsec² for the Coma, Cygnus, and Perseus clusters, respectively. These findings suggest that CFRSs are unresolved radio sources with minimal physical sizes. The CFRSs identified in this work are hypothesized to be either low-luminosity radio galaxies or young, low-luminosity radio jets. The CFRSs in the Coma and Cygnus clusters are likely low-luminosity radio galaxies, while those in the Perseus cluster may represent young, low-luminosity radio jets. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are probabilistic frameworks where hidden states, evolving over time via a transition distribution, generate observable outputs according to an emission distribution. This paper introduces a generalized framework, the \emph{abstract hidden Markov model}, in which these distributions are represented as \emph{monads} from category theory. We demonstrate that AHHMs provide a \emph{q-IF} (quantitative information flow) characterization of such models, linking them to probabilistic non-interference. Specifically, we establish a Martinet-style \emph{probabilistic strong simulation} between AHHMs; this relation ensures that although individual outputs from a specific model path may leak information, the average output remains information-safe across all possible paths. Furthermore, we introduce \emph{Markov functors}, which are categorical structures capable of abstracting various Markov models, and utilize this framework to define probabilistic simulation for them. Finally, we outline the connections between our proposed framework and existing extensions of HMMs. This work serves as a companion to [1], which offers an equivalent construction using probabilistic monads within the category \textbf{Prob}. Together, these papers illustrate the power of a categorical approach to probabilistic programming. This methodology facilitates a high-level, uniform definition of information-safe probabilistic programs and algorithms, while also providing intuition for the axioms used in existing if-and-only-if results in probabilistic programming.

We present a category of stochastic advection problems suitable for analyzing turbulent transport. The flow field's statistics are defined by the dynamical coherent structures (DCSs) of a nonlinear stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) and the multiplicative noise spectrum. Our analysis centers on the mean residence time (MRT) distribution of a passive scalar transported by the flow. We demonstrate that the MRT distribution lacks additivity across spatial scales, a phenomenon we attribute to the statistical nonlocality arising from the interaction between large-scale DCSs and small-scale turbulent fluctuations. This statistical nonlocality offers a framework for understanding how large-scale features influence small-scale behavior in turbulent systems. Specifically, we examine two distinct regimes: (i) large-scale coherent structures exerting control over small-scale dynamics, and (ii) small-scale turbulent structures significantly affecting large-scale dynamics. Our methodology is applied to turbulent transport within the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes (NS) equations and the two-dimensional shallow water (SW) equations. In both cases, we utilize the standard coherent vorticity field as the basis for the flow. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the MRT distribution and the spatial correlation function of the passive scalar. Finally, our findings indicate that the MRT distribution is universal for the NS and SW equations, remaining independent of the specific large-scale DCS selected. These results are corroborated by numerical simulations. Our methodology provides a quantitative approach to characterizing the interaction between large- and small-scale turbulent features. Furthermore, the MRT distribution derived here holds potential for application in other nonlinear hydrodynamic systems, including those involving shallow water equations, baroclinic instability, and the advection of heat flux by large-scale coherent vortices. Finally, we extend the analysis to three-dimensional NS equations. In this context, the MRT distribution is contingent upon the specific large-scale DCS under consideration. However, we observe that the three-dimensional DCS selected in our analysis—large-scale vortex rings—still exhibits statistical nonlocality. This three-dimensional extension underscores the critical role of large-scale coherent structures in turbulent transport. Our methodology is applicable to a broad range of nonlinear hydrodynamic systems. Moreover, the MRT distribution can serve as a quantitative metric for assessing the impact of large-scale coherent structures on small-scale turbulent transport. This research investigates electromagnetic radiation thermodynamics accounting for the Casimir effect. Our findings indicate that radial pressure drops to near-zero levels close to the plate separation, while radiation energy density remains only marginally affected. We further demonstrate that the grand potential, Helmholtz free energy, and entropy align with Planck's law, confirming that radiation remains a blackbody distribution even under the Casimir effect. In fact, the Casimir force can be derived from the system's thermodynamic potentials. Additionally, we observe that the energy density of electromagnetic radiation increases as one approaches the Casimir plates. Finally, our results indicate that the thermal radiation wavelength is significantly reduced near the plates compared to regions farther away. These effects are most pronounced at small plate separations and high temperatures. Ultimately, the derived expressions for thermodynamic potentials and entropy may prove valuable for developing quantum devices that leverage electromagnetic radiation and its interaction with the Casimir effect. This study paves the way for future research into quantum thermodynamics incorporating Casimir force effects. Furthermore, future investigations should explore the potential to enhance quantum efficiency in quantum thermodynamic devices through the manipulation of electromagnetic fields via the Casimir effect. Specifically, we propose that the thermal wavelength of radiation can be adjusted by selecting an appropriate plate separation. Finally, we suggest that Casimir mirrors could be utilized to generate and manipulate quantum radiation. To achieve this, one could employ two sets of mirrors: a hot mirror pair and a cold mirror pair positioned at specific distances to manipulate quantum radiation. The resulting radiation could then be directed into a working substance, such as a Bose-Einstein condensate. This approach may enable the manipulation of quantum radiation characteristics, including energy density, pressure, and the compressibility factor. Ultimately, these capabilities could facilitate the development of quantum thermal machines with improved efficiency. In conclusion, we have established a framework for analyzing the influence of boundary conditions on quantum radiation thermodynamics through the lens of quantum statistical mechanics. This study not only deepens our understanding of quantum radiation thermodynamics but also offers a pathway for the future design of quantum thermal machines. We anticipate that the findings of this work will contribute to the advancement of quantum technology. Ensuring that users understand how their data is utilized is a fundamental aspect of data privacy. This is especially critical for advanced machine learning (ML) methods, which necessitate extensive datasets to function effectively. This study examines the primary issue of conditional prior (CP) — a form of prior knowledge — within the context of spatio-temporal point pattern (STPP) data, a common format for user-generated content on online platforms. Drawing on a privacy framework for online services, we demonstrate the fundamental tension between privacy and utility when estimating STPPs using CPs. Our analysis reveals that the trade-off is influenced by the correlation structure of the data and the spatial-temporal scale at which patterns are identified. We conclude that the primary risk associated with CPs arises when they are employed to infer private information about individuals. These findings hold significant implications for online platforms regarding the design of their ML models. Specifically, we offer practical guidance for online services on selecting appropriate models to mitigate privacy risks while maintaining utility. Additionally, we present an application case study involving the online service OpenStreetMap to validate these insights. This case study illustrates the trade-off between privacy and utility and demonstrates the efficacy of our proposed privacy-preserving models. Overall, this work provides online services with the necessary knowledge to strike an optimal balance between privacy and utility when utilizing CPs in their ML models. Furthermore, it serves as a proof of concept for online services committed to safeguarding user privacy. By implementing privacy-preserving models, services can effectively address privacy concerns while delivering valuable services to their users. This approach serves as a concrete example of how online services can protect user privacy, thereby fostering trust in the platform. Additionally, we provide open-source code to assist other services in implementing similar privacy-preserving models. This accessibility will enable other services to learn from our implementation and adopt comparable strategies to protect their users. Ultimately, this work serves as a practical guide for online services seeking to balance privacy and utility, offering code that can be readily implemented to protect user data. This implementation can help other services address privacy concerns and build trust with their users. Finally, by making our code open-source, we enable other services to benefit from our implementation and contribute to the broader field of privacy-preserving ML. This could lead to the development of other privacy-preserving models that can be compared and evaluated against our approach, further advancing the field. While recent advancements in 3D point cloud localisation have leveraged implicit 3D shape understanding through Normal Distribution Transforms (NDT), these methods are often restricted to specific maps due to limited training data. This study introduces a large-scale NDT-based point cloud localisation approach that utilizes a Transformer architecture trained on diverse urban NED maps. By employing a hierarchical Transformer that processes NDT histograms at both 2D and 3D levels, the method effectively captures plan view and vertical geometry while filtering out irrelevant sensor data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach can be trained to output multiple NDT parameters—specifically position, rotation, and uncertainty—simultaneously. Additionally, we present a new benchmark comprising 1,000 datasets across three diverse cities, covering various sensor types and map configurations. Our results indicate that a single model can achieve an average translation error of 0.42m and a mean angle error of 0.15 rad during inference. Our findings suggest that future research should prioritize (i) developing more diverse and representative benchmark datasets, and (ii) enhancing the robustness of the end-to-end learning pipeline. Finally, we argue that end-to-end learning offers a promising avenue for overcoming the challenges associated with traditional handcrafted NDT-based localisation methods. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) connectivity serves as a robust biomarker for brain disorders. While group comparison methods have established robust group differences in rs-fMRI data, these findings often lack clinical utility because treatment decisions are made at the individual level. Consequently, rs-fMRI connectivity metrics hold promise for enhancing prediction accuracy in clinical settings. However, a significant challenge remains in translating group-level effects into high prediction accuracy at the individual level, particularly in multisite studies where rigorous assessment of prediction accuracy and power is essential. This study addresses these challenges by employing a rigorous cross-validation framework that accounts for potential multisite effects, thereby enabling the simultaneous evaluation of group comparison power and prediction accuracy. We first apply this framework to a large, well-controlled rs-fMRI study to assess the relationship between the two. Subsequently, we introduce a novel method that leverages statistically significant group effects to boost prediction accuracy by incorporating effects-informed edges into the predictive model. We apply this approach to two new rs-fMRI datasets and demonstrate robust prediction using clinically relevant markers: age and diagnosis. Finally, we develop a simulation framework to elucidate how various data characteristics influence prediction accuracy and power, offering guidance on optimizing experimental designs for clinical applications. These results significantly enhance the utility of rs-fMRI as a clinical tool. By improving prediction accuracy while maintaining statistically robust group effects, our methodology advances the application of machine learning in rs-fMRI research and offers a generalizable framework for translating group-level effects into individual-level predictions. Our findings suggest that the prediction accuracy achievable with rs-fMRI connectivity is superior to that of many other established neuroimaging modalities. This enhancement in prediction accuracy can be realized without compromising group comparison power or effect size. Furthermore, multisite effects do not hinder the achievement of statistically robust group effects or high prediction accuracy when using this prediction framework. These results have profound implications for the future use of rs-fMRI as a clinical tool. By optimizing experimental design and rigorously assessing group effects and prediction accuracy, rs-fMRI can yield clinically actionable metrics that are both statistically and clinically significant. This marks a pivotal step toward the widespread adoption of rs-fMRI as a standard clinical tool. Additionally, our methodology is broadly applicable to other neuroimaging modalities, including structural imaging, and can be extended to other imaging tasks beyond classification and regression. This work was conducted using the Nipype and Scikit-learn libraries. The accompanying code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/ahmedfahim123/Power_and_Pred

A single-hop beeping network is a distributed communication framework where all nodes interact by transmitting single-bit messages, known as beeps. This paper addresses two core challenges in distributed computing: naming and counting. Our primary objective is to minimize both the energy consumption and execution time of algorithms solving these issues. We present randomized algorithms that achieve optimal performance for both naming and counting on networks of $n$ stations, with a running time of $O(n \log n)$ and an energy complexity of $O(\log n)$. Additionally, we propose randomized algorithms for both problems characterized by a running time of $O(n)$ and a broadcast energy complexity of $O(\log \log n)$. Finally, we establish lower bounds for randomized algorithms, demonstrating that any such algorithm requires a running time of $\Omega(n)$ and a broadcast energy complexity of $\Omega(\log \log n)$. To the best of our knowledge, all proposed algorithms operate in a fully synchronous environment where every node possesses $O(n)$ bits of memory. Our findings represent the first randomized algorithms that resolve both naming and counting with running times and energy complexities that are optimal in at least one dimension. Notably, we prove that achieving optimality in both running time and energy consumption is impossible. Furthermore, our algorithms are straightforward to implement and can be readily adapted to address other fundamental problems in distributed computing. The primary obstacle to applying NLP on code-mixed languages is the failure of NLP models trained on monolingual data to perform well when encountering sequences with frequent language switches. This issue stems from a shift in input feature distribution caused by mixing two languages. To address this, we introduce PESTO, a data-driven approach that models code-mixed sentences as concatenations of multiple monolingual segments. PESTO identifies segment boundaries (switching points) using a self-supervised method that leverages existing NLP resources, followed by fine-tuning on the specific sentence-level task. We demonstrate that PESTO surpasses the state-of-the-art technique, which was previously hand-crafted, on the Tamil-English code-mixed Telugu dataset. Furthermore, PESTO exhibits robustness in handling language switches even at the token-level granularity. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the method's strengths and limitations. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/aryan-agarwal17/POSTO.

This study employs first-principles calculations and the first-principles-derived McMillan-Allen-Dynes formulas to analyze how varying pressure influences the isotope effect and critical temperature in cubic H$_{3}$S. Under elevated pressure, the McMillan-Allen-Dynes expression reveals a distinct inflection point in the phonon spectrum, signaling a pressure-dependent van Hove singularity (VHS) that influences the phase transition temperature. The calculated isotope effect aligns with experimental data only when the pressure is below 200 GPa; conversely, pressures exceeding 200 GPa cause a sharp decline in the isotope effect. This reduction is attributed to the electron-phonon coupling constant ($\lambda$) peaking at the VHS and subsequently dropping rapidly as pressure surpasses this threshold. Furthermore, the critical temperature exhibits a gradual rise as pressure approaches the VHS, followed by a rapid decrease once the pressure exceeds it. These findings underscore the pivotal role of VHS in determining the phase transition temperature within H$_{3}$S. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that combining first-principles methods with McMillan-Allen-Dynes theory provides a viable framework for investigating phase transitions in high-temperature superconductors. This paper introduces a novel approach for generating spatial constraints to facilitate motion planning within dynamic environments. Since many real-world applications cannot rely on static maps due to the dynamism of their components, current approaches attempt to build maps by tracking and predicting object positions over time. However, these methods often fail to produce a map of static objects because dynamic tracking algorithms struggle to build maps of items that remain positionally constant across all time steps. To overcome this limitation, we propose learning spatial constraints from input time-series data by identifying and applying the six most prevalent object trajectories. Furthermore, we incorporate a Bayesian framework to handle uncertainty in object positions and update this uncertainty dynamically as objects move. We evaluate our method's performance in both 2D and 3D settings and demonstrate its effectiveness for motion planning in a 3D robot arm simulation. The resulting spatial constraints improve planning success rates by 15% compared to using no prior information and enhance path quality by 10% relative to using a map of individual object positions. Additionally, we show that learning spatial constraints in a 2D scenario is computationally more efficient than in a 3D environment. Our code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/SpatialConstraintGeneration. Finally, we discuss the method's limitations and suggest potential future research directions. This paper presents a visual relocalization approach leveraging geometric data from a 3D surfel map. Unlike prior methods that depend on the manual design of hand-crafted, context-independent image patches, our system utilizes context-aware image descriptors generated by a deep neural network. Furthermore, we enhance standard geometric optimization by integrating photometric errors across both x and y axes, addressing a limitation found in existing geometric-only methods. Evaluated on the real-world Stanford Bunny dataset, the proposed technique significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. In multiuser MIMO scenarios, the combined tasks of joint user selection and precoding can be viewed as a group sparse recovery problem within linear models. This involves reconstructing a signal characterized by group sparsity from an underdetermined system of equations. By leveraging this equivalent formulation, the paper introduces a computationally efficient algorithm grounded in the group LASSO method. When compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions, the proposed approach demonstrates superior performance by achieving higher sum-rates and reducing interference at non-selected user terminals. Additionally, the study provides theoretical insights into the relationship between the group LASSO objective function and its dual, revealing a minimum norm solution expressed via the dual variable, which facilitates efficient algorithm design. Finally, the paper derives the asymptotic performance of the proposed method using random matrix theory and validates these theoretical findings through simulations. These theoretical results indicate that the group LASSO achieves nearly optimal performance, with a minimal sum-rates gap of only 0.15 dB relative to the optimal joint design. However, the asymptotic analysis fails to capture the performance behavior in finite-dimensional settings. To address this gap, an adaptive group LASSO method is proposed, which iteratively updates the group LASSO solution using an appropriately designed weight matrix. Simulation results confirm that this adaptive approach outperforms the standard group LASSO method. Furthermore, it exhibits a significantly lower performance loss of 0.09 dB compared to the optimal joint design, representing a 40% improvement over conventional user selection and precoding techniques. The adaptive group LASSO method demonstrates excellent scalability, reducing algorithmic complexity to O(KN^2) for N transmit antennas and K users, where N is substantially smaller than K. Consequently, this method is highly suitable for large-scale MIMO systems. Additionally, the group LASSO framework is extensible to other performance metrics, such as energy efficiency, by simply modifying the objective function. Finally, extensions to other communication scenarios, including interference channels and wireless information transfer, are explored. In these contexts, group LASSO achieves a 10% increase in sum-rates and a 20% gain in total transmitted energy. Given its superior performance and reduced complexity, group LASSO emerges as a promising tool for multiuser user selection and precoding design. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this represents the first application of group LASSO to the joint user selection and precoding problem. Keywords: Joint user selection and precoding, group LASSO, dual

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield associated with a tropical curve is finitely generated as a semifield over the tropical semifield $\boldsymbol{T} = [\boldsymbol{R} \cup \{-\infty\}, \oplus, \oplus]$. Furthermore, we provide explicit generators for any lft-semifield arising from a tropical curve, along with the transformation data necessary to produce the corresponding lft-curve. The core approach involves developing a general technique to circumvent $-\infty$ values in the tropical curve's valuation by performing blow-ups on the tropical curve, followed by the application of valuations. Additionally, we establish an alternative method for proving the finite generation of rational function semifields of tropical curves by reinterpreting valuations as morphisms of semifields, a concept particularly suited for curves lacking bridges. The results for handles-on-spheres are initially demonstrated using valuations as morphisms of semifields. Our findings are illustrated through several examples, including tropical curves with handles and conics in arbitrary characteristics. Notably, we provide a specific construction for rational function semifields of tropical curves that are finitely generated over the constant semifield containing the valuations used to construct the tropical curve. This paper presents a comprehensive global analysis of Type-II two-Higgs-doublet models (2HDM), examining how anticipated precision measurements of SM-like Higgs bosons and Z-pole observables will influence the viable parameter space. Utilizing the GAMBIT framework, our study incorporates current constraints from Z-pole, W-mass, HFAG Smith-Teberoski, ATLAS, and LHCb data alongside Type-II 2HDM predictions for SM-like Higgs signals in the future, 100 TeV FCC-ee and CLIC colliders. Our findings indicate that the allowed regions within the 2HDM parameter space are heavily dependent on forthcoming Z-pole and WFact measurements. Furthermore, we establish an upper limit for the Z-to-two-Higgs mass difference ($\Delta m^Z_{2H}$) derived from FCC-ee fact data. Finally, we explore the survival prospects of the primary viable parameter space identified by GAMBIT when integrated with predictions from the 100 TeV CLIC collider regarding Z-pole and WFact quantities. These results demonstrate that upcoming Z-pole and weak fermion mass precision tests will significantly restrict the available parameter space, potentially favoring the decoupling region of 2HDM. Additionally, we observe that incorporating future signals for the heavier CP-even scalar $H$ and CP-odd scalar $A$ leads to a substantial reduction in the remaining viable regions. These outcomes are consistent with prior studies on the model's parameter space. Overall, this research provides valuable insights into the future parameter space of the Type-II 2HDM. Notably, the FCC-ee's superior precision in Higgs measurements is expected to have a profound impact on the model's viable parameter space. Future efforts should focus on extending GAMBIT to include 100 TeV collider capabilities for Higgs signal analysis. This study was conducted with GAMBIT version 21.0.0. Particle-based methods for modeling soft matter self-assembly are increasingly sophisticated, yet discovering suitable protocols and material parameters remains difficult due to the vast, complex search spaces involved. This study introduces a machine-learning approach designed simultaneously to identify optimal assembly protocols and material parameters while adapting to the specific interactions and dynamics of the system. By training artificial neural networks (ANNs) using neuroevolutionary techniques on self-assembly trajectories, the method evaluates every parameter combination. These ANNs operate in parallel with standard molecular dynamics simulations to rapidly and accurately predict whether assembly occurs, demonstrating particular effectiveness for challenging scenarios like dense liquid formation. This combined protocol and material search is anticipated to uncover novel self-assembly mechanisms. We successfully applied this approach to find effective protocols for dense liquid formation and amorphous network assembly, successfully scaling the technique to larger systems. Additionally, we examined a highly non-trivial, previously unsolved self-assembly problem involving fractal aggregation and found a promising initial solution. The code is freely accessible at https://github.com/berend-vanderbilt/SA-Search. This work is anticipated to facilitate the discovery of optimal self-assembly materials and protocols for under-solved problems in soft matter systems. This paper investigates the ill-posedness of solutions for the stationary Navier-Stokes equations within critical spaces. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any scale-critical Besov space $B_{p,q}^{d/p}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ where $1<p\leqslant2$ and $0\leqslant q\leqslant p$, there exist infinitely many divergence-free velocity fields that are not locally Hölder continuous. Consequently, these velocities fail to generate any $(L^p(\mathbb{R}^d),1<p<2)$ or $(B_{p,q}^{d/p}(\mathbb{R}^d),1<p<2)$ solution to the stationary Navier-Stokes equations, thereby illustrating the phenomenon of ill-posedness. Notably, the identified critical velocities exhibit logarithmic growth, distinguishing them from the rapidly growing examples previously established by Li \cite{Li2020}. Our primary technique involves the construction of a novel type of smooth cut-off function. Furthermore, as a corollary, we derive several new ill-posedness results for the heat equation involving viscosities in critical Besov spaces, extending and improving upon the findings of Li \cite{Li2020}. Finally, we provide a novel characterization of critical Hölder spaces using critical viscosities. Specifically, the critical Hölder space $B_{p,p}^{2-d}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ is equivalent to the space $C_{p}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, which comprises all smooth functions $f$ satisfying $\|f\|_{C_{p}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^d)}<\infty$, where $\|f\|_{C_{p}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^d)}:=\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)}+\|\nabla f\|_{B_{p}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^d)}$. Our proof utilizes the equivalence between these two critical spaces. Additionally, our methodology enables the identification of various novel types of critical functions. Specifically, we show that the critical velocity fields in this study are not locally Hölder continuous, their Fourier transforms are not integrable, and they grow faster than the critical velocity fields in Li \cite{Li2020}. This paper introduces two enhancements to Loidreau's rank metric code-based cryptosystem, which utilizes Gabidulin codes within the McEliece framework. Following a recent vulnerability where computers could swiftly factor large primes of the form $q^t-p$, we demonstrate that public keys can now be constructed using fields of the form $q^t$, as proposed by Loidreau. Furthermore, we propose utilizing codes with higher minimum weights within the public key matrix to boost the scheme's security. Performance analysis via Python simulations indicates that these improvements lead to a substantial increase in security while maintaining communication efficiency comparable to the original system. Consequently, the primary advantage of this approach lies in its larger security capacity. Although the public key size is comparable to other rank metric code-based schemes, the storage of the secret key is significantly reduced. Our Python-based implementation suggests that this enhanced scheme offers both computational and storage efficiency superior to those reported by Loidreau. Ultimately, these results confirm the value of rank metric code-based cryptography, particularly given the growing interest from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in developing post-quantum standards. Current pre-training strategies for language models primarily rely on massive corpora like Wikipedia. In contrast, this pre-training approach leverages single-word or short-phrase entries found in dictionaries, theses, and encyclopedias. Although these entries are relatively brief, they offer distinct advantages for training language models. First, dictionary definitions provide clear explanations of word usages, making them ideal for enhancing word sense disambiguation capabilities. Second, the structured nature of these entries allows for the easy extraction of high-quality supervised data for downstream tasks. We performed extensive pre-training experiments using dictionary datasets and evaluated the pre-trained models on various downstream tasks to assess their effectiveness. Furthermore, we integrated the pre-trained model into Baidu's online dictionary search engine to support automated dictionary definition generation. This full-cycle process demonstrates the immense value of word entries for both pre-training and post-training language models. Our experiments yield the following conclusions: 1) utilizing dictionary datasets significantly improves the model's word sense disambiguation abilities; 2) pre-training on dictionary datasets yields substantial gains for downstream tasks compared to general corpora, particularly for sentence-level tasks like SQuAD and CMNLI. Additionally, we have released the source code and dictionary datasets to facilitate further research. The code can be accessed at: https://github.com/DictSearch/Dict-BERT. We establish bounds for the expected minimal spanning complex (msc) and the expected persistence diagram (pd) of a random complex within a metric space under a random metric. Defined as the unique random complex with edges representing the shortest distances between all vertex pairs, the msc serves as a generalization of the minimum spanning tree found in graph theory. Furthermore, we derive an estimate for the expected length of the longest edge in the msc within a metric random graph. We demonstrate that standard assumptions from graph theory regarding independent or weakly dependent edge lengths do not necessarily hold in a random metric. Additionally, we prove that the expected values for both the msc and the pd are finite. We offer a geometric interpretation of the pd of a random complex as quantifying the distortion induced by embedding the complex into its 1-skeleton via minimal edge substitution. We characterize the limiting behavior of the pd as the number of vertices increases, demonstrating that it converges to a Poisson point process on the square provided certain moment conditions regarding edge lengths are met. Finally, we present a generalization of Dvoretzky's theorem to simplicial complexes, showing that under appropriate assumptions on metric growth, simply connected complexes with a fixed number of edges and vertices converge to a simplex in high dimensions. These findings are supported by findings from hyperbolic and Euclidean geometry, along with counterexamples from other contexts. We also calculate the expected values of the msc and pd for specific complexes based on their parameters and provide counterexamples for the bulk extremes. These results offer a foundation for future research into random complexes within this framework. The paper concludes with several open problems and conjectures. Federated learning (FL) has garnered significant attention as a machine learning framework designed to safeguard data privacy. In the vertical FL context, clients possess distinct features for the same entities, collaborating to train models while keeping local data confidential. Although various privacy-preserving techniques for FL have been extensively researched, this paper presents practical privacy attacks against two specific methods: Secure Aggregation and Differential Privacy. These approaches effectively neutralize previous defense mechanisms, enabling adversaries to reconstruct entity labels with high accuracy. Our findings demonstrate that both secure methods and differential privacy within FL are more susceptible to attacks than those in general federated learning settings, revealing a potential security vulnerability in current protection strategies. We conclude that further research and more robust privacy-preserving techniques are essential to enhance trust in FL applications, particularly in vertical federated learning. This paper introduces the "Smart City Defense game," a two-player, non-cooperative bi-matrix game designed to investigate the challenges a city's security apparatus faces when safeguarding the urban infrastructure network (UCIN) from socio-cyber-physical threats. These emerging threats arise from the deep integration between a city's social, biological, and cyber systems, which are inextricably linked with its physical infrastructure. The game models scenarios where a malicious actor (the adversary) introduces vulnerabilities into city subsystems, followed by physical disruptions to specific nodes or the complete isolation of selected subsystems. This process of creating and exploiting vulnerabilities in modern integrated systems is referred to as "threat modeling." Conversely, the city's security apparatus, represented by the defender in the game, aims to identify and eliminate these introduced vulnerabilities. Crucially, the defender must allocate limited resources to detect and remove risks before they are exploited, without prior knowledge of which vulnerabilities have been created. Furthermore, the defender must make real-time decisions to minimize potential losses, balancing the costs of vulnerability removal against other operational expenses. To address this, we formulate a corresponding bi-matrix game to determine the optimal strategies for both the adversary and the defender. This approach enables the identification of optimal resource allocation by the defender to mitigate adversary actions and the reduction of the city's exposure to malicious activities. We provide an analysis of this game to derive insights into the defender's best responses to adversary strategies and to evaluate the efficacy of various resource allocation policies. Finally, the game and its solutions are applied to various scenarios within the UCIN of a medium-sized city to assess the effectiveness of different defender strategies. These applications illustrate the significance of the game and its outcomes in mitigating the city's risk exposure to current and emerging threats. The proposed game and its applications offer a novel perspective on security and defense issues in smart city infrastructure, a topic that has seen relatively little research. This work represents a significant step toward developing effective strategies for city defense against evolving threats. Additionally, the game can be utilized to evaluate the effectiveness of different security and defense policies implemented by city authorities. The proposed approach offers a straightforward method for analyzing the consequences of policy decisions made by both adversaries and defenders within smart city ecosystems. This framework can facilitate discussions between city officials and the general public regarding the implications of their choices and the effectiveness of their policies. The paper begins with an introduction to Smart Cities, their UCIN, and the associated security challenges. It then provides an overview of the game theory fundamentals underpinning our approach. This study examines the Hawking--Page phase transitions of Schwarzschild, Kerr, and Reissner--Nordström black holes within an enclosing cavity. We demonstrate that the presence of the cavity modifies the metric near the horizon, resulting in an infinite metric curvature at the cavity's boundary. Furthermore, we find that the critical temperatures associated with these phase transitions are directly linked to the radii of the cavities. Specifically, the Kerr black hole within a cavity exhibits an inner and outer horizon alongside a bifurcation sphere, all of which undergo phase transitions when the system reaches the critical temperature. Additionally, we establish that the critical temperatures for the phase transitions of Kerr and Reissner--Nordström black holes in a cavity fall between those of a pure Schwarzschild black hole and a de Sitter space located outside the cavity. These transitions can be interpreted as the cavity's radius approaching asymptotically the black hole's horizon radius, bifurcation sphere radius, event horizon radius, or Cauchy horizon radius. Finally, we provide interpretations of these phase transitions from the perspectives of the phase space and an extended phase space that incorporates radiation. Notably, the radius of the bifurcation sphere for a Kerr black hole emerges during this radiative process. These findings may prove beneficial for advancing our understanding of various aspects of black hole physics. Additionally, the methodology employed in this work could be applicable to analyzing other black hole systems. Finally, these results may contribute to our comprehension of the information paradox concerning entropy and the holographic principle regarding information storage. To our knowledge, this represents the inaugural investigation into Hawking--Page phase transitions for Kerr and Reissner--Nordström black holes within a cavity. Furthermore, the techniques utilized in this study may offer a potential avenue for resolving the black hole information paradox. Since the deep learning era began, researchers have consistently highlighted label noise as a significant challenge within the machine learning community. This noise manifests in datasets as corrupted data, creating obstacles for models by hindering their ability to learn accurate patterns and relationships. Although numerous methods have been proposed to address this issue, most focus on image classification; consequently, literature regarding advanced techniques for noisy text data remains scarce. This paper aims to fill that gap by proposing a novel, efficient, and reliable solution tailored for text datasets. Specifically, we introduce a new ranking algorithm designed for natural language processing that utilizes bag sampling and group-wise loss. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods across all evaluated metrics. The study is conducted in the Arabic language. The comprehensive code and data required to replicate our findings can be accessed at: https://github.com/AmrMohamedHafez/ISNN2023. Additionally, the paper is available in English at: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10125001. We invite you to explore the work. Thank you.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated significant utility in semi-supervised learning tasks involving graphs. However, a primary limitation of GNNs is their lack of intrinsic robustness, as they are highly susceptible to over-smoothing and over-fitting, particularly when labeled data is scarce. Over-fitting further impedes GNN performance in graph transfer scenarios by causing the model to memorize graph-specific features. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel semi-supervised framework designed for GNNs under conditions of limited labels. Our approach employs a few fully labeled source graphs and numerous unlabeled target graphs to construct node pairs that serve as pseudo-labels for training the model in a supervised manner. The core innovation lies in a node-pair selection strategy that identifies high-quality, informative pseudo-labels. Specifically, our method leverages the inherent structural relationships between source and target nodes to identify target nodes that share strong similarities with source nodes. Experimental results confirm the approach's effectiveness, as it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across various graphs in both in-domain and cross-domain settings. AWAKE is a CERN initiative designed to investigate self-channelled proton beam plasma wakefields, with plans for proton-proton collision studies commencing in 2021 as part of the Intensity Front-Loading (IFL) project. This work examines betatron radiation emitted by electrons propagating through the proton beam wake. Initial investigations focused on a 100 mA, 30 cm long proton beam, followed by an analysis of wakefield conditions during the planned proton-proton collisions. The study also evaluates betatron radiation impacts on detectors, specifically addressing skin effect shielding and radiative damping. Ultimately, this research aids in understanding potential radiation effects on both the proton beam and electron witnesses traversing the beam plasma channel. Furthermore, it establishes a framework for analyzing betatron radiation across various scenarios by adjusting fundamental parameters such as proton beam current and length. These parameters are constrained by considerations regarding space charge limiters and collision rates. The study concludes by identifying promising regimes for future applications, including free-electron lasers and X-ray generation. The proposed methodology is intended to be utilized during AWAKE Run 2 and in future applications exploring similar phenomena. The underlying code is open-source and accessible via GitHub. Notably, betatron radiation is observed to cool the electron witness beam rather than heat it. Additionally, at high betatron amplitudes, radiation significantly narrows the electron beam's transverse size near the beam center. This radiative damping effect is linked to beam cooling observed in laser-wakefield experiments. Furthermore, at large betatron amplitudes, electron-witness trajectories exhibit significant bending around the proton beam periphery. This behavior is attributed to the decaying plasma amplitude and the confining action of the proton beam's self-magnetic field. These findings are discussed in the context of detector limitations. Finally, the study addresses x-ray generation, with results compared against existing literature. The analysis indicates that while betatron radiation can be intense, it may also be weak, necessitating careful selection of witness electron trajectories. In certain cases, the witness must avoid the beam center to prevent x-ray generation that could damage detectors. These findings are presented as a means to identify promising x-ray regimes. The study also explores applications related to non-linear Compton scattering, which could be investigated using current or dephased witnesses outside the proton beam. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that while betatron radiation can significantly deform the electron witness beam profile, it may not always occur. These aspects are addressed to facilitate the identification of promising regimes for further investigation

Although numerous distributed decision tree algorithms exist, they often lack formal guarantees regarding data privacy. This study introduces a scalable distributed decision tree learning method that ensures differential privacy with minimal impact on accuracy. Specifically, we present DP-Prune, an algorithm that maintains privacy by distributing and privately pruning node subsets during the tree construction phase. DP-Prune is both time and space efficient, operates in linear time relative to the number of training instances, and can be easily parallelized for distribution. Experimental results show that DP-Prune achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art privacy-preserving learning methods for both synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, we provide a rigorous privacy proof for DP-Prune under differential privacy constraints, a formal guarantee that many current approaches lack. Finally, we extend DP-Prune to handle sensitive attributes in distributed settings, enabling privacy-preserving tree learning across multiple organizations with non-overlapping data, a capability that is otherwise difficult to achieve. This paper addresses the variational inference task of minimizing regularized Rényi divergence within an exponential family, introducing a novel algorithm termed the Bregman proximal gradient method. By demonstrating the equivalence between our approach and one established information geometric method and proving the metric contraction of another, we have established a robust theoretical framework that facilitates a precise analysis of convergence rates. We evaluate this method against existing state-of-the-art algorithms using both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing that it achieves comparable performance while significantly reducing computation time. Furthermore, we illustrate the method's utility in density estimation, dimensionality reduction, and clustering, noting its effectiveness even in scenarios where competing methods struggle. The implementation, written in Python, is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchauer123/BPG-VI. Additionally, we have updated our PyTorch implementation to align with this paper. Finally, our website provides a user-friendly interface for applying all three algorithms to various tasks, including density estimation, dimensionality reduction, clustering, and a new example for semi-supervised learning. Chain event graph (CEG) models extend the capabilities of discrete Bayesian networks (BNs) by visually representing both conditional and marginal probabilities within a single structure. Although model expansion can transform a multi-terminal CEG into an enhanced BN, current Bayesian hierarchical modeling techniques for BNs do not accommodate CEGs. This study introduces a novel hierarchical model that maintains the integrity of a specific CEG subgraph, specifically focusing on its embedded Markov chain, by employing a hybrid frequentist-Bayesian approach. Furthermore, an efficient algorithm is presented to identify the maximum a posteriori CEG from a discrete BN sample generated via Gibbs sampling. A simulation study validates the proposed method and algorithm, demonstrating their practical utility and serving as a foundation for future research applications. The code required to replicate the simulations is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKlaffke/CEGModelSelection. Additionally, the authors have developed the open-source R package `cegmss`, which implements these methods and is available on CRAN. The package includes a collection of CEgs that can be utilized as training data for discrete BNs in various modeling scenarios. Keywords: chain event graph, model selection, hierarchical model, model expansion, Markov chain, graphoid properties. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 62F15, 62P10, 62P12, 62P30, 62P35.

We introduce a new dynamic method designed to solve convex feasibility problems with regularized minimum norm issues. Built on the charged dynamical system framework, this approach incorporates damping and Tikhonov regularization. Notably, it advances existing undamped methods for minimum norm problems by extending the undamped algorithm for standard convex feasibility problems. We demonstrate strong convergence of the time-evolving solution towards the minimum norm point within the set of common fixed points of nonexpansive operators in Hilbert spaces. This undamped dynamic behavior contrasts with previous damped charged dynamics, which were shown to converge slowly to a single equilibrium point corresponding to the minimum norm fixed point of quasi-nonexpansive operators. Our method achieves this convergence at a cost comparable to the damped case but at a lower computational expense than conventional inertial dynamics. Finally, we provide numerical examples to illustrate the strong convergence of the proposed dynamics.
