This paper investigates how chaotic transitions emerge in the control systems of wall-following robots. A three-dimensional autonomous dynamical model was constructed to simulate the robot's motion during the execution of a basic wall-following task. By analyzing the robot's orientation state, we demonstrate the presence of a band merging crisis followed by type-II intermittency, which leads to a transition across a control parameter boundary. Furthermore, a crude scaling law was employed to estimate the critical exponent associated with this type-II intermittency. Finally, we show that the evolution of Lyapunov exponents during the crisis can be approximated using the well-established universal scaling function. These dynamics were simulated and visualized using a 3D visualization tool. The research concludes by suggesting potential applications of wall-following robots in future security and surveillance systems. Additionally, the mathematical model and visualization techniques developed here may serve as a foundation for studying other autonomous mobile robots and wall-following behaviors. The accompanying computer code is available at: https://github.com/alejandro-fernandez-rincon/Research-Projects-2020-2021. Investigating the impact of extended impurities on the microwave conductivity of superconductors within the energy range near the Dopaned kinetic energy gap minimum ($\sigma_M(E_D)$), we observe that at low temperatures, impurities with sizes comparable to the coherence length can diminish this conductivity. This reduction is particularly significant in chiral kinetic energy driven superconductors, such as those in the $k_x+ik_y$ state, where extended impurities preserve magnetic symmetry while disrupting momentum conservation. Consequently, a characteristic peak in microwave conductivity emerges as Dopant concentration varies, a feature essential for distinguishing between superconducting mechanisms and identifying the specific superconducting state. Furthermore, in multiband systems, extended impurities can transfer carriers from the normal metal band to the kinetic energy driven band, thereby enhancing multiband superconductivity. This mechanism may also contribute to the observed increase in microwave conductivity in certain high-$T_c$ cuprates upon entering the superconducting state. Finally, we demonstrate that the specific shape of the impurity potential, whether screened Coulomb or rectangular, does not alter these general findings. These theoretical predictions can be experimentally validated using nano- or micro-fabricated obstacles on the surfaces of kinetic energy driven superconductors. Ultimately, measuring microwave conductivity serves as a potent tool for identifying the superconducting mechanism and determining the superconducting critical temperature. These results are applicable to any kinetic energy driven superconducting state, including $k_x+ik_y$ and $isotropy+realsym$ states. Additionally, the influence of extended impurities on microwave conductivity in the pseudogap phase of high-$T_c$ cuprates warrants experimental verification. We anticipate that the insights gained from studying microwave conductivity in kinetic energy driven superconductors will significantly advance the understanding of high-$T_c$ superconductivity. Finally, our findings regarding extended impurities in kinetic energy driven superconductors align with the proposed mechanism for the local restoration of momentum in high-$T_c$ cuprates. We examine a category of anisotropic curvature flows known as crystalline curvature flows, offering a survey that prioritizes the well-posedness of their initial value problems. Our analysis highlights the primary metric space frameworks employed in this field, with a specific emphasis on the* $L^\infty$-metric. Furthermore, we outline the strategies utilized to establish existence and uniqueness within these spaces. The structural characteristics of these solution spaces mirror those of the classical* (isotropic) mean curvature flow, and we draw parallels between the two frameworks where appropriate. Finally, we address select aspects of the associated heat equation, noting that the properties of these solutions provide additional insight into the behavior of crystalline curvature flows. This text serves as a survey of existing literature. No prior knowledge of the subject is assumed, although a background in non-smooth analysis would be advantageous. Plants are vital for human survival, yet they are sensitive to environmental factors. Optimizing growth conditions can enhance plant size and robustness, benefiting both agricultural yields and medicinal potential. We introduce GrowSpace, a growth simulation environment designed for both interactive human use and reinforcement learning. This tool enables users to interact with simulated plants in real-time by adjusting various environmental conditions. We involved human participants in a shaping task to investigate their strategies and goals, revealing that they prioritize multiple objectives such as increasing size, minimizing energy usage, preventing disease, and avoiding collapse. Subsequently, we applied reinforcement learning to tackle this shaping problem. Our results demonstrate that an agent trained on this task can effectively predict plant responses to specific environmental inputs. Furthermore, we explored shaping this simulated biological system using both human intuition and agent-based approaches, highlighting the complementary nature of human and artificial intelligence. Our contributions include the release of the GrowSpace source code, which facilitates interaction with biological systems and empowers reinforcement learning agents to solve tasks that mirror human intuition. Ultimately, this work advances our ability to model biological systems and deepens our understanding of their growth dynamics. The source code and video demonstrations are available at https://growspace.org. GrowSpace is accessible via Apple's Arcade platform. We demonstrate that the SLE loop measure emerges naturally from the conformal welding of two quantum disks. This proof builds upon the classical concept of welding a Brownian disk, which was established by Miller and Sheffey and recently expanded by her with her collaborators. Our findings provide an alternative, conceptually distinct derivation of Miller and Shen's formulation of the universion problem. Specifically, we establish that the volume of a Brownian disk created by welding two quantum disks corresponds to the product of their individual volumes, thereby resolving a longstanding conjecture regarding the measure on free boundary harmonic disks proposed by Miller and Sheffey. Furthermore, we offer a conceptually different derivation of Lewis's formulation of the unversion problem and confirm that the loop measure on the SLE disk is the unique welding measure capable of simultaneously satisfying the multiplicative property for quantum disk volumes and the uniqueness axiom in Lewis's framework. Consequently, we establish the equivalence between the welding measure on Brownian disks and the equivalence between Miller and Sheffey's and Lewis's formulations of the unversion problem. Additionally, we introduce a novel formulation of the SHEF measure on Liouville Quantum Gravity and establish an integration by parts formula that extends the Liouville First Passage Percolation formula to include boundary terms. This formula facilitates the derivation of several properties of the SHEF measure, such as the equivalence between Liouville and boundary reparametrization invariant measures and various consequences of the Ward identity. Finally, we provide a concise overview of the quantum Dyson-Schwinger equation, which encapsulates all these properties. This equation can be viewed as a first-order formulation of Miller and Sheffey's problem that explicitly incorporates boundary contributions. Solving this equation yields a solution to the welding problem, thereby recovering the welding measure on Brownian disks. This approach offers a fresh perspective on Miller and Sheffey's framework and establishes a bridge to the study of Liouville Gravity. In this context, the boundary terms in the boundary decomposition formula for quantum disk partition functions correspond to the boundary term in the Ward equation for correlation functions in Liouville Gravity. This connection elucidates the relationship between boundary terms in the boundary decomposition and the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov equation governing conformal blocks in Liouville Gravity. The Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative (IBSI) functions as an independent global collaboration dedicated to standardizing the extraction of image biomarkers from medical imaging data. This effort supports both research and clinical applications by facilitating reproducibility and comparability in imaging outcomes, thereby enabling the effective utilization of image data for various purposes, including clinical trial recruitment. The initiative involves experts across the spectrum of medical imaging, such as radiologists, software and image analysis developers, and the research and clinical communities. Additionally, the IBSI promotes education and training in image analysis and serves as a neutral forum for exchanging information and fostering collaboration. To achieve these objectives, the IBSI produces consensus guidelines and code for calibrating and validating image analysis methods, along with reference datasets and an information portal. This document outlines the IBSI's vision, strategy, and core activities. Furthermore, it explains how to join the initiative and obtain IBSI resources, while also addressing common misconceptions regarding its role. Finally, this work serves as an introduction to the series of papers in Radiology: Artificial Intelligence that detail IBSI concepts and their application to image analysis for clinical trial support and other uses. For further information, visit https://www.imagebiomarker.org. The contributors are the IBSI Expert Group and IBSI Steering Committee. Contact: info@imagebiomarker.org.

We conducted two-body $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction calculations using a relativistic framework that incorporates $S$ and $P$ wave amplitudes, delta resonances, as well as the high-spin $N(4440)$, $N(4650)$, and $N(5000)$ baryons. The resulting $S$ and $P$ wave contributions align with existing experimental data, whereas the delta resonances and high-spin $N$ states significantly influence the helicity doublets. To ensure PBHs constitute a significant portion of the dark matter density, we also analyze the constraints imposed by gravitational wave observations. Finally, we examine constraints derived from the missing satellite problem and the core density cusp observed in dwarf galaxies. Our model offers a unified explanation for multiple cosmological phenomena, including the CMB power spectrum, SST radio data, gravitational wave data, and astrophysical evidence regarding dwarf galaxies. Consequently, this research holds significant potential for future astrophysical investigations. Our findings also suggest that SST may be incompatible with standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. Analyzing how students move from high school to college and into specific careers is vital for both policy-making and research. While individual-level data from the High School and Beyond (HSB) study allows for tracking these transitions, the latent academic interests of high school seniors remain unobserved, forcing researchers to infer them indirectly. This paper introduces a latent class model to characterize these high school interests and examines two approaches for integrating this latent variable into a Hawkes process to forecast academic trajectories. The first approach employs a Bayesian Hawkes process that accounts for uncertainty in latent variable estimation by treating the latent class assignment as a parameter to be inferred alongside other model parameters. The second approach treats the latent variable as fixed and calculates predictive probabilities for each possible assignment. The Bayesian method is demonstrated to yield more accurate predictions than simple model alternatives. Finally, the study explores applying these models to specific subgroups within the HSB dataset. The developed Bayesian framework is made available as an open-source package. By offering tools to estimate latent academic interests and their progression over time, this work advances the understanding of academic pathways, thereby assisting researchers and policymakers in designing interventions to support high school students. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a widely used optimization method in machine learning, particularly for logistic regression (LR). However, its performance degrades significantly when regularization terms are involved. This paper introduces a specialized SGD variant designed to maintain robust convergence even with logistic regression's non-linear, non-smooth regularized cost function. For both stochastic and batch scenarios, we establish that this proposed algorithm achieves a convergence rate superior to SGD under weak convexity conditions. Nevertheless, SGD retains advantages in terms of storage and computation efficiency. To address this, we enhance the SGD approach by minimizing communication overhead without compromising storage or computational efficiency. Specifically, we reduce the parameter update frequency in SGD while simultaneously increasing the frequency of gradient frequency updates. We demonstrate that this modified SGD achieves a performance comparable to, or better than, the specialized SGD algorithm, while featuring reduced storage requirements and increased computation efficiency. Extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that our algorithms outperform existing methods in terms of storage, computation, and convergence efficiency. Furthermore, we validate that these proposed algorithms deliver superior prediction accuracy compared to SGD on large-scale datasets. Finally, we discuss how these methods can be extended to other generalized linear models. Empirical results indicate that our algorithms achieve an order-of-magnitude improvement in both convergence and prediction accuracy over SGD when applied to L1-regularized LR on large-scale datasets. We also highlight the potential for these algorithms to be utilized within distributed optimization frameworks. We introduce a novel, end-to-end system for detecting text generated by large language models (LLMs). Our findings indicate that while traditional automatic salience-based detection methods perform poorly on LLM output, state-of-the-art category-representation learning (CRR) techniques effective for detecting non-human authors like crowdworkers or GPT2, when adapted to this task, achieve strong results. Specifically, our best-performing model secured an F1 score of 0.922 on Evolv.ai's headline detection challenge, outcompeting all other submitted models. Through a detailed analysis of headlines produced by various LLMs across numerous prompts, we observe that current detection models rely more heavily on the text's input context than on the signal that the text itself was LLM-generated. Furthermore, we demonstrate that lLMs produce outputs where local n-grams and semantic relationships are nearly indistinguishable from human-written samples, whereas lLM text exhibits slightly lower category-representation similarity compared to human text. Finally, we show that increasing the diversity of LLM prompts can enhance the difficulty of detecting LLM-generated text. These insights into the characteristics of LLM-generated text may guide future research aimed at improving the reliability of identifying LLM contributions. The Evolv.ai dataset and associated code are accessible at https://github.com/evolv-ai/nlp-eval-lime-later/tree/main/data/llm-detection. Additional code for human vs. LLM detection is available in Evolv-AI/detection-challenges. Our results underscore the urgent need for robust methods to identify the various contributions of large language models. Given the rapid evolution of LLMs, we anticipate that n-gram-based and CRR-based detection will continue to lag behind category-representation similarity learning, which leverages Transformer architectures. We also note that semantic-based detection outperforms n-gram-based approaches, as LLM-generated text displays only marginally lower category-representation similarity than human text. We conclude that further research is necessary to better understand the semantic and syntactic properties of LLM-generated text. Finally, to enhance the reproducibility of results in future evaluations of large language model contributions, greater diversity in task prompts and data should be prioritized. We hope this work inspires greater efforts to accurately identify the various contributions of large language models. Evolv.ai's commitment to promoting transparency and accountability in the use of large language models is evident through this competition, and we look forward to their continued advocacy for responsible AI development. We suggest that chiral spin liquids (CSLs) can be realized in both amorphous and polycrystalline form-factor plaquettes by applying a finite magnetic field. In random bond Kitaev models, the CSL phase diagram relies on the ratio of the transverse field to the magnetic field, alongside the value of the longitudinal field. We propose that near-amorphous samples, achievable through vapor deposition, combined with an external magnetic field, offer a viable route to creating CSLs in real-world materials. Furthermore, we anticipate that CSLs in both polycrystalline and amorphous form-factor plaquettes exhibit a finite-field thermal Hall effect. This phenomenon arises from the emergent chiral Majorana modes within the CSL, which can be probed using non-local boundary conditions in the thermal Hall operator. We illustrate this using a one-dimensional effective field theory that captures the low-temperature physics of the CSL phase. Additionally, we demonstrate that thermal Hall conductance can be tuned in amorphous Kitaev models by adjusting the longitudinal field. Finally, we show that in the presence of a finite magnetic field, the thermal Hall conductance of the CSL phase in form-factor plaquettes diverges from that of the Chern insulator phase, even at zero fields. This distinction stems from the fact that in the Chern insulator phase, thermal Hall conductance is governed by the sum of the Chern numbers of occupied bands, whereas in the CSL phase, it is determined by the emergent emergent field. We argue that form-factor plaquettes are promising candidates for realizing a magnetic field-tunable chiral topological phase, as evidenced by their thermal Hall conductance, which is a signature of a topological spin liquid. We suggest that vapor-deposited samples offer a practical means to achieve CSLs in Kitaev models. Our proposals for detecting and characterizing CSLs in form-factor plaquettes may be applicable to other materials, such as the quantum spin liquid candidate $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$. Future radio observatories utilizing large arrays of antennas on a regular grid will generate massive data volumes due to visibilities scaling as $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$. To mitigate this computational burden, calibration schemes with linear complexity in array size—specifically $\mathcal{O}(N)$—can be developed, analogous to those used in optical interferometry. This work extends such schemes to radio arrays positioned on a regular 2D grid, achieving $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$ complexity for gain estimation. By deriving visibilities for calibration sources under specific instrumental errors, gain estimates can be obtained via fast convolution using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). Similar rapid computation applies to correlation errors; while a single correction iteration may not suffice, these calculations remain efficient. Although the proposed scheme assumes a regular grid, it is not limited to synthetic apertures formed by such grids. When combined with advanced calibration techniques, it will facilitate the construction of large arrays capable of imaging with a complexity independent of array size. Additionally, the method is applicable to radio imaging algorithms designed for large arrays on regular grids, such as OPTICS. Both the method and a proof-of-concept implementation are available in the Python package `pycalib`. Furthermore, the framework can be extended to address other systematic errors, including antenna pointing errors and array imprecision. Antenna pointing errors can be corrected with $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$ complexity, whereas addressing array imprecision will require the use of convolutional integrals supported by rapid multipole methods. Ultimately, the approach is applicable to any radio array built on a regular grid, including non-coplanar configurations. However, the specific calibration measurements utilized in both the algorithm and imaging process are tailored to the data format of radio interferometers. Consequently, this solution is not applicable to other instruments, such as optical interferometers employing baselines with specific spacings, like AMBER. This study presents the results of applying a novel Bayesian neural network (BNN) to classify Fermi-LAT blazar sources, analyzing data across three energy bins spanning 100 MeV to 100 GeV. The model was trained on a comprehensive dataset comprising 1,000 blazars and 1,000 non-blazar sources. By evaluating posterior probability distributions, the BNN achieved a classification accuracy exceeding 90%. This exceeds the performance of traditional machine learning algorithms, including support vector machines, random forests, and artificial neural networks, as well as that of the Fermi Science Tools blazar source classification module. Furthermore, we estimated the credible intervals for the posterior probabilities of the BNN's classification outcomes. The BNN's optimal three-layer architecture, designed to process vector inputs, is detailed alongside a discussion of the uncertainties inherent in the classification process. These uncertainties stem from two main factors: the influence of nearby sources on the source count map (SCM) used to generate Fermi-LAT photon maps, and the model's sensitivity to variations in the spectral energy distribution (SED) of the training sources. Our findings suggest that Bayesian neural networks are a highly effective method for source classification in the gamma-ray sky. Additionally, the BNN's ability to generate highly probable classifications in all three energy bins indicates its potential to identify multi-energy spectral features within a source's SED. This capability could facilitate the detection of spectral breaks in gamma-ray sources, a task previously limited to the most luminous and bright objects. Finally, the BNN's capacity to produce a probability distribution for each classification allows researchers to assess the confidence level of the source type assigned to a given object. The source count map (SCM) employed in this work was constructed using an optimized Gaussian beam deconvolution technique, which significantly enhances the BNN's classification accuracy. This paper presents three tensor-based operations on hypergraphs, which we demonstrate are equivalent to the tensor product (also known as the direct, box, or Cartesian product) of adjacency tensors. We analyze the properties of these operations and establish their relationship with traditional hypergraph products. Furthermore, we derive connections between the eigenvalues of the adjacency tensor under each operation and those of the factor tensors. Finally, we investigate tensor-invariant sequences of hypergraphs, exploring their links to several well-known deterministic constructions. Additionally, we construct specific $q$-designs by tensoring independent hypergraphs and prove that tensor powers of the adjacency tensor of a perfect code remain constant. These findings suggest that the complexity of tensor-invariant sequences grows at a polynomial rate, contrasting with a lower bound on the complexity of $q$-designs formed by direct sums. We also provide an algorithm for resolving the equivalence problem for hypergraphs. Our findings indicate that our construction represents the most efficient method for generating $q$-designs, with a time complexity of $O(n^{k-1})$. Finally, we examine the feasibility of extending these results to weighted hypergraphs. To our knowledge, this work represents the first application of tensor methods to the classical problem of constructing $q$-designs. Our approach is highly adaptable, and we anticipate that these methods will yield further significant results. We have made our code available online.

This study introduces natural cubic splines as a method for modeling time in longitudinal clinical trials involving Alzheimer's disease patients. The approach addresses issues related to unknown visit schedules and negative visit times, ensuring the model remains proper at the boundary. Additionally, the authors develop predictive distributions for future visit times and the corresponding responses. A real dataset from the Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study (ADCS) is utilized to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed framework. The results are compared against models employing other time scales and those using standard cubic splines. Given the practical application in Alzheimer's disease trials, the paper also examines how visit schedules influence the results. Ultimately, the findings indicate that the choice of time can significantly affect outcomes, and the use of predictive visit times alongside clinical measurements offers valuable insights for clinical decision-making. Finally, the methodology is extended to accommodate longitudinal clinical trials with multiple outcomes. Simulations confirm that the proposed methods achieve the nominal coverage level for confidence intervals and maintain the nominal size for treatment effects. Furthermore, these methods exhibit superior power compared to both standard cubic splines and alternative time-scale approaches. The study concludes that the proposed methods are broadly applicable to any longitudinal clinical trial. We introduce a novel technique for identifying dominant transition pathways by globally optimizing the most likely path action with respect to the elevation function that defines the geometry of the transition state ensemble (TSE). We demonstrate that this approach converges to the dominant transition pathway when the elevation function is constructed using forward-sampling weights derived from a preliminary run of the method. Applications to both simulated and real molecular systems confirm the method's efficacy in correctly identifying dominant transition paths. Furthermore, we establish a connection to the majorization method, showing that the dominant path identified by our approach aligns with majorization theory when the elevation function is linear. These findings suggest the method can isolate a single transition pathway among multiple dominant paths by strategically selecting the elevation function. Finally, we illustrate how this technique can be employed to map the free energy landscape of nanodrop formation on lattice sites. The method is implemented in TransitionPathways, which integrates popular sampling and analysis tools. This paper addresses the question of whether a topological group structure can be defined on the normal structure space of a topological group. We introduce the concept of a normal structure space (N.S.) for topological groups and investigate its fundamental properties. Furthermore, we provide a partial solution to the aforementioned problem by constructing a N.S. for semi-Hausdorff groups, albeit under certain restrictions, and demonstrate that the product of two separation groups is not necessarily separation by explicitly defining two specific separation groups whose product fails to be separation. An appendix is also included, which presents a method for constructing a N.S. on the normal structure space of a Hausdorff group using a base of closed sets, given a finite closed bi-base of neighborhoods of empty set. Additionally, the appendix outlines a method for constructing a Hausdorff group structure on the normal structure space of a normal Hausdorff group, provided the group possesses a bi-base of compact neighborhoods of the empty set. The resulting structure space is shown to be homeomorphic to the original space, and the continuous homomorphism mapping one group onto the other is demonstrated to be open. Through this approach, we offer a positive resolution to the problem posed earlier.

**Keywords:** Topological group, Normal structure, Normal structure space, Bi-base of compact sets.

Ensuring safe navigation in multi-robot systems remains a significant challenge, particularly when robots lack precise knowledge of one another's future states. While existing risk-aware navigation methods often depend on specific risk metrics—such as those derived from risk-sensitive control, Bayesian optimization, or Monte Carlo tree search—this research introduces a distinct approach. We propose a data-driven algorithm rooted in risk-sensitive optimization, designed for safe navigation within multi-robot environments. This method enables the derivation of risk-aware trajectories by necessitating only a single future state prediction per robot. The necessary risk assessment data is gathered through simulation. We validated the algorithm's efficacy using a two-dimensional multi-robot system featuring dynamic obstacles. The results demonstrate superior collision avoidance capabilities compared to standard model-predictive control (MPC) and established risk-aware navigation techniques. Furthermore, our risk-aware trajectories outperform those produced by a state-of-the-art risk-aware MPC approach that relies on specific risk measures. Additionally, our method maintains safety guarantees even when future states are predicted via Monte Carlo sampling. We report the discovery of a new ultrafaint dwarf galaxy within 1.1 Mpc of the Milky Way, designated Andromeda XXV (And XXV). This galaxy features a compact, nearly face-on stellar disc with a radius of 160 parsecs and a total stellar mass of $4.5 \times 10^4 M_\odot$. Based on M31's stellar density, we estimate a stellar mass of $(3.0-10) \times 10^4 M_\odot$ within a 100 kpc aperture. The galaxy exhibits a high star formation rate of $0.004 \pm 0.001 M_\odot \text{ yr}^{-1}$, evidenced by H$\alpha$ luminosity of $(1.1-1.9) \times 10^{-4} M_\odot \text{ yr}^{-1}$ and the presence of 11 O/B stars. Our analysis of the stellar velocity dispersion ($\sigma = 1.8 \pm 0.3 \text{ km s}^{-1}$) and tidal acceleration suggests a mass of $(1.0-1.5) \times 10^7 M_\odot$ within 1 kpc. This mass is primarily attributed to dark matter, as dynamical friction and tidal drag account for only a minor portion of the observed stellar kinematics. Consequently, And XXV possesses a low central dark matter density of $(0.001-0.003) M_\odot \text{ pc}^{-3}$, making it the least dense known dwarf galaxy. We propose that And XXV was accreted by M31 approximately 1.5 Gyr ago and is currently undergoing minor-merger induced star formation. Its existence challenges the standard $\Lambda$CDM model, which predicts that such low-density galaxies should have been tidally disrupted by the Milky Way. Furthermore, And XXV joins a growing list of dwarf galaxies that may have been accreted by the Andromeda galaxy. These findings underscore the need to refine our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution, particularly regarding the interaction between dwarf galaxies and larger systems. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for constraining the mass of primordial black holes. \textit{Key Words}: galaxies: individual (And XXV) — galaxies: haloes — galaxies: kinematics and dynamics

Current modelling efforts to forecast the thermodynamic behaviour of moist air frequently rely on approximations that lack a solid thermodynamic foundation, a shortcoming highlighted by earlier research. This study examines the consequences of applying such methods, specifically the distinction between modelling dry and adiabatic processes, as well as adiabatic cooling and the relationship between water vapour pressure and humidity. It demonstrates that specific heat calculations are heavily influenced by whether these approximations are employed. Furthermore, the research establishes a clear relationship between the magnitude of relative humidity and the extent to which these approximations deviate from rigorous thermodynamic principles. Finally, the study illustrates the effects of these deviations on the potential temperature of moist air within both the boundary layer and convective clouds. The authors conclude that a model utilizing these approximations is insufficient for accurately describing the thermodynamics of moist air, particularly in scenarios involving significant supersaturation. A key application of this finding is shown to be the calculation of potential temperature within convective clouds. The paper provides a term representing the lapse rate of potential temperature in adiabatic moist convection, which accounts for the energy required to generate supersaturation. This formulation is particularly valuable for modelling convective clouds, as it enables the development of a thermodynamically consistent closure scheme for turbulent mixing within them. The validity of these theoretical findings is confirmed by comparing calculated values of the supersaturation-induced lapse rate of potential temperature against values derived from the bulk thermodynamic approach. A suite of numerical experiments was conducted to test these theoretical results. These simulations, which modelled a convective cloud within a stably stratified environment, demonstrated that the thermodynamic effects of supersaturation are significant. Specifically, the results indicate that the lapse rate of the potential temperature of turbulent eddies is reduced by a factor of approximately 1.5 to 2 due to supersaturation. These outcomes align closely with the theoretical predictions. The concept of exterior algebras, originally developed within vector spaces, is adapted here for matroids. This adaptation facilitates the examination of homogeneous polynomials defined on matroid spaces. Specifically, certain characteristics of these polynomials enable a more streamlined demonstration of the Strong Rank Theorem. Furthermore, this methodology offers a straightforward alternative to traditional proofs of several fundamental matroid theoretical principles. Notably, it provides a direct establishment of the Strong Rank Theorem itself. Additionally, it serves as an effective means to illustrate the relationship between matroid rank functions and their corresponding polynomial expressions. Although automatic dialogue state tracking (ADST) offers a promising future for natural language-based human-computer interactions, it remains underutilized in current automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. Since ASR and ADST rely on identical audio-input-to-output mappings, leveraging ASR hybrid models as shared representations could enhance ADST accuracy and efficiency. However, because ASR models are pre-trained to ignore ambiguity, they fail to capture the full range of potential utterance meanings required for effective dialogue state tracking. To address this, we introduce the Word Confusion Network (WCN), a novel technique that adapts the ASR model's weight matrix to model utterance ambiguity. By applying a layer-adaptive, layer-wise optimization process, the WCN refines the network's mapping from a single target meaning to multiple alternative interpretations. Experimental results demonstrate that WCN achieves significant performance gains, yielding improvements of 1.5 to 2 points in F1 scores for both slot F1 and transition F1 metrics. Furthermore, WCN offers a speedup of approximately 2.5 to 3 times in inference time compared to using separate ASR models. Finally, we analyze the WCN network to elucidate its internal mechanisms. Our findings indicate that WCN enhances attention network focus on semantically relevant words and utilizes cross-entropy loss to drive weight matrix optimization, thereby producing outputs from the softmax layer that better reflect utterance ambiguity. Additionally, we find that a WCN model fine-tuned with only a small portion of the dataset outperforms one fine-tuned on the complete dataset. A critical challenge in distributed computing involves coordinating multiple users who access a shared resource, such as a single server. An access structure defines the eligibility of user subsets for this resource, and a universal access structure allows a centralized controller to manage any specific request while maintaining average waiting time at the minimum level, regardless of the specific user requesting service. This paper examines the computational complexity of identifying universal access structures within fixed frameworks. We derive new necessary conditions for universality applicable to any access structure, establish the computational intractability of this identification problem across all possible structures, and determine the complexity of deciding universality for symmetric access structures. Furthermore, we address the associated optimization problem: given a universal access structure, minimize the number of users required to achieve all possible average waiting times. Our findings reveal that this optimization task is generally intractable, though it becomes solvable in polynomial time for universal access structures composed of disjoint chains. Additionally, we demonstrate the existence of universal access structures that cannot be decomposed into such disjoint chains as per any partition. Finally, we formulate and solve a specific instance of the broader decomposition problem. Applying this method to continuously variable systems, we demonstrate that the precision of the reconstructed Wigner function entanglement reaches the optimal quantum limit achievable through any estimator of a quantum channel. In this scenario, we demonstrate the reliable estimation of the Concurrence measure for systems residing in the Bell diagonal subspace. Finally, we compare the distributions of Concurrence values derived from our probabilistic method against those obtained via standard estimators. These findings are relevant to applications in quantum information theory, quantum cryptography, and the certification of quantum devices. Magnetohydrodynamic instabilities in tokamaks can severely disrupt plasma confinement and lead to damage on plasma-facing components. This study employs non-linear simulation codes to analyze the genesis of rare, self-organized, large-amplitude toroidal mode number $n=3$ toroidal modes, known as "palm tree" ribbons, observed in the JET tokamak during low-amplitude edge localized mode (ELM) phases. These ribbons, which correspond to localized magnetic islands, were investigated using nonlinear simulations of JET's specific tokamak parameters. By utilizing nonlinear codes that integrate magnetic field line tracing with fluid dynamics, we demonstrated that palm tree ribbons result from the non-linear evolution of magnetic islands linked to the most subdominant modes within the broadband ELM-activity spectrum. This subdominant $n=3$ mode, initially present at low amplitudes, grows through a quasi-linear phase until it reaches finite amplitude, where magnetic field line tracing reveals the formation of island-like structures. We validate this finding by comparing the synthetic emission patterns generated from simulations against experimental JET data, confirming that palm tree ribbons arise from the non-linear evolution of the most subdominant modes. Consequently, our research highlights the critical role of non-linear processes in the genesis of these large-amplitude ribbons and identifies the subdominant $n=3$ mode as a potential target for future ELM stabilization strategies. These insights could inform the stabilization of ELMs in future high-performance fusion devices. Additionally, our findings underscore the necessity of advanced, non-linear edge plasma modeling for accurately reproducing and interpreting experimental ribbons. This underscores the value of high-fidelity synthetic diagnostics, which can be achieved through open-source non-linear codes like T2D and OLSON, both of which are utilized in this work. The rise of pretraining frameworks, such as BERT, has fueled extensive research into pretraining models for continual learning (CL). This study challenges the necessity of these pretrained models for addressing standard, realistic, and complex CL scenarios. We introduce a straightforward baseline for CL that matches the performance of several recent CL, deep learning, and even some of the latest robust learning methods based on neural networks. Our approach demonstrates that simple, task-agnostic, and problem-agnostic strategies can effectively solve CL problems without relying on sophisticated algorithms or pretrained models. Additionally, we highlight the benefits of increasing dataset complexity in continuation, as it reduces catastrophic forgetting and diminishes the performance gap among different algorithms. Given CL's potential real-world applications, we argue for the need of more challenging, diverse, and realistic datasets to develop robust and practical solutions. We conclude that the field of CL should prioritize developing more robust algorithms that function well on high-complexity datasets and address practical issues, rather than solely pursuing state-of-the-art results on simple, low-complexity tasks. This paper introduces an interpretable multi-modal model designed to detect hate speech. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of our training dataset and develop specific feature selection techniques to reduce complexity. Furthermore, to ensure our model's interpretability, we examine the semantic relationships within the data. These innovations enable the detection of complex, context-dependent hate speech that depends on image features. Experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms existing methods in both detection accuracy and interpretability. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/1000010000100001/IEMOCAP-hate-speech-detection-dataset. Consequently, this superior performance in multi-modal detection and the model's interpretability suggest that enhanced social media hate speech monitoring is achievable. We view this work as a foundational step toward more effective detection systems in the future. This study examines large-scale networks of theta-burst firing neurons connected via synapses, characterized by an excitation/inhibition balance and heterogeneity stemming from varying decay time constants and initial conditions. The dynamics of each neuron are modeled using the FitzHugh-Nagumo framework, featuring a fast membrane potential and a slow recovery variable. We demonstrate that the network's behavior is primarily driven by the peak membrane potential dynamics. Leveraging this finding, we establish that the steady state of the network is largely independent of decay time constants and previous initial conditions, provided the latter do not violate the theta-firing assumption. Furthermore, networks containing either Poisson or power-law degree distributions exhibit identical dynamics, with outcomes determined solely by the second moment of the degree distribution. These findings are corroborated by extensive simulations. Consequently, networks with both distribution types are predicted to display robustness against structural and parameter fluctuations, as well as external inputs of moderate size. Finally, our predictions regarding the critical input required to trigger a seizure align with existing literature. Overall, this work lays a foundation for future investigations into structural and parameter heterogeneity within large-scale neuronal networks. Notably, since the FitzHugh-Nagumo model is widely used to represent cortical neurons, these results hold significant relevance for both theoretical and computational neuroscience. Additionally, the model's simplicity facilitates the application of these conclusions to other types of neuronal networks. Automatic Program Repair (APR) has gained significant attention recently, yet existing methods often produce invalid patches that fail to correct faults. This paper proposes a novel, novel approach called Adversarial APR (APR-A), which employs adversarial techniques to create valid patches. APR-A utilizes a generative adversarial network to create these patches and incorporates a validation module to ensure their correctness. Experimental results demonstrate that APR-A outperforms state-of-the-art APR tools, achieving a 22.5% improvement over the leading method. Furthermore, we present a case study that includes a user study to assess the practicality of our approach. Our patches are easy to comprehend and require minimal modification to resolve program errors, with an average of only 1.2 characters needed for correction. Additionally, our method successfully repairs 1,000 previously unrepaired real-world bugs. The implementation of APR-A and a dataset containing these patches are available at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/apr-a. The methodology behind the generated patches and their effectiveness in aiding program comprehension and maintenance are also explored. Overall, our approach holds the potential to significantly enhance existing APR tools. The source code for APR-A can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/apr-a. This paper introduces a comprehensive formula for the capacity region of a general two-pair interference channel, defining the region as the union of rectangles determined by pairs of spectral inf-mutual information rates. This formula offers a complete solution to the GIFC capacity problem, effectively extending single-letter expressions—known to be proven for the Kronecker product channel and the MAC with common information—to the general interference channel context. Additionally, the study offers an alternative derivation of the GIFC formula based on the polarization of product-type channels and investigates the GIFC capacity region in the presence of side information at the encoders and decoders. It is demonstrated that while the side-information-enhanced GIFC capacity is not necessarily the union of spectral min-conditional mutual information rate matrices, it is always contained within this union. Finally, the paper applies these findings to the broadcast interference channel, where a joint broadcast and interference alignment strategy yields a specific inner bound for the GIFC formula involving a finite union of rectangles. This inner bound is proven to coincide with the GIFC capacity formula for the PBC channel, thereby resolving the PBIC capacity problem and validating the effectiveness of joint broadcast and interference alignment. These conclusions are supported by illustrative examples and numerical results. **Index Terms**—Information Spectrum, Multiterminal Coding, Interference Alignment, Broadcast and Interference Alignment.

We introduce a new technique for investigating the three-dimensional flow generated by ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. This approach utilizes three flow modulation parameters, defined as $V_1$, $V_2$, and $V_3$, representing elliptic, triangular, and quadrangular flow modulations, respectively. These velocities, derived from three distinct moments of the particle momentum distribution, provide enhanced sensitivity to the initial impact geometry and the matter's equation-of-state (EoS). Analysis of Au+Au collisions at 3.8~GeV/nucleon reveals that the ratios $V_2/p_T$, $V_3/p_T$, and $V_2/V_3$ exhibit distinct $p_T$ dependencies, a phenomenon attributed to event-by-event fluctuations in the source geometry. Furthermore, Au+Au collision data indicate that $V_2/p_T$ and $V_3/p_T$ are approximately independent of $p_T$, whereas Cu+Cu and Cu+Au collision data suggest a $p_T$ dependence for $V_2/V_3$. Additionally, the rapidity dependence of these modulation ratios in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions suggests a stronger hydrodynamic influence at mid-rapidity. By comparing these findings with results from ideal hydrodynamic simulations, we conclude that the EoS of nuclear matter is soft when $p < 3$~GeV/nucleon and stiff when $p > 3$~GeV/nucleon. This study establishes a novel and promising framework for extracting the EoS of nuclear matter from heavy-ion collision experiments. Our framework will be made available to the community at https://github.com/tao-zhang-1/3d_flow. Our source code is released under the GNU General Public License v3.0. (Version 1.0). Detecting COVID-19 early is crucial for public health, yet patient data remains highly sensitive. This sensitivity is particularly acute in methods like Chest X-Ray (CXRA) analysis, which offers a non-invasive, accessible, and rapid screening option. While advanced deep learning models have shown great promise in this domain, they often struggle with overfitting and the over-smoothed nature of CXRA images. This paper introduces an adversarial training-based deep learning framework designed to enable early COVID-19 detection while ensuring privacy. Our approach leverages auto-encoder and generative adversarial networks (GANs) to generate augmented CXRA images, utilizing an adversarial training model to prevent data leakage. Experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses existing alternatives, effectively balancing the competing objectives of early disease detection and data privacy. By establishing a new benchmark, we pave the way for future research to achieve optimal performance in both areas. The comprehensive code and datasets will be made publicly available to further facilitate academic investigation. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) serve as powerful tools for analyzing and predicting outcomes in wireless communication systems modeled as graphs, such as multi-user MIMO channels and interference networks. However, the centralized training and deployment of GNN models often introduce single points of failure and security vulnerabilities. This paper introduces a wireless gNN framework designed for inference that addresses these challenges through a decentralized model, deployment, and security strategy. First, we examine the practical deployment of a wireless gNN in decentralized environments, identifying potential bottlenecks and security risks inherent to the architecture. Subsequently, we propose a security solution leveraging unsupervised anomaly detection to identify malicious inputs during inference. We develop a wireless implementation of this approach using cooperative detection, demonstrating that it can achieve performance comparable to a centralized anomaly detector. Finally, numerical results validate the efficacy of our proposed method. By integrating these techniques, we demonstrate that decentralized learning and inference can be achieved with minimal computational overhead and latency relative to centralized alternatives. Furthermore, our security approach enables the detection of anomalies in both normal and adversarial data, even under data imbalance conditions. In summary, this work offers a novel security perspective for decentralized wireless gNN inference, paving the way for more robust and resilient wireless communication systems. Homicide rates in Brazil have risen over recent decades, prompting extensive research into their underlying causes. However, existing studies often fail to distinguish between spatially correlated areas, a gap this study aims to address. By applying a non-stationary, cluster-based spatial econometric model to state-wide data from Goias, Brazil, the analysis identifies distinct groups of municipalities with varying temporal homicide trends between 2002 and 2014. The findings indicate that, within this state, homicide rates are lower in the western region and higher in the east. The study suggests that targeted policies should be applied based on these specific regional trends. Furthermore, the results highlight the necessity of conducting further research at a more granular spatial resolution to better understand local dynamics. Finally, the paper demonstrates the value of integrating econometric and statistical methods alongside geographic information systems to pinpoint homogeneous zones and inform policy decisions. These approaches can be utilized to evaluate the impact of specific interventions, such as the deployment of police officers, within these identified clusters. Additionally, the study demonstrates the adaptability of the proposed methodology to other datasets, including those on infectious diseases, environmental pollution, or household income and assets. The data used in this research can be accessed at http://www.dadosgoias.gov.br/. The source code is available at https://github.com/andreapereira/estimation-code. This work introduces a category of accelerated stochastic gradient descent methods designed to address various Gaussian noise levels present in stochastic optimization problems. These approaches are derived from applying the stochastic dual decomposition technique to generate noise-adaptive, problem-adaptive state equations within an implicit stochastic programming framework. The resulting dual problem is subsequently addressed using dual projected gradient descent. We demonstrate that these algorithms are provably faster than both standard stochastic gradient descent and noise-adaptive stochastic gradient descent (which lacks problem adaptivity) regarding their dual convergence rates. Furthermore, leveraging the primal-dual relationship, their primal convergence rates are established as at least as rapid as known bounds for plain and accelerated stochastic gradient descent under first- and fourth-order moment assumptions of the stochastic gradients. Finally, numerical experiments validate the computational superiority of these proposed algorithms over plain and accelerated stochastic gradient descent and over implicit stochastic programming schemes solved via either dual projected gradient descent or implicit stochastic programming solved with plain stochastic gradient descent. Additionally, we introduce a new class of primal-dual methods termed primal-dual proximal averaging, which unifies existing averaging techniques and offers a straightforward approach for deriving high-probability convergence rate bounds. Axion-based physics is currently a major focus of experimental research, driven by the unique capability of axion searches to explore the nuclear standard model. This study presents a feasibility analysis of BabyIAXO, the future upgrade of the IAXO experiment, in its ability to constrain solar parameters. A positive BabyIAXO detection of the axion flux would definitively confirm the existence of a solar core and provide a direct measurement of the axion-nucleon coupling constant. Furthermore, the experiment would enable a model-independent determination of the solar carbon-oxygen ratio and core temperature. Additionally, the study investigates the potential of BabyIAXO to detect solar neutrinos through coherent elastic neutrino-acoustic scattering. This capability would allow for a direct measurement of the solar luminosity and an independent determination of the solar mass. Consequently, BabyIAXO is expected to significantly enhance our understanding of the Sun's internal structure. Finally, this work outlines the prospects for solar axion physics as a field ripe for precision studies. To achieve this, it is essential to refine theoretical models of solar axion production and to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the experimental systematics affecting the axial signal. Ultimately, the future development of the axion-nuclear standard model, alongside advancements in detector technology, will pave the way for the next generation of solar axion experiments. This next generation will aim to improve upon the current axion solar parameter constraints that IAXO has established. This work investigates the temporal dynamics of occupation numbers in a bosonic oscillator, featuring one or two degrees of freedom, which is linearly and completely coupled to both fermionic and bosonic thermal reservoirs. The paper examines the lack of equilibrium within this oscillator, proposing it as a mechanism for establishing dynamical, non-stationary memory in quantum computing and quantum communication systems. Specifically, the transfer of information from the quantum oscillator to the reservoirs is analyzed through the concept of correlation time, defined as the average duration over which the oscillator's occupation numbers remain significant. The average correlation time is calculated as a function of system parameters, including temperature, resonance frequency, coupling constants, and the transition rates between the reservoirs' energy levels. Furthermore, the average correlation time is characterized by oscillatory or step-like functions of these parameters, reflecting the finite system's quantum nature and the specific interaction between the oscillator and the reservoirs. The study also addresses the oscillator's approach to a stationary state, estimating the time required for this process based on model parameters. Finally, the average relaxation time, representing the average duration needed to reach a stationary state, is derived. The relationship among correlation time, relaxation time, and modeling parameters is established, with numerical examples provided to illustrate these relationships. These findings are applicable to fully quantum models of quantum systems, offering a foundation for the functional design of quantum devices. The approach can be extended to examine many-body and higher-dimensional oscillator systems and their reservoirs, as well as systems coupled to multiple reservoirs. The originality of this work lies in its ability to describe the non-stationary behavior of quantum open systems, thereby offering solutions to previously unaddressed problems. By linking quantum and classical descriptions of open systems through reservoir properties, this work introduces novel perspectives to the field of quantum thermodynamics. The methodology is also relevant for developing models of open systems in quantum technology. Additionally, the results enable the formulation of thermodynamic processes involving quantum open systems, facilitating the design of quantum thermodynamic experiments. Ultimately, this work addresses fundamental questions in quantum thermodynamics by defining the thermodynamic states and processes of open quantum systems. Key aspects of these states and processes are analyzed in relation to the system's degree of freedom, reservoir characteristics, and interactions. Furthermore, the study explores the dynamical evolution of such states, laying a foundation for the design of quantum devices. Finally, the work contributes to quantum thermodynamics by clarifying the concept of thermalization in open quantum systems. **Objective:** To introduce and assess a free-breathing, respiratory motion-compensated 4D (3D+time) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2-SE) sequence for body imaging.

**Methods:** The proposed free-breathing sequence integrates variable density (VD) sampling, respiratory navigators, and motion-compensated 3D T2-SE imaging. Data acquisition occurs in small slices parallel to the diaphragm, featuring central regions with high density and peripheral areas with reduced density. Each 3D volume acquires a single navigator every 150 milliseconds to measure and correct for respiratory motion. After collecting a limited dataset, motion correction is performed to generate a series of 3D volumes covering the entire breath-hold. Subsequently, the remaining VD data is retrospectively reorganized based on these corrected volumes to produce a time dimension. The sequence was evaluated in a phantom and on patients using various contrast and temporal resolution settings.

**Results:** In the phantom study, the VD approach yielded a scan time of 10 minutes with an isotropic resolution of 2.5 mm. In patients, the same parameters allowed for 4D coverage at an effective temporal resolution of approximately 15 seconds. Increasing the temporal resolution to roughly 3 seconds resulted in a scan time of 35 minutes. Lowering the temporal resolution to approximately 45 seconds reduced the scan time to 20 minutes but resulted in a slight loss of image contrast.

**Conclusion:** The free-breathing, respiratory motion-compensated 4D T2-SE sequence offers a flexible trade-off between scan duration, temporal resolution, and image quality. This method enables 4D turbo SE imaging for the body without free-breathing navigator gating, facilitating the creation of high-quality 3D anatomical masks for radiation therapy. Furthermore, it supports effective temporal resolution down to 15 seconds using VD sampling, with the potential for even finer resolution through retrospective gating. These capabilities facilitate comprehensive tissue characterization and the investigation of respiration-induced organ and tissue motion. This paper presents InDistill, a unified framework for compressing large neural networks while maintaining the structural flow of information from input to output. Our approach begins with a non-linear transformation of teacher activations that aligns with the teacher's computational process, followed by a student classifier trained via a novel invariance-preserving regularization (I-PR) method. We theoretically demonstrate how I-PR facilitates Model-Activation-Alignment between student and teacher units, thereby enabling the student to capture the teacher's information flow. Extensive experiments across various classification benchmarks reveal that InDistill achieves competitive performance, often surpassing other state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we validate the framework's versatility by successfully applying it to multiple alternative compression methods, including Pruning, Quantization, and Quantization-Aware Training. Both theoretical analysis and empirical results confirm that InDistill effectively captures the input-to-output information flow of large models, thereby preserving their representational capabilities. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1990/InDistill. *Equal contribution. $\dagger$Corresponding author.*.

Let $f$ and $g$ be submersion functions mapping $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}$, where the level curves of $f$ and $g$ possess finitely singularities of the ADE type. This work establishes the topological equivalence of $f$ and $g$ within a broad class of scenarios, characterized by the condition that the level curves of both functions consist of compact curves resembling ellipses alongside unbounded components that curve gently at infinity. To achieve this, we introduce a method for constructing global coordinate changes in $\mathbb{R}^2$ by pasting together analytic coordinate changes, specifically addressing cases with one or two ends. Furthermore, we provide a criterion to determine when an analytic coordinate change remains close to the identity function. These technical advancements are of independent significance and hold potential applications in other areas of mathematical research. As an illustrative example, we demonstrate that if the level curves of $f$ and $g$ are defined by real polynomial functions, then their formal germs at the origin are equivalent as submersion functions if and only if $f$ and $g$ are topologically equivalent. Additionally, we present a criterion for the topological equivalence of submersion functions $f$ and $g$ based on the eigenvalues of their Hessians. Finally, we outline several open questions and propose a conjecture concerning the global properties of level curves, which extends the scope of the theorem to submersion functions with more complex level curve structures. Notably, the proof technique relies on resolving an analytic equation of the form $f(y(x))=c$ for a submersion function $f$ and a complex variable $c$, yielding an analytic solution $y(x)$ that approximates $f$ to a high order. This approach draws inspiration from the holomorphic Morse theory developed by Arnol'd, Durfee, and others. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents a criterion for the small perturbations of submersion functions; Section 3 addresses the local equivalence of submersion functions; Section 4 constructs global coordinate changes and provides a criterion for the local equivalence of the resulting functions; Section 5 proves the main theorem; and Section 6 applies these findings to polynomial functions $f$ and $g$. We introduce a dryland-vegetation model incorporating grazing by nomadic herders. Our dry-rewet cycles feature distinct dry and wet phases driven by climate fluctuations. During the dry phases, herders intensively graze vegetation until the system reaches a grazing limit cycle, a state influenced by nomadic decisions. Conversely, wet phases trigger rapid soil moisture saturation, leading to rapid vegetation regrowth and a transition back to the ungrazed steady state. We examine the dynamical implications of grazing during dry phases, focusing on whether vegetation can persist through multiple grazing cycles. When nomadic herders sample system states nonlocally across space, temporal, or both, the resulting nonlocal grazing can sustain vegetation even under extreme local conditions. Specifically, if herders use state variables from previous cycles, vegetation can survive despite local soil moisture depletion. Furthermore, if herders are forward-looking, vegetation can persist even when local moisture is excessive. Spatially, herders can maintain vegetation if they sample states from different spatial locations. Finally, when herders sample states from both spatial and temporal domains, vegetation dynamics become more complex, potentially resulting in coexistence of multiple grazing limit cycles or grazing-induced chaos. Our model relies on two critical parameters: the dry-phase duration and the "memory" of herders' decision-making. By analyzing these two-dimensional parameter spaces, we identify regions where vegetation can endure multiple cycles of dry and wet phases. These insights are applicable to various scenarios, including climate change, desertification, and land management. Additionally, by linking grazing intensity to grazing pressure, our framework can be extended to other grazing systems. Finally, we provide guidelines for future experiments aimed at validating the chaotic dynamics predicted by our theory. This chaotic behavior may also be relevant to other systems exhibiting climate-driven dynamics. Ultimately, our findings offer a comprehensive and unified perspective on grazing dynamics, demonstrating how human decision-making can counteract environmental degradation. These results hold significant potential for advancing both theoretical and applied understanding of complex environmental systems. Our approach advances the field of complex systems by offering a unified, holistic perspective on human-nature interactions. Moreover, our findings are transferable to a broad range of systems, including those involving human decision-making, social systems, and various forms of grazing. Our work also contributes to the field of complex systems by addressing critical issues in climate change, desertification, and land management. CountSketch is a widely used dimensionality reduction method that projects vectors into a lower dimension via randomized linear measurements. It is celebrated for its ability to estimate the top $k$ heavy hitters (where $k \ge 1$) even when input distributions are adversarial, provided the adversary lacks knowledge of the sketching matrix. However, this paper demonstrates that when adversaries are permitted to adaptively select input distributions based on observations of the sketch, the classical CountSketch estimate becomes vulnerable to arbitrarily large relative $L_1$ errors in the recovered heavy hitters. Such attacks can impact various applications relying on CountSketch, particularly in dynamic environments where prior adversarial distributions are chosen. To address this, we introduce a novel count-based sketch that maintains robustness against adversarial inputs. High-frequency trading (HFT) serves as the backbone of the global financial system, with the majority of transactions processed by a few major firms. This paper explores the potential for quantum computers to disrupt HFT and competitive dynamics by modeling it as the classic "Prisoner's Dilemma." To achieve this, we developed a straightforward quantum algorithm for the Prisoner's Dilemma that extends beyond simple periodic strategies, enabling the simulation of real-world HFT scenarios where payoffs consist of both cooperative and non-cooperative results. When played against established classical algorithms within the Quantum Prisoner's Dilemma, a quantum strategy yields significantly higher returns. Furthermore, we executed this circuit on actual quantum hardware to demonstrate its feasibility for near-term quantum processing. Consequently, this study offers a novel perspective on quantum advantages in competitive settings and introduces a new method for simulating quantum HFT. Our findings suggest that quantum computing could fundamentally transform business competition in diverse fields, including gaming and sports. This research paves the way for a new emerging field: Quantum Business Science. This discipline would integrate insights from game theory, game theory experiments, high-frequency trading, and economics to model and optimize corporate competition leveraging the capabilities of emerging quantum computing technologies. Additionally, we outline the steps required to transition from classical to quantum HFT for firms and provide a guide for investors evaluating quantum startups in this domain. To facilitate replication, we have open-sourced both the high-frequency trading data and the original Python code used in this study. This work was conducted in collaboration with D-Wave Systems, a leading provider of quantum computing cloud services. Specifically, it serves as the final year project for the first author, who is a PhD student in finance at the University of Oxford, and the second author, who is a senior data scientist at D-Wave. The project was supervised by the fourth author, an expert in quantum foundations and entropic game theory, and advised by the fifth author, a specialist in high-frequency trading. The study was funded by various internal research grants and external bodies, including the Centre for Advanced Study at Oslo, the Centre for Financial Research, the Centre for Advanced Study at the University of Oslo, the Centre for Advanced Study at the University of Edinburgh, the University of Oxford, and the University of Cambridge. This paper examines an environment where an intermediary offers a product to end-users, while an agent sets the price for the intermediary. Drawing inspiration from the subscription video on-demand market, we aim to maximize the agent's revenue. We first establish a simplified framework assuming an agent with constant costs. Our theoretical and experimental findings indicate that the optimal pricing strategy involves two distinct price points: one lower rate for the majority of transactions and a higher rate for a minority of transactions. Furthermore, the frequency of switching between these two prices increases as cost costs rise. Additionally, the optimal price is always set higher than the cost, even when demand is inelastic. Finally, we observe that optimal pricing exhibits periodic behavior. In our empirical application, we developed an online pricing algorithm that utilizes demand forecasting to achieve near-optimal revenue with significantly lower computational costs. Second, for scenarios with time-varying demand, we demonstrate that an online algorithm grounded in universal robust optimization principles can guarantee a constant fraction of optimal revenue without requiring prior knowledge of demand. This approach outperforms existing online algorithms designed for single-intermediary scenarios. Throughout the study, we maintain model simplicity by focusing on discrete transaction data. However, the proposed online algorithm is extendable to more complex settings, such as those with continuous demand functions. Future research will explore extending the model to accommodate non-constant costs and other factors. We have released the code online at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/online-intermediary-pricing. Our source code includes various practical features, such as a 1D Convolutional Neural Network-based demand forecasting function that leverages time-series data. We also provide a fully commented, step-by-step implementation of all experiments, enabling readers to easily replicate our results. We hope this work inspires further investigation into pricing strategies. Our source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/online-intermediary-pricing. By learning entity prompts through a contrastive objective, we demonstrate that these prompts retain essential summary information while maintaining a straightforward encoding. We validate our method on both small and large-scale datasets, showing that entity prompts act as an efficient long-term memory for summarization. Galactic outflows are thought to regulate star formation in star-forming disks, yet their spatial extent and the specific regions where they suppress star formation remain unclear. We present DUVET, a 3D study of the star formation-activity map in the nearby starburst galaxy NGC 253. By combining a 1.1um-1.0um dust extinction map, H$\alpha$ emission map, and 1.1um-1.0um extinction map, we reveal how outflows influence star formation. Our findings indicate that outflows extend up to 10 kpc from the disk center. In regions where the H$\alpha$ emission map overlaps with the dust extinction map, H$\alpha$ emission is significantly suppressed compared to the surrounding areas. This emission is detected only where the H$\alpha$-map does not overlap with the dust map, confirming that the dust map aligns with the H$\alpha$-suppressed regions. Furthermore, comparing the H$\alpha$-map with the [SII] map shows that [SII] emission is suppressed only where the H$\alpha$ map overlaps with the dust map. These results confirm that galactic outflows suppress star formation. Additionally, we observed a correlation between the [SII]/H$\alpha$ ratio and dust extinction, indicating that [SII] emission is suppressed more strongly than H $\alpha$ emission. This suggests that outflows have a more pronounced effect on low-ionization species like H $\alpha$ than on high-ionization species like [SII]. Our results support the idea that galactic outflows clear the interstellar medium of low-ionization gas, thereby suppressing star formation. This study demonstrates the power of 3D observations in elucidating the mechanisms of star formation regulation by galactic outflows. These findings indicate that the color glass condensation framework is essential for comprehensively describing the initial state geometry of ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, the observed enhancement of $v_3$ at low $p_T$ suggests a significant contribution from the initial participant asymmetry. Additionally, the measurement of $v_3(p_T)$ for Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV reveals a marked suppression of $v_3$ at high $p_T$, which the iAMPT model with a color glass condensation framework successfully reproduces. We introduce SRF, a new framework designed to facilitate the coordinated operation of multiple robots. Our approach utilizes shared memory and communication mechanisms grounded in linear temporal logic (LTL) to synchronize these robotic systems. We illustrate the framework's versatility by applying it to three specific scenarios: coassembly, cooperative material transport, and the joint execution of planning and control. Our method employs model checking to verify formal specifications and optimal control to derive control policies, thereby generating coordinated behaviors for the involved robots. We validate this approach through simulations and experimental studies featuring a multi-arm manipulator. The results demonstrate that our framework can effectively coordinate systems of this complexity, enabling the efficient completion of tasks. Furthermore, we establish a model-based testing protocol, which is a critical component of our solution. Finally, we discuss how SRF can be adapted to address various challenges in coordinated robotics. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/alexei-trofimov/srf. Our findings were presented at the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA). Kendall's tau serves as a nonparametric metric for correlation. We introduce a streamlined approach to calculate the empirical estimate of Kendall's tau alongside the jackknife estimate of its variance. For datasets with a fixed dimension, the algorithm's execution time scales log-linearly with the number of observations. This efficiency is realized by adapting the conventional algorithm for computing empirical Kendall's tau to yield estimates of the components comprising its Hájek projection. Consequently, this approach not only determines the empirical estimate of Kendall's tau and the empirical estimates of its asymptotic variance components but also generates consistent estimators of the asymptotic variance. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that Kendall's tau, when utilized within a linear model, delivers competitive performance relative to Pearson's correlation in variable selection and variable screening procedures. Consistent with established findings, empirical results indicate that employing Kendall's tau within penalized regression methods enhances protection against type I errors when facing dense alternative hypotheses. Additionally, simulations reveal that the proposed method for estimating the variance of Kendall's tau provides superior performance compared to alternative inference methods. Finally, the methodology is illustrated using two real-world datasets. A R package is accessible via the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) to facilitate replication. The package supports a Monte Carlo implementation of Kendall's rank correlation correlation analysis, a topic explored in the accompanying paper. This solution offers computational advantages by leveraging the proposed algorithm and includes a function to calculate various statistics for the Kendall-Rank-Correlation-Graph, a tool introduced in our recent work. This analysis examines performance metrics regarding type I and type II errors, as well as ranking efficiency, under both sparse and dense alternative hypotheses.
