The computational efficacy of the finite Hex method hinges on the quality of the hexahedral mesh. However, computational meshes are inherently generated for specific problems and require no special attention to underlying topologies, resulting in irregular meshes characterized by cells with varying sizes and shapes that often fail to conform to the computational domain, creating hanging nodes. This study introduces a novel algorithm to reorganize these messy hexahedral meshes into a highly structured format suitable for the application of the finite Hex formulation. By treating each hexahedral cell as a "tet," the algorithm transforms the mesh into a collection of "tets" featuring "Hex faces" on "Hex nodes," thereby establishing a new data structure for finite Hex method applications. The core of this method involves subdividing irregular tets into up to 58 structured tets, thereby eliminating hanging nodes and enhancing the overall structure of the mesh. A thorough investigation into the theoretical basis for the 58-tets subdivision is provided, and the algorithm's validity is confirmed through various practical examples. Furthermore, the numerical accuracy of the finite Hex method on the resulting structured mesh is demonstrated using the classic Poisson equation on a unit cube. The results indicate that for a given mesh count, the computational accuracy of this new structured mesh is comparable to that of a mesh with the same number of elements. Additionally, the 58-tets subdivision enables the finite Hex method to achieve the optimal second-order accuracy in both space and time, a target previously unattainable with existing hexahedral meshes due to hanging nodes. Consequently, the 58-tets subdivision serves as a vital step toward realizing the full potential of the finite Hex method. Notably, both the 58-tets subdivision algorithm and the resulting structured mesh (via the "tet on Hex node" organization) are freely available for public use. Given their nature as general-purpose tools, they hold significant promise for diverse applications. For instance, in fluid dynamics, they can facilitate the highly structured mesh required for applying the finite Hex method to complex flow problems, such as flow around aircraft. In this specific context, the algorithm can convert existing unstructured Lagrangian mesh-based finite volume schemes into a highly structured Eulerian Hex mesh framework, where a broad range of established and emerging computational fluid dynamics schemes based on the finite Hex method can then be readily applied. This capability to convert established hexahedral mesh-based schemes into a highly structured Hex mesh framework represents a significant advancement in the field. Relation extraction (RE) focuses on identifying the relationship between a subject and an object within a sentence. Specifically, we introduce a joint pre-training framework that handles both tasks within a unified framework, which also serves to generate an effective sentence representation tool for downstream RE applications. By leveraging the co-occurrence of words across numerous sentences during pre-training, the model learns robust word embeddings without relying on external word embeddings or language models. We conducted comprehensive experiments on three public relation extraction datasets to assess the performance of these derived word embeddings. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach yields competitive performance on standard RE tasks. Principled decision-making in continuous state-action spaces relies on the assumption that environmental rewards and transitions vary smoothly with respect to states and actions. However, standard smoothness definitions, which depend on Lipschitz constants, are often difficult to estimate, leading many reinforcement learning algorithms to rely on heuristic methods for smoothness adaptation. This work proposes a metric-based coarse-grained smoothness concept that captures standard smoothness while remaining robust to Lipschitz constants. We present a gradient-descent rule that leverages this property and achieve competitive results on both model-based and model-free continuous control tasks. Furthermore, we develop adaptive algorithms for various reinforcement learning contexts, including off-policy learning, policy optimization, and the exploration-exploitation dilemma. Empirical evidence demonstrates that our approach outperforms baseline algorithms in these settings. Additionally, we apply a metric-derived Lipschitz constant to enable a metric-based variational policy optimization algorithm to surpass existing methods. Overall, our contributions provide both a theoretical and practical framework for achieving principled, high-performance continuous control and decision-making. Code is accessible at: https://github.com/SebastianSchmid1992/CoarseGrainedSmoothRL.

The mechanisms governing animacy organization in the ventral temporal cortex (VTC) are not well understood. While recent research suggests that animacy categories are derived from shared object properties, the specific nature of these categorical dimensions remains uncertain. This study examines whether the animacy structure of VTC is governed by a single dimension or multiple dimensions. Using functional MRI and multivariate pattern analysis, we assessed the similarity of neural representations for faces, bodies, and objects. Our results indicate that the animacy structure in VTC is essentially one-dimensional, with face, body, and object representations arranged along a continuum rather than split into distinct clusters. Furthermore, the relative positions of these concepts align closely with the relative similarity of their conceptual definitions, reinforcing the notion that concept similarity drives neural similarity in VTC. Finally, we demonstrate that a deep neural network trained on the same task replicates our findings, underscoring the significance of common semantic attributes in VTC organization and hinting at the brain's reliance on explicit semantic knowledge. These findings collectively bolster a continuous, representational view of the mind, where animacy categories emerge from the continuous variation of dimensions defined by shared object attributes. By integrating empirical data with computational modeling, we offer a step toward elucidating the intricate mechanisms underlying visual and conceptual categorization. Our work also introduces a computational framework for modeling conceptual similarity, which holds promise for advancing future research in this domain. Finally, we argue that the brain's explicit knowledge of concepts may play a more central role in cognition than currently acknowledged. By employing explicit conceptual representations, our approach paves the way for a unified framework that bridges the gap between implicit neural computations and explicit conceptual knowledge. Ultimately, this research advances our understanding of the neural basis of visual and conceptual categorization and fosters a more holistic understanding of the relationship between neural representations and concepts. The study's data and code are accessible at https://github.com/zhongliangwang/animacy_VTC. The code is also available at https://github.com/zhongliangyang/catvisor. Our computational approach to modeling conceptual similarity holds potential for advancing our understanding of the explicit nature of concepts. Specifically, our method for characterizing conceptual similarity can enhance the brain's understanding of concepts and foster a more comprehensive grasp of the relationship between neural representations and concepts. The data and code used in this study can be found at https://github.com/zhongliangwang/animacy_VTC. The code is also available at https://github.com/zhongliangyang/catvisor

This study introduces a structure-preserving filter (SPF) designed for finite element simulations across various spatial dimensions, grounded in convex optimization. The approach leverages the broad applicability and robustness inherent in convex optimization frameworks. Our methodology defines a filtering property that guarantees the output of the nonlinear filter remains within the input's convex hull. To achieve this, we construct the filter using a constrained convex optimization problem that minimized while respecting the aforementioned property, alongside an efficient implicit algorithm for its resolution. Notably, our implicit solver avoids the need to explicitly define the convex hull constraint, thereby maintaining a compact representation and enabling a robust solution even for discontinuous finite element fields. We demonstrate that this filtering property preserves essential physical characteristics, such as non-negativity and mass conservation, which are frequently critical in simulation applications. The theoretical findings are substantiated by several numerical examples in two and three dimensions, including simulations of incompressible viscous fluid flow, thin elastic shell structures, and elastic contact problems. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability to recover solutions with sharp interfaces from filtered data, even under significant noise conditions. A key advantage of the proposed convolution-type filter is its compatibility with standard post-processing, allowing for direct comparison of physical quantities between filtered and unfiltered solutions. To the best of our knowledge, no other existing structure-preserving filter shares this distinctive characteristic. The SPF exhibits robustness and stability, as evidenced by numerous numerical tests, and is readily adaptable to diverse physical phenomena and conservation laws. Additionally, the SPF is computationally efficient for both 2D and 3D simulations. Finally, we demonstrate that the filter can regularize solutions in a way that mitigates numerical instabilities in sharp interface simulations, a feature not achieved by smoothing splines or Gaussian kernel methods. To our knowledge, no other structure-preserving filter possesses this capability. The theoretical results are validated through various fluid and solid mechanics simulations in 2D and 3D. Our approach extends the concept of optimal transport to convex optimization, offering a novel and versatile tool for simulation-based design and optimization. A Python implementation of the SPF is available at https://github.com/andreafioravanti/structure-preserving-filter. Type-soft (Type-S) and Type-intermediate (Type-I) corona models are established paradigms for soft (soft-to-soft) and hard (hard-to-soft) state transitions in black hole accretion systems. However, the nature of the transition from Type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) to Type-S or Type-I states remains uncertain. This study investigates the evolutionary path of the corona in the black hole X-ray binary MAXI J1535-571, which exhibits Type-C QPOs, during its 2018 outburst. We utilized data from the Insight-HXMT observatory, analyzing the evolution of the corona through spectral fitting and the tracking of Type-C QPOs. Our results indicate that the corona in MAXI J1553-571 evolves from a thin, thin-dominant, or thick-dominant configuration to a thick corona, followed by a thick-thin-dominant or thick-corona configuration. This transition is accompanied by the disappearance of Type-C QPOs. Additionally, we observed a significant inverse correlation between the energy centroid of the QPO and the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) radius, alongside a positive correlation between the QPO's full width at half maximum (FWHM) and the distance between the inner and outer (20 $r_g$) radii of the accretion flow. These findings suggest that Type-C QPOs may serve as an indicator of the presence of a thick corona. Furthermore, the inverse relationship between the QPO's FWHM and ISCO radius implies that Type-C QPOs could arise from resonances within the accretion flow. Finally, our results support the hypothesis that the soft component of Type-S and Type-I QPOs originates from the thermalization of the hard component. These conclusions are supported by the substantial and consistent data obtained from Insight-HXMT. Future research should continue to explore the evolution of Type-C QPOs to better understand the physical mechanisms governing black hole accretion. This study explores cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) within the context of communication-free dynamic transfer scenarios. In these settings, an agent must reliably replicate the impact of a partner's actions to effectively cooperate, even when the partner exhibits unpredictable behaviors. To address this, we introduce a method for identifying the optimal behavior replication strategy through a meta-reinforcement learning approach. By adapting the concept of "transfer empowerment" from single-agent model-based RL, we develop a modified version of the intrinsic motivation framework known as TEA. This approach is considered "social" because it relies on the empirical cross-empowerment between agents, enabling the agent to infer how its actions influence its partner. We validate the efficacy of our method, termed Transfer Empowerment of Action Influence (TEAII), in a simple two-agent card game. The results demonstrate that TEAII enables reliable behavioral transfer during interaction, even when the partner's behavior changes. Furthermore, our method facilitates the automatic acquisition of this capability without requiring any manual design of the agent's intrinsic motivation. Finally, we examine the theoretical properties of TEAII within the multi-agent Markov decision process framework. By establishing the relationship between transfer efficiency and the discount factor, we offer a guideline for selecting the discount factor in dynamic transfer MARL problems. Additionally, the empirical results indicate that TEAII achieves performance comparable to methods that do require the manual design of intrinsic motivation. We introduce MatSim, a material simulation dataset designed to generate images representing samples from any material placed on any surface. Our goal is to enable material property recognition even when the sample is completely unfamiliar, a task we frame as few-shot (one-shot) recognition to align with contemporary machine learning terminology. To build MatSim, we developed a physics-based renderer capable of simulating diverse material combinations and applied contrastive learning to automate the supervision process. This approach yields two outcomes: (1) a customized material simulator that accelerates the simulation of material appearances, and (2) a novel few-shot recognizer for material properties that surpasses existing methods by an order of magnitude in top-1 accuracy while requiring only 10 images per material. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our recognizer successfully identifies materials in real-world images, fulfilling our one-shot recognition objective. The MatSim dataset and material simulator are publicly accessible at https://mat-sim.github.io. Our code and papers are available at https://github.com/jaychen123/mat-sim. We begin by revisiting Lie 2-algebras, also known as strict Lie categories, which serve as the 2-categorical extension of Lie algebras. Subsequently, we review the equivalence between strict Lie categories and Lie groupoids that possess vanishing Lie algebra bundles. Furthermore, we examine the concept of weak Lie 2-algebras by presenting the equivalent characterization of relaxed Lie groupsoids. In the final section, we provide an explicit construction of the 2-functor connecting the category of strict Lie 2-algebras to the category of Lie groupoids with Lie algebra bundles. This work serves as a comprehensive guide to the author's paper arXiv:1905.06774 [math.AT].

We introduce a new approach for local image feature matching that bypasses the traditional sequential steps of detection, description, and matching. Instead, our method directly establishes pixel-to-pixel correspondences between images using global context. To achieve this, we developed LoFTR, a transformer-based model. First, we apply a multi-scale transformer to each image to generate large-scale global context and locate potential correspondences. Subsequently, a fine-scale transformer refines these matches by leveraging detailed local context. A simple global matching mechanism filters out incorrect matches, while a local disambiguation mechanism strengthens valid ones. A differentiation layer ensures context consistency across different scales. We evaluated our method on the Pascal VOC and COCO datasets for self-training, and on several public datasets across diverse domains as well as on publicly available datasets to demonstrate generalization. Experimental results show that LoFTR outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative and qualitative assessments. The code and models are accessible at https://github.com/lucasb12/LoFTR. This study examines the bias inherent in the aliphi algorithm, which is widely used to derive vector magnetic field measurements from extreme ultraviolet images captured by the Solar Telescope on the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory. The authors demonstrate that aliphi introduces a systematic error when applied to the SHAO's extreme ultraviolet imagery, causing inferences in regions lacking a field line to consistently display a field line direction. This results in a systematic overestimation of the magnetic field strength. The authors identify the specific image characteristics that trigger this bias and propose a mitigation strategy: applying an ultraviolet filter prior to inferences. They validate the efficacy of this method by comparing the ultraviolet-preprocessed results with aliphi inferences across various solar regions, including the quiet Sun, active regions, and near solar filaments. The analysis confirms the method's success, demonstrating that it effectively eliminates the aforementioned bias. Furthermore, the authors develop a model to quantify the impact of this bias on the resulting magnetic field strength. Finally, they illustrate the consequences of this bias by analyzing the magnetic field evolution within an active region over a 24-hour period. The study concludes that the influence of bias is more pronounced in areas with weak magnetic fields, such as the quiet Sun and filament regions, whereas its effect is minimal in strongly magnetized areas. These findings are critical for the accurate analysis of helicity and free magnetic energy. Additionally, the authors provide a Python implementation of alipfi, which is available on GitHub. This paper introduces a new demand-side management framework where autonomous smart appliances on the consumption side enhance their performance by exchanging information with smart generators on the supply side. Simultaneously, flexible loads within the system optimize their operations by trading energy with the generator. To manage total consumption, the framework employs an aggregative game to determine a stable state where no load can improve its performance by unilaterally deviating. Furthermore, to safeguard system security, an explicit constraint is imposed to prevent any load from exceeding its rated power. Simulation results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in reducing total energy usage while maintaining a Nash equilibrium. Additionally, the study confirms the global convergence of the proposed learning algorithms for both smart generators and flexible loads, even under constraint conditions. These findings suggest the approach is well-suited for deployment in microgrid environments. A case study of the "Smart Village" at the University of Central Florida illustrates the method's real-world applicability. In this setup, autonomous smart loads achieve performance improvements by exchanging data with their smart generator, while the learning algorithms for both loads and the generator are proven to be globally convergent. Furthermore, loads can reduce overall consumption by trading energy with the generator. The paper also addresses the challenge of modeling the impact of inter-temporal demand-side management on generators, specifically accounting for the generator's cost to meet additional load demands. This cost accounting structure ensures that increased total consumption remains economically viable. Finally, load flexibility is safeguarded through the enforcement of both technical and operational constraints. In this design, loads utilize learning-based methods to optimize their performance by trading energy with the generator. Promising outcomes indicate that the proposed approach can achieve a significant reduction in total consumption without violating constraint violations. The results of this approach are presented in the simulation results section of the paper. Ultimately, this approach is particularly suitable for deployment in microgrid environments. The paper concludes by discussing the advantages of this approach for microgrids. We demonstrate that the power-law decay exponents in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems correspond to the pointwise scaling exponents of a spectral measure at the spectral value $1$. Furthermore, we establish a quantitative link between the asymptotic behavior of a spectral measure at $1$ and the convergence rate within von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem. These findings are illustrated using self-similar and self-affine measures, which serve as spectral measures for family dynamics arising from iterated function systems. Additionally, we generalize prior results regarding self-similar measures on $\mathbb{R}^d$ driven by matrix systems to encompass general matrix systems. Finally, our results provide a quantitative version of the open set condition. Specifically, we derive formulas for the rate of convergence in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for spectral measures associated with self-similar measures on $\mathbb{R}$ generated by contractive affine mappings, expressed through the open set condition, the relative positions of images, and box counting numbers. Finally, we examine the case of self-affine measures on $\mathbb{R}^2$ generated by two families of contractive mappings, analyzing the rate of convergence in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem relative to box counting numbers. In this context, we also address the convergence rate of discrete approximations of the spectral measure. However, we note that no comparable result exists for higher-dimensional cases involving $\mathbb{R}^d$ and matrix systems. Our work extends the findings of J. Strahov and J. S. Shao [20], who linked dimension and discrete approximation of self-similar measures on $\mathbb{R}$ with a single family of contractive mappings to power-law exponents in Fourier decay. We also present a quantitative version of this extension. Finally, we highlight the applicability of our results to fractal strings and their associated spectral zeta functions. We introduce a novel approach to identify metal-poor stars ($[Fe/H] < -2.0$) within the billion-star catalog of the second data release of the \textit{Gaia} Extra-Tial Dimension (Gaia-EDD). This method relies on stellar spectra obtained from Gaia's Blue/Purple and Red/Purple instruments, specifically targeting the strength of the Ca II H and K lines. By analyzing these lines, we determine stellar masses and derive a proxy for metallicity, $Z_{\rm{b}}$, which strongly correlates with actual metallicity ($[Fe/H]$). Our analysis of 1,000 stars with valid spectral data reveals that $Z_{_{\rm{b}}}$ is a robust proxy, showing a linear relationship with $[Fe/H]$ for stars with masses between 0.5 and 2.0 solar masses. This technique is particularly effective for low-mass stars, where we can confidently distinguish metal-poor stars from those with intermediate metallicity ($-2.0 \leqslant [Fe/H] \leqslant -1.0$). This capability significantly enhances the ability to select candidates for future follow-up observations. We have developed an open-source tool to apply this method to the \textit{Gaia}-EDD catalog. Our findings indicate that approximately 1,000 low-mass metal-poor stars exist in this release, with a completeness of 90\% for masses exceeding 0.7 solar masses. The majority of these stars are likely to be found in the \textit{Gaia}* DR2 HRZ catalog. We conclude that this selection of low-mass metal-poor stars represents a valuable resource for advancing our understanding of stellar evolution. Future work will involve spectroscopic follow-up to calibrate the metallicity proxy and investigate the physical properties of these stars. This dataset is especially pertinent to the ongoing debate regarding the existence of a metallicity gap in low-mass stars. Our results confirm that such a gap exists within the \textit{Gaia}-EDD catalog, with a distinct boundary separating metal-poor stars from intermediate-age, low-mass stars at $Z_{\rm{b}} = 0.15$. This separation aligns with theoretical predictions regarding the initial mass function of low-mass stars. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to assess and predict global fire season severity. Utilizing Climate Data Records (CDR) from NASA's Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), we represent fire severity as the count of active pixels across eight monthly snapshots per season. Addressing the scarcity of publicly accessible fire severity forecasting tools, we develop an Autoencoder-based Transformer model. This model forecasts seasonal active-pixel counts using Climate Data Records of temperature, humidity, and vegetation cover, with each season limited to eight predictions. To overcome the challenges of imbalanced datasets and varying active-pixel volumes, we implement an attention mechanism that dynamically adjusts focus based on seasonal variations. We further refine the Transformer's feed-forward attention layers to enhance its predictive accuracy. Finally, we validate the model's performance through cross-validation and comparative analysis against baseline models. The source code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1234567890/GlobalFireSeasonForecasting. We offer an analysis of eight corpus-based metrics for quantifying morphological complexity in natural languages, which differ in their annotation requirements and the specific aspects of complexity they capture. Through visual inspections and both linear and nonlinear statistical analyses, we demonstrate that these measures are fundamentally interconnected, sharing between 40% and 100% of variance. This suggests that all measures effectively reflect the same two primary dimensions of morphological complexity: morpheme richness and morpheme diversity. We also establish a link to typological morphological complexity by integrating our corpus data with the Mapuche-Typology. Finally, we correlate these measures with syntactic complexity, finding that they account for 30% to 80% of the variance in syntactic complexity metrics. Our results indicate that measures capturing morpheme diversity also strongly predict morphological interlanguage similarity, thereby supporting the Morphological Diversity Hypothesis proposed by Siewierska (2018). Our findings underscore the utility of diverse corpus-based measures for uncovering specific dimensions of grammatical complexity and their connections to typological patterns. Furthermore, the high correlations among these measures facilitate the development of a unified metric for morphological complexity, which we implement in the open-source library `natural-languages-complexity`. This library calculates all eight measures via a vector space model grounded in morpheme inventories and usage statistics, allowing for efficient computation without the need for corpus annotation. Its source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/robertkagey/natural-languages-complexity. Additionally, we provide a detailed description of the vector space model and a collection of precomputed vector spaces for 2,250 languages, available at https://github.com/robertkagey/nlc-vectors. We investigate the optical properties of self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) within galaxy clusters. By analyzing strong gravitational lensing observations of the Abell 2744 cluster, we place stringent limits on both the self-interaction cross section and the mass of dark matter mediators. Our study employs ray-tracing techniques to generate high-resolution synthetic lensed images, which are then compared against observed images to constrain these parameters. Our results indicate that a significant amount of self-interaction is disallowed by lensing data, even when mediators possess a mass as low as a few eV. We further demonstrate that discrepancies between cosmological simulations and galaxy cluster observations can be resolved through spatially varying self-interaction cross sections. Additionally, we highlight the benefits of gravitational lensing as a tool for probing dark matter self-interactions in galaxy clusters. Finally, we discuss the potential for further constraining SIDM properties in future cosmological surveys that include lensing data. Specifically, we predict that the COSMOS-LOCI survey will be able to detect dark matter self-interactions with a cross-section-to-mass density ratio ($\sigma/m$) as low as $0.01 \, \mathrm{cm^3/g/GeV}$, provided the mediator mass is at least $10 \, \mathrm{GeV}$. This level of sensitivity represents an order of magnitude improvement over current constraints derived from galaxy cluster observations. Additionally, we find that the median mediator mass capable of being probed by a given $\sigma/m$ value scales with the redshift of the target sample as $(1+z)^{1/3}$. This trend reflects the combined influence of higher lensing surface density and increased mediator redshift in higher-redshift samples. We conclude that upcoming optical surveys will significantly enhance our ability to test self-interacting dark matter models. Finally, we demonstrate that lensing data can simultaneously constrain both the self-interaction cross section and the mediator mass, thereby mapping out a broad region of parameter space where SIDM models are viable. This approach allows us to address small-scale issues such as the core-cusp problem and the missing satellite problem. Specifically, we show that a simple form of self-interaction can naturally produce cores in dwarf galaxies while maintaining cuspiness in galaxy clusters. We anticipate that future lensing surveys will significantly improve our understanding of dark matter self-interactions in both galaxies and clusters. This study addresses the model reduction of nonlinear dynamical systems that exhibit spatially distributed behavior under partially distributed sensor observations. The objective is to construct a low-dimensional nonlinear data-driven reduced-order model capable of reproducing the original system's outputs at unsensed locations. The proposed framework integrates machine learning techniques with traditional projection methods, remaining agnostic to specific system dynamics or observations. It relies on two primary components: a correction map that predicts system outputs at unsensed regions based on local neighborhoods, and a projection operator that constructs the reduced model by embedding the correction map into a linear projection scheme. Results are validated using two numerical experiments derived from real-world data, along with an extensive numerical test involving random systems and observations to assess the approach's generalizability. Furthermore, the work provides validations from both numerical and experimental perspectives. Although the primary application targets spatially distributed systems, the methodology is fundamentally data-driven and can be extended to other domains. The authors believe this model holds significant potential for applications in model-based control and optimal design. This research introduces the "m-ar-K-FastICA" algorithm, an enhanced variant of the "FastICA" method tailored for m-ar-K-Feature Independent Component Analysis (m-ar-K-ICA). While standard ICA aims to separate independent sources from mixed data, m-ar-K-ICA further incorporates specific statistical characteristics, denoted as m-ar-K-features, into the decomposition process. In this study, the m-ar-K-feature is defined as the number of data points. Although previous work by the authors developed "m-ar-K-FastICA" to enable local source separation, this paper restructures that approach by redefining the probability density function (PDF) and the non-linear mixing function. The proposed method utilizes the K-th order cumulative distribution function (K-CDF) rather than the standard cumulative distribution function. This work represents the initial investigation into applying K-CDF-based m-ar-K-ICA to solve specific problems. The results indicate that "m-ar-K-FastICA" with the k-CDF variant demonstrates superior performance in specific scenarios compared to other models. Furthermore, both theoretical analysis and experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed algorithm achieves local source separation. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through an image denoising application. The findings suggest that the proposed method is particularly effective for denoising tasks when noise exhibits varying intensities across different image regions. The source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/SeijiKawai/m-ar-K-FastICA. This paper introduces two event detection methodologies based on geographic social media streams, aiming to identify events within specified spatial and temporal contexts using automated techniques. The first approach is real-time, utilizing a machine learning model to predict events as new data arrives, alongside algorithms for localizing spatial regions and determining when events commence. The second approach is offline, applying a similar machine learning strategy to discover event time sequences and, through a dedicated spatial algorithm, identifying the corresponding geographic areas. Both systems were evaluated against a benchmark dataset from the Real-Time Event Detection on Geographic Social Media (RTDDGSM) challenge, with performance measured by success rates in event identification, spatial region localization, and the timing of event initiation. The proposed methods achieved competitive results, with an average accuracy of 60% for event identification. This surpasses the average performance of the top three winning teams in the RTDDGSM challenge. This paper establishes optimal regularity results for solutions to the additive measure problem and adds measure problems within trace spaces on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$. These findings yield novel regularity insights for the polyharmonic, sub-elliptic, and weighted additive (specifically) sub-elliptic measure problems. Furthermore, we investigate the uniqueness of the n-Laplacean, sub-elliptic, and weighted multiplicative (respectively) measure problems. The analysis relies on fundamental estimates concerning the behavior of the Poisson kernel on $\Omega$ and associated fractional Sobolev spaces. Additionally, we present a series of counterexamples demonstrating the failure of these results when the domain $\Omega$ is non-tangentially accessible. Finally, an appendix offers a comprehensive review of key concepts regarding finiteness measures on trace spaces, encompassing their definitions, equivalent characterizations, and characterization theorems. These concepts are derived from a significant characterization theorem by Bourgain, Nirenberg, and Pismen, which serves as a cornerstone of our research. We also highlight its applications to the uniqueness of the n-Laplacean, sub-elliptic, and weighted multiplicative measure problems. Notably, this characterization theorem is instrumental in advancing current research on measure problems in trace spaces, as it resolves a long-standing open question by Bourgain, often referred to as the "measure problem." Specifically, it clarifies the necessary and sufficient conditions for a function to belong to trace spaces, a topic of fundamental importance in regularity theory. Furthermore, this theorem has applications in other areas of analysis, including measure theory, geometric measure theory, and geometric analysis. This characterization was achieved through a combination of novel and refined arguments by the three authors, building upon earlier contributions by various researchers. We anticipate that these results will serve as a valuable resource for future research on measure problems in trace spaces. These techniques may also have broader applications in regularity theory, particularly for additive measure problems. Real-time bidding (RTB) has emerged as a dominant approach for digital display advertising, enabling advertisers to set prices for individual impressions. However, the prevalence of budget constraints within RTB remains a significant concern for the industry. Existing research on budget allocation in RTB is limited, with most current methods merely setting a price and relying on bidders to enforce the budget constraint. This study proposes adaptive risk-aware bidding strategies for display advertising that ensure budget constraints are met. Specifically, we introduce a new method called ARAB (Adaptive Risk-Aware Bidding), which utilizes adaptive risk adjustment to achieve strict budget compliance. Our arithmetically simple yet effective method sets a bid price that is both risk-aware and adaptive, contingent upon the advertiser's budget status. We validate our approach through simulations using real-world data, comparing our methods against adaptive risk-aware bidding techniques based on adaptive risk adjustment. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed bidding strategies. Furthermore, we reveal the optimal bidding behavior under adaptive risk adjustment and argue that our adaptive risk adjustment method can be seamlessly integrated with other bidding strategies to achieve real budget constraints. Finally, our adaptive risk adjustment method is also applicable to English auctions to prevent overspending. Notably, it achieves this budget constraint adherence without requiring any modifications to the standard bidding process. The arithmetically simple method can be directly applied to ensure budget constraints in RTB without compromising advertiser privacy. Additionally, our method is compatible with the Generalized Linear Budget Constraint (GLBC) framework. By simply setting the advertiser's risk aversion coefficient to zero, advertiser risk is eliminated, thereby preventing budget overspending. Our paper offers valuable insights for practitioners aiming to enforce budget constraints in RTB. The source code is publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/ChenchenLi1990/ARAB}. Quantum nonlocality and contextuality are both fundamental elements of quantum theory characterized by asymmetric correlations between distant observers. This contextual aspect manifests as steering, where measurements performed by one observer enable another to remotely manipulate, or "steer," the conditional states of their shared system. This phenomenon is considered a precursor to nonlocality. This letter investigates the link between Wigner negativity and the steerability of bipartite quantum systems by defining and analyzing a variant of steerability based on the convex hull of conditional states, termed geometric steerability. We demonstrate that for a specific class of local quantum systems, the steering polytope and its corresponding Wigner-like probability distribution are directly correlated. Furthermore, we extend the concept of geometric steerability to the Wigner-negative region, revealing that the maximum maximum-entropy state within the steerability region of a bipartite quantum system is uniquely determined by its Wigner-negative boundary. These findings offer a promising framework for investigating steerability and its relationship with Wigner negativity in quantum systems. Additionally, the study provides a systematic approach for generating N-partite nonlocal models that exhibit nonlocal correlations. Finally, we examine a scenario in the quantum key distribution problem involving Gaussian states, illustrating the significance of geometric steerability in the context of entanglement harvesting. These results provide a promising avenue for exploring the interplay between steerability and Wigner negativity in quantum systems. Geometric steerability is anticipated to play a pivotal role in quantum information theory, quantum sensing, and fundamental physics. In quantum key distribution (QKD) systems employing privacy amplification, the seed randomness required for generating the final key is typically supplied by a random number generator. When this device produces non-uniform random variables, the security bound must be adjusted to ensure protocol safety. This paper examines secure bound analysis for the BB84 protocol under conditions of non-uniform seed randomness. We demonstrate that the secret key rate can be derived using either the bias or probability distribution function of the random seeds, with an upper limit determined by the Shor-Preskill method combined with the bound analysis presented in this study. Furthermore, we compare these findings against bound analyses based on the Lo-Kudner-Vyakhushev (LKV) and Devetak-Wagner (WD) frameworks. Finally, our results indicate that the security bound calculated via the Shor-Preskill approach is more conservative than those offered by the LKV and WD methods. These findings were validated through simulation using a decoy-state BB84 model. Additionally, the proposed bound analysis method is applicable to other QKD protocols that utilize random seeds for privacy amplification. We examine the diffusion process governed by the forward equation $u_t(t,x)=x u_{xx}(t,x)+(m-2)xu_x(t,x)$, where $m>0$ is a parameter and $u_0(x)$ serves as the initial condition. This equation models a standard Feller diffusion with an additional repulsion of strength $2m-4$ directed away from infinity. We demonstrate that the coalesence time $T_n$ for a system of $n$ particles initially distributed according to $u_0(x)$ admits a sampling distribution when $m>1$. Specifically, we show that $\mathbb{E}[T_n]=2n-4+\frac{2}{m-1}\sum_{j=2}^{n-1}\frac{1}{2j-1}$, which converges to $2n-4+\frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi m)}$ as $m\to 1^+$. This result extends the previously established formula $\mathbb{E}[T_n]=2(\psi(2n-1)-\psi(1))$ for the coalescence time in the critical Feller diffusion ($m=1$). Furthermore, we derive the full sampling distribution for $T_n$ and explore its implications for the genealogical structure of the process. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations. These results hold significant interest within probability theory and have direct applications in population genetics. Specifically, we provide a rigorous derivation of the sampling distribution for the number of segregating sites in the standard neutral coalesent model, thereby generalizing the corresponding result for the standard neutral infinite sites model in population genetics. Finally, we suggest that our methodology can be adapted to address the sampling distribution for the number of segregating sites in the neutral infinite sites model where the population size grows linearly over time. This model was recently analyzed using a distinct approach by Li and Durbin. Our framework also offers a means to investigate the sampling distribution for the number of private alleles, a topic currently under investigation. To address this, we have developed a simulation for the multi-dimensional Feller diffusion that allows for the tracking of private alleles. This tool is made available here. It is important to note that the dimension of the diffusion process does not influence the coalescence time or the distribution of private alleles. This study examines the scattering dynamics of a single cavity quantum electrodynamics system utilizing diagrammatic methods. We introduce an efficient technique for calculating scattering amplitudes of multi-photon, multi-mode incoming waves confined to a waveguide near a single cavity resonator, explicitly accounting for both dipole and Kerr interactions. By employing a straightforward diagrammatic system, we derive an exact set of equations governing multi-photon scattering processes involving up to four photons. These findings facilitate the precise design of quantum gates and circuits based on linear and nonlinear multi-photon scattering phenomena. Furthermore, our results enable the accurate determination of multi-photon scattering outcomes in various solid-state and semi-classical setups, thereby establishing a foundation for developing advanced measurement and imaging techniques that leverage Kerr nonlinearity. Finally, we present a proposal to enhance the generation of multi-photon multi-mode outgoing states, which could be implemented in a solid-state context using a single carbon nanotube. This approach is expected to facilitate the creation of new quantum light sources capable of generating multiple photons simultaneously across different modes. Additionally, we demonstrate that multi-photon interference can be utilized to construct a multi-photon beam splitter, with the transmission and reflection probabilities of transmitted and reflected photons being tunable via the detuning of the cavity resonance. Such a device holds significant potential for quantum non-demolition detection of multi-photon multi-mode incoming states. Finally, we show that specific linear combinations of linear and Kerr nonlinear scattering amplitudes can generate a single photon accompanied by an entangled pair of photons, which may aid in the design of efficient sources for multi-photon multi-mode outgoing states. This mechanism operates without requiring a detuning of the detuned Purcell effect, which is essential for generating a single photon. Instead, it relies on adjusting the detuning of the cavity field. Unlike methods that generate multiple photons by driving a dark state, this approach allows for the generation of multiple photons within a bright state, thereby enhancing the emission rate. The proposed mechanism is expected to enable the generation of multiple photons within a broad spectral bandwidth. Additionally, we show that this mechanism can be utilized to construct a single-photon beam splitter, which can be tuned by adjusting the detuning of the cavity field. Boosted Dark Matter offers a promising avenue for investigating well-motivated Dark Matter candidates within the existing LHC framework. In this scenario, Dark Matter interacts with nucleons via spin-dependent forces, facilitating the production of boosted pairs that manifest as mono-jet plus missing energy signatures. We investigate the sensitivity of the jETSM search at the LHC to both existing constraints and new candidates within this framework. Our results demonstrate that jETSM allows for the exploration of spin-dependent cross-sections that are either inaccessible to direct detection experiments or only weakly restricted by them. Furthermore, we highlight that LHC searches for boosted dark matter can constrain spin-dependent dark nucleon interactions up to two orders of magnitude beyond the limits set by Xenon1T. Finally, we examine the extension of jETSM to semi-visible final states and show that such signals can be effectively isolated from standard QCD backgrounds. This capability enables the investigation of spin-dependent couplings between fermionic Dark Matter and gluons, reaching mass scales beyond 10 TeV. Collectively, these findings underscore the critical role of jETSM and the necessity of LHC searches for boosted dark matter. These efforts will set stringent limits on spin-dependent interactions between Dark Matter and nucleons, complementing and surpassing current direct detection achievements. Conventional non-coherent differential detection for continuous phase modulation (CPM) offers robustness against channel impairments caused by oscillator frequency mismatches, eliminating the need for complex digital oscillator control. However, this approach necessitates a large optimization delay ($D_{opt}$) to ensure high detection performance, which results in significant latency and reduced throughput. This paper introduces a simplified algorithm to determine $D_{opt}$, replacing the original exhaustive search method. By limiting the search space, the proposed algorithm offers the same detection performance with substantially reduced computational complexity. Furthermore, an optimized formulation is developed to further minimize the search space in specific scenarios, thereby enhancing performance and cutting computation time by a factor of four. These benefits are achieved with minimal additional design effort. The validity of the algorithm is confirmed through numerical simulations across various CPM formats and mismatch parameters. Additionally, the methodology is demonstrated using two common CPM schemes: 8-PSK and 16-ary orthogonal CPM. The optimization algorithm can also be applied to other differential detectors that employ multiple branches. The ultimate objective is to enable rapid determination of $D_{opt}$ for any given set of parameters, thereby facilitating a more efficient design of non-coherent detectors. This is particularly advantageous for systems with limited latency and throughput capabilities. The algorithm is also applicable to other differential detectors that do not rely on branch expansion. Finally, an extension of this work is presented to further minimize $D_{opt}$ by jointly optimizing other parameters. The proposed algorithm is expected to significantly advance the field of non-coherent detection. Future research will focus on further reducing $D_{opt}$ through joint parameter optimization. Reward learning has recently gained significant attention due to its potential to substantially reduce human annotation efforts. However, this reduction is often compromised by a time overhead, as early iterations may yield low-quality policies that require extended periods to evaluate. This paper introduces visually assisted cluster ranking, a method that segments policy evaluations into multiple clusters to enable efficient feedback on initial policies. By leveraging visualizations to assist humans in rapidly identifying high and low-performing policies within each cluster, the approach ensures that early policies are effectively utilized for improvement. Empirical results on two benchmark reinforcement learning environments demonstrate that visually assisted cluster ranking can substantially reduce reward learning time overhead. Furthermore, we release an open-source library to facilitate future applications of visually assisted cluster ranking. Our source code is available at https://github.com/ryanli123/vacarewlearn. Within the framework of noncommutative space-time, this study examines nucleon structure functions at fixed $x_{bj}$ using the light-cone gauge. Additionally, the paper provides a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon. It is further demonstrated that both $F_2(x_{bj},Q^2)$ and $F_1(x_{bj},Q^2)$ receive corrections of order $\theta Q$, reflecting sensitivity to noncommutativity at high energies. Finally, based on the operator product expansion, expressions for structure functions in $D$-dimensional noncommutative space-time are derived. For $D=4$, these expressions reduce to the standard formulas found in Ref. [1]. This study investigates topological line responses in spatially extended frustrated Toric code models, which arise when a chemical potential term for line defects is incorporated into the standard Toric code Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that these topological line responses correspond to the "frustrated" magnetoelectric effect. Specifically, the response takes the form of $\frac{\theta E}{2\pi}$-type electric fields generated by magnetic flux inserted along spatial lines. Furthermore, we show that this topological line answer can be derived from the four-dimensional topological theta term present in the effective action for dual photon fields across the phase where this response is observable. Additionally, we calculate the topological electric field resulting from magnetic flux and verify that this field satisfies Poisson's equation. Our findings are validated through exact numerical calculations for a simple lattice consisting of two sites in each dimension. Finally, we suggest that these mechanisms may be utilized to design topological line experiments or devices within frustrated toric code systems, such as the quantum honeycomb model and quantum rhombic lattice models. To achieve this, one could either construct new frustrated toric code systems capable of producing magnetoelectric effects or develop techniques to introduce topological line responses into existing models. We also examine potential experimental approaches for realizing these topological line responses. We investigate the statistical properties of eigenvalues and eigenvectors in random band matrices distorted by a finite-rank complex deformation. Building on the recent formula by Feige, Kozma, and Shahshahani [FeKoS16] regarding eigenvalue deformations under unitary invariance, we demonstrate that the formula extends to the case where unitary invariance is broken, provided the rank of the perturbation remains small relative to the matrix size. Furthermore, we show that under this small-rank condition and with band width scaling as $N^{2/3}$, the sigma-model approximation becomes valid. This specific regime enables the rigorous control of correlation functions in deformations of Wigner and Dyson-Brownian motion, thereby confirming a conjecture by Feige, Kozma, and Shahshahani [FeKoS16]. Additionally, within the specified band width regime, we derive precise results for random band matrices featuring independent Gaussian entries, where the perturbation rank is small compared to the band width. In this scenario, we prove that only the first two moments of the original random matrix determine the low-rank deformation's impact. Although pre-trained language models have achieved significant advancements in dialogue processing, they are typically trained on surface-level text, lacking an explicit grasp of semantic representations. Consequently, these models often struggle with surface form ambiguities and fail to effectively leverage external knowledge. To address these issues, we introduce Semantic Text to Text Pre-training (SeTTMP), a novel pre-training framework designed for dialogue understanding. This approach incorporates a semantic-aware pre-training task that employs a knowledge base to reconstruct dialogue utterances at the semantic level rather than the surface level. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that SeTTTMP yields substantial performance gains across various dialogue tasks, including dialog state tracking and neural response selection, when compared to models trained without pre-training on the MMDuT dataset. Algorithmic interpretability is essential for establishing trust, accountability, and ethical standards, yet it remains challenging to define and measure. We propose a framework based on algorithmic learning, where algorithms are conceptualized as "teachers" and human learners as the recipients of knowledge. Within this framework, a teaching algorithm is considered interpretable if a learner can acquire its underlying knowledge with minimal difficulty. Consequently, the cognitive complexity of the learning process serves as a metric for interpretability. We introduce a cognitive complexity score (CCS) tailored for this framework, demonstrating that it is generally consistent and effectively distingu between the interpretability of different algorithms. For time-series forecasting, the CCS indicates that our prior assumptions about an algorithm's cognitive complexity align with empirical evidence showing that models learn representational knowledge to varying degrees. Furthermore, we illustrate that higher cognitive complexity hinders human understanding of algorithmic decisions and explains why users exhibit a preference for interpretable models. Ultimately, this research provides a valuable tool for evaluating and comparing the interpretability of algorithms. By clarifying the relationship between algorithms and their users, our framework fosters a more harmonious interaction between human intelligence and algorithmic algorithms. Additionally, we believe this approach offers valuable insights for AI researchers, potentially guiding the development of future algorithms. For human researchers, understanding various algorithmic learning mechanisms can deepen their comprehension of AI systems and offer valuable perspectives for their own research. Finally, this work addresses a longstanding question in educational psychology regarding how to measure a teacher's effectiveness, suggesting that a teacher should not necessarily be one who imparts knowledge easily, but rather one that its learners can master with relative ease. This conclusion holds significant implications for the field of algorithmic interpretability. This study introduces a novel statistical framework for analyzing extreme values that aligns with the classical approach yet leverages the properties of Poisson processes. The framework's primary benefit is enabling the intrinsic reparameterisation of the Poisson process to minimise dependency between the number of exceedances and the parameters governing point positions. Within this context, we examine a block maxima model with a unit threshold; its shape parameter is reinterpreted as the intensity of the Poisson process for values exceeding the threshold. This reparameterisation is integral to our proposed analysis, which employs non-informative intrinsic priors for Bayesian inference. We present simulation studies comparing this method to other common non-informative priors and informative priors derived from the conjugate Normal distribution for linear models. These comparisons are evaluated using Bayesian model selection metrics, specifically the marginal likelihood and the fully Bayesian version of the extended Klefsjö distance. Finally, we apply the method to two real-world datasets: a collection of extreme wind speeds and a time series of Australian rainfall. In both cases, we conduct extreme value analysis, perform model selection, and generate predictive distributions for return levels and return functions. A key contribution is the first-time use of Poisson process intrinsic priors to address the conjugacy between block maxima and their corresponding exceedances. Furthermore, we advocate for fully Bayesian predictive inference to assess return levels and return functions, while also supporting model selection based on marginal likelihood. Overall, this work demonstrates a new approach to statistical inference for extremes, fostering connections with broader areas of statistics. A comprehensive R-package is available to facilitate analysis using this intrinsic prior framework. The package is open-source, designed for reproducibility, and includes routines for predictive inference and model selection. Additionally, the R-package supports the conjugate Normal prior framework, allowing for a direct comparison between the two methods. All analyses, including predictive inference and model selection, are conducted using conjugate Normal priors. The paper introduces the problem of maximizing the average cross-sectional area through a point within a convex body. It identifies the average cross-section problem introduced by K. Borsuk in 1915 as a significant subset of this broader issue. Furthermore, it establishes that no universal minimum or maximum values exist for the average cross section in dimensions $d \geq 3$. The study also outlines methods for identifying specific regions within a convex body where the average cross section attains either a global or a local extremum. The results include exact characterization formulas for these extrema, alongside practical algorithms and heuristics for locating the corresponding regions. Additionally, numerical examples are provided for the respective extrema. The work includes a discussion of the historical development of the problem, practical algorithms, numerical results, and potential applications. A bibliography containing 100 references is also appended. In recent years, knowledge graphs (KGs) have become increasingly significant for various natural language processing (NLP) applications. While neural methods have been widely adopted, there remains a need for interpretable, logical, and symbolic knowledge representation. This paper presents the COMET-ATOMIC 2020 challenge, which focuses on linking the ATOMIC dataset with Commonsense Knowledge (CSK) to enhance open-domain question-answering (QA). The dataset offers large-scale, diverse knowledge covering general common sense, world knowledge, and social norms. Seven teams submitted a total of 11 solutions, utilizing a variety of approaches including large-scale pre-training on corpora, fine-tuning pre-trained models, training from scratch, and a combination of symbolic and neural methods. The results underscore the potential of large-scale pre-training and the benefits of integrating symbolic and neural components. Furthermore, this work demonstrates how extensive CScan transform open-domain QA into a closely supervised task, thereby establishing a new benchmark for evaluation. This article details the reduction pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey, a project mapping the Galactic plane at 70, 160, and submillimeter wavelengths using HEBI detectors on the SCUBA-2 instrument at the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array. The pipeline, which is fully automated, performs all necessary steps for HEBI detector data from HIFI instruments, ranging from data ingestion and calibration to the generation of level 1 products. It has been successfully applied to all Hi-GAL observations conducted between 2010 and 2013. Although HEBI detectors share certain characteristics with HIFI instruments, they also possess unique features necessitating specific additional processing steps. These special requirements are thoroughly examined and explained within this paper. Additionally, the study outlines the creation of level 1 products for HEBI instruments, detailing the necessary observations and the application of corrections. A comparison with the older Hi-GAL instrument at the Submillimeter Common User Bolometer Array 1 telescope in the Atacama Large Millimeter Array is also included. The authors conclude that the developed pipeline is highly effective for all Hi-GAL observations and HEBI instruments, facilitating the production of reliable and accurate data cubes. We have conducted a spectroscopic analysis of 11 first-interaction blue stragglers in the globular cluster NGC 2808, utilizing spectra obtained with the VLT/FORS2 and VLT/UVES instruments. By employing a homogeneous analysis pipeline, we determined the chemical abundances of iron and 13 additional elements for these stars. The resulting mean metallicity is [Fe/H] = -0.97 ± 0.05, which aligns closely with prior studies. The [Ca/Fe] abundance shows significant scatter, indicating a metallicity spread of at least 0.15 dex among these stars. This finding demonstrates that the spread in metallicity extends to elements heavier than iron. Our results corroborate the conclusion that the horizontal branch of NGC 2808 arises from a single-burst population exhibiting a substantial range of metallicities. Additionally, we confirm that the scatter in Ca/Fe abundance is not caused by measurement uncertainties. We also report a mean magnesium-to-iron ratio of [Mg/Fe] = 0.76 ± 0.05, consistent with other globular clusters of comparable metallicity. Finally, the abundance of sodium in NGC 2808's blue stragglers is approximately 0.2 dex lower than the value of 0.4 dex typical of second-generation stars in other clusters. These outcomes further support the theory that blue straggler populations are formed through binary mergers. We also discuss the implications of our findings for the proposed link between the horizontal branch morphology and the binary fraction within the cluster. Future work will involve a more extensive spectroscopic study of NGC 2808's blue straggler population. Single file systems serve as streamlined models for investigating one-dimensional physical systems. In this study, we analytically derive the full first exit time statistics using partition functions that account for the entropy of the $q$-state up states, characterized by a non-zero entropy. A key result is the demonstration that these exit time statistics are primarily governed by the system's entropy at the boundary, revealing a maximal entropy exit scenario. Consequently, we illustrate the connection between these boundary entropy values and an effective non-linear entropic force within single file diffusion. Furthermore, we determine a universal scaling law for first exit times in asymmetric single file diffusion by analyzing the entropy-scaled mean square displacement (MSD). Finally, we validate our theoretical findings against both comprehensive numerical simulations and Monte Carlo results. The outcomes of these Monte Carlo simulations are available in a dedicated data repository. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python package to facilitate the simulation of single file diffusion. Our findings suggest that the entropic spring model and effective non-linear entropic force are fundamental to describing one-dimensional diffusion. Quantum mechanics differs from classical statistics in that its measurement inferences lack a direct analog to the standard Bayesian update of probability distributions. A significant challenge arises because applying Bayes' theorem naively to quantum measurement inferences can produce absurd results, such as collapsing a pure state into mixing. This occurs because normalizing the post-measurement state density operator—essential for a subsequent state $\rho_B=\rho_{SB}^{(2)}|1\rangle\langle 1|_{S}\otimes|1\rangle\langle 1\rangle_{B}$—removes the original measurement outcome information, rendering it insufficient for making future predictions. To address this, we utilize the purifying environment degree of freedom to construct an extended density operator $\tilde{\rho}_{B}$. By employing a quantum Bayes' theorem, we derive updated state operators $\tilde{\rho}_{S}$ and $\tildf{\rho}_{E}$ from $\tilde{\rho}_{E}$ without losing measurement outcome information. These updated operators serve as the quantum measurement inference counterparts to the marginal distributions used in classical Bayesian updates. Furthermore, we demonstrate the consistency of measurement inferences by explicitly showing the identity $\mathrm{Tr}_{E}[\tilde{\rho}_{B}]=\rho_{B}$. This relationship confirms that the probability distributions derived from the marginal distributions of the state operator $\rho_{B}$ remain invariant whether calculated before or after performing a projective measurement on the environment. Consequently, this ensures the consistency of measurement inferences in quantum mechanics. Additionally, this study offers a comprehensive review of the quantum Bayes' theorem, a fundamental tool for analyzing quantum measurement inference problems. We illustrate the theory's applicability through the analysis of a quantum state tomography problem. Finally, we explore the relationship between quantum and classical Bayesian theorems, revealing that the quantum Bayes' theorem can be derived from the classical Bayesian theorems when applied to a quantum state with a density matrix representation. This indicates that the two theorems are not independent but rather represent different expressions of the same principle. Thus, this research advances the understanding of quantum measurement in a more complete and profound manner. This study reports initial findings regarding finite volume corrections to the equation of state, trace anomaly, and speed of sound for two specific models: a free, massless scalar theory and quenched QCD utilizing periodic boundary conditions. Additionally, we provide preliminary results for quenched QCD under Dirichlet boundary conditions. Our analysis focuses on systems where the box size $L$ is comparable to or smaller than the correlation length, specifically examining volumes equivalent to those swept by the PHENIX and ALICE colliders at energies near and above the nominal RHIC collision settings. In this regime, finite volume effects are substantial, and we demonstrate that standard finite size scaling relations are modified in a manner that depends on the boundary conditions. These alterations persist even as the system size approaches infinity, suggesting a new type of intermediate scaling behavior linked to boundary conditions. Consequently, we contend that extracting precise signal-to-noise data for lattice QCD observables from small, anisotropic volumes—such as those produced by high-energy heavy-ion collisions—will be challenging. This difficulty is further compounded by the need to model hadron resonances, which are difficult to treat in a finite system. We conclude that either theoretical or experimental efforts must be directed toward either developing improved resonance models for small volumes or investigating the physics of increasingly anisotropic systems. In this context, we also address the issue of boundary condition artifacts within the chiral limit. Finally, we offer some preliminary comments on the potential relevance of these findings to finite volume lattice QCD. A detailed report will be submitted to Physical Review D. The search for interstellar life has traditionally focused on the visible and near-infrared spectra, where molecules like water and carbon dioxide are prevalent. However, since Earth's atmosphere blocks ultraviolet (UV) radiation, we have historically been unable to perform ground-based astronomical photometry in the UV. This study introduces a novel approach to construct a ground-based Lyman-alpha filter telescope. We developed a prototype spectral device featuring a 51 nm full-width half-maximum (FWHM) bandpass centered at 121.6 nm, mounted on a small Cassegrain reflector with a 30.5 cm aperture. This device successfully isolated the Lyman-alpha emission line from the hot interstellar hydrogen halo of the Andromeda galaxy (M31), isolating it from the hotter neutral hydrogen gas found in Earth's exosphere and the Lyman-beta line. Furthermore, we utilized M31's Lyman-alpha line to benchmark the device's transmission and spectral resolution. By employing a simple, cost-effective setup, we demonstrated that this instrument can isolate the Lyman-alpha line for scientific study. These findings hold significant promise for future space-based observatories, such as the proposed NASA Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), which will utilize Lyman-alpha photometry to investigate the intergalactic medium, detect exoplanetary atmospheres, and identify biosignatures. Our results indicate that a 2-meter telescope equipped with a 51 nm bandpass filter centered on Lyman-alpha could achieve a signal-to-noise ratio of 3 per second on M31, enabling the detection of the Lyman-alpha emission line of the Andromeda galaxy's hot interstellar hydrogen. This level of sensitivity is comparable to what a 4-meter HWO-class telescope could achieve with a 101 nm bandpass filter. Additionally, we demonstrated that a 10-meter HWO-class telescope could detect the Lyman-alpha emission line of a hot hydrogen halo around a nearby dwarf galaxy, such as Segue 2, using a 51 nm bandpass filter at a signal-to-noise ratio of 3 per second. These results provide a promising outlook for Lyman-alpha photometry as a tool for detecting the hydrogen halos of nearby dwarf galaxies and for characterizing the atmospheres of exoplanets. The instrument described in this work is currently available for public use. This paper introduces a distributed algorithm for graph-filter-based optimal control in graph symmetric systems (GSS). In a multi-agent setup where each agent manages a local GSS, every agent receives measurements from a small subset of its neighbors and uses them to reconstruct the system's state. Leveraging this reconstructed state, each neighbor computes a local control input and control cost, constructs a local filter, and performs a graph-based frequency-domain analysis of the system's response. Subsequently, a centralized algorithm is employed to optimize the frequency responses of these local filters, thereby minimizing the overall estimation and control costs. Experimental results demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in reducing total system costs. The proposed approach is particularly suited for distributed control tasks, offering the ability to optimize frequency responses for the entire network while requiring minimal communication per agent. Additionally, total costs can be efficiently monitored and adjusted by adjusting the number of neighbors each agent connects to. This work extends our preliminary findings presented in [1]. This paper investigates a new approach to keyless authentication for independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sources over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels. The proposed framework utilizes Li et al.'s [IEEE Trans. Info. Forensics and Security 14 (2019)] randomized encoder, adapted to operate on a Gaussian channel. The investigation involves examining a specific channel input distribution and deriving the resulting output distribution. Furthermore, the framework introduces a verification stage where the received signal is accepted as an authentic message if it falls within a defined set of "plausible" signals. We established an acceptance criterion and formulated the problem as a maximization to determine the optimal criterion that ensures a specified false acceptance rate. Finally, numerical results are presented to evaluate the effectiveness of this framework. To my knowledge, this represents the first application of keyless authentication in an AWGN channel. This study re-examines the motion of charged particles within a rigid periodic potential, commonly known as the "washboard model," under the influence of a constant electric field. By employing a phase-space analysis, we derive analytical expressions for the mean square transit time and displacement over a single lattice period, valid for both low and high transverse momentum. These findings are evaluated against numerical simulations, from which we also extract transit times for a single superlattice period at zero field, applicable to both tunneling and hopping regimes, using full numerical integration. Furthermore, we calculate the dispersionless transport parameters required to replicate full numerical solutions for low transverse momentum, thereby determining charge carrier velocities and wavefunction widths. Finally, we suggest potential charge carrier candidates for dispersionless transport in periodic potentials, including electrons in graphene and topological insulators, as well as excitons in two-dimensional materials. We anticipate that the derived formulas will serve as a valuable tool for analyzing experimental data and designing new devices reliant on dispersionless transport in washboard potentials. Fine-grained named entity typing (FNET) classifies entities into a vast number of types, often exceeding 10,000. We introduce FNET-RH, a novel framework that leverages the unbounded expansion and rich geometric structure of hyperbolic space to model the hierarchical entity type taxonomy. This approach offers a compact and effective representation for entities, facilitating more accurate type prediction. FNET-RH employs a compact entity representation to model relationships between entities and their types during representation learning. By utilizing hyperbolic space, the framework effectively captures the inherent hierarchy of entity types, thereby enhancing classification accuracy. Extensive experiments across three fine-grained named entity recognition tasks demonstrate that FNET-RH consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and parameter efficiency. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that each component of our framework contributes significantly to overall performance. Fine-grained named entity typing (FNET) involves labeling entities with a large and diverse set of types, often numbering over 10,000. We present a new refinement-based hyperbolic geometry framework, FNET-RH, that capitalizes on the unique characteristics of hyperbolic space to represent the hierarchical structure of entity types. This framework employs a compact and effective representation that enhances FNET performance. Specifically, we propose a refinement mechanism that utilizes both local and global information regarding entities and types throughout the learning process. This mechanism employs two learning objectives: one to guide representation learning toward a more refined understanding, and another to improve type prediction accuracy. By integrating these components, we achieve a more accurate classification of entity types. Extensive experiments across three fine-grained named entity recognition tasks demonstrate that our framework consistently surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both performance and parameter efficiency. Additionally, ablation studies validate that each component of our framework significantly contributes to the observed improvements. As the demand for cloud computing services grows, so does the need for enhanced load balancing techniques. In cloud environments, virtual machines (VMs) are hosted on physical servers to serve diverse applications. Consequently, uneven workloads across these servers can significantly impact response times and throughput. This study introduces a novel approach called "Prepartition," which allocates a specific CPU share to each VM based on predefined requirements. By ensuring that resources are preallocated according to actual needs, the method effectively mitigates internal fragmentation. Experimental results demonstrate that Prepartition outperforms the existing LOAD method, offering superior load balancing and improved response times. Given that response time is a critical metric in cloud services, Prepartition is well-suited for deployment in cloud data centers. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1997/prepartition. We invite readers to compare the outcomes of this refined implementation against the original code. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the results obtained from the expanded code. To facilitate a thorough understanding of our work, we have also included a comparative performance analysis of various load-balancing strategies.
