This paper introduces the Fixed Point Network, a new architecture designed to compute game-theoretic equilibria in normal-form games, including Bayesian variants. We demonstrate that the team of agents maximizing expected payoffs in both the main game and its associated decision problems corresponds to the equilibria of a specific stochastic game. Consequently, we leverage a recent reinforcement learning method for stochastic game equilibrium computation to propose an efficient deep network capable of predicting these equilibria. Empirical results indicate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and sample efficiency. Furthermore, we apply this method to the task of equilibrium prediction, showing that it helps large language models more effectively acquire decision-theoretic knowledge. Finally, we utilize the learned equilibrium prediction network as an inductive bias within a question-answering system. Experimental evidence confirms that the system can answer equilibrium-related questions in natural language that previous methods failed to address. Notably, we also observe that the system is able to derive new games and theoretical results. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of such a system being able to perform these tasks. The complete code is available at \url{https://github.com/Chen-Yang-Lin/Fixed_Point_Network}. This study addresses two primary objectives. First, we establish tight bounds for various causal effects within stratified populations. Unlike most existing literature that relies on strong assumptions such as bounded potential outcomes or utility functions, our approach focuses on the covariance between causal variables and stratification indicators. We derive tight bounds under the constraint that the joint distribution of causal variables and stratification indicators follows a Gaussian model. These findings yield actionable insights for high-dimensional settings and offer a novel perspective on causal inference using deep learning. Second, we introduce a new framework for estimating causal effects in highly dimensional environments where causal variables interact with covariates. In such contexts, causal variables often depend on covariates, making traditional methods like linear regression or simple MLPs inadequate. To overcome these limitations, we propose a neural architecture where causal variables are represented as the outputs of neural networks trained on covariates. We apply our derived bounds within this framework to derive an efficient algorithm for causal inference. We validate our method's efficacy through extensive numerical experiments and two empirical case studies involving real-world data. Specifically, we perform causal inference on two deep learning benchmarks: ImageNet and CIFAR100, where we examine how causal variables respond to changes in input images. Additionally, we address a real-world medical challenge by determining the causal impact of radiation therapy on prostate cancer survival. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of applying causal deep learning to a medical domain. Finally, we have open-sourced all relevant code for this project. Attacking critical infrastructure has become a significant security concern, yet most existing research focuses on detectable attacks. In contrast, stealthy attacks are designed to remain invisible to standard monitoring systems. This paper introduces a predictive monitoring framework capable of detecting stealthy attacks on linear-time invariant systems, leveraging the fact that such attacks typically leave minimal physical traces. The core concept involves using an accurate system model to generate reference signals that, when compared with actual sensor data, can reveal attacks even if they evade conventional defenses. The study also examines the impact of measurement noise and modeling errors, which can mask attack signatures and reduce the effectiveness of predictive monitoring. To address these uncertainties, predictive monitoring is compared against current detection methods. Furthermore, a real-world experimental case study validates the approach by successfully identifying stealthy attacks on a DC microgrid, demonstrating the efficacy of predictive monitoring in such scenarios. Finally, strategies for optimizing sensor placement to enhance detection capabilities are explored. Overall, this work provides a novel and effective method for detecting and mitigating advanced persistent threats against critical infrastructure. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions and applications of predictive monitoring.

Document summarization focuses on selecting the most significant paragraphs to create a concise yet representative overview of an information source. While many state-of-the-art methods exist for English, there is currently no superior generalizable solution for non-English languages. This study introduces GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised model designed specifically for Indian languages. GAE-ISumm utilizes an enhanced version of the EchoGraph+ algorithm, featuring novel graph construction strategies and modified edge weighting mechanisms. It incorporates both semantic and lexical information through the integration of pre-trained language models with the salience computation process. We evaluated our approach across six Indian languages using a newly developed, large-scale, high-quality dataset gathered from news articles, religious texts, and government documents. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms the standard EchoGraph+ and other leading techniques in both qualitative and quantitative metrics. Furthermore, we show that increasing the size of the training corpus continues to improve the model's performance. The dataset and implementation are made publicly available to support future research. GAE-ISumm is expected to advance document summarization research by providing a robust, high-performing, generalizable solution for Indian languages. **Aims.** This study seeks to restrict the masses and orbital separations of potential binary companions for the accelerating stars $\zeta$~Teach, $\zeta$~For, $\zeta$~Ori, $\zeta$~Tau, and $\zeta$~Cen. **Methods.** We conducted a systematic search for companions by analyzing archival data from 2MASS, WISE, Gaia DR2, and Gaia DR3, alongside new observations from Gaia DR3, the USNO-B1.0 Catalog, and the USNO-A2.0 Catalog. Additionally, we performed astrometric fitting using Gaia DR3 and conducted follow-up near-infrared imaging of the $\zeta$~Teach, $\zeta$~For, $\zeta$~Ori, $\zeta$~Tau, and $\zeta$~Cen fields with the Gemini South and Very Large Telescope. **Results.** We identified a likely binary companion to $\zeta$~Ori and established upper limits on the masses and separations of potential companions to $\zeta$~Teach, $\zeta$~For, $\zeta$~Ori, $\zeta$~Tau, and $\zeta$~Cen. **Conclusions.** The detected binary companion to $\zeta$~Ori is a low-mass M dwarf, suggesting that the astrometric wobble observed in $\zeta$~Ori and $\zeta$~Ori~A is driven by this low-mass object. Consequently, the previously hypothesized massive brown dwarf or low-mass star orbiting $\zeta$~Ori~B is ruled out. Furthermore, the non-detection of companions to $\zeta$~Teach, $\zeta$~For, $\zeta$~Tau, and $\zeta$~Cen constrains the existence of any unseen companions to these stars. These findings offer valuable insights into the formation and evolution of stars and their binary systems. The research data and outcomes are accessible via https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/staf1008. This work contributes to the broader investigation of accelerating stars, a topic highlighted in the 2023 Astronomers' Telegram (ATel) #14545. The autoencoder serves as a fundamental element in various machine learning tasks, including clustering, outlier detection, and dimensionality reduction. In a standard autoencoder architecture, the hidden state is derived from an unconstrained transformation of the input data. This study extends that approach by introducing a regularized transformation, which enables the modeling of specific characteristics within the input data. Specifically, we integrate a regularized least-squares matrix transformation into the input layer and assess its performance on real-world datasets. Empirical results indicate that this enhanced architecture surpasses the conventional autoencoder architecture. Furthermore, we demonstrate its utility in a clustering task, where it successfully identifies the optimal number of clusters for a given dataset. Additionally, we find that this approach is robust to noise, accurately recovering the underlying manifold structure even when noise is present. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1992/LSVAE. Our methodology is particularly well-suited for scenarios where data distribution is unknown. We also provide a repository of pre-trained models for several common datasets, which can be accessed at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1992/LSVAE-Pretrained-Models. Both repositories are maintained by the corresponding author. We acknowledge that this approach may be less effective when dealing with datasets where the data distribution is known. Keywords: autoencoder, outlier detection, clustering, manifold learning, dimensional reduction.

The growing adoption of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies has significantly enhanced daily life by offering numerous practical applications. However, security and privacy within smart home environments remain critical yet underdeveloped issues. This paper introduces a low-cost, secure, and private framework for smart homes that leverages the distributed nature of private blockchains. By employing the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) algorithm to localize smart home appliances, the study demonstrates their ability to detect anomalies such as unattended cooking and missing children. Furthermore, it utilizes machine learning and the Random Forest (RF) algorithm to identify these anomalies and forecast children's movements. This approach offers a secure, privacy-preserving solution for monitoring and managing smart homes, effectively detecting abnormal activities and predicting user behavior. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework outperforms existing solutions in both security and privacy. The proposed method is evaluated against two alternatives: a centralized blockchain and Fog Computing. To ensure the method's viability for real-world deployment, an analysis of its computational complexity was conducted. The findings reveal that the EKF algorithm is the most efficient for smart home monitoring and management tasks. The contributions of this work include: i) designing a secure, privacy-preserving framework for smart homes; ii) developing an efficient strategy to predict child movements within these homes; and iii) proposing a novel security and privacy framework for smart home management. This framework employs the EKF algorithm for appliance localization, Random Forest (RF) for anomaly detection, and HyperLogLog (HLL) for data summarization. Additionally, it addresses the primary security and privacy challenges currently facing smart home systems. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed approach was performed to demonstrate its superiority over existing solutions. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 details the proposed solution; Section 4 presents the evaluation and discussion; and Section 5 provides the conclusion. This study introduces a deep learning-based quantization method for calculating likelihood values associated with Gray-coded modulation formats. By employing a customized convolutional neural network, the approach effectively reduces computational complexity while maintaining state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, the research investigates the potential of integrating auxiliary layers into the architecture to achieve like-as-possible performance with an even smaller model size. The method is evaluated across a variety of conditions, including Gaussian and Gabor noise, G.652 and G.655 standard optical fibers, and fiber characteristics found in real-world transmission systems. Additionally, the analysis covers multiple modulation schemes, such as G4, G8, and G12, as well as G.652 fibers exhibiting Gordon-PM4 effects. The results demonstrate significant computational advantages, with complexity reductions of 60%, 70%, and 75% for G4, G8, and G12 modulations, respectively, compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the achieved like-as-possible performance surpasses that of non-Gray-coded schemes by 0.1, 0.2, and 0.2 dB, and also outperforms existing Gray-coded approaches by 0.1 and 0.2 dB. Finally, tests conducted on G.652 fibers under Gordon-PM4 effects in G4 and G8 configurations confirm results consistent with standard scenarios. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengzhijun1992/Deep-Learning-Quantizer. Notably, the authors emphasize the method's successful application and validation within a real-world transmission system.

This study introduces novel parameterized algorithms for the classical problem of determining if a directed acyclic graph possesses an upward planar drawing. The findings encompass a new fixed-parameter algorithm based on the count of sources, a XP-algorithm defined by treewidth, and another fixed-parameter algorithm utilizing treedepth. All three methods stem from an innovative framework that integrates SPQR tree-decompositions with parameterized techniques. This approach not only unifies but also extends prior tractability results for series-parallel digraphs, single-source digraphs, and outerplanar digraphs. Additionally, we present a straightforward reduction demonstrating that upward planar recognition is FPT-hard when parameterized by the number of feedback arc sets, and it is para-NP-complete parameterized by feedback vertex set size. This paper presents a method for analyzing noisy, crowdsourced data, which is increasingly accessible but often annotated by unreliable participants, resulting in probabilistic labels rather than definitive class assignments. To address the uncertainty inherent in individual annotator reliability, we employ ensemble modeling. We treat the distribution of an annotator's historical labels as a soft-max distribution, defining the annotator's confidence as the annotator's soft-max. We introduce a novel ensemble strategy that leverages these soft-max distributions to dynamically weight the contributions of individual annotators. Furthermore, we propose a new metric that quantifies the uncertainty within an annotator's historical labels using entropy. This method is applied to a contemporary dataset from the NLP community that has recently gained significant attention. The findings demonstrate that our approach yields superior classification accuracy and robustness compared to existing methods. Additionally, the proposed method offers a straightforward mechanism for identifying and filtering out unreliable annotators. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/EM-HM-EU. Finally, we provide a tutorial on using our method to analyze and filter labels from a dataset via the AWS serverless platform on which our method is deployed. This tutorial is available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/EM-HM-EU. By offering a user-friendly deployment for a method popular among NLP researchers, we aim to facilitate its adoption by the community. We provide step-by-step instructions to analyze and filter the dataset's labels. This framework enables researchers to quickly and easily experiment with their own datasets, allowing for a more rapid comparison of our method against baseline approaches. Given that our method relies on standard classification techniques, it can be readily adapted to any dataset. We have made our method available on AWS Lambda, allowing researchers to deploy it with a single command. This eliminates the need for complex coding or the maintenance of personal servers, thereby significantly lowering the barrier to entry for researchers. We believe this accessibility will substantially enhance the adoption of our approach within the community. We provide a high-level walkthrough of the method's execution on the dataset and a high-level overview of the deployment process on AWS. The execution time is approximately 10 minutes, and the command required to deploy the method is `aws lambda invoke --function-name EM-HM-EU /dev/stdout sample-data.json results.json`. The tutorial is available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/EM-HM-EU. We conclude by outlining the method's advantages, such as enhanced accuracy and reliability through the dynamic weighting

We demonstrate exponential decay in the Hölder norm for transfer operators acting on smooth observables within uniformly and nonuniformly expanding semiflows that exhibit exponential decay of correlations. This decay arises from a fractal structure formed by points that do not experience exponential contraction along the stable direction, encompassing all nontransient points under the stated conditions. These findings generalize prior results from rapidly mixing semiflows to systems with exponential (but not rapid) decay of correlations, covering examples like geometrically exponential mixing Anosov semiflows and uniformly mixing reversible Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) torus winding flows. Additionally, we establish a novel example of a nonhyperbolic uniformly expanding semiflow demonstrating nonquadratic decay of correlations, alongside insights into the relationship between transfer operator norm decay rates and correlation decay rates for semiflows. These methods also apply to one-dimensional nonhyperbolic maps, yielding, alongside quadratic mixing rates, an example map with nonhyperbolic fixed points, mixed contraction and noncontraction, subexponential mixing, and transfer operator decay rates that vary with regularity. The validity of these results extends to semiflows defined on manifolds with boundaries, provided specific boundary conditions are met. Notably, we establish polynomial mixing for uniformly expanding reversible Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) torus winding flows, achieving a faster rate than previous studies. These systems consist of maps with hyperbolic and weakly nonhyperbolic fixed points, subject to decay of correlations, and are linked to transfer operators on smooth observables. The proofs rely on fractal splitting lemmas, shadowing lemmas, and fractal covering lemmas, with all results generalizable to semiflows on manifolds with boundaries. The methodology also applies to one-dimensional maps, offering a unified approach to maps with monotonic, piecewise monotonic, parabolic, and weakly nonparabolic fixed points, thereby unifying and extending existing work on transfer operators, fractal structures, and mixing rates. These insights are applicable to maps with monotonic fixed points, piecewise monotonic maps, parabolic maps, and weakly nonparabolic maps. Strong $t$-covering arrays serve as generalized orthogonal arrays (OA). While Small Size Strength $2$ Orthogonal Arrays have been extensively studied, research on generalized OAs remains limited. This work investigates the structure of Small Strength-$2$ Covering Arrays (CS2CAs) with specific levels and $v$ values, where the count $v$ represents the range of symbols for any pair of columns. We demonstrate that for CS2CAs with 4 columns, the value $v$ cannot take odd primes as factors. The findings in this study lay a foundation for analyzing the structure of CS2CAs with 5 columns. Furthermore, we present a new approach for constructing generalized OAs using CS2CAs and provide additional examples. We demonstrate that every nonlocal game utilizing a noisymaximally entangled state is decidable, meaning the gap between the highest quantum and classical winning probabilities can be closed in polynomial time. This result stems from a novel transformation of nonlocal games into matrix inclusion problems, which enables the application of algorithms developed by Kaltofen and Lee for computing the greatest invariant of a matrix family. Our findings also hold for games based locally equivalent noisy maximally entangled states. Additionally, we present a distinct proof of the strong quantum value additivity theorem for bipartite systems, a result that facilitates the calculation of quantum values for certain specific games. Finally, we examine the computational complexity associated with estimating the classical value of nonlocal games under noise. While the classical value of a noisy Bell-KS scenario is known to be undecidable, the classical values of noisy Bell-CHSH and Bell-polygones are respectively solvable in polynomial time and NP-hard. We further address the complexity of the epsilon strong quantum value problem for these same game classes. Our conclusions are supported by an extensive library of Python and C code. This decidability result extends to nonlocal scenarios involving any finite number of parties, arbitrary finite input and output sets, and either fixed or unfixed measurement numbers. Notably, our findings also apply to the quantum and classical correlation sets defined by any collection of bipartite states and channels. Furthermore, the epsilon strong quantum value problem is classified as FP^PP^#P for bipartite scenarios and as FP^#P for arbitrary finite scenarios. Importantly, these complexity classifications do not require a uniform epsilon. The code library is available at https://github.com/SebastianSchmidt1992/noisy_bell_codes. The existence of a vortex lattice within unconventional superconductors remains a contentious topic. In this study, we demonstrate compelling evidence for such a lattice inside a high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate superconductor, YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6-y}$, containing nanoscale nanoparticles. This lattice was identified through the observation of periodic peaks in both magnetization and magnetization noise as a function of applied magnetic field, with its presence confirmed via magnetization microscopy. We developed a model that accounts for these findings by proposing two distinct regimes of vortex ordering linked to a square-square transition, mirroring the electronic pseudogap phase transition. Furthermore, our findings strongly suggest that vortex lattices can be engineered to switch between different ordered states. These results bolster the hypothesis that the vortex lattice adheres to universal properties governed by the superconducting critical fields, independent of the specific material. Additionally, our results provide compelling evidence for a universal scenario involving competing vortex lattice and electronic orders in high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate superconductors. Finally, the demonstrated control over vortex lattice ordering may facilitate the creation of novel, stable devices for energy harvesting and storage. These outcomes are consistent with a model incorporating electronic pseudogap physics, offering a viable explanation for a broad array of previously reported phenomena associated with vortex lattice behavior in high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprates. Specifically, these results align with a framework where an optimal vortex lattice transition occurs at a critical magnetic field $H^\ast$, which is lower than the upper critical field $H_{c2}$, thereby facilitating an energy gap within the vortex core states. This framework also elucidates a recent report of lattice-induced giant magnetoresistance in cuprate superconductors. Consequently, our findings offer a comprehensive explanation for an extensive body of prior research. In this model, vortex cores possess an energy gap that can be expressed as a fraction of $H_{c2}$, a relationship we establish through analysis of the magnetization data. This gap enables the vortex lattice to exhibit two distinct ordering regimes separated by a square-square transition, a phenomenon that has been widely reported in high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprates. We also discuss the implications of our results for recent reports of lattice-induced giant magnetoresistance. Finally, we outline the implications of our findings for recent claims of lattice melting and demonstrate that our results can account for these observations. Photons are anisotropically emitted from a viscous fluid expanding in local thermal equilibrium. Specifically, thermal photon anisotropy offers a unique window into the specific volume-dependent ratio of shear viscosity to entropy density ($\eta/s$) of the quark-gluon plasma. Unlike heavy ions, thermal photons traverse the entire medium without being significantly influenced by the later-stage hadronic gas, allowing them to probe the strongly-coupled QGP more sensitively. By analyzing STAR data from Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV, we determined that the anisotropic flow coefficients $v_1$ and $v_2$ for photons with $p_T < 5$ GeV/$c$ are $(-0.04 \pm 0.01_{stat} \pm 0.01_{syst})$ and $(0.08 \pm 0.01_{stat} \pm 0.01_{syst})$, respectively. Hydrodynamic models utilizing the iEBE-VISH2 viscosity engine successfully reproduced these experimental $v_1$ and $v_2$ values across various centralities. Our findings indicate that the specific viscosity of the QGP is comparable to the perturbative QCD prediction, with an upper limit of $\eta/s < 0.2$ (90% C.L.). Furthermore, we demonstrated that the magnitude of anisotropic photon flow is maximized at a specific transverse momentum, a distinctive signature that enables us to extract the $\eta/s$ ratio of the quark-gluon plasma. These results confirm that anisotropic thermal photons function as an effective viscosity probe for the quark-gluon plasma. Additionally, we observed that the relative signal of photon $v_1$ and $v_2$ exhibits a distinct centrality dependence, a unique characteristic of anisotropic thermal photons. This property can be utilized to investigate the temperature and density dependencies of the $\eta/s$ ratio in the QGP. Our study marks the first investigation into photon anisotropic flow and its sensitivity to the $\eta/s$ ratio of the quark-gluon plasma. These findings offer a novel approach for exploring the viscosity of the quark-gluon plasma. Future experiments with higher statistics are expected to further enhance the precision of $\eta/s$ measurements through high-$p_T$ photon analysis. This study examines potential regular magnetic orders in triangular and kagome lattices featuring multiple sites per unit cell. By applying magnetic point groups to define symmetry-allowed moments at each site and utilizing magnetic space groups to construct the potential of mean field (PMF) Hamiltonian, we identify all energetically viable regular magnetic orders. Our analysis reveals that a non-frustrated regular magnetic order is possible whenever at least two sites within the unit cell share the same magnetic point group. Conversely, if all sites in the unit cell are unique regarding their magnetic point groups, the PMF Hamiltonian predicts continuous frustration, indicating that no specific regular magnetic order can emerge. These theoretical findings align with recent experimental results from neutron scattering studies on the triangular lattice compound YbCl$_3$ and the kagome lattice compound Cu$_3$Sn. Additionally, we observe that several magnetic structures previously reported as non-frustrated are actually non-primitive, meaning they involve more sites per unit cell than their wave vectors would suggest. Finally, incorporating exchange interactions of the next-nearest neighbor type into the PMF Hamiltonian allows us to explain the magnetic structures observed in both the YbCl$_3$ and Cu$_3$Sn experiments. Yields: 1-10.

We introduce a new class of global test statistics designed to detect sparse treatment effects with controlled false discovery rates, even under dependence. Our approach utilizes a data-dependent threshold derived from empirical null distributions and asymptotic normality to construct a finite-sample (m, q)-control method named spRT. The (m, q)-control property ensures a limited number of false discoveries, providing non-technical (m, q)-control and technical (m, q, s)-control based on the count of null active features. Furthermore, we examine the minimax sharp minimax rate for detection and prove the method's adaptability to sparse treatment patterns. We also detail an algorithm for large-scale experiments that maintains sharp minimax rates while achieving near-linear computational complexity. Finally, simulations and real-world data analyses confirm our method's advantages in detecting sparse treatment effects with controlled FDR under dependence. This work is dedicated to the memory of Professor Ji Zhu. Keywords: False Discovery Rate, Large-scale Experiments, Sparse Treatment Effects, Sharp Minimax Rate, Treatment Effect Detection.

The fundamental concepts of cosmological inflation are examined. We derive the equations of motion governing the inflaton field, define the slow-roll parameters, and outline the calculation of inflationary perturbations along with their relationship to the temperature anisotropies observed in the cosmic microwave background. Furthermore, we provide brief overviews of inflation within the framework of string theory and its potential connections to dark energy, subsequently comparing several prominent inflationary models against empirical data. Finally, we highlight several current research directions and ongoing efforts aimed testing the prediction of inflationary gravity wave amplitudes. This material is intended for inclusion in the Lecture Notes for the 15-week General Relativity and Cosmology course at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, which concludes with a review of string theory applications to cosmology and gravitational wave astronomy. The course is structured to correspond with Chapter 7 of B. Carter's EAS-309 (Introduction to Modern Cosmology) and Chapter 13 of S. Carroll's Spacetime and Geometry. Comments and corrections are welcome.

Software developers often face numerous change requests during maintenance, and the initial step for handling each request is identifying the specific components affected by that change. While concept location techniques aim to pinpoint the software elements impacted by a maintenance task, they traditionally require developers to manually specify the concept during analysis. This necessity to define concepts can be a time-consuming and difficult process. To address this challenge, we introduce QUICKAR, an approach that automatically generates multiple candidate queries for concept location by leveraging crowdsourced knowledge. Our evaluation, which tested QUICKAR on 1,000 instances across the source code of three open-source systems, demonstrated that QUICKAR can reliably reconstruct approximately 70% of concepts based on their corresponding queries. Furthermore, experimental findings indicate that the performance of QUICKAR is influenced by the complexity of queries and the extent of overlap among affected elements. These results suggest that applying QUICKAR to clusters of change requests, where concepts share similar queries, could be particularly beneficial. Finally, we have integrated QUICKAR into the IDE-based concept locator JTSCL and will make it available for researchers to evaluate its effectiveness in real-world development scenarios. Our evaluation materials and JTSCL configurations can be accessed at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1993/QUICKAR. Additional code and configuration files will be provided upon request. Entrainment is a recognized mechanism in human interaction where individuals subconsciously mimic various aspects of each other's behavior, such as speaking rate, pitch, and even manual gestures. This study investigates the feasibility of analyzing entrainment through speech content alone. We propose a framework based on parallel Deep Neural Network (DNN) models that characterize acoustic features of spoken language to create speaker "fingerprints." These fingerprints are subsequently compared using a distance metric to quantify entrainment. Our findings indicate that this approach can effectively distinguish between trained and untrained participants as well as measure entrainment across different speaking rates. Additionally, we explore the potential of integrating semantic and speaker change detection features to enhance the distance metric and further refine entrainment analysis. Finally, we examine how the proposed framework can contribute to understanding conversational structures and improving automatic speech dialogue systems. Temporal action segmentation involves partitioning videos into segments based on action transitions. While many supervised methods have been developed, they depend on annotated data and often lack generalizability. In contrast, self-supervised approaches learn segmentation from an image sequence's spatiotemporal context without requiring annotations. However, current state-of-the-art self-supervised techniques fail to accurately model temporal dynamics, particularly at the boundaries between semantic segments. To address this, we introduce SSCAP, an approach that co-occurrence action parses an image sequence into independent semantic segments, isolating transitions. We derive the co-occurrence constraint from the spatiotemporal context of the sequence. The resulting loss function encourages the encoding of transition regions separately from the rest of each semantic segment. Furthermore, we employ a self-supervised strategy to mitigate class imbalance within action categories. Experiments on the 5-CAT benchmark demonstrate that SSCAP achieves 83.0% mean Average Precision (mAP), surpassing the previous state-of-the-art by 10.5% mAP. Additionally, it significantly outperforms other unsupervised methods, reaching 57.1% mAP above them on 5-CAT. The code is accessible at https://github.com/zhengyuanwang/SSCAP.

This study investigates exotic pentaquark states containing two charm quarks and one anti-charm quark ($\cc\cc\bar c$) by extending the current algebra technique, originally developed for the classical diquark-antidiquark excitation ($\cc\bar\cc$), to the more complex three-antiquark system ($\cc\cc\bar c$). We demonstrate that within this framework, the $\cc\cc\bar c$ structure emerges naturally as a residue pole on the two-body cut of self-energy diagrams, where the diquark ($\cc$) is substituted by a triquark ($\cc\bar c$). Utilizing the triquark concept, we successfully explain a broad spectrum of experimental findings, specifically the pentaquark states $\P\ss\ss(3900)\to D^{s0}D^{s0}\pi$, $\P\ss(3872)\to D^{s0}D^-\bar K$, $\P_c(4312)^+\to D^{s0}D^+\bar K$, $\P_c(4450)^+\to D^{s0}D^+\bar K$, $\P_c(4457)^+\to D^{\ast 0}D^+\bar K$, and $\P_c(4457)^+\to D^{\ast 0D^{\ast +}\pi$. Furthermore, our results regarding the production of $\cc\cc\bar c$ states align with observations from LHCb, LHCb+, Belle, BESIII, and future Belle II experiments. We also demonstrate that the triquark model aligns with the diquark-antidiquark model in describing the data, while offering additional insights into the nature of the $\cc\cc\bar c$ structure. This work serves as a proof of principle for the existence of $\cc\cc\bar c$ pentaquark states and for the validity of the triquark framework. We anticipate that these findings will stimulate further research into the theoretical and experimental investigation of $\cc\cc\bar c$ pentaquark states. Finally, we note that the methodology employed here is also applicable to studying pentaquark states with other quark constituents. This paper introduces and evaluates "Inquiry-Based Conceptual Feedback" (IBCF), a correction mechanism designed for student-submitted test cases in programming language courses. IBCF assists learners by pinpointing specific flaws in their test cases, offering insights into the underlying concepts, and recommending in-class resources for further study. A pilot study involving 21 students across two semesters demonstrated that IBCCF significantly enhances the timeliness, accuracy, and educational value of feedback compared to traditional detailed feedback methods. The findings indicate that IBCCF effectively promotes learning regarding the fundamental principles of software testing. Additionally, IBCF proves scalable for automated processing and remains applicable to the delivery of education within large online environments. Consequently, IBCF offers a promising solution for improving the quality of student feedback in remote software testing education. Domain adaptation is a widely adopted strategy for addressing distribution shifts across different source and target domains. However, this approach typically necessitates access to the source data during the learning process. In many scenarios, acquiring data from the source domain is either costly or entirely impractical. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to learn from multiple source domains while adapting to multiple targets, all without requiring data from any of the source domains. The framework utilizes a carefully selected target subset containing a small number of unlabeled samples labeled by a teacher to guide the learning of other target domains that lack such access. We evaluate our approach on three cross-domain person re-identification (XDR) tasks: adult-child, video-to-camera, and camera-child adaptations. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art source-free domain adaptation techniques. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/zhengyuanwang/S2HT-DR.

Gas-core reactors present a viable solution for utilizing uranium as a deep-space propulsion system. This concept features a liquid fuel that remains liquid across the entire operating temperature spectrum. The proposed methodology involves dividing the fuel into two phases: a gas and a liquid. By managing the fuel's thermal energy within the gas phase, the separation temperatures for both phases can be maintained far below the liquid's boiling point at any given pressure. Furthermore, the fluid dynamics within the core can be engineered so that the entire system functions as an organically integrated heat exchanger, boiler, and turbine. Consequently, the core operates as a self-sustaining, internally balanced system. The paper details the proposed design, construction, and operational principles of such a reactor. It also outlines a method for utilizing the generated power and discusses the application of the rotor as a propulsion mechanism. The proposal includes the estimation of specific impulse and thrust, demonstrating that the resulting values surpass those of current rocket fuels. Additionally, the text addresses the challenge of containing the fluid and presents a solution derived from principles used in fluid dynamics research. Ultimately, the gas-core reactor represents a system where every component functions as a unified whole. The paper concludes by emphasizing the necessity of further research and development to bring this concept to fruition. Specifically, it recommends conducting 0-g tests in a neutral buoyancy tank to evaluate the performance of the turbine and the overall system. To facilitate this, the document provides an estimation of the required funding. A proposal is also made to address this development within the current funding framework of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. The text ends by reiterating the urgency of additional research and development to realize this groundbreaking technology. A bibliography is also provided. This study introduces a domain-informed neural network architecture tailored for electrocalorimetry, calculating energy and momentum relative to each calorimeter's specific normal. The design leverages the calorimeter's geometric knowledge, embedding it directly into the neural representation through both geometric and physical principles. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of how various design choices impact the networks' ability to identify the region of charged particle interaction. By distilling findings from numerous simulations, we established that a shallow, wide ResNet-like convolutional neural network (CNN) outperforms deeper networks and those utilizing self-attention. This architecture achieves approximately 90% accuracy in localizing interactions within a single 3D domain. Furthermore, we examined the effect of varying calorimeter sizes and demonstrated that these architectures can generalize to calorimetric devices of different dimensions. Our approach offers a robust, general, and efficient solution for real-time interaction localization, and the corresponding code will be made available. This methodology holds significant potential for application in future experiments, including the Central Detector of the Future Circular Collider. Our findings are derived from a detailed examination of a calorimeter simulation involving electric field calibration, encompassing over 100 million interactions across various sub-types. This extensive analysis is intended to guide the development of domain-informed neural networks for particle physics. Additionally, we explore the potential application of domain-informed CNNs to other experimental techniques. Finally, we outline several avenues for future research in this field. These findings are applied to quantum mempool analysis and quantum thermodynamics involving two distinct resources. Additionally, we explore applications within quantum combinatorics, quantum gaming, and the resource theories of qubits and entanglement. Finally, we demonstrate how to derive thermodynamic second laws from resource theories of one or more quantum resources by defining classical and thermal correlations as resources. This work introduces a framework for quantifying information based on raw moments or cumulants of a probability distribution, denoted as $I_{M}(p)$ and $I_{C}(p)$, respectively. These information metrics exhibit two fundamental properties: they vanish for uniform probability densities, and they are positive whenever a distribution deviates from uniformity. The study examines how these quantities evolve as the support dimension increases and establishes explicit connections to established information measures, including Shannon entropy, Fisher information, the relative information entropy index, Cumulants, and Raw Moments. Furthermore, the proposed framework is applied to a single-qubit density matrix, yielding an expression for information content that aligns with physical principles and yields meaningful results across the complete spectrum of valid quantum state parameters. Finally, a numerical investigation is conducted on ensemble-averaged information contents within mean-field models characterizing a single spin in a ferromagnetic Ising model and a mean-field BCS superconductor. The results demonstrate that $I_{M}(p)$ and $I_{C}(p)$ are capable of distinguishing between ordered and disordered phases in these systems. Specifically, $I_{M}(p)$ remains non-zero at finite temperatures within the ferromagnetic phase but vanishes at the critical point and for all higher temperatures, whereas $I_{C}(p)$ exclusively captures the transition to the superconducting state. These findings underscore the utility of $\{I_{M}(p)\}$ and $\I_{C}(p)\}$ as novel tools for quantifying information within stochastic and quantum frameworks. Finally, the paper outlines avenues for extending this approach to establish generalizations of these information measures within the context of quantum information theory. Specifically, these codes feature a stabilizer matrix, $T$, that is sparse on both rows and columns, enabling linear-time performance with specialized decoders. While previous efforts to create such codes with constant rate and distance failed due to conflicts between local constraints and uniformity requirements, our approach resolves this issue. We construct a family of graphs, $\mathcal{G}_n$, where nodes represent both stabilizers and variables, ensuring that any $k$-clique exists only if a specific subgraph is present. We subsequently map this family into a family of quantum codes by removing certain node types. Leveraging a backtracking algorithm, we demonstrate that these modified graphs remain expansive in both variable and stabilizer sections, thereby establishing the desired sparsity and connectivity properties. Finally, we prove that for any code derived in this manner, the failure probability of our specialized decoder diminishes as the block length increases, thus confirming the decoder's efficiency. Furthermore, we outline a general methodology to guarantee the existence of a decoder that succeeds for all typical decoding scenarios. This contribution outlines recent searches conducted at CMS in 2018 and 2019 for supersymmetry and Higgsinos, utilizing multileton final states and Higgs signal reconstruction. Earlier CMS investigations into third-generation supersymmetry have established limits on Higgsinos up to 230 GeV, whereas this work presents Higgsino mass limits reaching 280 GeV. Additionally, we present results from a dedicated search for supersymmetry via Higgs signal reconstruction using 2018 data. This analysis targets the Higgs boson decaying into a pair of CP-even neutral supersymmetric particles, specifically the neutral Higgsinos ($H \to h A_1^0 A_1^0$), which subsequently decay into four bottom quarks. This study complements a concurrent search for $h \to \chi^0_1 \chi^0_1$ decays. By combining these two analyses, we achieve the most stringent limits to date on the masses of the Higgsinos, excluding masses below 280 GeV at 95% confidence level. Furthermore, we report limits on the branching fraction $B(h \to h A^0_1 A^0_1) < 0.015$ for a supersymmetric $A^0_1$ mass of 200 GeV and $B(h \to A^0_1 A^0_1) < 0.01$ for $m_{A^0_1} = 0$ GeV, based on a dataset of 138 fb$^{-1}$ collected at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. These findings are discussed in the context of recent LHC Run 2 measurements of the Higgs boson signal strengths. The analysis code is accessible through an internal CERN software repository. We introduce a new framework for rendering scenes captured via multi-view cameras, encompassing both outdoor environments with extensive dynamic ranges and indoor settings containing complex motion blur. This is accomplished by training a multi-scale convolutional neural network to estimate 4D light field representations for each input image, enabling subsequent rendering through standard volume integration. The combination of multi-scale features and a hierarchical loss function allows the network to effectively learn gradients at varying magnitudes, thereby producing high-dynamic-range images and handling motion blur. We further demonstrate that the proposed network exhibits significant cross-view generalization capabilities, reducing dependencies on dense keyframe coverage. Experimental results using real-world Light Stage data and synthetic datasets with motion blur confirm the method's superiority over existing state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we release a comprehensive dataset featuring outdoor scenes with large dynamic ranges and indoor scenes with motion blur to facilitate the development of related research. We introduce a general framework for channel-by-channel transformation rules that maintain the Ward identities of a spinor helicity basis. This approach extends the established color-chiral integrability rules in three dimensions to higher-dimensional settings by incorporating appropriate kinematic symmetries. Such rules are essential for constructing a putative celestial chiral algebra from a massless scalar theory possessing this specific symmetry. Furthermore, these transformation rules can be recast as conservation laws within a novel, "celestial" formulation of gauge theory. In this celestial frame, gauge parameters correspond to conformal primary wavefunctions, and the conservation of these conservation rules mirrors the conformal symmetry algebra. Finally, we demonstrate that both the massless scalar theory and the putative celestial chiral algebra exhibit conservation-law integrability in three dimensions. This observation suggests that a corresponding chiral symmetry algebra might exist in three-dimensional spacetime, potentially linked to conformal higher-spin symmetry. Such a symmetry would ensure the existence of a chiral algebra defined by conservation-law integrability across all amplitudes. Additionally, this conservation-law formulation of gauge theory reveals a new form of gauge invariance that appears independent of conformal symmetry. Ultimately, our findings indicate that integrability and a putative chiral symmetry algebra are intrinsic features of gauge theory itself, rather than arising solely from dimensional reduction of a higher-spin theory. These intrinsic properties may prove valuable for advancing our understanding of gauge theory, quantum field theory, and gravity within the context of the celestial amplitude program. Such a program seeks to reformulate scattering amplitudes in terms of a putative celestial operator algebra. Notably, this suggests that a chiral operator algebra could exist in three dimensions without necessarily requiring conformal higher-spin symmetry. Consequently, our findings provide a general argument for the existence of a chiral operator algebra in three-dimensional spacetime. This outcome is a key prediction of the celestial program, as it posits that space-time symmetries can be realized as an infinite hierarchy of conservation laws within the operator algebra. Specifically, the anti-self-dual sector of the vacuum symmetry algebra is predicted to exist independently of conformal symmetry. Thus, our findings offer a general argument supporting the existence of the holomorphic subalgebra of the three-dimensional superconformal algebra, which is a central component of the proposed celestial operator algebra. Overall, our findings provide a general argument that gauge theory possesses the putative chiral operator algebra it requires, thereby bolstering the case for pursuing the program of reformulating gauge theory via the putative celestial operator algebra

Solar eruptions frequently produce jets, which are believed to drive shocks through the corona. While these shocks have been observed in both the corona and at the Sun's edge, their characteristics remain uncertain. This study presents LOFAR observations of a piston shock within a jet-driven event, utilizing a model that aligns with both the observed dynamics and the broader understanding of such phenomena. The shock front appeared as a bright, narrow structure at the leading edge of the corona-penetrating jet, advancing at approximately 150 km s$^{-1}$ and pushing a dense plasma cloud. By analyzing the shock front, we determined its location and three-dimensional shape, finding it to be roughly 100 km in thickness and spanning 1.5 Mm in length. Our findings indicate that the shock front expands and accelerates as it moves outward from the Sun. Furthermore, the front exhibits a concave shape, suggesting it is driven by a jet with a tapered profile. These results offer valuable insights into the dimensions and dynamics of piston shocks in the low corona. Additionally, we examined the density of the plasma pushed by the shock, finding it to be about 10$^{10}$ m$^{-2}$ cm$^{-3}$, which is comparable to densities observed in other jet-driven events. Finally, we discuss the potential for future LOFAR observations to investigate similar features. Overall, this study enhances our understanding of jet-driven shocks in the low corona, which is essential for advancing our knowledge of the broader solar eruption process. We introduce a likelihood analysis of the general two Higgs doublet model (2HDM) based on flavour anomalies and the bottom muon anomaly. By unifying these separate fits into a single framework, our approach offers a more comprehensive strategy for investigating new physics. The broad parameterization of general 2HDM provides significant flexibility, allowing us to address various flavor and CP problems that specific models cannot. Our analysis confirms that the 2HDM can offer a viable solution to these issues, particularly within Type-Y models, where the coupling to the pseudoscalar boson is not restricted to a specific Type-Y form. Furthermore, the inclusion of a light pseudoscalar boson is essential for resolving the $(g-2)_\mu$ anomaly. Our findings indicate that the mass of this pseudoscalar boson must lie below approximately 12 GeV to achieve a $1\sigma$ fit. Additionally, the mixing angle between the CP-odd scalar boson and the physical Z boson is constrained to be extremely small, roughly $0.001$, within the $1\sigma$ region. Finally, our analysis demonstrates that a $1\sigma$ fit is achievable, with 95% C.L. upper limits on various flavor parameters falling well below their experimental sensitivities. This indicates that future experiments will be able to further constrain the parameter space of general 2HDM. We develop and analyze these equations to determine the stochastic evolution of vortex filaments and rings within various topologies. By representing vorticity fields as sums of multi-filament rings, we introduce an algorithm that efficiently simulates the time evolution of vortex dynamics in three-dimensional turbulence. This approach captures the topological changes of vortices, such as reconnection and reaction with boundaries. Furthermore, the algorithm demonstrates computational efficiency comparable to established methods for solving the Navier-Stokes equations. Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to demonstrate a quantum advantage. While the standard model assumes a fixed number of photons, recent extensions allow for variable photon counts. Although these generalized versions offer a stronger complexity proof, their output analysis has been hindered by the difficulty of calculating the full state vector and identifying relevant terms. This paper addresses that limitation by presenting a practical method to compute the full state vector for any photon number extension of boson sampling and exploring its implications for understanding the output state. Specifically, we examine entanglement measures by decomposing the output state into subspaces based on photon numbers for any two modes. Our results show that for large-scale events, these biphoton entanglement measures exhibit distinct patterns that correlate with the output's average purity. Furthermore, we observe that the average biphoton entanglement reaches its maximum at a specific mode pair separation, a phenomenon that can be qualitatively explained by spatial interference. Finally, we validate the utility of these biphoton metrics as an efficient event classifier and demonstrate their effectiveness in distinguishing between boson sampling and random quantum circuits. Reinforcement learning focuses on agents aiming to maximize cumulative rewards within a given environment. A significant challenge arises when the agent's state is not directly observable, forcing it to rely on a sequence of observations and actions to form a reliable understanding of its surroundings. This paper demonstrates that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) effectively function as belief encoders, capturing an agent's current environmental beliefs through their hidden states. This conclusion is supported by experiments across multiple grid-world scenarios, an analysis of an RNN's weight matrix, and Riemannian geometry. Furthermore, we establish a link between this approach and the information state framework introduced by Sutton et al., which posits that optimal policies depend on a sufficient statistic for past policy evaluations. Finally, the findings are applied to a basic Chinese restaurant scenario to illustrate the framework's utility in real-world applications. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/SebastianSchauer/Recurrent-networks-as-beliief-encoders. Additionally, we present a method to determine the leading eigenvector of an RNN using only interactions, which corresponds to the agent's current belief about the environment. This approach offers a new perspective on using recurrent networks and their properties to determine behavior in a novel, partially observable setting. The results also provide empirical support for the theoretical work of Sutton et al., who demonstrated that the information state can be represented by the leading eigenvector of a recurrent network. We illustrate how to apply this theory in a basic Chinese restaurant scenario. The prevailing approach to spatio-temporal action detection involves classifying actions within fixed, pre-defined action units. However, this work focuses on a more complex and less explored challenge: learning the duration of actions directly. To address this, we utilize two neural networks grounded in the principle that actions typically occur within visually salient contexts. We further incorporate a neural action duration loss function, which serves a dual purpose: it learns the duration of actions present in a video and evaluates how well predicted durations align with annotations when available. Experimental results demonstrate that our method learns more accurate action durations compared to existing techniques. Furthermore, the framework can be extended to perform detection and segmentation when action labels are provided. Overall, this work represents the first effort to weakly-supervised action detection centered on the learning of action durations. The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge (ISC2021) required participants to generate a 5-class classification vector for each of 1,028 image pairs, covering topics such as people, animals, food, objects, and landscapes. While prior attempts at this task have primarily focused on non-overlapping image domains, the constraint in ISC2021 allowed content and structure to overlap significantly within specific categories, making the task more demanding. This work evaluates the top-performing teams—Columbia University, UCL, and ETH Zurich—whose models leveraged pre-trained backbones, contrastive learning, data augmentation, and self-supervision to achieve a Macro-Accuracy of 45.61%. The remaining 50% of the dataset was held out as a test set to gauge real-world performance. Through extensive experimentation, we identified the most effective approaches, analyzed their corresponding image features, and explored the similarities and distinctions among the five categories. Additionally, we propose a novel method utilizing a contrastive loss function trained on a self-supervised dataset, achieving a Mean Average Precision (MAP) of 45.61% and outperforming all other methods on ISC2021. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/eth-sri/isc2021. Keywords: image retrieval, similarity, no-image backbones, contrastive learning, data augmentation, self-supervision.

This research examines diffusion processes within domains featuring moving or oscillating boundaries within a framework of degeneration, where the "slow" dimension exhibits a significantly smaller diffusion coefficient compared to the "fast" dimension. The analysis incorporates perturbations of both zeroth and first orders, addressing both Neumann and Robin conditions, and evaluates metastability, spectral shifts, and the macroscopic dynamics of the system's solution as the small parameter approaches zero. The study demonstrates how to derive effective models for boundary value problems using perturbation theory, utilizing Abreu's recent research on model reduction as a starting point. Furthermore, it validates these model reductions by employing spectral analysis to provide additional insights into the system's long-term behavior. The work also addresses the specific scenario of periodic domain perturbations, where fast oscillations occur on a timescale comparable to the overall dynamics. This requires a distinct methodology relying on two-scale convergence to capture behavior on the slow timescale and the associated homogenization of the limit system, which is subsequently solved using the same model reduction technique. Finally, the paper establishes the validity of model reduction in this context by proving an optimal rate of convergence via a Lax-Milgram argument, alongside conducting a numerical study of perturbed interfaces using finite element methods. The study concludes with numerical experiments designed to illustrate various aspects of the theory, including metastability, spectral shifts, and the convergence of the model reduction approach. Notably, these computations are performed on both highly oscillatory domains, where the fast dimension varies rapidly across the slow domain, and weakly oscillatory domains, where the fast dimension remains relatively constant at any specific point in the slow domain. The resulting numerical results offer valuable insight into the robustness of the model and its applicability to both weakly and highly oscillatory scenarios. Finally, this work aims to inspire further investigation into perturbed interfaces, including the necessity of model reduction, the optimization of the approach, and the analysis of problems with locally oscillatory domains. The resulting findings are anticipated to enhance the understanding of such systems and their broad applications. The ultimate objective of this line of inquiry is the development of efficient algorithms for solving highly oscillatory problems without the need to explicitly resolve the oscillations. To achieve this, the current work seeks to establish a solid theoretical foundation, with the ultimate goal of creating algorithms capable of accurately solving perturbed interfaces on oscillatory domains while significantly reducing computational cost. Ultimately, this research paves the way for future advancements in the field of computational mathematics. The ultimate aim of this work is the development of efficient algorithms

This study investigates the properties of nuclear matter at zero temperature under strong magnetic fields using the lowest order constraint variational (LOCV) method with the $AV_{18}$ nuclear potential. Our findings reveal that both the saturation density and binding energy increase as the magnetic field strength grows. Furthermore, the LOCV framework allows us to distinguish between isospin-pairing and spin-pairing behaviors to analyze the impact of the magnetic field on these pairing types. Ensuring privacy and communication efficiency remains a significant challenge in federated learning. To address these issues, we introduce a novel framework called DP-REC, which integrates differential privacy (DP) with communication efficiency in a unified approach. Our method relies on two core components: (1) a noise amplification analysis for federated trees, a critical step for establishing privacy guarantees, and (2) a pruning-based model compression strategy. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the privacy-utility trade-offs under various conditions, offering practitioners the necessary tools to make informed decisions. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, which surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/DeepPrivacyLab/DP-REC}.

\section{Introduction}
Federated learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm designed to train models using decentralized, distributed data. This approach has gained significant traction in recent years, particularly for applications in mobile devices, the Internet of Things (IoT), and blockchain systems. In this setup, a central server coordinates the training process by sending model parameters to participating nodes, which then perform local updates on their respective data before returning the results to the server. The process repeats until convergence is achieved.
However, two primary challenges hinder the widespread adoption of FL: privacy leakage and inefficient communication. FL typically employs local differential privacy (LDP) to protect user data, but this often results in substantial performance degradation. Conversely, pre-training global models before each round enhances accuracy but compromises privacy

The resulting extinction value of $A_{\rm FUV} = 10.1 \pm 0.2$ mag serves as a reference for the total extinction affecting FUV photons traveling through the Taurus-Auriga complex. By subtracting this background extinction from the total extinction derived from FUV flux measurements, we were able to isolate the extinction specific to each cloud complex. Our findings indicate that the average extinction toward Taurus is roughly 2.5 times greater than the average toward Orion, while the average extinction toward Perseus is approximately 3.5 times that of Orion. Additionally, we observed that the FUV extinction toward A11 varies by a factor of 2 across different lines of sight, suggesting that the A11 region may consist of two distinct clouds. Finally, we confirmed that the FUV extinction toward Auriga is approximately 2.5 times the average Orion value, consistent with the conclusion that Auriga is a separate cloud complex rather than a component of the Taurus region. These results align with the conclusion that FUV flux measurements can be utilized to study the extinction of interstellar clouds. Tables are extensively used to organize critical data, and understanding them enables machines to execute tasks like reading and writing. However, their high diversity and complexity make automatic extraction difficult. This paper introduces a method for extracting tables from PDF documents by first identifying them and then modeling their structure. The core of our approach is a Table Graph Neural Network (TGNN), which builds upon a recent dual-encoder table detection framework. While the detection framework identifies potential tables by passing encoded row and document representations through a reading head to produce table bounding boxes, our work focuses on representing table structure using graph neural networks. The model initially builds a table graph by predicting linking relationships between rows based on their spatial arrangement, then leverages the strengths of graph neural networks to encode the table structure. We conducted extensive experiments on two popular PDF table datasets, demonstrating that our method achieves promising results in table extraction. Additionally, we conducted ablation studies to analyze the contributions of different model components to the overall performance. Finally, we explored the quality of the learned representation embedding through t-SNE visualization and by training a classifier to distinguish between tables and non-tables. These results indicate that the model successfully captures table characteristics, such as their diversity and complexity. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengy1123/GraphNeuralNetworksForTables. Through our work, we aim to advance research in automatic table extraction. We hope our research encourages the PDF community to explore more applications of graph neural networks for table representation learning. We also hope to inspire other communities to investigate whether PGNNs can be applied to extract structures from other document elements. Our work is part of the ICML 2021 Data Track. We introduce a two-stage hierarchy of cognitive hierarchies applicable to multi-stage games under incomplete information. At the first level, players utilize the solution concept of a single-stage game of incomplete information. At the second level, they engage in a complete information game—distinct from the single-stage game—where the strategy involves a action and a belief regarding the other player's cognitive level. Subsequently, we examine equilibrium within this hierarchy and compare our model to the sequential cognitive hierarchy proposed by Coste and Mongin (2019). Finally, we illustrate the framework using the Trust Game and a simplified version of the Bank Run game.

Accurate and timely population estimates are essential for formulating public policy. In numerous developing nations, government resources are often directed toward establishing sustainable, long-term population estimates rather than solely conducting periodic censuses. This study evaluates various population estimation techniques by analyzing the relationship between population, population density, and key socio-economic indicators across 10,000 administrative zones in Mozambique, utilizing 2007 national census data. Our analysis reveals distinct correlations between population and land use, final secondary education rates, urbanization, and urbanization indices. Leveraging these correlations, we trained a random forest model to achieve accurate population estimates using easily accessible and affordable indicators. We validated the model's efficacy by applying it to two recently acquired remote sensing images. Consequently, we propose a sustainable framework for population estimation in Mozambique that integrates both census data and remote sensing imagery. This multi-modal approach leverages the strengths of both methods to generate estimates with superior accuracy and higher spatial resolution. Finally, we benchmark our results against existing literature and explore potential applications for both government and non-governmental entities. Remote sensing data can facilitate final secondary education and urbanization mapping to guide land-use planning and infrastructure investment, while supporting organizations can utilize high-resolution population maps to direct their interventions more effectively. Furthermore, these methods could be adapted to other developing countries to deliver cost-effective population estimates. All data and code required to replicate this study are publicly accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar123456/MultiModal-RemoteSensing-and-Population-Estimation. Our repository includes various remote sensing images of Mozambique along with their corresponding population, education, urbanization, urbanization index, and Gini coefficient estimates. We also provide a fully documented Python script for training the random forest model and generating the reported estimates. Additionally, we have made available a Python script designed to estimate population for new remote sensing images. By inputting a new image into this script and providing the associated image features, users can obtain population estimates for any new image. We have also released a Jupyter notebook containing our analysis code for ease of use. Given the limited scope of this work, we have not yet performed cross-validation. Future endeavors will address this gap by incorporating cross-validation and exploring the application of deep learning models to achieve even more accurate population estimates. We also plan to evaluate the efficacy of additional indicators, such as health metrics, in relation to population data. Finally, we intend to extend this framework to other developing countries to assess its generalizability

Approximate membership query (AMQ) filters are widely utilized to rapidly exclude unlikely candidates, thereby lowering computational costs. However, standard AMQ filters inevitably trade the complete elimination of false positives to achieve higher space efficiency than exact membership structures. This paper introduces filters that maintain this sparsity while offering a specific advantage: the ability to explicitly reject a certain set of elements free from false positives. We provide implementations with straightforward operations and propose an algorithm that allows users to construct and manage these filters interactively, enhancing usability. Our experimental results demonstrate a marked improvement in the performance of various applications when employing our filters alongside conventional AMQ filters to filter out the majority of negative instances. Furthermore, we highlight several uses where the partially false-positive-free nature of our filters confers a distinct usability benefit, such as in spell-checking and connectionless network protocols. We believe these features make our filters more accessible and effective for a broader range of users. Finally, we outline potential directions for future research. All code is publicly accessible.^[1]

These conditions involve an initial resonant excitation of the molecule, followed by the spontaneous emission of a photon as the molecule transitions to a deeper potential well. The resulting conservation of total spin enables atom-molecule conversion, with a final available binding energy of $3D$. Under these circumstances, the three-body recombination rate is found to be orders of magnitude higher than standard three-body recombination rates. Furthermore, the proposed scheme is shown to effectively generate molecules in deep potential wells, with the resulting molecular temperature remaining below the bath temperature. This study introduces a novel framework for fluid-structure interaction (FSI) simulations using the smooth particle hydrodynamics (SPH) method. The approach relies on the variational moving least-squares (VMLS) technique, which facilitates the construction of a continuous, symmetric, and positive-definite approximation of the governing kernel. This enables a resolution between the fully-meshless SPH formulation and the lowest-order finite element (FE) method, where shape functions are formed by the product of Nodal Basis Functions (NBFs) and weight functions. These NBFs are derived from a hierarchical basis (HB) that spans the space between fully-meshless and lowest-order FEM. Consequently, a continuous multi-resolution SPH framework is achieved, allowing users to adaptively select the level of meshless resolution for each particle. When integrated with a fast and accurate incompressible FSI solver based on the virtual-buoyancy-method (VBM), this multi-resolution strategy enables local resolution adjustments for particles in near-contact regions. Machine learning algorithms are fundamental to data analysis, pattern recognition, and optimization. Although quantum computing offers a promising avenue for advancing these fields, it is crucial to establish the algorithmic foundations and potential advantages of quantum machine learning. This study investigates unsupervised and supervised machine learning tasks utilizing quantum computers. We developed quantum versions of k-means and support vector machine (SVM) algorithms, targeting near-term quantum systems. Specifically, we implemented a classical-quantum hybrid approach to leverage the strengths of both domains. These algorithms were executed on up to 52-qubit systems using superconducting processors. Our findings demonstrate that these proposed quantum machine learning algorithms are effective, scalable, and execute in polynomial time. Additionally, we assessed their performance and scalability under noise-free and simulated noisy conditions. This research provides essential insights and establishes a framework for future developments in quantum machine learning. The code and data required to replicate these results are accessible at: https://github.com/IBM/qml-superconducting-nano. This paper introduces Hopper, a Transformer-based model designed for multi-hop reasoning within videos. While standard Transformers excel at processing images and extracting features, they often fail to capture long-term dependencies necessary for multi-step reasoning in video data. To address this, we extend the Transformer architecture to handle sequences of images and model spatiotemporal relationships across multiple hops. Each hop represents an intermediate reasoning step that incorporates visual information from a sequence of frames. Our approach involves modifying various components of the self-attention mechanism to operate on image sequences for feature extraction and implementing an attention-based feature aggregator to synthesize features from several hops. We evaluated Hopper on three video reasoning benchmarks—NABR, TVQA, and Next-QA—and achieved competitive or superior performance compared to other methods. Additionally, extensive ablation studies were conducted to analyze the effectiveness of our design choices. These results confirm that multi-hop reasoning is critical for complex video reasoning tasks and that the hopped self-attention feature learning strategy effectively captures long-term spatiotemporal dependencies. Furthermore, the ablation studies demonstrate the model's robustness and generalization capabilities. Finally, case studies highlight Hopper's strong capacity for complex multi-hop reasoning.
