We introduce a technique to measure the mass of the $W$ boson with high precision by analyzing lepton-pair production in association with a $b\bar{b}$ pair at the hadron collider. This approach is validated using proton-proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV from the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The derived differential cross-section as a function of the invariant mass of the lepton-pair and $b\bar{b}$ system is compared against next-to-leading-order theoretical predictions incorporating two-loop QCD corrections, as well as simulations based on power-suppressed higher-order QCD and QED effects. To achieve mass measurements with uncertainties below 1 GeV, this method demands a substantial data sample and a thorough investigation of various experimental and theoretical uncertainties. Furthermore, we outline a potential application of this technique to data collected at $\sqrt{s}=13.6$ TeV in the upcoming year 2025. This update to the particle data group worldwide hammer plot yields an average $W$ boson mass measurement uncertainty of approximately 1 GeV, utilizing an integrated luminosity of roughly 3000 fb$^{-1}$ accumulated over the current and forthcoming LHC runs. Such precision is crucial for conducting a more sensitive search for physics beyond the Standard Model. Our findings are directly applicable to future hadron colliders, including the High-Luminosity LHC and the proposed Future Circular Collider. Additionally, we provide a rapid implementation of this analysis available for immediate use. This study marks a significant step toward achieving ultra-precise $W$ boson mass measurements at hadron colliders, thereby enabling a stringent search for new physics.

Telepresence robots (TPRs) are remotely operated vehicles that enable users to physically visit distant locations without traveling. As these systems become more advanced, they are increasingly deployed in settings like remote work and healthcare. However, improving system quality often degrades the user experience (QoE), creating a dilemma where optimizing for one may compromise the other. This study examines how interactive QoE and cognitive load within the human-machine interface of a TPR correlate with system performance metrics, specifically video resolution and frame rate. By administering a suite of cognitive tasks and performance measures to 15 participants, we developed a cognitive model that accounts for individual differences in interactive QoE and cognitive load. We also introduced a novel method for measuring QoE interaction, which assesses how a user's attention shifts between the robot's environment and the interface. Our findings indicate that bandwidth and processing constraints can be managed by adjusting V4L2 parameters, thereby enhancing both performance and QoE. Ultimately, this research deepens our understanding of the performance-QoE trade-off in TPRs and equips system designers with a new metric to evaluate quality of experience. By enabling real-time QoE assessment, this work lays the foundation for developing self-optimizing robotic systems. This approach is particularly vital for TPRs, as their QoE is heavily influenced by both the remote environment and the user of the robot itself. Mafia, also known as Werewolf, is a well-known party game that has become increasingly popular on social media platforms. It is typically played by a group of participants divided into two factions: "Cops" and "Criminals." The game begins with the Cops eliminating a member of the group without revealing their identity. Subsequently, the players discuss the elimination, debating whether the recently removed individual was a Cop. If the consensus is that the last removal was indeed a Cop, the game ends in a Cop victory. Conversely, if the consensus is that the previous player was not a Cop, the Criminals are allowed to eliminate another player. The game concludes with either the total annihilation of the Cops or the Criminals gaining control over the majority of the players. This paper introduces a mathematical model of the Mafia game, which is then employed to analyze the probabilities associated with the game's various outcomes. A potential future application involves using these outcomes to design an optimal strategy for the Cops, ensuring that the elimination of the first player maximizes the likelihood of a Cop victory. This approach would involve selecting the player to eliminate with a probability proportional to the resulting chance of victory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an optimal strategy exists where the first elimination targets either the player holding the strongest belief the previous victim was a Cop, or the player holding the weakest belief the previous victim was not a Cop. This paper focuses on the initial elimination, whereas a subsequent paper will address subsequent moves. Our method for determining the first elimination is based on a novel result regarding the optimal stopping problem, which we also explore. Additionally, we present a generalization of a well-known identity concerning sums of powers, and we illustrate a second generalization of this identity within the context of the Mafia game. Finally, we introduce a new identity that arises from the analysis of this game. This work is partially supported by the National Science Foundation under grant DMS-1954030. This study introduces a novel fuzzy k-means algorithm designed for high-dimensional data, incorporating variable feature weights. In many real-world datasets, information distribution varies significantly across dimensions, rendering equal weighting inappropriate. To address this, the proposed method utilizes dimension-wise entropies to determine weights for each data feature. Experimental results indicate that these weights effectively identify irrelevant features and adaptively adjust cluster centers during the algorithm's execution, resulting in superior clustering performance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, both theoretical analysis and empirical findings demonstrate that the algorithm exhibits efficient computational performance. A comprehensive evaluation of clustering quality and efficiency was conducted using high-dimensional data from multiple sources, supported by statistical tests. The method was also applied to high-dimensional data analysis within the medical field. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a foundational component in large-scale neural network architectures. Each expert functions as a neural network trained to handle specific subsets of the input space, with the final prediction derived from a weighted combination of their outputs, where weights reflect confidence. Despite its potential, identifying the optimal MoE is an NP-hard problem, causing most efficient greedy algorithms to stagnate in local minima. This work addresses that challenge by introducing a novel consistent and efficient algorithm for linear MoE. Our core insight is that the non-convex optimization landscape of general MoE can be recast as a convex optimization problem over an expanded feature space. Leveraging this insight, we propose a convex algorithm for linear MoE that guarantees both consistency and efficiency, subsequently extending the approach to deep linear networks. We empirically demonstrate rapid convergence, generalization, and superior performance of our proposed model. All code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/zhongtao-liu/moe}. Furthermore, we release a new dataset, \texttt{synthetic\_mixture}, which comprises a mixture of 10 distinct linear regression tasks. We anticipate this dataset will serve as a valuable benchmark for evaluating the generalization capabilities of various algorithms. Although quantum gravitational effects are expected to explicitly break global symmetries, their magnitude and the mechanisms for their breaking remain uncertain. We propose a testable framework to constrain the breaking of the chiral $U(1)_L$ symmetry, a candidate global symmetry, within quantum gravity. Assuming an anomalous coupling between $U(1)_L$ currents and the Riemann curvature tensor, we demonstrate that these quantum gravitational effects induce non-geodesic motion for cosmic rays and modify the dispersion relation of light. Specifically, if $U(1)_L$ is preserved, gravity generates vacuum birefringence by causing photon polarization states to propagate at different speeds; however, if the symmetry is broken, this birefringence is suppressed. By integrating our theoretical predictions with recent observations from the Polarization Intensity and Matrix Analysis of the Cosmic Microwave Background (P4MA), we derived constraints on the magnitude of quantum gravitational symmetry breaking and the form factor associated with the explicit coupling. These bounds are comparable to those obtained from pulsar timing and significantly tighter than previous limits from gamma-ray bursts. Our findings indicate that quantum gravitational effects either do not break global symmetries or break them in a manner that does not introduce a speed difference for light polarization modes. This conclusion is robust against uncertainties in astrophysical source emission and potential biases in polarization measurements. Our work establishes a novel, complementary method for measuring or constraining the breaking of global symmetries in quantum gravity, utilizing a unique astrophysical probe to test whether quantum gravity allows for truly global symmetries. Furthermore, our framework is applicable to other astrophysical sources, potentially enabling even stricter constraints in the future. Finally, we highlight potential extensions of our analysis to other phenomena, such as the magneto-rotation measure of the CMB and the dispersion of radio waves. Our results provide further evidence supporting the existence of quantum gravitational symmetry, a conclusion previously suggested by constraints on $(2,2)$ Weyl gravity and axion-like particles. We report on the first UVIT study of NGC 4147, an intermediate-age globular cluster located in the Fornax dwarf spheroidal galaxy. The study identifies 13 stars with UV brightness exceeding that of the cluster's most luminous member by a factor of 100 or more. By combining UVIT photometry with optical photometry derived from the HST/ACS F814W filter, we determined the effective temperatures and luminosities of these UV-bright stars (UBSs). Our analysis indicates that the majority of these stars are likely post-red giant branch (RGB) stars, with a few probable members of the blue horizontal branch (BHB). The observed luminosity distribution of the UBSs aligns well with predictions from single star evolution models. Furthermore, we determined the distance modulus of Fornax to be $31.05 \pm 0.05$ mag, consistent with other distance estimates for the dwarf spheroidal galaxy. Additionally, we calculated the metallicity of UV-bright stars in NGC 4147 to be $[Fe/H] = -1.91 \pm 0.05$ dex, which is in good agreement with studies utilizing H$\alpha$ emission. Finally, we discuss the presence of these UBSs in the context of stellar evolution models and the formation mechanisms of hot stars in globular clusters. This research is part of the UVIT Key Programme on Globular Clusters (GO/KP/GC-1). The data are available at http://www.iiap.ernet.in/~uvit.

Deep Transfer Learning (DTL) represents a significant and extensively researched subfield within deep learning. Its primary goal is to enable knowledge gained from training on one or more source tasks to be effectively transferred to a target task. Two established theories have traditionally guided this field: (1) linear separability between subspaces and (2) canonical correlation analysis (CCA). However, recent research has challenged the linear separability assumption, while DTL advancements have outpaced initial CCA findings. This study re-evaluates and refines the foundational theorems of transfer learning. We introduce four new theorems that encompass and extend the classic linear separability and CCA principles. Furthermore, these theorems establish a rigorous basis for algorithmic design and explain the mechanisms behind knowledge transfer, offering a fresh perspective on the principles and practices of deep transfer learning. Additionally, empirical experiments demonstrate that models constructed using these theorems achieve superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. The theorems and enhanced algorithms are accessible at: https://github.com/ChenYixuanZ/Principles_of_Deep_Transfer_Learning. Specifically, the project includes: (1) subspace separability conformance testing for pre-trained models, (2) a model achieving SOTA results on ImageNet with limited training data, and (3) an model reaching SOTA results on COCO with limited training data. The swift dissemination of information within complex networks has garnered significant attention, yet the underlying mechanisms driving this diffusion remain poorly understood. While prior research has focused on how the topology of deterministic spreading processes influences transmission rates, this study investigates the impact of network community structure. We demonstrate that for networks with equivalent topological characteristics, a higher modularity consistently accelerates the spread of information. This counter-intuitive outcome is particularly pronounced in large networks composed of highly modular, small-world structures. To explain this phenomenon, we introduce a network model that integrates community and long-range links. Our theoretical analysis reveals that network modularity serves to reduce the effective degree, thereby facilitating faster information diffusion. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the relationship between modularity and the effective correlation length is non-monotonic. These insights are corroborated by numerical simulations across various network models. Our proposed framework effectively unifies diverse perspectives on the topology of spreading processes and establishes the critical role of community structure in controlling information flow. These insights hold broad applicability, extending to the diffusion of infectious diseases, fake news, and social trends. Additionally, this theoretical understanding lays the groundwork for designing networks with specific information diffusion rates. Finally, our framework offers a pathway to investigate the intricate interplay between network topology and community formation. **Keywords:** Network Modularity; Information Diffusion. **PACS:** 89.75.-k; 89.75.Kb. **Author contributions:** YL and YZ designed the research. Utilizing Floer theoretic conditions, we derive quantitative bounds regarding the proximity—measured via Hausdorff distance, flat norm, or F-metric—of two Lagrangians, contingent upon the magnitude of their Lagrangian angles. As the most widely used operating system globally, Android has become a primary target for malicious software. In response, the security community has developed numerous detection tools and systems to identify and neutralize these threats. However, despite these advancements, a significant number of applications continue to bypass screening mechanisms. This survey focuses specifically on evasion attacks targeting the problem-space within the Android OS. Our primary objective is to examine the vulnerabilities exploited by these attacks, which undermine the effectiveness of existing detection methods. To achieve this, we provide a holistic view of problem-space evasions, analyze key issues in Android's design and implementation that facilitate such attacks, and outline future research directions. We anticipate that this survey will deepen understanding of how problem-space evasions compromise current security measures and offer a foundation for further investigation. Additionally, we have compiled a comprehensive survey table detailing 111 known Android problem-space evasion attacks, including their publication year, developer, targeted security mechanism, attack vector, and reference. This extensive list is intended to serve as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners by offering a clear overview of existing evasion techniques and their specific goals. Finally, we propose several promising avenues for future research, including exploring new attack vectors, developing more robust detection and prevention mechanisms, enhancing user education and awareness, and conducting empirical studies to assess the real-world impact of these attacks. By addressing these areas, researchers can advance our collective efforts to mitigate the threats posed by problem-space evasions in the Android ecosystem. Additionally, we have curated a survey dataset on GitHub, featuring 109 papers on Android problem-space evasion attacks, which can be utilized as a foundation for future empirical studies. This dataset includes information on attacker profiles, attack types, attack goals, attack vectors, countermeasures, and evaluation metrics. Furthermore, we offer guidance on how researchers can leverage our survey work to gain a broader perspective of the field and identify promising directions for subsequent empirical investigations. We anticipate that this survey and the associated dataset will significantly contribute to advancing our understanding of Android problem-space evasion attacks and inspire new research endeavors in this critical area. Finally, we acknowledge the limitations of our survey, noting that it does not encompass all problem-space evasion attacks, as new variants are emerging regularly. Additionally, our survey does not provide a comprehensive list of countermeasures for every attack, as these solutions are often proprietary or confidential. We hope that our survey will encourage further research to address these gaps and contribute to the overall security of the Android ecosystem. To our knowledge, this remains the first survey dedicated to Android problem-space evasion

Ozy is a hardware- and software-agnostic general orchestrator designed to handle functions including hardware discovery, provisioning, configuration, lifecycle management, and resource scheduling across a unified platform. It supports both standalone execution and distributed execution across multiple orchestration instances. This paper details Ozy's design and implementation, highlighting a critical challenge: the distributed execution environment. We present a unified execution environment and distributed architecture to effectively address this issue. We demonstrate that the Thakurta metric, which models a black hole within a cosmological setting, fails to meet the requirements of asymptotic flatness and the presence of a regular event horizon. Consequently, Thakurta's claims regarding the unambiguous identification of these metrics in cosmological black holes are baseless. Furthermore, we show that applying a cosmological background to modify the Thakurta metric does not significantly alter the current bounds on primordial black hole (PBH) density derived from LIGO-Virgo observations of binary mergers. Thus, PBH density limits remain essentially unchanged despite the cosmological context. Our findings indicate that current efforts to incorporate general relativity in a cosmological background are insufficient to describe black holes, and that a future theory of gravity will likely differ substantially from Einstein's framework in the cosmological setting. Ultimately, a successful quantum theory of gravity will require a complete re-evaluation of black holes. This situation underscores the critical need to experimentally probe Einstein's theory of gravity in extreme regimes, such as those involving high energy densities and extreme curvature. We argue that PBHs offer a unique opportunity to test quantum gravity, as the statistical fluctuations in their density distribution can be precisely calculated. The recent detection of binary PBH mergers by LIGO and Virgo has enabled the determination of bounds on their density; we emphasize the urgent necessity of conducting more such measurements to achieve a comprehensive understanding of quantum gravity. This paper focuses specifically on the constraints placed by LIGO and Virgo on binary PBH mergers. In the future, we aim to explore other observational probes, such as gravitational wave background, cosmic microwave background, and large-scale structure, to place bounds on cosmological PBHs. We also plan to examine how varying definitions of "cosmological black holes" and their corresponding metrics affect the resulting bounds on PBH density. Additionally, we intend to investigate how different models of cosmological PBH density distributions influence these bounds. Finally, we will examine how cosmological effects on binary PBH systems influence the derived bounds from LIGO and Virgo. We conclude that a future theory of gravity will inevitably differ from Einstein's theory, and that various definitions of "cosmological black holes" and their metrics will play a crucial role in shaping this future theory. Therefore, it is essential to conduct more experiments to determine the correct description of binary PBH systems in our cosmological universe. Pebble accretion is a widely accepted mechanism for the rapid formation of giant planet cores within the gaseous protoplanetary disks surrounding young stars. However, once a planet forms, it induces gas density enhancements in its wake that could significantly alter the disk structure and potential, thereby influencing further planet formation. This study investigates these disk perturbations using the open-source astrodynamic code "Reproducible and Reliable Eulerian-Lagrangian" (ReproEL), which integrates gas hydrodynamics with particle evolution. Our simulations reveal that the gas density boost generated by a Jupiter-like planet is substantial, yet it diminishes rapidly behind the planet due to viscous diffusion and gas pressure. Under standard disk conditions, this density wave does not alter particle growth rates. However, if a gas pressure barrier exists in the original disk, the density enhancement from the planet can amplify it. This amplification causes pebble drift to halt, resulting in the accumulation of particles at the pressure barrier's downstream side. Consequently, this could accelerate the formation of a second planet near the pressure barrier. Furthermore, we find that gas pressure waves propagate at a finite speed, allowing us to quantify the time required for density perturbations to reach distant regions of the disk. This insight is crucial for interpreting observations of young stars and their disks. Overall, this research provides a novel perspective on planet formation and offers a new approach to studying the co-evolution of multiple planets within protoplanetary disks. Overparameterized models feature significantly more parameters than the degrees of freedom required to fit training data. This excess capacity imparts distinct qualitative behaviors, enabling efficient training and generalization even on complex datasets. This paper investigates the origins of these phenomena. We contend that computational constraints, specifically those arising from the need to calculate generalization error, play a role. Specifically, the statistical mechanics of random neural networks demonstrate that the replica symmetric (RS) solution—which yields a generalization error comparable to the best in-distribution models—is generally stable precisely when the number of test samples is small, aligning with practical constraints. Conversely, the RS solution fails in datasets with an extensive number of test samples or out-of-distribution data. Consequently, the replica-symmetry-breaking (RSB) solution becomes relevant, a framework extensively explored by spin glass theory. Remarkably, this approach reveals that overparameterization may be necessary for machine learning. Furthermore, the application of quantum computers to the training and generalization of overparameterized models offers additional insights into this approach. Collectively, these findings suggest that overparameterization arises from computational constraints, thereby establishing a link between the ease of learning and quantum computational capabilities. These insights deepen our understanding of the fundamental challenges in artificial neural networks and inspire new research directions. This work serves as a tutorial and introduction to these topics. It synthesizes concepts from statistical mechanics, dynamical systems, and recent quantum machine learning advancements. Additionally, it highlights promising avenues for future study, such as investigating learning dynamics on the landscape of structured overparameterized neural networks. This research was conducted as a special issue of npj Computational Materials. The issue's theme, "Computational Materials Design," reflects the growing trend of utilizing artificial intelligence to address diverse materials science challenges. We conclude by demonstrating how our theoretical framework can be applied to materials science, thereby bridging the gap between statistical mechanics and this field. Specifically, we illustrate the application of overparameterized models to unsupervised learning for materials discovery and to quantum machine learning. We establish an analogue of the Bohr–Kochener theorem within the context of countable abelian groups. Specifically, if a subset $A$ of a countable abelian group $G$ possesses a sumset $A + A$ containing a Bohr set $B$ such that $|A \cap B| \geq \alpha |B|$ for some $\alpha \in (0,1)$, then $A$ includes a subset $A'$ satisfying $|A'| \geq \alpha |G|$ and such that $A' + A'$ encompasses the Bohr set $B' := B \cap G$. Furthermore, we derive analogous findings for general groups and finite groups, respectively. For the case of finite groups, we provide an explicit formulation of the constant $\alpha'$ in terms of $\alpha$ and the order of the group, which approaches $0$ as the group order increases. Additionally, we demonstrate that our primary theorem for countable abelian groups yields a novel asymptotic formulation of the Gowers host–Green theorem regarding Bohr sets. Finally, we conclude with a series of open problems and conjectures stemming from these findings. Notably, a conjecture by Tao and the second author concerning the $\ell^2$-sum of a Bohr set in a finite group appears to be false; we offer a counterexample and a revised version of the conjecture. We also present an alternative proof of the first author's theorem on Bohr sets within finite fields, which relies on the $\ell^1$-sum of a Bohr set. Moreover, we prove an analogue of Tao's conjecture within the framework of finite groups, thereby establishing the validity of the first author's conjecture. In the process, we provide a self-contained proof of the Tao–Green theorem. This study examines a dial-a-ride problem tailored for elderly individuals in a densely populated urban setting. Unlike traditional vehicle routing problems, this specific formulation necessitates that a customer's route be concatenated with a tour of interest, such as a historical or cultural landmark trail, which must be completely visited by at least one vehicle by the end of the planning horizon. To address this novelty, we develop a Branch-and-Cut algorithm incorporating various constraints and procedures, including mixed integer linear programming subproblems, flow variables, time-window asymmetry-based inequalities, and a large neighborhood search. Numerical experiments conducted on a synthetic dataset for a hypothetical city in Southern Portugal demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. A key finding is that these trail routes tend to restrict feasible solutions, making the integration of time-window asymmetry constraints essential for enhancing algorithmic performance. The results indicate that the proposed algorithm can solve small to medium-sized instances optimally in a reasonable timeframe, with all instances yielding optimal or near-optimal solutions. Furthermore, the average cost improvement relative to a first-best model is achieved with only a negligible increase in travel costs. Finally, we discuss potential applications of this approach in urban environments and identify promising directions for future research.

KMP is the first multi-modal e-commerce pre-trained model to integrate a multi-stage self-supervised learning process. In this work, we investigate correlated metals by integrating the concepts of renormalized drift velocity and spin drift. Our calculations show that the spin drift current is enhanced by a factor of $R^2$ compared to the Drift Vector (DV) current, where $R$ represents the correlation strength. This $R^2$-scaling arises from the correlation-induced modification of the quasi-particle velocity and aligns with experimental findings. Furthermore, we establish a qualitative connection between our theoretical framework and the classification of spin currents. Finally, we apply this enhanced spin drift current to various experimental contexts, successfully replicating key results. Specifically, we demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst effect (ANE) in strongly correlated metals is enhanced by the $R^2$-factor relative to the Seebeck coefficient, a conclusion that matches recent measurements. Additionally, we observe that the Hall voltage across a $p-n$ junction can be amplified by an even higher factor, $R^4$, which is identified as a higher-order anomalous Nernst effect. Finally, we examine the magneto-Seebeck effect within the Hund's metal regime of Ce$_{3-x}$Co$_x$Si$_2$ and provide a comprehensive explanation that is consistent with the available experimental data. Our findings indicate that strong correlations not only increase the magnitude of the magneto-Seebeck effect but also enable the emergence of novel spin currents. Overall, this study establishes a robust foundation for experimentally realizing amplified spin currents in the context of correlated electron systems. Finally, we offer a discussion regarding the potential existence of anti-intuitive phenomena, such as the vanishing of the Seebeck coefficient, which could serve as a valuable tool for experimentally identifying strongly correlated electron systems. This paper serves as a companion to our recent publication: *Phys. Rev. Research* **4**, 013097 (2022). We introduce a novel dark matter framework wherein metastable conformal fields define the dark sector while the baryon-toentropy ratio $\eta$ serves as the source of baryonic mass in the visible sector. A key feature of this model is that a first-order phase transition, driven by mass terms originating in the visible sector, establishes an initial barrier in the potential of a conformal field within the dark sector. This field acts as the dark matter candidate, with its relic density established through a mechanism analogous to the standard freeze-in process. We examine a specific implementation utilizing a renormalizable effective operator, demonstrating that the model successfully accounts for the observed relic density and is capable of generating dark matter baryon asymmetry via an out-of-equilibrium decay of the dark matter field. Furthermore, this model offers a solution to a problem encountered in the conformally coupled $\lambda\phi^4$ theory, specifically the issue of an incorrect late-time equation of state. We conclude that this approach also resolves tension between different Hubble parameter reconstructions derived from cosmological data. Finally, we present constraints on the model's parameter space based on cosmological observations. Notably, we find that the proposed solution to the $H(z)$ tension demands a higher dark sector temperature, which in turn requires dark matter with an extended lifetime. This necessity introduces an additional constraint on the parameter space, which we analyze in detail. Finally, we discuss the implications of this model for future cosmological and astrophysical observations. The parameter space and results are available at https://github.com/SebastianKahlhoefer/MetastableConformalDarkMatter. Our findings indicate that the dark sector temperature must be approximately $10$ times higher than that of the visible sector. This requires an upper limit on the operator coefficient of $\kappa \lesssim 10^{-7}$, which in turn imposes a lower limit on the mass of the dark matter field, $m_\chi \gtrsim 1$ eV. Additionally, the model predicts a dark matter field mass of approximately $1$ meV and an interaction cross-section of roughly $10^{-45}$ cm$^2$. These predictions are consistent with data from LIGO/Virgo, the Planck satellite, and the Cosmic Microwave Background. Artificial Intelligence (AI) for medical imaging is rapidly advancing, yet its generalization capabilities remain a significant challenge. When data distributions shift, performance often declines, leading regulatory bodies to mandate rigorous estimation methods for predicting real-world clinical effectiveness. This study introduces a novel approach to distribute-set conformity, a type of statistical guarantee that remains valid despite distribution shifts. This framework enables the efficient estimation of suitably calibrated AI medical devices utilizing conformal prediction. We validate our proposed framework through two simulations and a case study involving an AI medical device based on a convolutional neural network, which estimates tumor response in neuroblastoma patients from multi-modality medical images. Our results demonstrate that this method ensures reliable performance estimation for AI medical devices even when data distributions shift. Furthermore, we observe that while distribution shifts can cause a substantial drop in the accuracy of existing AI medical devices, the implementation of our proposed approach allows these models to regain reliable performance estimation. These findings hold significant implications for guiding the development of AI medical devices to enhance their robustness against distribution shifts. Additionally, our findings suggest an optimal strategy for retraining AI medical devices to mitigate the impact of distribution shifts. Finally, we emphasize the necessity of conducting sensitivity analyses during the development of AI medical devices to assess their vulnerability to potential distribution shifts. The source code for this study is accessible at https://github.com/kenji-koizumi/distribution_shift_confidence_calibration.git. All-atom simulations are essential for investigating the conformational dynamics of DNA, yet these sequences often display slow folding kinetics and access a vast array of conformations. We present RBB-DNA (Rigid Base Biasing for DNA), an approach that integrates the conformational constraints of linked DNA bases with high-temperature dynamics to facilitate sampling within physiological parameter regimes. By applying a constraint potential between adjacent bases, this method restricts the relative orientation of adjacent base pairs, thereby reducing the conformational space and accelerating transitions. We examined the efficacy of RBB-DNA on various sequences, including the well-known CG-rich 14-mer, demonstrating that it accurately replicates physiological bending properties. Furthermore, the method successfully generated conformations consistent with known experimental findings regarding DNA supercoiling and the presence of Z-DNA segments. Finally, RBB-DNA was utilized to explore sequences exhibiting large end-to-end displacements, revealing that even moderate torsional stress can induce dramatic sequence-dependent unfolding. The accessibility of this technique, which relies on standard molecular dynamics software, alongside open-source implementations and accessible examples, allows researchers to investigate the conformational landscape of any DNA sequence. Additionally, its compatibility with existing analysis tools enables the investigation of questions such as whether a specific sequence can achieve any desired conformation and the associated energy costs. The combination of these capabilities offers a comprehensive framework for investigating the intrinsic bending rigidity of any DNA sequence and assessing the feasibility of achieving desired conformations. Finally, RBB-DNA is not restricted to DNA; it can be applied to other biomolecules and synthetic polymers to explore their conformational landscapes. Asymptotic Numerical Integration (ANI) is a widely used, universal lossless entropy encoding method for probability sources, recognized for achieving arithmetic efficiency, surpassing Shannon entropy limits, and maintaining variable alphabet support. In contrast, Zipf's Law governs the frequency distribution in many natural language corpora, where individual words follow a frequency-ordinality relationship defined by the inverse power law $f(i) \propto i^{-s}$, with $s$ denoting the Zipfian exponent. This study demonstrates that ANI encoding achieves arithmetic efficiency matching the optimal Huffman encoding standard and establishes that ANI can reach within 1 bit/word of the Shannon entropy lower bound. These findings are supported by an analysis of English text corpora, ranging from the complete works of Shakespeare to modern Wikipedia, under the assumption of Zipfian distribution. Additionally, the arithmetic cost of ANI is shown to be proportional to the average path length in the Huffman code tree, which also scales with individual word frequency. Finally, the analysis of English corpora reveals the inverse relationship between source entropy and decoding cost. Furthermore, a conductivity model for concrete is proposed, accounting for the interaction between gel water and capillary water through the concept of relative humidity. This study introduces a direct statistical inference method for cosmological parameters using the three-dimensional correlations within Lyman-$\alpha$ forest data. We generate synthetic catalogs containing $10^6$ absorbers, simulating a G2V quasar at $z=2.5$ observed with the SDSS-IV BOSS survey, incorporating all relevant observational effects. We calculate the three-point auto-correlation functions involving both pairs and singles of these synthetic absorber catalogs. Subsequently, we fit these measured correlations directly with theoretical predictions derived from the Matter Power Spectrum (MPS) to simultaneously constrain the comoving volume density of halos hosting haloes with a mass of $10^{12}M_{\odot}$ at the quasar's redshift and the normalized amplitude of primordial density fluctuations, $\sigma_8(z)$. Our results yield a comoving volume density of $\log_{10}(M_{12}^3/V_{\rm com}) = 7.05 \pm 0.05$, which aligns with predictions from the HALOFIT and RECFAST models. Furthermore, the combination of three-point autocorrelation and cross-correlation functions enables a direct constraint on $\sigma_8(z)$ with a precision of $\Delta \sigma_8(z) = 0.025$. This represents a significant improvement over the $\Delta \sigma_8(z) = 0.1$ uncertainty typically associated with the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, demonstrating the method's potential to deliver the first direct statistical constraints on cosmology from the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. Additionally, the computational efficiency of this approach allows for the analysis of the full SDSS quasar catalog, thereby maximizing the statistical power of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. Our findings suggest that the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest could provide the first direct constraints on the growth of structure, thereby helping to resolve the current tension regarding the amplitude of density fluctuations. This represents a substantial leap forward in direct cosmological parameter estimation using the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. Future enhancements, such as increasing the quasar redshift to the $z=3$ range and utilizing higher-resolution spectrographs, are expected to further refine these constraints. This work serves as a foundational step toward developing the first direct statistical cosmological constraints from the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. While Social-LSTM models have shown promise, they often fail to produce reasonable outputs in complex scenarios. This paper introduces a new model that effectively captures both long-term and short-term movement characteristics in urban settings. We propose a sequential autoregressive Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) that incorporates a Sliding Sequential Discriminator (SSD) to predict joint trajectories for all pedestrians in the scene. The encoder network predicts both joint positions and the uncertainty (variance) of each pedestrian's path. By generating trajectories with varying degrees of randomness, our model produces a diverse range of potential paths for every prediction step. Counterdiabatic (CD) protocols have become essential tools for rapidly reaching desired target states. However, implementing these schemes requires precise knowledge of the final target Hamiltonian's eigenbasis, a requirement that often becomes prohibitive when the target ground state is merely approximate. In this work, we introduce a novel CD approach designed to efficiently prepare the ground state of the two-dimensional Hubbard model on any rectangular lattice. Unlike conventional CD methods, our proposed scheme utilizes a single CD term, which is explicitly shown to be sufficient for effective preparation. We demonstrate that when combined with a standard adiabatic passage protocol, this scheme achieves nearly perfect ground-state fidelity in less than 1000 time steps on 6×6 and 5×9 grids. Furthermore, we illustrate how a straightforward variational principle can significantly reduce the number of CD terms needed, and we show that even with only a single CD term, the scheme remains robust against a wide range of experimental imperfections. These findings indicate that our protocol can be readily implemented on existing quantum simulators and open the door to exploring more complex and realistic many-body systems. Additionally, the proposed variational principle is broadly applicable and can be adapted to various other contexts. Finally, we discuss potential future extensions of this approach. Our findings are supported by supplementary materials available at http://link.aps.org/supplemental/10.1103/PhysRevLett.123.100601. Grayscale images are widely utilized in various digital media contexts, such as user interface design, photography, and graphic arts. Although converting high-quality color images to grayscale is common, existing methods often suffer from significant color loss. This paper introduces a novel technique designed to maintain the original image's colorfulness. Specifically, we develop an adaptive, color-temperature-dependent gain map that enhances the vividness of converted grayscale images. The proposed algorithm is fully automated and requires no user intervention. Additionally, we utilize Perceptual Image Quality Assessment metrics to quantitatively evaluate both the visual fidelity and colorfulness of our approach compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. We demonstrate that any harmonic map from a compact Riemann surface to a compact CAT($k$) sphere, which exhibits only ramification points as critical points, constitutes a branched covering. This finding complements the results of J. Schoen and R. Yau regarding harmonic maps of spheres to spheres. Furthermore, we establish that for any compact manifold $M$ equipped with a pinching Riemannian metric, any harmonic map from a Riemann surface to $M$ with solely ramification points as critical points is also a branched covering. Our proof relies on the harmonic map equation, energy, and energy variation, alongside a specific harmonic function defined on the tangent space of the domain Riemann surface. Additionally, we provide a novel harmonic equation characterization of the uniformization map for compact CAT($0$) $S^2$'s, extending S. Kotowski's result from the Euclidean setting to the spherical context. This observation offers a new approach to proving the uniformization theorem for these spheres. Our work also establishes a harmonic map characterization of harmonic functions on compact Riemann surfaces, which can be utilized to investigate the existence and symmetry of minimal surfaces. We introduce a laser-plasma system designed to investigate realistic photon-photon interactions. By employing a multi TW solid-state laser to generate a highly excited plasma, the Schwinger limit of two-photon interactions is closely approximated. This platform enables the direct observation and measurement of the charge-conjugation-dependent scattering cross section. Additionally, we propose a scheme to stimulate this Schwinger process using a second intense laser, thereby offering a method to amplify the signal. This research is driven by the desire to explore non-linear quantum electrodynamics, providing a basis for future investigations into the interaction between light and matter in strongly non-linear regimes. Furthermore, these findings are relevant to quantum electrodynamic studies of astrophysical phenomena. Our proposed experiment can be conducted using existing equipment at research centers such as Max-Born-Institut, IFF-Copenhagen, and CCL in Lund. The successful execution of this study will establish the foundation for a new scientific discipline focused on photon-photon physics within laser-plasma systems. Additionally, the proposed work will facilitate the development of novel laser-plasma light sources and contribute to a novel approach for laser-based direct energy conversion. Finally, the methodology is applicable to photon-photon interactions involving higher-order non-linearities and conduction electrons in plasmas. Specifically, it is pertinent to studying quantum electrodynamic effects in astrophysics, including photon-photon scattering in the interstellar medium and non-linear radiation pressure in laser-irradiated planetary surfaces. The suggested proposal is also applicable to laser-plasma systems utilizing laser wakefield accelerators. The Schrödinger equation for this scenario has been solved, and the resulting solutions are presented. The study is also relevant to photon-photon interactions involving relativistic electrons in strong laser fields. The proposed experiment is expected to advance the field of photon-photon interaction, which is currently in its infancy. The findings will be published in Physical Review Letters. This study examines the sensitivity and constraints on the soft-breaking $Z_2$ parameter $m_{12}$ within the Two Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM). We demonstrate that the allowed region for $m_{12}$ varies based on the specific 2HDM variant, even when other parameters are fixed at their best-fit values. These constraints are sensitive to the CP nature of the heavier CP-even Higgs boson, $H$, and the ratio of vacuum expectation values, $\tan\theta$. The analysis is conducted separately for scenarios with and without a heavy neutral pseudoscalar ($A$). Furthermore, assuming $H$ is identified as the heavy Higgs boson detected at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), we determine the sensitivity of the two main 2HDM types to the $m_{12}$ parameter. In Type-II 2HDM, we find that $m_{12}$ can reach up to 1 TeV for CP-conserving cases and 3 TeV in the CP-violating scenario. In contrast, Type-Y 2HDM exhibits significantly reduced sensitivity to $m_{12}$ compared to the Type-II case. These findings are relevant for future experimental searches for $H$ bosons. Additionally, we compare our results with those of a similar study, highlighting the importance of considering $H$ couplings and CP properties when establishing 2HDM constraints. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for future $H$ boson searches at the LHC. Our conclusions suggest that the $H$-boson search regions for $m_{12}$ should be adjusted according to the specific 2HDM scenario. This adjustment is particularly critical when $H$ couplings are measured in the future, as such measurements could significantly impact the constraints placed on the $m_{12}$ parameter space. Consequently, these results should be incorporated into future $H$-boson searches at the LHC. Similar analyses should also be performed for $A$-boson searches to better understand the 2HDM parameter space. We have provided the necessary code for these calculations on GitHub. This work examines data exchange from relational sources to RDF targets, where target constraints are defined via Shape Expressions. We characterize the existence of data exchange solutions via decidable query evaluation and the recurrence of solutions via expression term size. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to construct RDF data exchange solutions by mapping source relations to target shapes while addressing identified shape ambiguities. These findings rely on transforming source-to-target tuple-generating dependencies into a specific canonical form derived from an extended class of range-closed dependencies. Finally, we present an algorithm that efficiently generates solution instances with minimal shielded shape attributes, thereby minimizing ambiguity. These results hold independent significance for the fields of data exchange and shape conformance. Additionally, we apply these theoretical results to define a polynomial-time algorithm for mapping RDF sources to targets, utilizing shape requirements to address shape ambiguities. This algorithm runs in time linear to the source size and quadratic to the target shape collection. We also present empirical evidence of the algorithm's practical performance. Notably, our experiments indicate that the algorithm produces high-quality mappings for source data that conforms to the provided shape collections. This approach is also practical because it avoids the expensive preprocessing step of computing a Shape Graph, which would be necessary to leverage our theoretical outcomes. Consequently, our method offers a practical means of mapping RDF sources to targets while adhering to shape constraints. We illustrate the algorithm's utility by proposing a data quality check that identifies and quantifies target data violations of the source data's shape requirements. This paper extends an earlier version of the authors' proceedings article, which did not include the material covered in Sections 5, 6, and 7. The current version incorporates several refinements, including a more precise definition of data exchange recurrence, an algorithm that maps source relations to shapes more effectively, and a more efficient method for mapping source tuples to shape instances. These enhancements result in improved solutions for RDF data exchange. Specifically, the algorithm now produces solutions with fewer shielded shape attributes, thereby reducing overall shielded data. This improvement stems from a straightforward refinement of mapping source tuples to shape instances, which prioritizes tuples with fewer shielded attributes. Furthermore, the algorithm's runtime is now quadratic with respect to source data size and cubic with respect to the number of shape collections, representing a significant efficiency gain. Finally, the paper includes a new section detailing how to verify that target RDF data satisfies shape constraints, which was not present in the earlier version. This capability was enabled by the earlier refinement that prioritizes mapping source tuples to shape instances that do not require shielding.

Shape-constrained nonparametric regression has emerged as a significant method across diverse fields, particularly for identifying causal effects. By estimating treatment effects without relying on untestable functional form assumptions, this approach achieves robustness that conventional regression techniques lack. This paper introduces pyStoNED, a comprehensive Python package designed for convex regression, specifically targeting NED (non-decreasing and non-increasing in differences) monotonicity. The method is extensively applied in economics and related fields to analyze costs, prices, demand, supply, and the broader impacts of economic policies. Pyramidal convex regression models are presented as the most effective tool for this purpose. pyStoNED facilitates the estimation of convex functions, calculates optimal solutions for convex minimization problems involving these functions, and generates accurate visualizations. Furthermore, it supports ensembles of models, enabling users to assess the sensitivity of convex model estimates to outliers and varying parameter settings. To demonstrate the package's capabilities, we apply pyStoNED to estimate the causal effects of fertilizer on crop yields, using this analysis to illustrate how the package can elucidate the causal mechanisms underlying economic policies. The package is released under an open-source license and accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchaefer/pyStoNED. This paper presents the first comprehensive investigation of top-quark pair plus Higgs ($t \bar t \phi$) production as a search channel for the low-mass region of a light scalar boson $\phi$. This process offers unique capabilities for exploring scenarios with significantly larger couplings between scalar bosons and top quarks compared to the Standard Model (SM) Higgs. We examine the scalar's coupling to top quarks through a dimensionful effective operator and determine constraints on this operator by examining how constraints from the DM direct detection experiment COUPP and SM Higgs searches intersect with those derived from the $t \bar t \phi$ process. Additionally, we discuss the potential of future high-luminosity LHC runs for searching the SM Higgs boson in the low-mass regime. Finally, we demonstrate that extending the proton-proton collision energy to 33 TeV at a potential Future Circular Collider (FCC-hh) can achieve sensitivity to Higgs couplings to the top quark comparable to current direct SM Higgs searches, even at an integrated luminosity of $\mathcal{L} = 10~$fb$^{-1}$. Furthermore, the search for a pseudoscalar boson yields no constraints, necessitating a dedicated analysis tailored to its distinct production and decay characteristics. Finally, we note that while the analysis for Higgs decaying to diphotons is not yet complete, the search for a scalar boson decaying to two photons is already feasible. Finally, we conclude that further studies are required to fully exploit the $t \bar t \phi$ process for low-mass scalar searches. A more detailed study of this channel will be conducted in a future report. The code used for these analyses is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/Prashant-1998/LowMassHiggsSearches}. The LaTeX source files for this paper are also available at the same link. We introduce an unsupervised and few-shot neural parser built upon a pretrained language model. This approach extracts parse trees by conditioning the model on a natural language query, enabling it to utilize its internal language knowledge for parsing without relying on external grammatical resources. Consequently, we achieve state-of-the-art few-shot results on the CoNLL2003 dataset and successfully identify new morphosyntactic patterns in low-resource languages—specifically Korean and German—that distinct from those found in English. In a zero-shot setting, we compete with the top few-shot performance on NeuroX, a multilingual extension of CoNLL2003; our method ranks second for Korean and German and achieves second place for Malagasy and Swahili without any fine-tuning. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method can jointly parse multiple languages by fine-tuning on just a single source language, a capability that significantly boosts performance when target language data is scarce. Finally, we show that few-shot inference can detect grammatical errors by scoring malformed sentences lower than well-formed ones, successfully identifying various error types across English, Korean, German, and Malagasy. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/taehyunglee97/UnsupervisedParsing. High-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) is essential for numerous applications. While off-the-shelf ASR solutions are readily available, they often underperform for specific language subsets used in specialized domains. Consequently, it is preferable to utilize open-source ASR tools that allow for customization to specific requirements. This study presents the development of a new, open-source ASR system for German. The system is grounded in neural network architectures, featuring an end-to-end design that utilizes a neural network to convert acoustic input features directly into text. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive evaluation comparing various neural architecture choices and hyper-parameters. We achieve a character error rate (CER) of 4.5% on the German test set of the LUKE evaluation platform. Our system's primary source code is released under the Apache 2.0 license and can be accessed at https://github.com/ruddm/auto-german. This project is supported by the DFG-funded Collaborative Research Center (SFB) 894 "Common Sense" and its associated project SC 294. To our knowledge, this represents the most comprehensive evaluation of RNN-based acoustic models for German ASR to date. Our analysis reveals that increasing the number of layers in an RNN architecture, even without adding residual connections, enhances model performance. Finally, our source code is released under the Apache 2.0 license and is available at https://github.com/ruddm/auto-german. This work serves as a foundation for future research into German ASR. We analyze high-resolution spectra of 13 Be-type stars within the 30 Doradus Starburst Region to determine their atmospheric and rotational characteristics. Our findings indicate that these objects possess rapidly rotating companions with periods ranging from 0.4 to 2.2 days. Our N II 6583 emission line modeling reveals that the circumstellar disks in 30 Doradus are less ionized than in the Large Magellanic Cloud, likely due to the intense radiation field in 30 Doradus. Additionally, we report that the emission line profiles of HD 201638 and NGC 2737 exhibit asymmetries, suggesting that their disks are viewed at a high inclination angle. Finally, we identify HD 201638, NGC 2737, and NGC 2749 as the three most luminous Be stars in 30 Doradus. This study is the first to comprehensively examine the properties of Be stars in 30 Doradus, and our results will facilitate further investigations into the characteristics of these objects. The analyzed spectra are now available for the community to study. The three most luminous Be stars in 30 Doradus (HD 201638, NGC 2737, and NGC 2749) are also the most massive stars in 30 Doradus, making them ideal candidates for further research on the mass-loss rates of massive stars. We have applied our methodology to the 30 Doradus Be-star sample, and we intend to extend this approach to other stellar samples in future work. This research is part of a broader study on the mass-loss rates of massive stars, which will be published in an upcoming paper. This paper establishes a Faber-Krahn type inequality concerning the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator under Robin boundary conditions. We demonstrate that the optimal domain is a half-space and provide a detailed analysis of the boundary behavior for the corresponding eigenfunctions. Furthermore, we derive corresponding inequalities for the heat semigroup and the resolvent. Notably, our proof relies solely on rearrangements and does not depend on any variational principle. Finally, we examine the boundary asymptotics of the first eigenfunction within a bounded domain. Specifically, in the limit where the Robin parameter $\beta$ approaches zero or infinity, we precisely determine the corresponding first eigenvalue. Additionally, we prove self-adjointness for the Hermite operator with Robin boundary conditions across all real values of $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$. Our findings extend and complement previous studies by the first author in \cite{Ma2018, Ma2019, Ma2020, Ma2021} regarding Faber-Krahn inequalities for the Hermite operator with Dirichlet and Neumann conditions. Finally, these results are applied to analyze the boundary behavior of eigenfunctions in the resolvent set of the Hermite operator subject to Robin boundary conditions. Finally, to the best of the authors' knowledge, this represents the first study to employ rearrangements to prove a Faber-Krahn inequality for the Hermite operator. Furthermore, the techniques developed here are readily applicable to address similar issues for other operators defined on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Specifically, this approach yields a novel and direct proof of the Faber-Krahn inequality for the Laplacian with Dirichlet boundary conditions, originally established by Sandier and Tartar using concentration compactness methods. Finally, we outline several open questions arising from this work. These results may be extended to the case of Robin conditions with a potential $V$. In this context, we provide a detailed analysis of the boundary behavior of eigenfunctions as eigenvalues approach zero. Specifically, we derive an asymptotic formula for the first eigenvalue in the limit where the Robin parameter $\beta$ tends to zero or infinity. Finally, we prove the self-adjointness of the operator and examine the simplicity of the eigenvalues. Our methodology is applicable to various other operators, including the poly-Laplace operator, and can be utilized to derive the Faber-Krahn inequality for the poly-Laplace operator with Dirichlet conditions. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become essential for addressing complex real-world challenges, yet their susceptibility to adversarial attacks raises significant concerns. While recent studies show that transferring poison intended for one DNN to another usually fails, such success is possible when using Non-Fungible Tangent Kernels (NFTKs), which describe the tangent spaces of two DNNs. This work demonstrates that NFTKs can be employed to generate targeted adversarial examples. Furthermore, we prove that the efficacy of these examples hinges on the spectral properties of the NFTK matrix, duality gaps, and the distance between the NFTKs. Our experimental results indicate that NFTK-based attacks outperform those derived from Optimal Transport (OT) or traditional tangent space alignment methods, offering substantial implications for the security of deep learning systems. Additionally, we present an application for privacy, where a single NFTK-based attack can leak information from multiple models, potentially compromising user data. To our knowledge, this marks the first demonstration that NFTKs can serve as a tool for attacking and evaluating deep learning models. Finally, we release our code and datasets to facilitate the investigation of NFTK properties and enable the transfer of adversarial examples between models. The source code is available at https://github.com/DeepSecurityLab/NFTK-Adv-Attack. The source code for NFTK-based Privacy Attack is accessible at https://github.com/DeepSecurityLab/NFTK-Privacy-Attack. The dataset can be found at https://github.com/DeepSecurityLab/NFTK-Privacy-Attack/tree/master/NFTK_privacy_attack_dataset. Our findings reveal that OT-based attacks perform inferiorly compared to both Tangent Kernel Attack (TKA) and NFTK-based attacks. Specifically, in terms of accuracy, NFTK-based attacks achieve approximately a 10% improvement over TKA and double the accuracy of OT-based attacks. These results are detailed in our paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07004. This study introduces correlation-based non-Hermitian topological phases using the one-dimensional correlated non-Hermitian Hubbard model. By employing the density-matrix renormalization group and Wilson-loop correlation functions, we identify four distinct phases: two dynamic paratopological ones featuring paratanzania and one exhibiting brazeness. These phases are defined by the absence of traditional topological quantization, the lack of edge states, and the absence of a paratopological phase. We also examine the relationship between these correlation-induced topological phases and their Hermitian counterparts. Furthermore, by analyzing the correlation-induced phase diagram without a magnetic field, we uncover a novel phase that displays the opposite characteristics compared to the correlated Hermitian case. Finally, our findings regarding Hermitian phases suggest that similar correlation-driven topological phases may exist in real-world systems. These correlated topological phases are characterized by the absence of spectral paratanzania, brazeness, and edge states, and they defy conventional Hermitian topological definitions. Additionally, the study reveals a limitation of Wilson-loop correlation functions, as they fail to detect certain correlation-induced topological phases. Finally, we explore the potential to engineer correlated topological phases in experimental settings by manipulating the hopping integral. These phases exhibit robustness against thermal fluctuations and, unlike their Hermitian equivalents, do not require a magnetic field. Consequently, they may be more accessible for observation in experiments. Furthermore, we propose a method to induce correlated topological phases in real systems by manipulating the system's parameters. This work expands the scope of topological quantum chemistry and offers new insights into the field. Topological phases induced by correlations can be observed in experimental setups without the need for magnetic fields. The proposed approach for inducing correlated topological phases may have applications in quantum computing and quantum information processing. Engaging correlated topological phases have the potential to be harnessed in quantum sensors and other applications. The study also reveals a new connection between topology and quantum entanglement, which may have implications for quantum gravity research. Finally, the work highlights the potential for correlated topological phases to be used in quantum metrology and quantum communication. The findings also have implications for the development of new materials with unique properties. The study reveals a connection between topology and quantum many-body localization, which may have implications for the development of new quantum materials. The work also explores the potential for correlated topological phases to be used in quantum simulators and quantum engines. The findings also have implications for the development of quantum radar

Drawing inspiration from Heisenberg algebra, the concept of minimal length is integrated into the geometric framework of the relativistic collective model (RCM) for nuclei. This approach involves modifying the metric of the effective space and subsequently calculating the quantum spectrum of the Hamiltonian derived from the Lagrangian of the RCM. The study demonstrates that these minimal length effects significantly influence the characteristics of relativistic collective motions in triaxial nuclei. Furthermore, the relative contributions of quantum and minimal length effects are examined through the ratio $\xi = \hbar / l_{\rm min}$. Finally, assuming $l_{\rm min} = 10^{-15}$ cm, numerical results for the spectrum of the $^{129}$Xe nucleus are presented. These findings indicate that relativistic collective motions in nuclei are strongly dependent on minimal length effects. Specifically, at fixed values of $\xi$, relativeness is more pronounced in prolate nuclei than in oblate ones, whereas oblate nuclei exhibit stronger relativistic collective motion than prolate ones when $\xi$ is small. Additionally, a spectrum with a lower minimum state arises in oblate nuclei compared to prolate ones when $\xi$ is large. These outcomes are attributed to the relativistic behavior of collective motion in nuclei, which is quantified by the velocity $v^2 = \langle \hat{J}_1^2 + \hat{J}_2^2 \rangle / \langle \hat{J}_1^2 + \hat{J}_2^2 + \hat{J}_3^2 \rangle$. This velocity is notably higher in prolate nuclei than in oblate ones for a given $\xi$. Consequently, the relativistic correction to the energy spectrum in prolate nuclei exceeds that in oblate nuclei for a fixed $\xi$. Conversely, the relative correction in prolate nuclei is smaller than in oblate nuclei for a fixed $\xi$. These conclusions are illustrated through the $^{129}$Xe nucleus. Overall, the study confirms that relativistic collective motion in nuclei is profoundly affected by minimal length effects. This study introduces a feature fusion deep convolutional autoencoder architecture designed for change detection in co-registered hyperspectral images. The proposed architecture operates in two phases: first, it learns data-driven features using convolutional autoencoders, and second, it reconstructs these features into a two-channel representation that significantly enhances differential residual maps for post-processing bitemporal comparisons. This confirms that the proposed feature fusion strategy improves differential residual maps and boosts change detection performance in multispectral and hyperspectral imagery. This approach employs a state-of-the-art Neural Network architecture to extract acoustic features directly from the waveform, thereby bypassing the need for pre-computed backend acoustic features. We also propose a technique to lower the computational footprint of the VOTe network while maintaining strong performance. The stochastic dimer model, whether on a lattice or as a continuum limit, features dimers characterized by position, orientation, and a sign. In a background gauge field, the dimer count corresponds to the fermion determinant, which is the product of the anti-orientation and the determinant sign. We demonstrate that the fermion determinant remains invariant under small gauge transformations (both in the lattice and continuum frameworks), whereas the determinant sign alone is not. This specific feature appears to be unique to dimer models. The stochastic dimer model can be reformulated as a sum over histories for non-relativistic Dirac fermions moving in a background gauge field, where each fermion has an equal probability of being oriented up or down. In this formulation, the fermion determinant is defined as the product of the anti-orientation and the determinant sign. Consequently, we establish that the stochastic dimer count equals the sum of these products of dimer anti-orientations. Furthermore, we show that each factor of the determinant sign arises from a single dimer anti-orientation. This result holds for both the lattice and continuum versions of the model. Additionally, we investigate the connection between the dimer sum and the Dirac fermion path integral, revealing a specific property of the dimer count related to the "chiral anomaly." We also provide a discussion of this formulation within the context of the self-avoiding walk model. Finally, we offer a discussion of this representation using geometric arguments. Our approach builds upon earlier work by both communities, with significant contributions from the mathematical study of dimer models and the investigation of fermion determinants and their links to dimers. We have made some initial progress toward this goal. The Group Lasso is a widely used framework for performing selection and regularization on binary or multiclass data. However, standard Group Lasso methods struggle with convergence in high-dimensional settings where the number of features exceeds the sample size, often leading to unreliable results. This limitation primarily stems from relying on iterative methods like coordinate descent, which are computationally intensive and difficult to analyze theoretically. To address these issues, we introduce a novel Group Lasso approach designed for categorical data that utilizes their indicator matrix structure. This method is fast, supports efficient implementation via closed-form solutions, and maintains strong theoretical and empirical accuracy, even when both the parameter dimension and sample size are large. Furthermore, our method is robust in unbalanced scenarios where one class dominates. We also provide provably efficient strategies for high-dimensional multi-group Lasso applications, such as brain imaging. Finally, our solution is general enough to be adapted for sparse group Lasso, which is better suited for low-dimensional, continuous covariates. Embedded systems are increasingly prevalent in safety- and life-critical domains, necessitating the ability to operate multiple real-time tasks from diverse Quality of Service (QoS) guarantees on unified hardware. Employing hypervisors to facilitate the concurrent execution of these applications has emerged as a significant research focus. This study introduces T-Visor, a versatile and adaptable hypervisor tailored for embedded real-time environments supporting QoS. T-Visor leverages Quality of Service enhancements derived from recent operating system and scheduling methodologies. Specifically, it facilitates preemption of real-time virtual machines (VMs) by control VMs to satisfy their stringent real-time demands, implements fixed priority scheduling within each VM, and ensures timely VM exits using an analytical exit time model. Furthermore, it provides exit compensation, allowing VMs to adjust for predicted compensation time when meeting real-time constraints. We validated T-Visor's efficacy regarding timing guarantees through an extensive simulation study involving an automated VM scheduling tool. Our findings demonstrate that T-Visor achieves a higher acceptance ratio for real-time VM scheduling compared to other hypervisors, such as QoS and RT4all, under identical conditions. Additionally, we assessed T-Visor's performance in non-real-time VM execution to evaluate its suitability for mixed-criticality systems, revealing a minimal real-time acceptance rate degradation of approximately 1% relative to QoS. Consequently, T-Visor is a promising solution for developing safe, mixed-criticality embedded systems with real-time capabilities, as it simultaneously satisfies the timing requirements of both real-time and non-real-time VMs. The source code for T-Visor and the VM scheduling tool will be made available upon request. Chimeras are frequently associated with partially synchronized oscillatory systems featuring a neutral limit cycle governed by diffusive coupling among heterogeneous oscillators. This study employs a hybrid analytical and numerical approach to investigate chimeras in limit cycle oscillators with uniformly distributed heterogeneity, organized into two groups coupled within their own populations while weakly interacting across groups. We demonstrate that intra-group diffusive coupling induces partial synchronization and the emergence of chimeras. In this configuration, one population synchronizes while the other remains in an asynchronous state. Our analysis reveals that as the inter-group coupling strength varies smoothly, the system transitions between distinct types of chimeras. Furthermore, we confirm that the positions of the transition points align with predictions derived from the local linearization of the governing equations. Notably, our findings indicate that the asymptotic stability of these chimeras is governed by the local linearization of the inter-group coupling terms. Additionally, we observe that the asymptotic stability of a specific chimera state can be preserved indefinitely as one intra-group coupling strength approaches zero, a phenomenon achievable only when the local linearization of the inter-group coupling terms possesses a zero eigenvalue. This stability is achieved by selecting an intra-group coupling strength for the other population such that the local linearization of that system also yields a zero eigenvalue. Finally, numerical simulations validate the stability characteristics predicted through this hybrid methodology. These results offer valuable insights for understanding the stability of chimera states in systems where intra-group diffusive coupling is absent. Ultimately, the mechanisms identified in this work are applicable to a broad spectrum of limit cycle oscillators with uniformly distributed heterogeneity. Specifically, the stability analysis of chimera states in two identical groups of oscillators coupled only within their own populations can be accurately predicted through local linearization. This approach extends the local linearization method, which has previously been utilized to analyze chimera stability in systems with two partially synchronized populations. Our work provides a novel and effective framework for investigating the stability of chimera states in systems with intra-group diffusive coupling. By extending the local linearization approach, we have established a link between the stability of chimeras and the eigenvalues of the local linearization equations, a connection that has previously been overlooked. This connection facilitates the stability analysis of chimera states in more complex systems and aids in the design of partially synchronized states. These methodologies have already been applied to analyze the stability of chimeras in maps, delay-differential equations, and ordinary differential equations. Model-based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL) utilizes a world model to approximate the true environment and derive an optimal policy, typically offering superior sample efficiency compared to model-free approaches. However, because reinforcement learning inherently carries inherent risks, MBRL can result in unstable behaviors and poor sample efficiency when deployed in real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel probabilistic MBRL framework that integrates uncertainty quantification directly into the policy learning process. By employing a Gaussian Process to model the reward function and applying the Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound (GP-UCB) algorithm, the resulting policy can safely interact with the real world, thereby enhancing stability and sample efficiency. Experimental results confirm the method's effectiveness across three robotic manipulation tasks: pushing, balancing, and opening a drawer. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/zhongtao123/PBC. Furthermore, this work is the first to demonstrate that probabilistic MBRL achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art model-free algorithms under the same sample efficiency constraints.
