The energy carried by solar wind plasma is a critical component of the total energy budget within the inner heliosphere, significantly influencing the energy transfer between the solar wind and solar system plasma and the subsequent heating of the latter. This component has been inaccessible to observation until the launch of the Parker Solar Probe, which has now begun in-situ measurements of solar wind energy flux in the inner heliosphere. Analyzing data from the Solar Field and Plasma Science instrument across 18 inner heliosphere encounters reveals energy fluxes ranging from 0.001 to 0.1 W/cm$^2$. These observed fluxes align with theoretical models and are comparable to the thermal energy flux derived from in-situ measurements of solar wind energy. The most frequent fluxes occur near 0.01 W/cm$^2$, consistent with findings from in-situ thermal data. Across all encounters, energy flux exhibits substantial variability on timescales of approximately one day, mirroring fluctuations in thermal pressure. These variations are linked to solar wind structures identified in existing literature, including switchbacks, magnetic clouds, and coronal mass ejections. Furthermore, solar minimum encounters display lower average energy fluxes than solar maximum encounters, whereas energy flux in solar maximum encounters shows a stronger correlation with radial distance from the Sun. These results establish a foundation for future investigations into solar wind energy flux and its impact on inner heliosphere plasma. The findings also offer constraints for modeling the evolution of inner heliosphere plasma properties and may inform the interpretation of data from current and upcoming missions, such as the Interstellar Boundary Explorer and the Heliospheric Imager on the Parker Solar Probe. Finally, these observations can help calibrate and constrain global heliospheric models. (A video summarizing these results is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=11422222190). Introducing $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems is anticipated to significantly influence both transparency and the velocities of slow and fast light. This study examines how QED-like transparency and fast or slow light phenomena respond to $q$-deformation within a QED optomechanical framework featuring a single cavity mode coupled to two mechanical oscillators. The results demonstrate that QED-like transparency can be controlled by adjusting the q-parameter, whereas the generation of fast and slow light is constrained by the mechanical oscillator temperature, the coupling strength, the q-parameter, the cavity reflection coefficient, and the cavity frequency detuning. Notably, the $q$-deformation parameter has a distinct impact on the group velocity associated with fast light events. These findings may advance the utilization of light transmission characteristics in $q$-deformed optomechanical environments. Furthermore, the proposed model holds potential applications in all-optical communication, optical computing, information processing, and optical switches. In prior research, I demonstrated that within the Two-Rotors Framework, specific -1 parity states with the maximum allowed $|M|=1$ function as rotors in a rigid-body configuration while accompanying a core rotation at $|M|=0$ behaves like a rotor in a deformed configuration. These states naturally emerge as scissors modes when utilizing a negative potential, exhibiting properties analogous to their positive potential counterparts, including the ability to be defined by two rotational frequencies and represented via the Wigner $d$-function. Consequently, this study establishes the existence of R-even, negative parity scissors modes, contrasting with the previously identified R-odd modes. Furthermore, I show that the 2-$\sigma$ state, previously thought to lack scissors character, actually displays scissors mode properties within certain regions of parameter space. Finally, the kinematic and dynamical characteristics of these new modes are examined and compared with their R-odd equivalents. This investigation into R-even, negative parity states in superfluid nuclei is conducted based on prior work regarding R-odd, negative parity states, which previously demonstrated that Negative Potential Rotors (NPRs) and Deformed Potential Rotors (DPRs) with $K=0$ and $M=\pm 1$ components can generate R-parity scissors modes in R-even negative parity states. This study extends that framework to include contributions from NPRs and DPRs with $K=1$. The findings may offer new perspectives on scissors isomers, the origin of which remain an active area of research. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the model; Section 3 details the eigenstate spectrum, focusing on R-even, negative parity states; Section 4 analyzes the dynamical properties of these states; Section 5 presents the results and their discussion; and Section 6 provides the conclusions. Additionally, Appendix A provides the explicit form of the Wigner $d$-function matrix elements, and Appendix B discusses the relationship between the Wigner $d$-function and the associated Laguerre polynomials. Inspired by the characteristics of finite-volume schemes, we develop a data-driven framework termed the cell-average based neural network (CV-NN). This approach employs finite-volume discretization to transform partial differential equations into a recursive form that explicitly defines cell-averages based on prior values and those of neighboring cells. By utilizing the finite difference property, the first-level approximations of right-hand side terms are generated. Subsequently, neural networks are trained to refine these initial approximations until the entire process aligns with the discrete evolution of cell-averages. This method demonstrates high accuracy and stability across various benchmark problems, including linear and nonlinear finite difference schemes for both parabolic and hyperbolic equations. Furthermore, a finite volume-consistent neural network (FVCN) approach is introduced; it feeds the entire CV-NN output into a neural network trained to predict the final cell-average based on the first-level approximations, achieving superior accuracy. Finally, the CV-NN method is applied to the Burgers equation with random initial conditions and two randomly generated initial profiles to evaluate its generalization capabilities. Collectively, these findings indicate that the proposed method performs robustly for both standard and atypical initial value problems. Additionally, the framework's versatility is extended to both homogeneous and inhomogeneous linear and nonlinear reaction-diffusion equations. The code implementation, built upon the DeepXDE library, is provided to facilitate reproducibility. Future research will explore extending the FVCN method to more complex scenarios. This work represents a significant advancement in data-driven approaches for solving partial differential equations. Notably, the algorithm displays finite-time behavior, enabling the resolution of high-dimensional problems. The ALICE Collaboration has completed the design and construction of its detector upgrade for the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) and has commenced initial data-taking operations. The primary objective of this upgrade is to achieve data collection and triggering efficiency during proton-lead and lead-lead collisions at an instantaneous luminosity of 100 nb$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ in lead-lead collisions, while also accommodating associated proton events. This paper outlines the performance of the reconstructed ALICE magnetic field, detailing how the upgraded detector has already met the design goals for luminosity handling. Furthermore, the current capability of the upgraded detector is presented, along with a proposal for future upgrades targeting the end of the LHC's operation cycle in 2039, which aims to address the anticipated data challenges from LHC Facility 3 (LHC F3). Specifically, the ALICE Future End of Cycle upgrade (ALICE-FEYC) is proposed to address data challenges related to an integrated luminosity of 10 ab$^{-1}$, a potential future scenario for the LHC Facility 3. To achieve this, the ALICE-FEYC upgrade will implement significant improvements to the current detector, including the installation of new tracking and vertexing systems, the development of advanced trigger and data acquisition technologies, and the creation of new experimental analysis tools. These upgrades are designed to facilitate new and advanced physics measurements focused on ultra-peripheral collisions (UPC), quantum phenomena, and heavy-ion collisions. The proposed ALICE-FEYC upgrade is expected to be ready for data-taking by 2035, with a total cost of approximately 100 million CHF. This proposal has been developed through a series of workshops involving the ALICE Collaboration and the ALICE Upgrade Committee, as well as discussions with the ALICE Advisory Board and other ALICE sub-Committees. Additionally, the ALICE Collaboration is actively developing the scientific case for the ALICE-FEYC, and this paper will provide an update on that development. The scientific case for the ALICE-FEYC upgrade is based on the anticipated data challenges resulting from the LHC F3 and the specific physics capabilities of the current ALICE detector upgrade that are necessary to address these challenges. The Unruh effect predicts that an accelerated detector perceives the vacuum as a thermal bath, even though no particles exist in the true vacuum. While Unruh-Davies-UNG thermicity criteria have been utilized to demonstrate this phenomenon, these methods often require calculating Unruh-Davies entropy, which involves complex procedures such as field mode decompositions in moving frames. In contrast, this study presents a straightforward protocol to detect the Unruh effect using the concept of Berry phases within a simplified detector model, thereby demonstrating that "something" akin to thermal radiation is indeed present in what should otherwise be a null state of motionless, cold vacuum. Specifically, the Unruh effect is evidenced by computing the entanglement between future and past light cones, which induces changes in the detector's internal state. This process generates coherence between the detector's internal configurations, giving rise to a dynamical Berry phase in a simplified Hamiltonian. To illustrate the relevance of this detection method, the Unruh effect is also examined in two specific scenarios: a uniformly accelerated detector in a Minkowski vacuum and a non-inertial observer in an entangled vacuum state across two Rindler wedges, where entanglement between the wedges produces a "timelike" Unruh effect. Furthermore, this work establishes a framework for developing entanglement-assisted detection schemes to explore the intricate relationship between gravity, thermodynamics, and quantum information. Finally, the findings are extended to quantum key distribution protocols, where entanglement between future and past light cones generates secret keys, offering a solution to the problem of distributing entangled particles between non-local observers. Overall, the research advances the field of experimental tests for the Unruh effect by offering a simple, fundamental, and feasible approach to uncover this subtle phenomenon. Additionally, the work introduces a novel perspective on entanglement between non-local regions, providing a solution to the problem of non-local entanglement distribution. Finally, the results are applicable to quantum computing architectures that rely on non-local entanglement distribution. The proposed scheme is compatible with existing optical quantum computing platforms, including those based on optical parametric oscillators, entanglement swapping, and entanglement-assisted quantum key distribution. This approach not only deepens our understanding of the Unruh effect but also holds significant potential for advancing quantum computing technologies. Event extraction remains a critical yet difficult aspect of information extraction, with most current research concentrated on monolingual English systems. This focus stems partly from the availability of large-scale datasets for English. In contrast, this paper addresses the challenge of extracting events from non-English, multilingual media texts. We introduce a novel multilingual dataset spanning ten languages—Hindi, Bengali, Pashto, Urdu, Tamil, Gujarati, Marathi, Nepali, Sinhala, and English—comprising 1,500 manually annotated articles gathered from news and news-like platforms. Upon completion of the data collection and annotation phase, we conducted a comprehensive experimental analysis of system performance across these languages. Furthermore, we evaluated various annotation strategies, including coarse-to-fine and fine-to-coarse frameworks, alongside multiple extractions models such as BERT, BERTweet, BERTJoke, and BART. Our findings indicate that fine-grained annotation frameworks yield superior performance compared to coarse-grained ones. Additionally, we demonstrated that pre-trained multilingual models, like BERT and BERTJoke, hold significant potential for multilingual event extraction. This study offers valuable insights into available data resources and effective data processing techniques for multilingual event extraction. The associated code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ashraful123/MEE. We anticipate this dataset will advance research in multilingual NLP. Stellar winds from companion stars represent a likely source of accreted matter in binary systems during their X-ray sources' hard states. This study investigates how such winds influence the spectral and timing characteristics of the most prominent 40-month dataset from the hard state of the Cyg X-1 black hole system. Using the X-ray spectral-timing simulation (XSTAR-TIMING) tool, we examined how varying wind densities and temperatures alter the absorption properties of interstellar material along the line of sight. Our results indicate that stellar winds can significantly affect the spectral and timing features of black hole candidates in hard states, a factor that must be accounted for when interpreting the fundamental continuum emission of these systems. Specifically, we demonstrate that low-density winds with temperatures below 100 eV can mimic the spectral and timing signatures attributed to ionized gas in Cyg X-1. These findings suggest that the previously reported evidence for an ionized gas wind in Cyg X-1 may instead be explained by a low-density, cool stellar wind. Furthermore, we show that stellar wind absorption can distort the observed mean time lag between 6 and 60 keV, causing it to deviate from the inverse proportionality to photon energy expected from Compton scattering in the Comptonization region. This effect must be considered when analyzing time-lag spectral-timing data from hard-state black hole X-ray binaries. Our findings provide robust support for the presence of a cool stellar wind around Cyg X-1 and highlight the critical role of stellar winds in determining the spectral and timing properties of hard-state black hole X-ray binaries. These results also establish a foundation for future research into the spectral and timing properties of stellar winds in other hard-state black hole X-ray binary systems. Finally, we introduce an open-source Python package named \texttt{XSTAR-TIMING} to facilitate these investigations. This tool allows users to simulate and analyze the spectral and timing properties of stellar winds, enabling constraints on wind density and temperature based on observed spectral and timing data. It can be utilized to determine the physical parameters of winds in Cyg X-1 and similar systems. The \texttt{XSTAR-TIMING} package is available at \url{https://github.com/fernando-fernandez/XSTAR-TIMING}. The study examines Yang-Mills-aether theory, focusing on the implications of a non-abelian, aether-like term that induces Lorentz symmetry violation within a thermal quantum field theory framework. By employing the Matsubara formalism and a cutoff scheme for momentum in spatial dimensions, the analysis calculates corrections to free energy and the stress-energy tensor at both zero and finite temperatures. Furthermore, a mean-field approach is utilized to investigate color deconfinement and chiral phase transitions within this non-abelian temperature-dependent aether model. Finally, the paper outlines the sources of instability arising from specific choices of the aether-like term and proposes generalized correction terms for the free energy and stress-energy tensor. As boundary conditions for the aether field are relaxed, a nonlinear gluing effect between gluons and the aether emerges, altering the interpretation of the non-abelian temperature-dependent phase transition. We introduce a joint approach to simultaneous syntetic and semantic parsing, modeling both processes within a single probabilistic framework. This method leverages shared subspaces that connect syntactic and semantic features, enabling mutual reinforcement between the two parsing outcomes. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves the state-of-the-art universal semantic parsing score of 61.6% on the Universal Semantic Roles dataset (UMR), while also showing promising accuracy on the Penn Treebank (PTB) syntetic parsing task. Furthermore, our framework exhibits greater resilience to dataset shifts than previous separate syntactic and semantic parsing methods. These findings indicate that joint syntactic and semantic parsing yields substantial benefits. Additionally, we provide a PyTorch implementation of our framework at https://github.com/zhijunliu/juSP.

We investigated the jet-driven disruption of magnetized neutrino-cooled accretion disks, focusing on how jet power and inclination angle influence jet dynamics and disk evolution. Our findings indicate that moderate-energy jets (10^50 erg/s) can directly eject material from the disk midplane at moderate inclinations (45°), while high-energy jets (>10^51 erg/s) may impact the midplane to form an extended outflow. Furthermore, if the disk retains significant angular momentum, a broad, fast-moving outflow (velocity >10^10 cm/s) may be generated. These fast outflows could potentially power a late-time electromagnetic signal, such as an afterglow. In most scenarios, the total mass ejected from the midplane ranges from 0.01 to 0.1 M_sun. Additionally, a substantial fraction of the disk mass may be lifted to the inner layers (r<10^6 cm) by the jet, where it forms an extended accretion disk. This lifted mass could contribute a few times 10^51 erg to the neutrino flux observed during the early afterglow phase. Our results suggest that a combination of high-energy jets (>10^51 erg/s) and moderate inclinations (45°) can produce powerful outflows capable of disrupting the accretion disk. This finding may help explain the early and late electromagnetic emissions from GRB 130603B. Finally, we propose that a scenario involving both powerful jets and rapidly rotating accretion disks may be necessary to simultaneously account for the high-energy gamma-ray burst and the high-energy afterglow observed from GW170817. In this context, a large-mass black hole is essential to generate the high-energy gamma-ray burst. Over time, the accretion disk could evolve into a thin, massive disk, potentially producing a high-energy afterglow. The accretion disk mass required to power an afterglow of ~10^50 erg/s is approximately 10^-2 M_sun. Our study demonstrates that powerful, high-energy jets can disrupt accretion disks, a process that may have occurred in GW170817. This implies that a rapidly rotating black hole, formed by the merger of massive neutron stars, may have existed during the early afterglow phase. This study continues a series exploring the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), which extends General Relativity by relaxing the principle of spherical symmetry. ASTG is derived by applying the azimuthal symmetry constraint to the Spherical Symmetric Einstein Spherically Symmetric Spherical (4D) frame. Within ASTG, the gravitation field equation retains the Spherical Symmetric Einstein Spherically Symmetric form but incorporates an additional term derived from the Spherically Symmetric Spherical frame. This extra term generates a gravitational force that increases with the inverse square of the radial coordinate, thereby acting as a repulsive force at large distances. This characteristic facilitates the explanation of the dynamical origin of outflows in star-forming regions and the subsequent emergence of planetary systems. Furthermore, ASTG offers a gravitational basis for the flywheel mechanism driving the formation of star-planet systems. The repulsive nature of this force gives rise to a gravitation potential that diminishes with the inverse square of the radial distance, creating a gravitation potential well. This well serves as the foundation for modeling the dynamical evolution of stellar systems, including stars, planetary systems, and their associated feedback and outflow processes. Additionally, ASTG successfully explains the dynamical origin of solar system formation and planetary orbits, while also providing a framework to investigate the impact of outflows on the dynamical evolution of star-planet systems. To achieve this, the paper introduces a model of star formation under ASTG, deriving the governing equations for star-forming disks and their associated bipolar outflows. The results indicate that ASTG provides a more comprehensive and detailed description of star formation dynamics compared to General Relativity. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion on the implications of ASTG regarding star formation. Overall, these findings demonstrate the significant potential of ASTG to enhance our understanding of fundamental astrophysical phenomena. This study examines the optical emission from ten fast radio bursts (FRBs) that occurred between 2019 and 2020, which were previously reported with radio signals originating from the same sky position. We analyzed deep optical imaging data collected during the peak of each radio detection, resulting in six non-detections and four detections. The detected fluxes range from 0.0001 to 0.0014 mJy, with two events showing upper limits of approximately 0.001 mJy. We demonstrate that all non-detections are consistent with a model predicting optical emission peaking at ~100 seconds with a total energy output of roughly $10^{39}$ erg. Furthermore, we establish upper bounds on the fraction of FRBs capable of producing both simultaneous and highly beamed optical emission. We also evaluate the likelihood that our sample contains a population of FRBs with optical emission lagging the radio signal by 100–1000 seconds. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the investigation of FRB 20210514A. These results suggest that the fast, highly beamed optical emission proposed to explain the early optical emission of FRB 20200110X is unlikely to be a common feature of FRBs. Additionally, the potential for a multi-messenger, multi-morphological transient event involving FRB 20210514A is considered unlikely. We suggest that future FRB surveys should be complemented by early-time, high-time-resolution optical observations. This approach would facilitate the early detection of fast, highly beamed optical emission and enable the direct testing of emission models. Furthermore, it would allow for the identification of optical emission arriving simultaneously with or shortly after the radio emission. We propose that the early optical emission of FRB 20200110X is unlikely to be beamed toward Earth, and that any optical emission from FRBs is generally expected to be delayed by approximately 100–1000 seconds relative to the radio emission. These conclusions are contingent upon the FRB radio emission being the primary emission mode. Future multi-messenger observations of FRBs will significantly advance our understanding of the universe. This will help identify the sources of FRBs, constrain their physical properties, and better understand the environments in which they reside. This paper introduces Delegated RingCT, a modified version of the RingCT protocol, which is a cryptographic method ensuring private payments on blockchains through the use of rings. The primary modification involves replacing secret rings by extracting information directly from public chains. This approach enables a two-step protocol: first, a non-interactive preparation phase where a sender and receiver generate a secret ring alongside a proof; second, the sender signs the value, the receiver adds a signature to the ring, and together they produce a signed ringCT proof. This mechanism ensures that only the transaction participants hold knowledge of the specific ring members. We name this approach "delegated RingCT" because the receiver delegates the ability to reveal the ring to both themselves and the sender. Compared to standard RingCT, Delegated RingCT offers nearly tenfold improvement in both time and space efficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the protocol is secure under two widely accepted trust assumptions: either the common knowledge base chain is sufficiently long, or there exists a trusted entity capable of attesting to the existence of that chain. Additionally, we establish the protocol's security through a generic security model. Finally, we outline two deployment scenarios: one where all transaction participants possess access to a public chain, and another where only the public chain holder possesses it. While participants in the latter scenario cannot individually see the ring, they collectively know its existence, allowing them to execute transactions without direct interaction. To our knowledge, Delegated RingCT represents the first application of public chain information for secret ring generation. We have implemented the protocol in Rust and made the open-source code available on GitHub. Given that most users on major platforms like Bitcoin and Monero are constrained by hardware limits, Delegated RingCT is particularly well-suited to address their performance bottlenecks. We anticipate that future research will explore variations of this protocol to enable public chain-based RingCT transactions for individuals who do not own the chain. Additionally, we plan to extend Delegated RingCT to facilitate joint value signing between a sender and a receiver who do not interact directly. Finally, we propose that Delegated RingCT can enhance privacy on existing platforms by allowing users to leverage the public chain to select an optimal ring. This capability to select the best ring is exclusive to Delegated RingCT, as general RingCT users cannot choose the specific set of members. We demonstrate this advantage with an example application. Overall, we believe Delegated RingCT will foster further innovation in secret ring technology and that it holds the potential to revolutionize anonymous transactions on public blockchains.

In 2018, the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) implemented a novel diagnostic system called the luminosity scan. This method works alongside other standard beam diagnostics to measure the vertical horizontal beam-beam interaction parameter, denoted as $\xi_{ver}$, a critical factor for LHC physics performance. This paper details the operating principles of luminosity scans and provides an overview of their initial application to the LHC during the 2018 physics run. The presentation will include an in-depth description of the technique, sample results, and a discussion of the method's advantages and constraints. Additionally, the role of simulations in designing and validating the technique will be highlighted. The discussion will focus on the transition from an initial proof-of-principle demonstration to a full diagnostic integration, addressing both technical and non-technical challenges. We will also explore how the technique was adapted for the Compact LHC (CLIC) Insertion Test Facility (CLIC-ITF) and its potential applicability to other accelerators. Finally, we will outline a future variant of the luminosity scan that leverages machine learning to enhance both the speed and precision of the measurements. Driven by advancements in machine learning, data-driven methods have emerged as a vital complement to traditional theory-driven approaches in modeling and control. However, the sheer volume of data and computational demands often make applying these methods to large-scale systems daunting. To address this, this work introduces a cooperative data-driven modeling framework designed for distributed systems. In this approach, the system is partitioned into subsystems, where local models are learned using split datasets. Subsequently, these local models are refined through online streaming data from neighboring subsystems. The efficacy of this cooperative strategy is validated across various distributed systems using both synthetic and real-world data, with results indicating superior performance compared to centralized methods. Furthermore, the theoretical analysis establishes the relationship between the convergence rates of this cooperative approach and both the communication between subsystems and the volume of streaming data. Ultimately, this research offers a promising solution for applying data-driven techniques to large-scale systems. Keywords: data-driven modeling, modeling error, convergence rate, cooperative. This study examines the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ decays where $n=1,2,3$, proposing that the $\Upsilon(10753)$ is a hadronic loop state. By incorporating a multipole expansion for the $\Upsilon(10753)\to^{3}P_{J}$ hybrid quarkonium ($J=0,1,2$) and $\pi$ loop contributions to the $S$ wave, we calculate the decay widths. Comparing our theoretical predictions with experimental data, we derive the contributions from the $P$ state, hybrid ($J=0,1,2$) loop, and $\pi$ loop components. Our findings indicate that higher $n$ values result in larger decay rates, with the $P$ state, hybrid ($J=0,1,2$) loop, and $\pi$ loop contributions accounting for approximately 1.1%, 1.3%, and 1.6% of the total, respectively. Furthermore, we analyze the effects of varying parameters, such as the radius of the $P$ state, hybrid ($J=0,1,2$) loop, and $\pi$ loop contributions on the total decay rate. Our results demonstrate that an increase in the $P$ state loop contribution leads to a higher decay rate, whereas changes in hybrid and $\pi$ loop contributions result in lower decay rates. These findings offer a reference for understanding the structure of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ and its decay properties. Additionally, the study investigates the influence of the number of loops on the total decay rate, revealing that incorporating more loops results in an increase in the overall decay rate. This work provides a foundation for interpreting the structure of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ and its associated decay characteristics. The findings of this research are valuable for advancing our understanding of quarkonium physics and its various manifestations. Ultimately, this research contributes significantly to the broader field of particle physics. Specifically, the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ decays induced by the hadronic loop mechanism provide crucial insights into the dynamics of particle interactions and decay processes. The implications of this work extend to multiple aspects, including the development of new techniques for studying particle decays and the refinement of existing models in quantum chromodynamics. This paper introduces AskewSGD, a novel algorithm designed to train deep neural networks using quantized weights. We address the interval constraints inherent in trained quantized networks, which result from the specific selection and distribution of neural features. By applying the fundamental laws of mean and variance, we derive a closed-form expression for quantizing neural weights while adhering to these interval constraints. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the distribution of optimal neural features can be approximated using the mean value theorem, enabling the application of back-propagation to optimize network parameters during the quantization process. Our empirical findings indicate that the trained quantized networks are not merely centered within their respective intervals but are shifted, or "askew," relative to their mean. Additionally, we observe that the distribution of optimal neural features is unimodal and skewed, a characteristic confirmed by comparing the empirical distributions of our trained quantized networks with the theoretical distributions of random quantized networks. Finally, AskewSGD outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods for training quantized neural networks. Specifically, when using 2-bit weights and 8-bit activations, our approach achieves an accuracy of 93.0% on CIFAR-10 and 71.2% on CIFAR-100, surpassing previous results by approximately 4%. For the MNIST dataset, it reaches an accuracy of 99.4%, improving upon the prior state-of-the-art accuracy of 98.9%. These methods are implemented in the Quantized Neural Network (QNN) package available on PyPI. The package includes implementations of AskewSGD and other state-of-the-art training techniques for quantized neural networks. Users can easily compare the performance of AskewSGD against these alternative approaches. The QNN package is licensed under the MIT license and is freely available. Continuum robots offer superior dexterity and dexterity, making them ideal for confined and unstructured settings. Their ability to conform to complex shapes and perform intricate maneuvers is essential for various applications in medicine, industry, and agriculture. The core advantage of these robots lies in their continuous structure, which enables smooth motion and interaction. However, this very characteristic complicates precise control, as continuum robots are highly flexible and difficult to model accurately. This difficulty stems from the presence of numerous degrees of freedom and the need to account for dynamic effects, as well as external disturbances and internal contact forces. Consequently, controlling such robots requires robust, intelligent, and efficient systems. This survey examines the current landscape of model-based control for continuum robots. It begins by detailing existing modeling approaches, including kinematic, dynamic, and hybrid models, before analyzing current research initiatives. Our analysis reveals that while model-based control has made significant strides in recent years, it is not yet universally applicable. For instance, robots without force sensors currently lack a definitive control structure. Furthermore, many proposed controllers are highly application-specific, limiting their generalizability. We also identify several critical challenges that must be addressed to advance the field: enhancing the precision of continuum robot models, developing more robust and intelligent controller architectures, and designing more efficient controller implementations. The remainder of this survey is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines the most prevalent control structures in literature; Section 3 provides a comprehensive review of modeling techniques; Section 4 highlights key challenges and research gaps; and Section 5 concludes the survey and proposes a roadmap for future research. We contend that a systematic understanding of model-based control is essential for researchers and practitioners to effectively utilize and further develop these robots. This survey serves as a foundational step in that direction. We conclude with a detailed roadmap for advancing model-based control in continuum robots, with the aim of fostering future research and innovation in this dynamic field. Our goal is to provide researchers and practitioners with the necessary tools to better understand and harness the potential of continuum robots. We hope this survey will act as a springboard for exciting new research and development in the realm of model-based control for these robots. (Readers should note that our review covers the state-of-the-art up to the publication date of this survey.) The real Jacobi group $G^J_1$ is defined as the semi-direct product of the first real unimodular group $S_1$ and the multiplicative group of non-zero real numbers. This paper begins an investigation into the representation theory and unitary irreducible representations of $G^J_1$ by demonstrating two alternative construction methods for the irreducible metaplectic operators acting on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, which are unified under a single algebraic framework. The first method relies on geometric phase-space operations, while the second is derived through a direct application of the polar decomposition theorem for elements within the unimodular algebra $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$. Furthermore, we examine the irreducible representations of $G^J_1$ by extending these metaplectic operators. Finally, we provide a classification of these representations based on whether they are square-integrable or induced. These findings may prove beneficial for developing a unified theory of angular momentum operators within quantum mechanics. Additionally, we outline a strategy for generalizing these results to the real second unimodular group $S_2$ and the multiplicative group of non-zero real numbers. Such an approach could be instrumental in advancing the investigation into generalized angular momentum operators in quantum mechanics and may also aid in developing a geometric theory of geometric phases applicable to any compact representation of a real unimodular group. Finally, we derive a formula for a real analytic function on a real unimodular group using a classical Dirichlet series associated with a Weyl element, and we prove a generalization of a real analytic Eisenstein series. These results hold potential applications in quantum field theory. Finally, we introduce a unified theory for metaplectic operators and metaplectic matrices, which generalizes both the Frobenius determinant formula and the Cassini formula. Keywords: real unimodular group, real Jacobi group, angular momentum, geometric phase, compact group, metaplectic operator, Dirichlet series, Eisenstein series. Verifying facts using structured data is crucial for ensuring the credibility of information sourced from tables in encyclopedic references like Wikipedia. This process involves comparing a claim's subject and predicate against table facts to determine its validity. We introduce a novel approach for verifying facts in a natural language context by breaking the task into two simpler sub-tasks: claim analysis and fact retrieval. Additionally, we present a method to re-integrate the outputs of these sub-tasks for fact verification, alongside an evaluation of three strategies for resolving the coordination between them. Our results demonstrate that the strategy yielding the best performance utilizes completely unsupervised components for both claim analysis and fact retrieval, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on the ChKB dataset without any training annotations. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that our unsupervised coordination strategy surpasses existing methods in both accuracy and interpretability. Finally, we explore applications in knowledge graph completion and information extraction, showing that it significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) generate samples by leveraging a learned data distribution governed by a generator network. While GANs are powerful, they often struggle with mode collapse and lack control over the specific characteristics of the generated samples. This thesis investigates two approaches to enhance GANs: gaining insight into the latent space and establishing control over sample attributes. The proposed architectures utilize an encoder network to map samples into a lower-dimensional latent space, which is optimized through an adversarial game between the encoder and decoder networks. The first method, a Variational Auto-GAN, integrates a KL divergence loss function into the standard GANAdversarial loss, resulting in a three-layer architecture. The second method, a Conditional Auto-GAN, functions similarly but conditions the sampling process on an one-hot label vector representing a specific sample attribute. Experiments conducted on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets validate the effectiveness of the latent space modeling approach, demonstrating that the encoder can represent the data distribution of both datasets and producing a circularly arranged embedding consistent with prior research. Regarding attribute conditioning, successful experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate the model's ability to manipulate sample attributes, though results on MNIST indicate a need for further refinement. Ultimately, this research offers a robust architecture for modeling the sample distribution of both MNIST and CIFAR-10 and provides a mechanism for controlling the attributes of generated samples. The findings suggest promising avenues for future work, including the potential to decouple multiple sample attributes and refine the attribute conditioning method. Keywords: Generative adversarial networks, latent space conditioning, attribute conditioning.

Nested Sampling (JSB+01) functions as a method for model comparison and parameter estimation, utilizing an importance sampling technique to explore high-posterior probability regions. While various enhanced samplers, such as transition nested sampling, have been developed to improve mixing and convergence, the relative merits of these approaches compared to basic algorithms remain unclear. This study evaluates seven algorithms across four distinct models, characterized by increasing complexity, employing four metrics to assess their performance. Our findings indicate that for model comparison, the advantages of enhanced samplers over the basic approach are marginal. However, regarding parameter estimation, the transition nested sampling algorithm surpasses all other methods. We further illustrate the efficacy of transition nested sampling in a nested Bayesian model selection context, named the Nested Algorithm for Enhanced Model Selection (NAEMS), which outperforms other enhanced algorithms. Additionally, we propose a parameter estimation metric based on the posterior variance of parameters, derived from the Fisher information matrix inverse, to facilitate more informed algorithm selection. Finally, we apply the NAEMS algorithm to estimate the parameters of a gamma distribution and a two-component mixture of Poisson distributions, both of which exhibit challenging feature spaces. The objective of fault-tolerant distance labeling is to assign compact labels to the vertices of a graph $G$ so that the distance between any two vertices $u$ and $v$ can be deduced from their labels and a third vertex $f$ representing a failed node, effectively computing the distance in $G \setminus \{f\}$. We demonstrate that any directed weighted planar graph, as well as any graph family exhibiting $O(1)$-bounded directed pathwidth, admits a family of labels satisfying $O(1)$-correctness under failures of any $k$ nodes, complete with an efficient algorithm to resolve a fault. Furthermore, for a class of graphs $G$ possessing $O(1)$-bounded directed path-treewidth and a corresponding directed path-decomposition tree $T$, we establish that faults can be addressed using $O(\log k)$ time by assigning labels of size $O(k)$ to the tree nodes and $O(1)$ labels to the graph vertices. These labels maintain $O(1)$ correctness even when $k$ faults occur. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of fault-tolerant distance labeling for planar graphs that scales efficiently with $k$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the labels can be precomputed in polynomial time, even when $k$ is unspecified. Our constructed labels also support a broader fault-tolerance model: any $k$ vertices $v_1, \ldots, v_k$ remain mutually reachable in $G \setminus \{f\}$ if and only if they are reachable via the labels in the original graph $G$. Finally, we present fault-tolerant distance labels for planar graphs with $O(\log k)$ correctness, utilizing labels of size $O(k)$ and enabling fault resolution in $O(1)$ time. To our knowledge, this marks the first result to bound the fault-tolerance trade-off by the fault response time. To our knowledge, this also represents the first result to bound the fault-tolerance trade-off by the label size. Our primary technical contribution involves a novel application of directed path-decomposition trees to manage fault tolerance. We anticipate that the proposed algorithm and fault-tolerance framework can be extended to address fault tolerance in broader classes of directed graphs. We investigate time- and frequency-domain two-particle correlations (structure factors) for a driven, dissipative Bose-Hubbard model. In this system, photons are injected into the two-dimensional optical lattice from the boundaries and are simultaneously removed through the basis sites. The interaction between driven and dissipative dynamics generates a non-stationary steady state. In the stationary framework, we examine two-particle correlations within both real and frequency domains, analyzing how driving strength, loss, and photon-number detuning affect the resulting patterns. Notably, the real-space structure factor can be derived from its frequency-space counterpart via the Fourier transform, although this relationship holds only for the field operator. However, for the normal-ordered field operator, this recoverability is lost. These findings are validated using exact diagonalization and a strong-coupling master equation approach. Our results indicate that structure factors serve as a valuable tool for characterizing the non-equilibrium steady state of open quantum systems. Furthermore, while structure factors are typically defined in the eigenbasis of the undriven undissipative system, they can be extended to arbitrary bases. Finally, we explore the model's applicability in quantum simulation and sensing. In this context, a non-ideal Fourier transform arising from finite sampling of the structure factor may hinder the reconstruction of the real-space distribution from its frequency counterpart. This limitation can be mitigated by employing a quantum non-demolition measurement scheme that allows for the characterization of normal-ordered field operators. Such an approach enables the derivation of quantum-enhanced quantum sensors capable of surpassing the standard quantum limit. Thus, this study establishes a foundation for the correlation analysis of quantum many-body systems and for the development of quantum sensors utilizing quantum entanglement. The computational code is publicly accessible. To prevent erroneous predictions, machine learning models used in safety-critical domains often employ out-of-distribution (OOD) detection to identify predictions lacking sufficient confidence and alert human operators. However, current state-of-the-art methods rely on probabilistic models, making them susceptible to overfitting and inefficient, as they cannot be easily integrated into end-to-end neural network training. This paper introduces a Gaussian process layer for neural networks that leverages the theory of distributional Gaussian processes. This approach enables the straightforward calculation of predictive uncertainty for OOD detection while facilitating a efficient variational training of Gaussian processes within deep networks. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves performance comparable to other state-of-the-art techniques for OOD detection and surpasses them when trained in an end-to-end manner. Additionally, unlike other methods, the proposed layer can be detached during inference to quantify the impact of additional training data on both accuracy and OOD performance. The implementation and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/DeepLearningRappers/dgl_gpl. The source code can be found at the corresponding link. Periodically driven quantum systems typically experience heating through resonant excitation of high-energy modes. While this Floquet heating is a well-established phenomenon, we demonstrate that it can be averted in open systems where specific initial states remain protected. These driven open systems possess "scar-like" states—labeled "condensable" because they facilitate Bose condensation in the driven regime. We illustrate this within a three-mode system where one mode connects to a dissipative environment. Driven away from both Floquet and dynamical decoupling limits, the expected heating is suppressed as the scar-like mode absorbs energy from the environment, resulting in a Bose condensation transition. This scenario could be experimentally realized using a three-color scheme in optical-lattice setups. Furthermore, our findings indicate that this behavior is not unique to this specific system but is a general feature of open driven systems. This insight may inspire the creation of new quantum devices capable of operating without heating. Finally, our insights regarding scar-like modes and Floquet heating are expected to be applicable to broader contexts, including many-body systems and higher-dimensional single-particle states. In the latter case, a scalar equation with a specific boundary condition yields a scar-like mode, while open single-particle systems lacking such a mode still exhibit a universal, albeit weaker, suppression of Floquet heating. These insights are anticipated to have wide-ranging general applicability. Additionally, we highlight a link between Floquet heating and the quantum Zeno effect, where engineered dissipation stabilizes the ground state. In this context, the scar-like mode acts as an effective decay channel for ground-state excitations. Our numerical results show that this driving scenario is distinct from the Floquet heating-free case, as it results in significant particle loss. Overall, our findings regarding scar-like modes and Floquet heating are expected to be broadly generalizable. Finally, we establish the relationship between Floquet heating and the quantum Zeno effect, noting that within the quantum Zeno scenario, a scar-like mode functions as an effective channel for ground-state excitation decay. Our numerical analysis indicates that this driving situation differs from the Floquet heating-free case, particularly regarding induced particle loss. In conclusion, our findings on scar-like modes and Floquet heating are broadly applicable. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a specific initial state can be isolated from Floquet heating by appropriately coupling it to an environment; this scenario is exemplified by a Floquet-engineered situation where an initial state relaxes to a Floquet-condensable mode. This paper examines the convex solution $u$ to the Monge–Ampère equation defined on an open, bounded, convex domain in $\mathbb{R}^n$ subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions, assuming the solution has a sub-solution with the same boundary values. We demonstrate that the convex solution $u$ exhibits uniform Hölder continuity with an exponent exceeding $1/2$ whenever the right-hand side function is bounded. Furthermore, if this function is Lipschitz continuous, the solution $u$ is Lipschitz continuous in the interior of the domain. These findings generalize and strengthen the classical Alexandrov maximum principle. Finally, we apply these results to establish regularity properties for convex solutions of the Monge–Ampère equation with bounded right-hand sides arising in Kähler geometry. Specifically, we characterize the Hölder continuity and Lipschitz continuity of both the solution and its second derivatives on an open, bounded, strictly pseudoconvex domain in $\mathbb{C}^n$. Our results recover and extend the well-known theorem by Evans and Yau, which characterized the regularity of plurisubharmonic solutions to the Monge–Ampère equation based on the regularity of the right-hand side. Additionally, our work extends these regularity results to a broader class of solutions, encompassing both weak and singular solutions. The primary innovation of this paper lies in the explicit nature of the exponents and constants involved. Finally, we outline several open questions and potential improvements regarding the exponents and constants in our findings. Defining time involves analyzing the evolution of a physical system. While classical physics treats this evolution as periodic, such behavior fails to address the "flow" of time. In contrast, non-periodic processes, particularly those involving aging systems, can address this question. This paper introduces a statistical time-domain framework for model-free, non-periodic optical clocks. We develop a time-domain formalization of these clocks, enabling the measurement of both temporal symmetry and the rate of aging (irreversibility). This approach handles experimental data from a JILA Strained Buffer He-Ne laser optical clock, with a relative frequency instability of $1.5\times10^{-15}$ at 1s. The discussion covers a general theory applicable to all non-periodic systems, alongside a practical protocol for optical clock measurements. Additionally, we explore the potential of this method to probe the time-related properties of quantum gravity. Ultimately, we argue that a time-domain formalism is essential for optical frequency metrology. Specifically, we demonstrate that an optical clock's temporal evolution can be characterized by its symmetry, irreversibility, and an associated entropy. Furthermore, we show that assuming an underlying thermodynamic structure within a time-domain framework provides a more accurate description of optical frequency metrology. Finally, we illustrate how this approach can be used to measure the "local" spacetime properties of quantum gravity. We emphasize that entropy serves as a sensitive probe for quantum gravity effects in both laboratory and space environments. The study concludes by outlining prospects for optical frequency metrology as a tool for measuring spacetime entropy. Specifically, we detail a proposed experiment to observe the evolution of optical frequency in orbit, thereby testing the invariance of optical clocks across different spacetimes. Such measurements would provide a new, sensitive test of quantum gravity. Ultimately, we demonstrate that quantum systems, including optical frequency metrology, can serve as sensitive probes for quantum gravity. This aligns with the emerging field of space quantum gravity tests. We emphasize that quantum systems can provide a new, sensitive probe of spacetime entropy, thereby testing the validity of spacetime symmetries. In conclusion, we show that optical frequency metrology can provide a sensitive test of spacetime entropy. This approach complements other tests of quantum gravity, such as tests of Lorentz invariance and tests of gravitational redshift. We emphasize that these tests are crucial for understanding the relationship between quantum mechanics and gravity. This paper introduces an energy-aware, real-time SFC deployment framework that leverages SDN and fog computing to enhance network flexibility and service quality. The design integrates feature correlation analysis, an online feature selection algorithm, failure recovery, fault prevention, and energy-efficient resource management, all synchronized through a real-time data analytics pipeline. This pipeline ingests time-series data from network monitoring systems, network management tasks, and control plane operations, processing it within a distributed environment to trigger dynamic network responses. Extensive simulations demonstrate the proposed approach's superior performance regarding energy efficiency and service quality, while fault prevention tests and ablation studies confirm the efficacy of network feature selection and the mechanism's effectiveness. The implementation is open-source and accessible at https://github.com/zhengyuanwang123456/SDN4SFC. Furthermore, to support subsequent research, we provide an open API for integrating the proposed method into existing SDN controllers. This API, which interfaces with the real-time data analytics pipeline, allows controllers to subscribe to network monitoring data and register tasks for automated service chain deployment, feature correlation analysis, and failure recovery. We anticipate this will foster collaborative research among diverse communities, including software-defined networks, fog computing, and advanced data analytics. Specifically, software-defined network vendors can incorporate our open API into their controllers to offer intelligent SDN solutions with built-in service chain deployment capabilities. Additionally, fog computing vendors can utilize the open API to provide intelligent cloud services utilizing advanced data analytics and service chains. Finally, data analytics vendors can extend their real-time data analytics pipelines with our open API to achieve intelligent data processing capabilities. This API is available in our open-source project, which also includes a simulation environment for network monitoring data and pre-trained machine learning models for fault prediction. We aim to facilitate advanced research by providing pre-trained models that have undergone extensive training and real-world testing. To enhance gradient surgery's ability to extract and augment useful gradients, we introduce two non-differentiable loss functions. These proposed methods are simpler and more effective than the current standard of separate L2 regularization and gradient reversal losses. Experimental results demonstrate that our approaches consistently improve fairness and accuracy for the primary groups, surpassing the performance of existing methods. Furthermore, our system is $1.7\times$ faster than prior art because it eliminates the need to compute regularized adversarial gradients during the hard-label back-propagation phase. We also find that our losses remain effective even when combined with the established Grad-Surgery framework. Additionally, we address and resolve several implementation challenges encountered during the development of this alternative gradient surgery variant. Finally, we highlight a significant bias inherent in the gradient reversal loss when used for downstream tasks. To mitigate this bias, we propose applying the gradient reversal loss in a two-stage training framework, which effectively reduces the bias introduced by single-stage loss applications. We anticipate that these insights into gradient surgery will encourage further research and exploration of its potential. Holographic error correction codes (HECCs) offer a compact framework for building codes with long-range entanglement, yet constructing them for large system sizes remains difficult. This paper addresses that challenge by developing an efficient circuit that generates approximately power-law correlated HECCKODs (specifically, $X$-HECCKODs with minimum distance $k$ and local code dimension 1). By layering these codes, we build a holographic tensor network (HTN) capable of correcting arbitrary correlated errors up to a certain threshold. Unlike the original MERA, this network does not exact; however, we demonstrate that it successfully solves the central problem of approximating power-law entanglement entropy via holographic principles. Furthermore, we propose a method to approximate the entanglement entropy of arbitrary subsystems and briefly discuss the extension of these networks to the quantum setting. These contributions are achieved through a variational approach utilizing symmetrical tensor contractions. We also show how to handle boundary conditions and entanglement with an external bath. Finally, we detail how to determine the network's parameters. Our approximate solutions are derived from an invariant subspace under the action of the unitary group, and we prove their existence and uniqueness. Additionally, we discuss the connection between our construction and the hypergraph state within the context of holographic error correction codes. Finally, we examine how to extend these results to general HECCKODs with non-trivial local dimension. Notably, our construction enables the definition of a new family of highly symmetric, efficiently constructible, and locally correctable quantum LDPC codes, known as the hyper-Steane code. The code family's parameters can be tuned to achieve the optimal trade-off between local recovery capability and non-local entanglement. We demonstrate this by calculating the entanglement entropy of arbitrary subsystems, including a comparison with the Penrose-Haag-Vishveshvaran (PHV) bound. Our approximate solution is built upon a hyper-Steane state, which serves as a many-body generalization of the Steane state. This work serves as a precursor to our subsequent study on the ground state of a many-body Hamiltonian realized through our proposed tensor network. In this paper, we focus solely on the tensor network construction, deferring discussions of the underlying physical model and its associated Hamiltonian to a future publication. While the occurrence rate of these structures is significant, the probability of simultaneous formation is low. Consequently, when observed, filaments often appear to have evolved for some time, exhibiting a population with a broad distribution of lifespans. This study aims to determine the average spacing between filaments within an hourglass system. To achieve this, we analyze the longitudinal distances between consecutive filaments in Hubble Space Telescope images of various starburst galaxies. This study introduces a distributed algorithm for solving Conservation Voltage Reduction (CVR) problems in power distribution networks. Such networks often incorporate distributed energy resources (DERs) alongside distributed electrical loads (DELs) like residential and commercial customers. The goal of CVR is to maintain optimal voltage levels across the network while maximizing the potential for DELs and DERs to reduce overall power losses. CVR optimization in these systems is complicated by secondary distribution connections (e.g., streetlights) and power limitations within specific nodes or branches. To tackle this, we first model CVR as an optimal control problem involving a large number of distributed agents, each subject to both local and global constraints. Subsequently, a distributed algorithm is developed to resolve this optimal control problem. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted on two test systems to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm. These systems evaluate CVR performance considering various DELs, DERs, and distribution configurations, with agent communication managed via both ideal bandwidth conditions and realistic packet-drop scenarios. The algorithm successfully achieves optimal voltage levels, loss reduction, and adherence to all local and global power flow constraints. Furthermore, simulation results confirm the method's ability to handle both constant and time-varying communication delays and packet drops. Agent performance is assessed using convergence time and the count of required agents to reach the desired voltage levels. The proposed algorithm demonstrates robustness against communication delays and packet drops, maintaining stability and convergence. Additionally, the results indicate that increasing the number of agents (DELs) in the network enhances CVR performance. Overall, the findings suggest that the proposed algorithm is highly effective for distributed CVR optimization in primary-secondary distribution systems. It facilitates the intelligent management of DELs and DERs to lower losses and improve power quality, all while adhering to local and global power flow constraints. This approach eliminates the need for a central coordinator, thereby reducing computational costs and enabling scalable solutions. Ultimately, the results show that CVR performance improves with a higher number of agents (DELs) within the distribution network. This study employs a multi-fidelity surrogate modeling strategy to simulate structure-sea-surface-solar-array-sailor systems for flexible offshore wind turbines. The dynamics of the submerged components—structure, sea, surface, solar array, sail, and sailor—are analyzed using chained Gaussian processes (CGP). The study demonstrates that this probabilistic surrogate model effectively captures the dynamic interactions between these submerged elements. Furthermore, CGP is utilized to identify the dependencies between the dynamics of these coupled subsystems. Finally, CGP is applied to identify the specific surface, sea, and sailor states that result in extreme loads on wind-turbine components. These findings offer valuable insights for the structural design of offshore wind-turbine systems. Additionally, the research confirms the broad applicability of probabilistic surrogate models in wind-turbine system design, including the identification of high-risk operational conditions. The proposed modeling framework is implemented within the OpenSystemSim platform. The study findings are derived from a series of design trades conducted for the U.S. Department of Energy's Ocean Systems Design and Demonstration (ODSD2) program. Social media has become a fundamental element of contemporary life. Data extracted from these platforms can be leveraged to investigate various phenomena, including natural disasters. This article presents a case study analyzing Twitter data related to the October 6, 2020, earthquake that struck Izmir, Turkey. The study examines a subset of Twitter data to identify user demographics and their interests concerning the event. Results indicate that individuals from the 18 to 29 age bracket were the most interested in the earthquake, with both males and females showing equal interest. Furthermore, users with elementary education or less possessed the highest level of interest. The paper concludes by suggesting potential future studies in this area. A group $G$ is said to possess the property $R_\infty$ if the count of twisted conjugacy classes, denoted by $R(\varphi)$, is infinite for every automorphism $\varphi$ of $G$. For non-aspherical nilpotent groups, determining the $R_\infty$ property is generally difficult. This paper investigates this property within the family of groups formed by nilpotent quotients of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups. Although previous research has not fully characterized the $R_\infty$ status of these specific groups, we demonstrate that their nilpotent quotients invariably satisfy this property. Consequently, we establish that any subgroup containing all cyclic normal subgroups also possesses the property $R_\infty$. Finally, we compute $R(\varphi)$ exactly when $\varphi$ acts as a $-1$-multiplication on the abelianization. Notably, while the property $R_\infty$ is not preserved under taking quotients, our findings indicate it can be acquired through such a process in this context. Specifically, for the group $G = \langle a, t \mid t^{-1}at = a^q, t^{-1}bt = b^{\pm q} \rangle$ where $\gcd(q, -1 \pm p) = 1$ (with $q$ assumed prime), the quotient $G / \langle a \rangle$ exhibits the property $R_\infty$. The proof relies on the fact that the first homology of this quotient is finitely generated, enabling the use of free rank calculations for twisted conjugacy classes. This approach yields a formula for $R(\varphi)$ applicable to any automorphism $\varphi$ of the abelianization, provided $\varphi$ fixes the rank-two subgroup at infinity. This formula allows us to characterize the property $R_\infty$ for a broader class of automorphisms, including those that map the rank-two subgroup to itself via a $-1$ multiplication. These results extend the findings of [1] and align with the $R_\infty$ properties of the groups in that reference. Furthermore, the $R_\infty$ characteristics of these groups exhibit a significant link to the sign of the trace of the automorphism's matrix representation. This paper introduces a new framework for robust inversion, specifically applied to reconstructing the temporal evolution of the initial conditions behind a snapshot recorded by a single sensor following a brief, impulsive excitation. We represent both the excitation and the resulting state in a trajectory basis derived from a reference system-response pair. By modeling uncertainties in both the excitation and system response as random variables within a Gaussian process framework, we derive the posterior probability distribution of the state given the observed snapshot, accounting for uncertainties in the initial conditions of the response basis functions. The inversion procedure is governed by an evidence-maximisation criterion, which is evaluated via Monte-Carlo sampling using forward-optimisation. This formulation is both conceptually straightforward and computationally efficient, as it avoids expensive matrix inversions. Furthermore, it facilitates a systematic assessment of uncertainty propagation from the data to the inferred quantities. We demonstrate the method's capabilities through a numerical case study involving a one-dimensional half-space. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive set of recommendations for selecting basis functions and determining hyper-parameters that optimize the uncertainty characteristics of the inversion. These recommendations are validated by applying them to multiple real-world datasets, including seismic seafloor recordings, blast-induced acoustic waveforms, and particle accelerator beam dumps. Across all examples, the forward-optimisation approach effectively recovers the temporal evolution of the initial conditions, while the propagation of data uncertainties is accurately quantified. In contrast, standard approaches that rely on minimizing a priori-constructed cost functions often yield biased results and produce incorrect uncertainty estimates. Our method offers a solution to these challenges, which are particularly acute in large-scale inverse problems. The proposed framework is applicable to any inverse problem where inference is conducted in a response basis, such as state reconstruction, feature extraction, or feature selection. The initial section of this paper outlines key aspects of our methodology, while the final section provides a detailed application to seismic data inversion. This paper introduces SceNDD, a scenario-based naturalistic driving dataset recorded in an urban setting. Data was gathered via an in-vehicle system from 100 drivers over the course of 12 hours, resulting in 135 driving sessions. The system comprehensively captured driver states, behaviors, and environments, including facial imagery, cognitive load, emotional responses, and driving performance metrics. The study demonstrates the utility of SceNDD for two applications: identifying driving emotion states and forecasting emotional responses. Results indicate that classification models trained on SceNDD achieve robust performance for driving emotion state identification, while regression models for predicting emotional responses significantly surpass baseline approaches. Furthermore, the paper outlines the dataset's composition and provides example visualizations of the collected data. The SceNDD database can be accessed at www.scedata.org. Boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) and interface conformal field theory (ICFT) have garnered significant interest due to their connections with the holographic principle and conformal fluid dynamics. Notably, boundary/defect conformal symmetry has been employed to derive the entropy of systems characterized by conformal fluids. This paper extends the calculation of reflected entropy to scenarios involving two boundary/defect conformal field theories. Furthermore, boundary/defect conformal symmetry is utilized to determine the entropy of two adjacent interface conformal field theories, offering a rigorous foundation for the entropy of conformal fluids separated by an interface. Ultimately, our findings provide a precise and rigorous framework for investigating system entropy through boundary/defect conformal field theory and interface conformal field theory. Additionally, boundary/defect conformal field theory serves as a valuable framework for exploring the entropy of conformal fluids at leading order. All results are expressed in terms of boundary entropy, OPE coefficients, and correlation functions. Finally, boundary/defect conformal field theory and interface conformal field theory may offer precise and rigorous insights into the entropy of interacting systems.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) represent a promising innovation for next-generation wireless communication systems. This article investigates channel estimation techniques for RIS-aided Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) links under practical constraints, including imperfect hardware and reduced cyclic prefix (CP) duration. Given the inherent ill-conditioning of the estimation problem, a standard ELM-based approach yields significant performance gains when the CP is sufficient. However, we demonstrate that further improvements are achievable by treating the ELM input as an observation from a lower-dimensional perfect observation, a concept applicable to other estimation scenarios. Specifically, we introduce an enhanced ELM-based method utilizing this reduced-dimension input to achieve additional performance gains in RIS-assisted OFDM systems with reduced CP. Our findings indicate that the proposed enhanced ELM-based estimator can effectively leverage the reflected signals to improve channel estimation accuracy. Additionally, we analyze the impact of imperfect hardware on both the standard and enhanced estimators, deriving a closed-form expression for the mean squared error (MSE) of the enhanced estimator with respect to hardware imperfections. This analysis confirms the robustness of the proposed enhanced ELM-based estimator against hardware imperfections. Simulation results validate the effectiveness of the proposed techniques. Specifically, the enhanced ELM-based estimator outperforms existing schemes by up to 1 dB in terms of MSE at a fixed bit error rate. Furthermore, the proposed hardware analysis reveals that the enhanced ELM-based estimator is more robust than other approaches when considering imperfect hardware. Ultimately, the proposed enhanced ELM-based estimator achieves a significant reduction in estimation error compared to other schemes. These results suggest that the proposed enhanced ELM-based estimator is highly effective for RIS-assisted OFDM systems with reduced CP and imperfect hardware. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: First, we propose an ELM-based estimator leveraging the reflected signal from the RIS, which outperforms existing schemes by up to 1 dB in MSE at a fixed BER. Second, we introduce an enhanced ELM-based estimator that utilizes the data from an ideal low-dimensional observation as input, achieving up to a 1.5 dB improvement over other schemes at a fixed BER. Third, we provide an analytical expression for the MSE of the enhanced ELM-based estimator regarding imperfect hardware. Finally, we show through numerical results that the enhanced ELM-based estimator achieves superior performance compared to other schemes, even in the presence of imperfect hardware. These findings highlight the robustness of the enhanced ELM-based estimator, achieving up to a 1 dB improvement

Since nearly parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$ structures correspond bijectively to real Killing spinors, the deformation framework can be expressed using spinors and Dirac operators. We demonstrate that the space of infinitesimal instanton deformations is isomorphic to the kernel of an elliptic operator. Leveraging this approach, we establish the rigidity of abelian instantons. Finally, we apply these findings to characterize the deformation space of the canonical connection on the five-dimensional Heisenberg group. These findings offer an alternative proof for the rigidity of instantons on five-dimensional Heisenberg and seven-dimensional Sally manifolds. Additionally, we explore the implications of our results for non-abelian instantons, noting their sole existence within warped product geometries. In this context, we compute the associated metric deformations and identify a specific instance where a family of non-abelian instantons emerges as the limit as the warping function approaches zero. Our methodology also facilitates the study of the deformation theory of anti-self-dual connections on seven-dimensional manifolds with half-flat $\mathrm{G}_2$ structures.
