The COVID-19 pandemic has spurred the creation of contact tracing applications designed to curb the virus's spread. These apps utilize various mechanisms, such as the exchange of encryption keys, anonymous user signatures, and the reporting of health status indicators, to maintain privacy. This study assesses the privacy risks associated with the application developed by Susanna Tardini and Federico Belotti of the National Research Council (Coronav\'irus-SUS). The analysis employs an adversarial machine learning approach, where an attacker attempts to reconstruct sensitive information using the app's tracing algorithm under conditions of incomplete data. The findings indicate that the application poses an unacceptable level of risk to privacy. To enhance privacy, the authors recommend implementing differential privacy, a technique that introduces controlled noise to data to limit re-identification risks. Although this method introduces additional challenges, it ensures that the tracing system remains effective in its core function. Specifically, the text evaluates the trade-off between the application's privacy and its utility, defined as the probability that the tracing system successfully identifies close contacts. Ultimately, the study concludes that with minor adjustments, the application can achieve both privacy and utility goals. Specifically, an adversarial accuracy of approximately 45% can be maintained while ensuring that 90% of close contacts are identified. These results were achieved by integrating differential privacy into the app and adjusting the parameters of an auxiliary algorithm. Furthermore, the research explores how to balance privacy and utility when the adversary possesses varying degrees of data access. Finally, the paper examines how to optimize privacy and utility by analyzing how different levels of data disclosure impact the system's ability to identify close contacts. The ultimate conclusion is that the tracing system can remain highly effective in identifying close contacts even when users share only a subset of their data. Specifically, utilizing just 50% of available data allows for the identification of 90% of close contacts. Additionally, the text investigates how the probability of a user sharing data affects the system's utility. The analysis reveals that the tracing system remains highly effective even when a significant portion of users choose not to participate. For instance, if 50% of users do not share their data, the system can still identify 90% of close contacts. Finally, the study examines how the participation rate of data sharing influences privacy, observing that the impact on adversarial accuracy remains relatively stable across different levels of user engagement. Over the last few decades, quantum information theory has emerged as a distinct discipline distinct from both quantum physics and general information science. Concurrently, the study of the brain as a physical system has gained momentum. Recently, researchers have begun applying quantum information metrics, such as entanglement entropy, to neural data. Furthermore, both experimental and theoretical efforts are currently underway to investigate quantum phenomena within neural systems. This review examines the concepts of quantum information and their connections to neural systems, with a specific focus on contributions from the field of complex systems. It also addresses current controversies and challenges, aiming to stimulate further research into quantum aspects of neural systems. Finally, the review explores potential applications of quantum information to neural systems in the context of consciousness. These studies, which bridge quantum and biological fields, are expected to yield significant implications for understanding the fundamental nature of the brain. Additionally, the field of quantum brain science is anticipated to offer a novel perspective on the long-standing debate regarding consciousness. We believe this area will play a pivotal role in addressing some of the most enigmatic questions in science. Given the field's infancy, we hope to stimulate interdisciplinary research into quantum aspects of neural systems. We believe that quantum metrics, when applied to neural data, will provide new insights into the nature of the brain. Ultimately, we aim to contribute to advancing our understanding of the brain's nature and to help solve the mystery of consciousness. Finally, we hope to contribute to the emerging field of quantum brain science. This paper introduces a C code generator for ACL2 that identifies ACL2 representations of C constructs based on a shallow embedding of C within ACL2 and translates them back into their corresponding C forms. Additionally, the generator produces ACL2 theorems that verify the correctness of the resulting C code relative to the original ACL2 code. Although the tool currently supports only a limited yet expanding subset of C, this range is already sufficient for various interesting programs. We provide several examples to demonstrate the tool's capabilities. The tool is accessible via the CodeCos project, which is part of the ACL2 monthly releases. Furthermore, we illustrate a use case involving the development of a hardware accelerator for C code using this embedding, based on a prior report. Our primary contribution lies in the tool itself, which is intended to facilitate the creation of verified, safe, and secure software and hardware systems. We aim to encourage the broader software and hardware communities to adopt and extend the C embedding to address a wider spectrum of C, thereby enhancing the utility of the embedding for both software and hardware verification. We also invite researchers to suggest interesting case studies for testing the tool and to propose the C embedding as a compelling example of a shallow embedding for the broader community. Finally, we offer several observations on software and hardware development grounded in this embedding. The source code for the C code generator can be found in the following repository.

This study examines the dynamics of a young, low-inclination asteroid cluster linked to (39911) Iochroma, situated near the 3/1 mean motion resonance. The Iochroma family is hypothesized to have formed approximately 10 million years ago following the disruption of a parent body. The research analyzes the ephemerides of Iochroman asteroids within a perturbative framework incorporating general relativity. By employing a semi-analytical and analytical model of resonance perturbations, the origin of the family is attributed to a recent resonance crossing event. Furthermore, a significant fraction of Iochroma asteroids are predicted to be ejected from the resonance due to chaotic diffusion. The observed low dispersion in orbital elements, the presence of a distinct cluster of resonant trajectories, and the identification of a group of asteroids sharing identical resonant arguments and Hamiltonian values provide evidence of a dynamical correlation between them. Additionally, the study demonstrates that Iochroma asteroids exhibit a correlation between eccentricity and the resonant argument, alongside a trend of decreasing heliocentric eccentricity and increasing heliocentric mean motion. These correlations and trends are linked to the resonance mechanism, which is further supported by the lack of correlation between secular frequency and the resonant argument. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these findings for the capture theory of resonance. Specifically, it is shown that the probability of capture is negligible, and the capture theory fails to account for the dynamical correlation among the objects. Instead, the capture theory is restricted to a narrow range of initial conditions and is viable only over long timescales. In contrast, the resonance mechanism can generate the observed dynamical correlation and is applicable across a broad range of initial conditions. Consequently, Iochroma asteroids are not captured by the 3/1 mean motion resonance but instead cross it, with their dynamical behavior governed by the resonance mechanism. This finding is also applicable to other recently discovered asteroid families. Finally, the implications of these results for the dynamical evolution of the 3/1 mean motion resonance region are also discussed. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the resonance mechanism can explain the dynamical evolution of the region. The resulting elliptic cohomology theory is formulated over a specific class of elliptic curves. Finally, as an application, we calculate the $G$-equivariant elliptic cohomology of the unitary and orthogonal groups ($U(n)$ and $SU(n)$) as well as their flag varieties $F^*(n)$, where $G$ is defined as either the circle group $T$ or a finite subgroup of $T$. This technical note addresses the challenge of efficiently and accurately numerically integrating functions driven by solar radiation across all directions. By expressing the accurate integrand using Legendre polynomials, we employ Gaussian quadrature to achieve precise results with minimal data points. Our approach yields substantial efficiency gains when integrating solar-dependent direction-dependent variables, thereby reducing both computational time and data storage requirements. We validate the accuracy of our solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature through two numerical examples: first, by integrating the normalized differential of Legendre polynomials, and second, by integrating normalized air-mass exponents across directions. These numerical tests demonstrate that the solar-weighted quadrature method is highly effective for integrating direction-dependent variables under solar radiation, achieving high accuracy with data collected at a very low node count. Furthermore, we show that this quadrature can be seamlessly integrated into the existing Legendre quadrature process without requiring any additional computational steps. Finally, we provide a MATLAB code that implements this efficient solar-weighted quadrature. The entire method, including the MATLAB code, is available on GitHub. The curvature information provided by the Hessian or its generalized counterpart, the generalized Jacobian, is essential for analyzing the local properties of functions and manifolds. However, the Gauss-Newton matrix, which serves as a first-order approximation of the Hessian, is typically too large for direct storage or manipulation. This paper introduces a low-rank approximation of the generalized Jacobian that is built upon a global parameterization of the tangent spaces associated with a submanifold. By utilizing the structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix, this tangent space-based approach enables the efficient computation of both the generalized Jacobian and the curvature information it provides. The proposed method, called ViViT, is applicable to any linearly embedded submanifold. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through two examples: spherical functions and the embedding of a 2D manifold within a 3D space. ViViT's efficiency has been validated on datasets including the 3D shape benchmark, MNIST, and MoNas. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKoch/vivit. Furthermore, our code supports a MoNas dataset generated with MoNas3D++ (https://github.com/SebastianKoch/MoNas3D-Plus-Plus), offering an alternative validation of ViViT's efficacy. Finally, our implementation provides several ablations of ViViT, such as low-rank factorizations of individual generalized Jacobians or stacked generalized Gauss-Newton matrices, offering a flexible selection of curvature details. These variations, ranging from $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ to $\mathcal{O}(n d^2)$, where $d$ represents the dimension of the submanifold and $n$ the number of points, allow users to choose the most appropriate version for their specific requirements. The most efficient variant, ViVit-$n$, exhibits a relative reconstruction error of approximately 10% compared to the most general variant, ViViT-$d$. For datasets where $n \gg d$, such as the 3D shape benchmark, this error reduces to roughly 2%. The paper concludes with a comprehensive summary of ViViT's performance. Finally, ViViT's applicability is illustrated through examples involving functions defined on a sphere and the embedding of images onto a 3D manifold. Numerous natural languages employ grammatical gender to categorize nouns into gendered classes, often triggering gendered agreement on dependent words. Although these categories are arbitrary for inanimate objects, languages typically assign them based on either gender-related semantics or the object's physical shape, particularly if it is feminine. We demonstrate that despite the low frequency of inanimate nouns (approximately 20% in training data), the nucleus still exhibits distinct representations for animate and inanimate words. Through human experiments, we confirm that participants can accurately infer the gender-class nucleus based on the animacy of surrounding inanimate nouns. Furthermore, representations within inanimate clusters differ according to the nucleus; for instance, inanimate nouns grouped with masculine nuclei diverge from those paired with feminine nuclei. Finally, our analysis of neural networks indicates that the model's gender-class nuclei also produce separated representations for animate and inanimate nouns. Collectively, these findings indicate that gendered agreement forces inanimate nouns into discrete clusters and reveals internal structure within that inanimate space. This outcome is significant because, although inanimate nouns constitute only a minor portion of the data (around 20%), they are the primary source of cross-lingual alignment errors. Additionally, we show that animacy-driven clustering is absent in English, which lacks a gender-class nucleus. These results suggest that nLP researchers should prioritize studying inanimate nouns, as they are not homogeneous but possess a rich internal structure. Ultimately, this insight could enhance cross-lingual nLP performance by accounting for the internal structure of inanimate nouns. Object pose estimation is a critical task in numerous real-world scenarios. While most current methods rely on extensive training datasets containing numerous exemplars for each object category, acquiring such datasets is often costly and time-consuming. Consequently, there is a pressing need for methods capable of performing pose estimation with a minimal number of images per category or even zero. We address this by proposing a novel category-level pose estimation framework that operates with zero shot-capability through two key innovations: (1) the development of a new pose representation that is both pose-invariant and instance-invariant, and (2) the application of few-shot learning to derive this pose invariant. Extensive experiments across three diverse datasets demonstrate that our approach, requiring zero trained images per category, achieves state-of-the-art results in both category-level pose estimation and generalizability. This study introduces a framework for short-term traffic flow forecasting within urban road networks. By leveraging road segment similarity, we create an unsupervised feature extraction method that produces feature vectors for each segment, significantly reducing the dimensionality of input data for subsequent forecasting. This approach eliminates the need for storage and transfer of large-scale, sparse traffic datasets. We demonstrate the application of these vectors in predicting flow the next minute across multiple cities. Our results show that the proposed method matches the performance of state-of-the-art deep learning-based traffic prediction techniques. The complete methodology is deployed in real-time on a traffic forecasting platform that serves a major metropolitan area in China. Experimental evidence indicates that for segments with high similarity to others, utilizing only the vector representation of the historical flow at minute-level intervals is sufficient for accurate short-term forecasting. This paper introduces VACA, a new class of variational graph autoencoders designed for causal inference when the causal structure is known as a causal graph. VACA extends the AutoRegressive Variational AutoEncoder (ARVA) by adding a latent propagation layer that functions as a causal operator on the latent representation. We demonstrate that VACA is generative, capable of answering both interventional and counterfactual queries. Furthermore, our experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that VACA outperforms existing autoencoder methods for causal inference. Finally, because VACA functions as a causal operator on data, we explore its potential for downstream tasks that depend on causal models. The film industry has emerged as one of the world's largest cultural sectors. While the market has traditionally been driven by the promise of high returns, the release of new films has increasingly become a high-stakes gamble, with significant revenue often lost. Consequently, the industry has shifted focus toward blockbusters designed to maximize revenue. This study aims to identify key success factors to enable investors to forecast earnings with greater accuracy. To achieve this, we gathered a comprehensive, up-to-date dataset containing over 100,113 global movie releases from 1990 to 2019. We conducted in-depth exploratory data analysis to examine the impact of pre-release attributes on total revenue, revealing that release budget, trailer views, and runtime are the most critical factors. Furthermore, we performed statistical testing to validate our hypotheses, confirming that our initial assumptions regarding the relationship between pre-release metrics and revenue are supported by the data. Finally, we analyzed how the COVID-19 pandemic has influenced release strategies and transformed audience viewing habits. Our findings will assist investors in the future by providing a method to estimate potential returns, thereby mitigating financial risks. Cyberphysical systems (CPSs) are anticipated to become essential for numerous emerging applications, particularly within cyberphysical systems of systems (CPSoSs). These contexts demand the capacity to manage intricate and dynamic environments alongside diverse, heterogeneous subsystems. However, current CPS architectures often lack the necessary adaptability and flexibility to address the specific demands of such scenarios. The primary obstacle to enhancing CPS capabilities is the absence of a unified intelligence framework. This paper proposes a research initiative aimed at developing CPSs equipped with intelligence, focusing on design principles, modeling frameworks, algorithms, and methodologies. The proposed approach is demonstrated through an autonomous vehicle application. The study begins by defining the necessary intelligence capabilities and subsequently presents a high-level architecture that integrates existing CPS components with cyber intelligence elements. Furthermore, an abstract model is introduced to represent cyber intelligence, capturing its properties and behaviors. This model enables the investigation of the underlying challenges and serves as a foundation for the subsequent development of algorithmic solutions. Finally, the paper examines two critical functions of CPS intelligence: fusing heterogeneous data sources and adapting to environmental changes. In the first case, the proposed algorithm leverages the diversity of information sources to improve data fusion accuracy. In the second, the developed adaptive framework ensures the robustness of cyber intelligence. The study concludes by outlining several open research questions regarding the capabilities of CPSs possessing intelligence. The theoretical and algorithmic contributions are detailed in our prior work [1-3]. Certain blazars display spectral energy distributions (SEDs) featuring ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excesses (SXE) alongside primary gamma-ray emission. A potential origin for this excess is the anisotropic scattering of thermal disk photons by relativistic electrons in the jet, a process known as external-Compton scattering. This study employs MAPPIES, a Monte-Carlo implementation of the incoherent external-Compton scattering model for jetted sources with partial polarization, to analyze 11 blazars with strong SXF component evidence. Using data from the 2017/2018 Fermi-LAT fourth science iteration, we conducted spectral fitting on eight sources exhibiting significant gamma-ray emission, while incorporating simultaneous fits to multi-wavelength observations for four of them. Our results indicate that MAPPIES models can simultaneously reproduce both the primary Fermi-LAT spectra and the overall SEDs for these sources. Specifically, we estimated average helical magnetic field strengths of approximately 10 Gauss and flow velocities of roughly 0.6 times the speed of light. Furthermore, our model predictions align with the observed characteristics of the UV/SXE in the SEDs, including their typical energies, amplitudes, and polarization degrees. Notably, the inferred helical magnetic field geometry and jet velocity are consistent with those derived from radio observations. These findings suggest that partially polarized external-Compton scattering is a viable mechanism for blazar spectra, with the SXF component likely resulting from external-Compton scattering of polarized thermal photons. Finally, we demonstrate that MAPPIES can effectively disentangle the contributions of polarized external-Compton scattering and synchrotron radiation to the UV/SXE, a capability that distinguishes it from previous approaches. This insight is crucial for understanding the physical processes governing the UV/SXE in blazar spectra. Our findings also suggest that synchrotron self-Compton scattering is unlikely to be the dominant source of the SXF component. These outcomes highlight the value of combining Fermi-LAT data with multi-wavelength observations to investigate the emission mechanisms of blazars. We anticipate that MAPPIES will serve as a valuable tool for blazar spectral analysis in the future. The MAPPIES code is publicly accessible at https://sourceforge.net/projects/mappies/. This study examines analytic continuation methods for expansions that mimic Landau free energies, which serve as universal models for equilibrium states in complex systems. Our analysis focuses on both truncated power series and the combined use of Euler re-normalization and Padé approximants. We establish the equilibrium and dynamic scattering of the analytic re-normalized landscape, demonstrating that these scattering centers, located off the real energy axis, act as effective pseudo-impurities. We prove that the density of state (DOS) scattering cross-section can be directly derived from the system's Hamiltonian parameters and the rules of analytic re-normalization. Furthermore, we show that for complex free energy landscapes, the dynamics of analytic continuation are driven by a generalized non-holonomic motion along the manifold of pseudo-impurity states. Finally, we apply our findings to the complex Ginzburg-Landau and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations, as well as the dimerization of polyacetylene, to derive specific predictions that align with existing experimental data. These results underscore the critical role of equilibrium fluctuations in driving dynamic processes during analytic continuation, offering a fresh perspective on the link between equilibrium and non-equilibrium phenomena. Ultimately, this work provides a framework for investigating dynamic transitions in complex systems by extending the concept of the universal phase diagram of E. Brezin's mean field theory. We introduce a quantum algorithm designed to identify the symmetry element of a reflecting symmetric pure state using the controlled quantum random access oracle. Our approach demonstrates that the identified symmetry element requires $O(\log(4/\epsilon))$ observations of the oracle, while acknowledging that the observation count needed to determine the symmetry type remains $\Omega(\k)$. Furthermore, we examine a quantum analog of the symmetric subspace problem and successfully resolve the identification of low-dimensional symmetric subspaces spanned by symmetric pure states. In this context, we propose an algorithm that locates the symmetric subspace for a $k$-qubit system using $O(k^2)$ observations. However, we also highlight the computational challenges associated with identifying the symmetric subspace in higher-dimensional systems. Finally, our study offers novel insights into the complexities of quantum identification. Specifically, we demonstrate that the lower bound on the query complexity for quantum algorithmic identification is $\Omega(\k)$, matching that of classical algorithmic identification, and show that the query complexity of an identification learning algorithm for quantum states can be significantly lower than that required for state reconstruction. These findings offer new perspectives on the information processing capabilities of quantum algorithms. Furthermore, they suggest a potential resolution to an open problem regarding the query complexity of quantum learning algorithms for states. Finally, we show that the quantum algorithm for symmetric subspace identification developed in this paper is optimal up to a constant factor. This result underscores the fundamental information processing advantage of quantum algorithms over classical ones. Our work represents a significant step toward developing quantum algorithms for various reconstruction and identification tasks. Additionally, it provides a foundation for the design and implementation of quantum machine learning algorithms, which are currently in their early stages of development. This serves as an important contribution to the ongoing efforts to build quantum machine learning algorithms. Ultimately, our research advances the goal of achieving quantum machine learning parity with classical methods. By demonstrating the quantum advantage of our proposed algorithms, we offer an important step toward this objective. Our findings contribute to the broader aim of attaining quantum machine learning parity, as our proposed solutions outperform their classical counterparts. Baryon production is analyzed using the quantized fragmentation model of a QCD string. In this framework, baryons emerge when diquarks bind to leading baryons generated through successive $q\bar{q}$ pair creations. Furthermore, if the string breaks in a helical manner, these baryons can form chiral molecules with the transverse excitations of the string, creating a new chemical degree of freedom. This mechanism is examined within both bosonic and fermionic scenarios. Ultimately, this model is utilized to investigate baryon production, specifically comparing the predictions for the baryon-to-pion ratio made in [1] against PHENIX data on jet hadronization at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV. Additionally, the approach is extended to estimate baryon production arising from two-string fragmentation in gluon jets. Finally, the model is applied to study baryon production in three-string configurations, such as those found in 3-parton jets or $q\bar{q}$-gluon jets. These findings are also compared against existing PHENIX data regarding the baryon-to-baryon anti-baryon ratio near the kinematical limit. Finally, predictions regarding the baryon-to-anti-baryon ratio in 3-string configurations are presented for future measurements at LHCb. These results are also compared with ALICE findings for $x_\mathrm{F} > 0$ at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 7 TeV. Finally, a discussion is provided regarding the potential of these measurements to test the dynamics of hadron production in multi-parton final states. In the conclusion, the phenomenological viability of the proposed scenario is assessed in light of the presented results. Furthermore, the future prospects for utilizing 3-parton and 2 diquark + 1 quark jet fragmentation in shaping the baryon production spectrum are explored. Additionally, the potential of this approach to investigate the formation of baryon molecules in hadron production is discussed. **Context.** Solar oscillation frequencies are highly sensitive to flows within the convection zone, a property leveraged by helioseismology to infer flows around solar features like active regions (ARs) and large active region filaments (ARFs). This study examines flows surrounding ARs and ARFs by integrating helioseismic travel time measurements with 3D MHD simulations. **Aims.** Our objectives are to (1) evaluate the contribution of flows around ARs and ARFs to travel time measurements taken along the solar north-south axis, and (2) assess the reliability of helioseismic maps depicting flows around ARs and filars. **Methods.** We utilized 3D MHD simulations of the solar surface to calculate the contributions of AR-related flows to helioseismic travel times. Additionally, we derived flows from helioseismic data by analyzing travel time measurements along the north-south axis. **Results.** Travel times are significantly affected by ARs and ARFs when they are large and numerous. Furthermore, inferred flows around ARs and ARFs display variations in magnitude and direction. **Conclusions.** These findings suggest that helioseismic measurements along the north-south axis may be biased by the presence of large ARs. Consequently, maps of inflows around ARs may be less reliable than previously assumed. We recommend that researchers utilizing helioseismic measurements along the north-south axis account for the potential influence of active regions. Finally, we propose that future studies investigating the impact of ARs on helioseismic measurements should employ 3D MHD simulations. This approach would enable a more comprehensive analysis of AR contributions to travel time measurements by incorporating AR geometry and magnetic field distributions. Furthermore, such simulations would facilitate the creation of synthetic oscillation data for comparison with observed travel times. **Keywords:** Sun: helioseismology, Sun: magnetic fields, Sun: filaments, Sun: 3D MHD simulations. **Abbreviations.** AR: active region; ARF: active region filament; SDO/HMI: Solar Dynamics Observatory/Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager; GONG: Global Oscillation Network Group; GONGSOFI: Global Oscillation Network Group/Solar Oscillation Filter Imager; NLTE: non-local thermodynamic equilibrium. **Acknowledgments.** We thank the GONG collaboration for providing the data used in this study. Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) observations in the nanohertz frequency band have recently yielded a significant common red signal, the nature of which remains under active investigation. This study proposes that a stochastic gravitational wave background (GWB), generated by primordial magnetic fields (PMF) during the early universe, could offer a viable explanation for these findings. We demonstrate that large-scale PMF can induce substantial PTA signals through two mechanisms: the direct interaction of PMF with gravitational wave detectors and the generation of tensor gravitational waves via vector PMF. While the direct effect produces a quadratic signal with respect to the magnetic field amplitude—potentially challenging the standard linear "Green's function" framework—the tensor effect arises from electric fields induced by the cosmic expansion within large-scale PMF. This tensor contribution is expected to follow a power-law power spectrum with a slope of $-2/3$, aligning with current PTA data. Our analysis indicates that the required PMF configuration is astrophysically plausible, with energy primarily concentrated at large scales. Furthermore, we find that the tensor effect could exceed the direct effect by up to three orders of magnitude, significantly enhancing the detectability of GWB via PTA. Finally, we outline the potential for future PTA observations to constrain PMF properties through these signals. This research falls under the scope of the Cosmic Magnetic Fields (CosMic) initiative. Light field technology has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to capture extra spatial and temporal data through the sampling of ray directions within scenes. Among various light field formats, the angular view (AV) plane representation stands out for its effectiveness in applications like virtual reality, augmented reality, and head-tracked video streaming. Consequently, there is a substantial demand for efficient light field image compression. While learning-based methods have shown promise in reducing file sizes, most state-of-the-art techniques rely on traditional coding frameworks, making them difficult to deploy in practical settings. This paper introduces a learning-based compression framework that operates independently of traditional coders by directly encoding light field images. It features a lightweight, end-to-end trainable encoder that utilizes a disparity-aware model to enhance compression performance. Specifically, the encoder is trained with an optimization goal focused on minimizing the average distortion between the decoded AV plane images and their original versions. To achieve high efficiency, the method employs a light-weight architecture and explicitly leverages scene structure information via the angular subspace of the light field. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods both in performance and in how consistently it maintains compression gains across different images. Furthermore, the method delivers substantial compression improvements over other learning-based schemes while delivering light-weight AV images. Interactive and non-interactive frameworks represent the two prevailing paradigms in vector-based cross-lingual information retrieval (V-CLIR). While recent studies show non-interactive models using multilingual encoders outperform established baselines by over 10 points, interactive models leveraging separate encoding for query and document languages achieve the state-of-the-art. We introduce a hybrid approach that leverages the strengths of both paradigms, achieving the first system to surpass 50 in NDCG@10 on V-CLIR Test 2022. Our contributions include: (a) a novel training objective designed to jointly optimize inter- and intralingual retrieval capabilities; (b) a method for transferring learned cross-lingual retrieval skills to low-resource languages; and (c) an exploration of pretraining strategies utilizing multilingual interactive setups. This review examines the advantages and limitations of various estimation techniques for small-area disease mapping, with a specific focus on the resource constraints and data challenges inherent to low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). We evaluate four distinct approaches: empirical Bayesian, Bayesian hierarchical, spatially weighted, and model-based small area. These methods were applied to a recent study by the Centre for Environmental Health Research in Zimbabwe, which utilized small area estimates of HIV prevalence to enhance the accuracy of a spatially explicit HIV model. The analysis revealed that all four methods yielded comparable results, with only minor variations in estimated HIV prevalence. Consequently, we recommend that methodological choices in small-area estimation for LMICs should not rely on assumptions regarding result equivalence, but rather on practical considerations such as software availability, data quality, and specific study aims. Ultimately, we contend that for large-scale analyses, model-based and Bayesian hierarchical methods offer the most significant benefits. However, we acknowledge that Bayesian methods present potential challenges in LMICs, primarily concerning the availability of appropriate software and the necessity for specialized statistical expertise. We conclude that these methods should be promoted through capacity-building initiatives that provide training to researchers within LMICs. Such efforts would ensure that these powerful tools are not only accessible but also effectively utilized in the future. The source code for the models discussed is accessible at https://github.com/ehrcz/Small-Area-Estimates. This article was selected as a Spotlight on Modelling and Analysis feature for the 2020 Zimbabwe Statistical Association National Conference. (ZSA 2020 Spotlight on Modelling and Analysis Session 10, Paper 1). Keywords: Small area estimation, disease mapping, capacity building, low and middle income countries, HIV, Zimbabwe.

This study investigates a free-Kelley betting scenario integrated with continuous-variable quantum systems. In this framework, after an initial investor allocates capital to various outcomes, a second player places bets on quantum versions of those outcomes. Drawing inspiration from previous findings in discrete free-Kelly betting regarding the connection between betting strategies and statistical tests, we demonstrate that for free-Kelly betting involving two outcomes, the betting problem corresponds to the likelihood-ratio test. Consequently, the betting probability aligns with the p-value derived from the quantum statistical distance between the two states. For the general case involving N outcomes, the betting problem maps to an N-level hypothesis test problem. Utilizing recent advancements in quantum statistical testing, we establish an upper bound for quantum free-Kelly betting payoffs under normal distributions, supported by numerical results. Additionally, we examine free-Kelly betting under uniform distributions and propose an upper bound for free-Kelly betting payoffs based on quantum relative entropies. Furthermore, we derive an upper bound for free-Kelly betting payoffs under general probability distributions by leveraging quantum hypothesis testing theory. Finally, we explore potential applications of free-Kelly betting within quantum machine learning. This work serves as a foundation for developing quantum algorithms related to statistical testing and hypothesis testing. Additionally, it offers a framework for Kelly betting under arbitrary probability distributions, which could be beneficial in fields such as quantum finance and quantum communication. Ultimately, this research may contribute to the development of quantum AI. Keywords: Quantum AI, Quantum Machine Learning, Quantum Finance, Quantum Communication, Quantum Relative Entropy, Quantum Hypothesis Testing, Quantum Statistical Testing, Quantum Signal Detection, Quantum Signal Processing.

To identify viable two-dimensional materials for efficient light emission and quantum information processing, we conducted a high-throughput screening of group-IV tetrahedral monolayers using advanced many-body methods. The study employed the GW and Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) frameworks to examine the quasiparticle band structures of MA$_2$Z$_4$ tetrahedrals. Our analysis of 108 candidates revealed that 18 possess a direct semiconductor band gap, with the energy gap between the valence band maximum (VBM) and conduction band minimum (CBM) spanning 1.0 to 3.0 eV. Notably, the MQ layers consistently exhibit higher energy levels than AZ monolayers, resulting in an exciton binding energy of 0.2 to 0.6 eV. The calculated optical absorption spectra for these materials display sharp, intense peaks, with peak positions varying based on the specific elements involved. Furthermore, the energy separation between the VBM and CBM in these QSMDs is significantly larger than that of the direct gap in monolayer MoS$_2$ (0.8 eV), a key factor in developing low-threshold two-dimensional lasers. Additionally, GW calculations indicate that the quasiparticle renormalization effect on the band gap is nearly negligible in QSMDs, a distinct feature compared to other two-dimensional materials. Finally, we demonstrated that QSMDs can be effectively doped with transition metals to induce magnetism, with a predicted magnetic moment of 2 per magnetometal atom. These findings suggest that GW/BSE calculations can rapidly and accurately identify high-performance two-dimensional optical and spintronic materials. The comprehensive dataset, including band structures, optical spectra, and magnetic moments, is available at http://www2.issp.ac.jp/~ykimura/QTetrahral/QTetrahral.html. The LHCb experiment analyzed $pp$ collision data collected at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 3 fb$^{-1}$ to search for the rare decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$. No significant local excess was observed near the signal region. Nevertheless, the result excludes the non-resonant next-to-leading-order Standard Model (SM) prediction at a 95% confidence level and sets an upper limit on the branching fraction of $\mathcal{B}(\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-) < 5.2 \times 10^{-7}$ at 95% C.L. This limit is comparable to the combined LHCb and Belle II limits on the rarer decay $\Lambda \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$. Furthermore, a limit is established on the product of branching fractions for intermediate states: $\mathcal{B}(\Sigma^+ \to p \pi^0) \times \mathcal{B}(\pi^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-) < 1.1 \times 10^{-10}$, which aligns with existing constraints. These findings support the development of new techniques for studying such rare decays of light hadrons in $p$-fixed target experiments. Additionally, the study investigated constraints on effective operators arising from physics beyond the Standard Model, finding that while some are limited to near SM sensitivity, others are constrained to within an order of magnitude. Notably, the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ channel is particularly sensitive to vector operators that contribute to the recent anomalous magnetic moment measurement of the muon. Consequently, this channel is a promising candidate for future searches aimed at detecting light hadron decays that may be obscured by hadronic backgrounds. Finally, upper bounds on the hadronic transition form factors for $\Sigma^+ \to p$ were derived, with the most stringent limit occurring at the minimum $q^2$. These constraints are consistent with predictions from lattice QCD and calculations based on chiral effective field theory. The study also examined the potential for enhancing sensitivity in future experiments through optimized detector performance and increased data collection. Furthermore, it addresses the need for improved $\Sigma^+$ production and reconstruction capabilities at $p$-fixed target facilities, such as the proposed LHC Fixed-Target Experiment (AFTER).

We examine disk formation resulting from the gravitational collapse of a prestellar core using high-resolution smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations, with the initial mass density profile modeled after an isothermal collapse under radiative cooling. Our analysis focuses on how the initial mass and total mass ejected influence disk properties, including mass, radius, and mass accretion rate, while also investigating disk formation in low-mass stars. These parameters are critical for understanding the requirements to initiate planet formation. Our findings indicate that the final disk mass and accretion rate rely on the extent of mass ejection, whereas the disk's radius is determined by the specific angular momentum of the retained mass. Furthermore, we confirm that mass ejection occurs during the collapse, with the ejected mass and its angular momentum decreasing as the star's mass increases. Finally, the angular momentum transport mechanisms required to form disks around low-mass stars are also addressed. Overall, the mechanism we study is more effective at forming disks with higher masses and larger radii compared to other collapse mechanisms. Additionally, the angular momentum problem is less severe in low-mass stars than in higher-mass systems. These outcomes are consistent with the notion that low-mass stars can form without significant angular momentum issues, whereas higher-mass stars require substantial angular momentum transport. This suggests that very low-mass stars are the most likely candidates to naturally form disks large enough to facilitate planet formation. However, we also note that the formation of massive planets is more complex, as it requires the retention of a larger disk mass, which in turn necessitates reduced mass ejection. Consequently, the conditions favoring disk formation may differ from those enabling planet formation. Ultimately, we conclude that the initial conditions of a prestellar cloud significantly impact the characteristics of the resulting disk. Finally, we address the necessity of including magnetic fields and self-gravity in hydrodynamic simulations of prestellar core collapse. These simulations serve as a valuable tool for understanding the initial stages of planet formation. Future work will expand the scope of this study to include more realistic physical processes. Specifically, we will analyze the relationship between disk formation and planet formation, and we will also explore whether disks formed through collapse can naturally produce the massive disks and high accretion rates necessary for planet formation. Ultimately, this research aims to clarify the initial conditions of the solar nebula. To achieve this, we will incorporate more realistic physical processes into our simulations, such as heating caused by the formation of a first hydrostatic core, which will be the subject of our next study. Atmospheric dispersion remains a critical issue for high-resolution spectroscopy, yet current models often fail to accurately represent on-sky conditions, leading to underestimated requirements for Automatic Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors (AADCs). This study presents measurements of spatial and temporal variations in up to 1000 nm bandwidths, derived from a comparison between spectrograph traces and a high-resolution solar atlas. The observations were conducted at the 3.6-meter telescope on La Silla during a campaign designed to test the performance of an AADC under development. A new model is introduced to quantify at least the mean bias of recent dispersion models, while existing models are assessed based on their ability to reproduce measured spatial and temporal variations. The findings indicate that all considered models are insufficient for AADC operation. Specifically, Rayleigh scattering is identified as a significant but often neglected contributor to dispersion, and significant spatial variations in air density are observed. Furthermore, the results highlight a substantial disparity between ground-level and top-of-atmosphere dispersion values. Finally, a new parameterization for both temporal and spatial variations in total column water vapor is proposed. This approach successfully reproduces the observed variations and is expected to enhance AADC performance. A Python library containing this new parameterization is made available to the community. The full assessment of these results will be published in a forthcoming paper. A companion paper provides the observations upon which this study is based. [abridged]

Modeling multi-period time series is crucial for forecasting across various domains. While numerous models exist for this purpose, a key challenge lies in determining the appropriate complexity, specifically identifying the necessary features to forecast a specific series without overfitting the data. To address this, we introduce a multi-layer recurrent neural network that models and predicts multi-period time series. This approach treats prediction as a joint probability distribution problem, where the observation distribution is conditioned on the input series and an auxiliary "key" series. By employing a Bayesian network, we can incorporate domain knowledge and prevent overfitting. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness using both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results indicate that our model, combined with Bayesian techniques, can automatically select the most important parameters and exclude irrelevant ones from the prediction process. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ashishgarg123/MLRTN. Furthermore, we have released a dataset for public use, accessible here: https://github.com/ashishgarg123/Multi-Level-Modeling-Data. This dataset contains 1,000 synthetic time series generated using our multi-period modeling method, each accompanied by the ground truth auxiliary key series and "true" non-zero parameters. We anticipate this data will be valuable for researchers developing or evaluating other multi-period time series models. Our model surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in the current literature regarding accuracy and stability. Additionally, we have made the dataset available on the Kaggle platform at the following link: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ashishgarg123/multi-level-modeling-data. We hope researchers will utilize this resource to compare their models against ours and to validate the effectiveness of our approach. Our model is particularly suited for scenarios where data is limited and overfitting is a significant concern. The model can be accessed at: https://github.com/ashishgarg123/MLRTN. We present Pontryagin duality as a specific instance of Stone duality within a continuous logic framework. Specifically, for an abelian topological group $A$ and a family $\mathcal F$ comprising its continuous homomorphisms into the circle group $\mathbb T$, we treat $(A, \mathcal F)$$ as a structure in continuous logic. We demonstrate that its corresponding bi-interpretation with the Pontryagin dual of $(A, \mathcal F)$ involves the Quasi-L2 topology. Furthermore, we examine the continuous first-order theory characterized by the sole axiom stating that the group is a non-discrete, locally compact, Hausdorff topological group. Finally, we establish that the theory of the dual structure, when equipped with a specific language of constant symbols representing all Borel probability measures on the maximal compact subgroup, forms a model complete expansion of the theory of the dual of a locally abelian affine group. This result follows from the fact that the bi-interpretation between these duals restricts to a continuous logic functor between the categories of such groups and their measures. Additionally, we provide an example of a non-compact group possessing a continuous logic bi-interpretation with its Pontryagin dual that cannot be reduced to the Quasi-L2 topology. Finally, we offer a negative answer to a question posed by van den Dungen, demonstrating that the class of topological abelian groups is not axiomatizable within continuous logic. Our proof utilizes the fact that the free group of rank 1, when viewed as a continuous logic structure, is interpretable in the group of integers.

The swift advancement of machine learning has significantly contributed to societal challenges, including bias, data intrusion, and inequitable outcomes. Federated learning (FL), a decentralized strategy, has emerged as a key approach to addressing these issues by enhancing data privacy, ensuring fairness, and boosting efficiency. Nevertheless, privacy risks persist within FL, as revealed by various attacks. Differential privacy (DP), a rigorous privacy framework, is recognized as a robust solution to mitigate these risks. This paper presents the inaugural comprehensive investigation of integrating DP into FL systems. We first examine how DP can safeguard FL, followed by the development of two DP-FL protocols based on multiparty computation, which distinguish themselves from existing DP-FL methods through a novel encryption strategy. We further explore the trade-offs among privacy, security, and communication overhead in DP-FL. Finally, we validate the efficacy of DP-FL by assessing FL models under DP constraints regarding their susceptibility to attacks, evaluating the impact of different aggregation rules on model performance, and analyzing the effects of data distribution and size on privacy and security outcomes. Our findings offer valuable insights for the future evolution of FL systems, particularly concerning privacy enhancement, security hardening, and performance optimization. This study offers the most comprehensive analysis of DP-FL to date, establishing a foundational reference for advancing FL systems, with a specific emphasis on privacy. We introduce a supersymmetric extension of the standard model, incorporating a right-handed neutrino and an additional U(1)$_X$ gauge symmetry. To ensure anomaly cancellation, a new right-handed electron field is introduced; this field carries charges under both the U(1)$_{Y}$ and U(1)$_X$ generators. We establish the necessary conditions for electroweak symmetry breaking and neutrino mass generation through a detailed analysis of the vacuum condition involving Higgs and $Z^{\prime}$ fields. Furthermore, we examine the mass spectrum and decay modes of neutral gauginos. Finally, we evaluate the viability of this model at the LHC and future neutrino experiments by considering the decay of a next-to-lightest neutralino into a $Z$ boson and dark matter candidate $Z^{\prime}$, as well as the subsequent $W$-boson mediated decay of the $Z^{\prime}$ into a $W$ boson and right-handed neutrinos. The EH user, equipped with harvest-then-transmit functionality, utilizes an IRS to secure a communication link. The objective is to maximize the average throughput of the EH user by jointly optimizing the IRS phase-shifting matrix, energy harvesting duration, and continuous power control of the interferer, subject to specific constraints. Given the high dimensionality and non-convex nature of the resulting optimization problem, an analytical solution is unattainable. Consequently, a novel deep unsupervised learning (DUL)-based approach is introduced, comprising two stages. In the first stage, a deep long short-term memory (LSTM) network forecasts the average channel power of the EH user. In the second stage, these predicted channel statistics, alongside pre-processed interference information, feed into a long short-term memory recurrent network (LSTM-RN) that has been trained offline via a DUL scheme. This scheme decomposes the original problem into two independent subproblems, which are subsequently merged using a penalty function method. The offline-trained model enables the system to rapidly and efficiently solve the problem in real-time, thereby achieving a high-throughput performance for the EH user. Simulation results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed DUL-based scheme. Furthermore, the impact of interference is analyzed by varying the number of antennas at the interferer and the rate of antenna array expansion. Finally, the proposed method is compared against existing state-of-the-art approaches, including an exhaustive search and a deep learning-based scheme. Notably, in scenarios with large-scale antenna arrays, the proposed DUL-based approach significantly outperforms the deep learning-based scheme. For the first time, the Gamow-Teller strength distribution for the decay of $^{186}$Hg into $^{186}$Au has been measured using total absorption gamma spectroscopy. A half-life of $T_{1/2}=32.4\pm1.2$~ms was established, aligning with theoretical predictions. The primary beta transition is a Gamow-Teller decay to the $3^{-}$ state at 1047 keV, which accounts for 95% of the strength. Systematic comparisons with beta-decay data from other Hg isotopes reveal an odd-even effect in logft values. Furthermore, this study offers a novel perspective on the evolution of Gamow-Teller strength distributions across different nuclear shapes. The findings are compared with beta-decay calculations based on shell-model wave functions. Additionally, the study reports the existence of two previously unknown isomeric states in $^{186}$Au at energies of 1047$\pm$10 keV and 1170$\pm$10 keV, with mean lifetimes of $\tau$=1.0$\pm$0.1 ms and $\tau$=1.0$\pm$0.15 ms, respectively. These results are interpreted using total absorption gamma spectroscopy. Finally, the discussion addresses the challenges of applying this technique to other exotic, short-lived nuclei. We interweave the mechanisms of leptogenesis and dark matter production within a unified framework featuring two heavy right-handed neutrinos and a new scalar multiplet. Following the decay of the lightest right-handed neutrino during the radiation-dominated epoch, the remaining heavier state is generated as dark matter through freeze-in during the matter-dominated era. Our analysis demonstrates that both the leptogenesis and dark matter mass parameters can be calculated in the heavy neutrino basis without relying on CP-violating mass matrix diagonalization. Furthermore, we establish that the mass of the additional right-handed neutrino sets an upper limit for successful leptogenesis and dark matter production. Finally, we outline a strategy to experimentally probe this framework using both current and future lepton colliders. Our findings indicate that a lepton asymmetry of $10^{-3}$ can be achieved, and we outline pathways to explore this scenario at both a 10 TeV lepton collider and an FCC-ee. These scenarios predict a lepton asymmetry exceeding $10^{-3}$ and a dark matter relic density within the range of $0.05-0.5$. Additionally, these signals may manifest as a lepton flavor universality violation in $B$ decays and Higgs decays into $\mu\mu$ and $ee$. Consequently, these channels offer the potential to detect the model at a 10 TeV lepton collider with 1 ab$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. Finally, we examine the feasibility of investigating this framework at the FCC-ee with 1 ab$^{-1}$ of data. We anticipate detecting these signals if the dark matter parameter space falls within $0.05-0.5$ and the higgsino parameter is below 1 TeV. This model successfully explains the observed dark matter relic density, CP-violating asymmetries in both neutrino and muon sectors, and the $m_{\mu}$ problem. Ultimately, our proposed framework offers a compelling target for future lepton colliders. Our findings suggest that the parameter space can be scanned without diagonalizing the mass matrix, and the model addresses multiple experimental anomalies, including those related to the $\mu$ mass, $\mu-e$ conversion, and Higgs decays. We introduce a learning-to-control method designed for systems with highly non-stationary dynamics, minimal data, and partial state visibility. Our approach employs a data-driven dynamic programming algorithm that utilizes a pre-trained generative model of system dynamics as a scalar cost function. This low-data resilience stems from the algorithm's capacity to rapidly adapt to non-stationarity by retrieving and reusing data segments that temporarily resemble the current system dynamics. To address state partial observability, the method integrates a cost function derived from hidden Markov model-based filtering to assess the compatibility of potential "true" states with observed data. Through numerical experiments involving multiple mobile robots and a human arm, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can learn to reach, swim, walk, and fly within a single trial. Furthermore, the resulting controllers are robust against data scarcity and partial state information. In contrast, model-based model predictive control struggles in these scenarios, and random exploration fails to produce a coherent trajectory. These findings suggest that learning to control in the presence of non-stationarity and data limitations is feasible, thereby expanding the scope of viable control applications. Additionally, the approach holds promise for designing controllers for human-robot collaborations, such as those between service robots and individuals with motor impairments. This paper serves as an extended version of [1]. The multiple mobile robots used in our experiments are detailed in [2]. Our approach is also a foundation for designing motion plans for a mobile robot assisting a person with motor impairments, as described in [3].

Toda conformal field theories represent natural extensions of Liouville conformal field theory characterized by enhanced symmetry. Within Toda theories, this higher symmetry becomes manifest through a set of non-linear constraints known as Ward identities. This article investigates specific Ward identities linked to weight 2 and spin 2 operators in the context of an $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda theory, with a particular focus on critical and near-critical regimes. The analysis reveals that the correlation functions of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda theory can be expressed as explicit functions of those from a higher-ordered $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Toda theory, alongside explicit functions of conformal data specific to the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ theory. These findings offer explicit, exact predictions for correlation functions involving arbitrary numbers of operators. Furthermore, these results align with predictions derived from conformal bootstrap methods and numerical findings regarding critical and near-critical correlation functions. Finally, the explicit correlation functions are connected to the partition functions of the corresponding statistical systems at critical and near-critical points. This connection facilitates a comparison with existing exact and near-exact computations across various critical and near-critical models, including the critical and near-critical Ising, eight-vertex, Potts, and FK models, as well as the Potts and FK models in the next-to-critical regime. Additionally, the work establishes explicit relations between partition functions and Toda correlation functions, a relationship supported by existing literature. These relationships enable the explicit construction of correlation functions for the Potts model using correlation functions from the $\mathfrak{sl}_2, \mathfrak{sl}_3$ and $\mathfrak{sl}_2, \mathfrak{sp}_4$ Toda theories, as well as free fermion correlation functions. This approach yields explicit predictions for various correlation functions within the next-to-critical regime. Finally, the explicit correlation functions are compared with those calculated via the conformal bootstrap method. Notably, numerical estimates for critical and near-critical correlation functions in the Potts model align well with predictions derived from Ward identity computations involving the free fermion theory and critical or critical-near theory components. These results suggest that significant simplifications of the Potts model's correlation functions may arise from specific Ward identity applications. Consequently, this work may stimulate further research into the explicit correlation functions of Potts models through the lens of Ward identities. This study introduces a novel image-to-image mapping framework called Relation GAN (RGAN), which integrates Relation Networks (RNets) with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to model complex relationships within data. While RGAN demonstrates strong versatility, we specifically apply it to the portrait styling task (PST), aiming to transfer artistic features from a source image to a target face under a specific artistic theme. To enhance the result's fidelity and structural quality, we incorporate a triplet loss function that leverages the inherent data relationships among faces, the target source image, and the source style image. Our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic datasets and large-scale benchmarks, significantly improving both fidelity and structural loss. Furthermore, extensive ablation studies and additional experiments confirm the model's robustness and reliability. We demonstrate that implementing quantum key distribution via the twin-field protocol does not necessitate phase locking when transmitting weak coherent pulses. By employing a detection method based on optimal linear optics, we show that twin-field quantum key distribution can achieve single-photon interference between transmitted pulses, facilitating key rate scaling linearly with the square root of the optical power. Consequently, this approach eliminates the need for sophisticated phase-locking techniques, thereby simplifying twin-field quantum key distribution systems. Furthermore, we compare the security of this variant against practical quantum key distribution methods and illustrate the single-mode nature of the optical field by calculating its Wigner function. These findings are derived from a classical analysis of the detection method alongside quantum key distribution security formalism. Finally, we contextualize our results within the broader landscape of quantum communication technologies. Overall, our study underscores the significance of optimal linear optics in achieving high-rate quantum key distribution. Our findings indicate that the quantum advantage of twin-field protocols stems from the interference of weak coherent pulses at the linear optics detector following optimal measurement, a principle applicable to other quantum communication schemes. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the viability of quantum key distribution without twin-field phase locking, a conclusion reached through optimal linear optical measurements and classical post-processing. This insight may prove valuable for the development of future quantum communication technologies. To enable the identification of objects beyond this limited set, it is essential to allow detection using open-vocabulary categories that are not confined to a fixed list. However, previous open-vocabulary approaches fail to address two critical challenges: (1) the absence of bounding box annotations for target categories, and (2) the excessive generation of hard negatives, which negatively impacts model performance. The remarkable success of Transformer models in natural language processing has spurred extensive research into adapting them for computer vision tasks. This paper provides a comprehensive survey examining both the theoretical foundations and application of Transformers in computer vision. Initially, we outline current computer vision challenges, highlighting their unique aspects and complexities. Subsequently, we detail the core mechanisms of Transformers, illustrating how different variants are designed to address specific problems. Following this, we present a survey of state-of-the-art studies across major domains, including image classification, object detection, image-to-image translation, and segmentation. The paper concludes by summarizing common design principles, identifying remaining unsolved problems, and offering insights and suggestions for future research. We anticipate that providing an all-encompassing review of Transformers in computer vision will serve as a valuable guide for both novices and established researchers in the field. Most current mortality forecasting techniques depend on extrapolating historical temporal patterns. Nevertheless, external factors like major pandemics or significant shifts in lifestyles and healthcare can cause these patterns to break, rendering predictions unreliable. This paper demonstrates that factor models are capable of mitigating overfitting and providing robustness against structural breaks. Furthermore, it reveals that allowing factor loadings to change over time enhances forecasting accuracy, particularly for short-term projections. Finally, the method is applied to four national datasets, generating one-year ahead forecasts from 2000 to 2019. This comparative analysis includes several factor models utilizing both time-varying and time-invariant loadings, as well as various uncertainty metrics. The study confirms the superior performance of the AR(1)-F(1,1) model with time-varyian loadings. Neural Architecture Search (NAS) utilizes reinforcement learning to automatically explore a space of neural network architectures, aiming to identify models that achieve high accuracy and efficiency. Because these architectures can yield complex interference patterns among performance metrics, they often conflict with one another. This study examines the interference between network performance and efficiency within Inception architectures and training time versus performance within ResNet architectures. By analyzing the characteristics of this interference, we offer insights into the underlying mechanisms of NAS. Furthermore, we investigate mitigation strategies by incorporating network ensembles into search time and output validation, particularly for Inception architectures. Our findings demonstrate that validity checks and ensembles can significantly reduce interference. Additionally, we establish that network ensembles are more effective at mitigating interference in performance-optimized search spaces than in performance-accuracy tradeoff spaces, as the latter already integrate validity checks. Finally, we release an open-source reinforcement learning-based NAS system that supports multiple architectures and enables custom search spaces through validity checks and network ensembles. Time series analysis serves as a critical method for addressing real-world challenges and making informed decisions. Although numerous techniques exist, including machine learning, the most effective approach for a specific decision often remains a statistical model. The `thefe` package supports statisticians, data analysts, and machine learning practitioners by integrating a wide array of time series methods from `forecast` and other sources with feature extraction capabilities. This report presents an applied demonstration of these capabilities. It highlights that decision support can be significantly enhanced by incorporating feature importance alongside forecasts. Furthermore, comparing models based on the stability of their key predictors can improve the selection process, ultimately leading to more robust decisions. The primary objective of this report is to illustrate various `thefe` functions and their utility in generating the necessary outputs. Finally, because model selection is a complex issue within the forecastable environment, utilizing alternative metrics such as feature stability can offer valuable insights. This analysis aims to facilitate a more informed decision-making process. Overall, this report seeks to raise awareness about the `thefe` package and the valuable insights it can contribute to model selection. Specifically, while every geodesically complete boundary of such a space possesses this property, certain subspaces fail to do so. Furthermore, in Theorem A, we establish that for any locally compact geodesically complete CAT(0) space with a compact core, its compactly supported second l²-cohomology with coefficients in $\Gamma$ is isomorphic to the second reduced $l^2$-cohomology of its boundary, provided $\Gamma$ is a subgroup of $\pi_1(X)$ whose commensurator is a lattice in Isom$(X)$. We illustrate the utility of this isomorphism by presenting a non-amenable group whose boundary has triadic curvature and is amenable. Additionally, we present a boundary with finitely generated homotopy groups and triadic curvature, alongside an example of a group where the boundary of a Cayley graph exhibits negative curvature and is finitely presented. The initial three examples were inspired by a question from Bridson and Oliver regarding the non-hereditary nature of non-positive curvature. Human Translators hold a critical role in the human-machine translation workflow. While reliability estimates are essential for their work, calculating them is challenging due to the confidentiality of professional translations. Consequently, assessing reliability is typically conducted collectively among translators. Although the traditional Crow/Bradley model is a standard statistical method for reliability analysis, it relies on maximum likelihood estimation, which often yields unreliable results when the number of translators is small. To address this limitation, this study introduces a Bayesian framework for Bayesian reliability analysis, applicable to small groups of translators. The approach enables more accurate reliability inference and supports decision-making by facilitating the ranking of translators and the identification of translation quality issues. The proposed model is demonstrated using real-world data, and a web-based decision support system has been developed to assist translators in analyzing and improving translation quality. Sum rules are fundamental for characterizing generic properties of physical systems and have been extensively utilized in various scattering contexts, including electronic transport within quantum dots, wave scattering in chaotic cavities, and noise correlations in ultra-cold gases. Recently, sum rules have also emerged as a crucial tool for identifying environmental signatures of quantum information processing devices by examining quantum evolutions along closed paths in configuration space. In this work, we extend these sum rules to a broader spectrum of open-system scattering scenarios, encompassing energy deposition and extraction from open quantum systems coupled to multiple reservoirs, as well as energy loss mechanisms in few-qubit systems interacting with environments. We demonstrate that these generalized sum rules are derived from an eigenvalue problem defined over the space of completely positive, trace-preserving maps. This formulation introduces "channels" as a new conceptual framework for analyzing open quantum system dynamics. Furthermore, we establish a link between these map eigenchannels and the eigenvectors of a specific non-Hermitian matrix, offering a tractable approach for numerical investigations. Finally, we illustrate the utility of these scattering-system eigenchannels as a versatile instrument for comprehending energy dynamics in energy relaxation processes. Specifically, we analyze a few-level system embedded in a two-level environment to reveal universal characteristics of energy deposition by the system into the environment. Our findings suggest that this specific scenario is particularly significant for establishing the fundamental limits of energy efficiency in superconducting qubits. Ultimately, we contend that these generalized scattering sum rules, along with the associated map eigenchannels, represent a novel and broadly applicable instrument for investigating diverse aspects of energy dynamics in open quantum systems. Additionally, the principles governing these map eigenvalues and eigenvectors may prove valuable in addressing fundamental issues regarding information and energy conservation during quantum operations. Our associated video offers a complementary visual exploration of these open quantum system eigenchannels. Supplementary materials are available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12401888. Supplementary Note 1 outlines a numerical algorithm to calculate map eigenchannels, while Supplementary Note 2 details a numerical study of energy relaxation in a two-level system within an environmental two-level system. Supplementary Note 3 demonstrates that an apparent violation of a sum rule arises from the non-Hermiticity of the associated matrix, which is subsequently rectified. Supplementary Note 4 explores the relationship between these map eigenchannels and the recently introduced "time crystals." Supplementary Note 5 examines the relationship between these map eigenchannels and the fundamental problem of information conservation during energy exchange

Pruning techniques aim to enhance network efficiency regarding memory usage and computational demands by eliminating redundant connections. While it is established that even minimal substructures within feedforward neural networks possess functional capabilities as "winning lottery tickets," the impact of pruning on feature extraction remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the effects of pruning on deep feedforward networks' ability to extract features. We contend that deep convolutional networks achieve efficient representations by retaining only a sparse subset of features found within shallow, fully connected architectures. To test the efficiency of deep convolutional features relative to deep and shallow fully connected ones, we developed an algorithm capable of identifying winning lottery tickets composed exclusively of features from either convolutional or fully connected networks. Our findings indicate that while deep convolutional features are indeed efficient, they achieve this sparsity through a distinct mechanism compared to winning lottery tickets in fully connected networks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that identifying the core substructure of functional networks can be accomplished by comparing the participation rates of features within active subnetworks. These results offer a novel perspective on the efficiency of deep convolutional networks and open avenues for new network pruning strategies based on feature participation. We introduce a data-driven framework for determining the optimal purchase time and distribution for lottery tickets to maximize expected value. Our approach treats the lottery as a multi-armed bandit problem, where each "arm" represents a draw from historical patterns of winning and losing. By utilizing predictive models to estimate the probability of success for unplayed combinations in an upcoming draw, we apply mapping functions to optimally purchase tickets based on these estimates. Furthermore, we propose the concept of "lottery heat maps," which visualize the geographic distribution of sold tickets. Our method for defining optimal heat maps relies on estimating local ticket success probabilities and the current market price of tickets. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through both simulated and real-world experiments, showing that predictive models can identify high-value ticket combinations and, by accounting for local saturation, establish optimal selling prices and locations. Additionally, we develop algorithms to accelerate ticket purchases, leveraging parallelization and GPU acceleration to increase throughput by several orders of magnitude. The practical utility of this work is particularly evident for syndicates, which can use it to identify when to buy and sell to optimize returns, while also offering players a mechanism to profit from informed decision-making. The methods are implemented in an open-source Python library, LibLottery, designed to speed up simulations and enable rapid prototyping of new strategies. The full paper and code are accessible at https://liblottery.github.io. Finally, we conclude by outlining several avenues for future research. Keywords: Lottery, Syndicates, Optimization, GPU.
