We compute the large-spin anomaling dimension $\gamma_Q$ for the product of $Q$ external spins in the $O(N)$ symmetric $\lambda\phi^4$ model up to order $g^6$ in the expansion around the critical dimension. This result yields five new terms for $\gamma_Q$ and enables the calculation of the ratio $R_Q = (\chi_{critical}-\chi)(\eta-1)/g^2$, which characterizes the subleading behavior of the leading twist dispersion relation at large spin. Our findings provide strong evidence for the validity of the recent $1/(2\ell)$ expansion of $\gamma_Q$ proposed in [J. Caetano, S. Komatsu, and J. Zinn-Justin, Phys. Rev. D 104, 026007 (2021)]. Furthermore, we observe that the structure of $\gamma_Q$ simplifies significantly when $Q$ is even, a feature that likely extends to other theories within the context of the large spin expansion. Finally, we derive the two-loop and three-loop equations governing the $g$-dependence of the anomalous dimensions for the $O(n)$ symmetric tensor operators $\phi^I\phi^J$ and the scalar operator $\phi^4$. These equations facilitate the calculation of the anomalous dimensions for the tensor operators $\phi^I\phi^J$ through three-loop order. Our results are consistent with existing computations for the $O(3)$ symmetric model and the $O(N)$ symmetric $\phi^4$ model with $N$ vector components. Additionally, we provide the three-loop anomaling dimensions for the tensor operators $\phi^I\phi^J$ and the scalar operator $\phi^4$, which were previously unknown. Our analysis reveals a striking simplification in the anomaling dimensions of the tensor operators $\phi^I\phi^J$ [arXiv:2301.07370] for even $N$, a pattern that also emerges in the large spin limit of $\gamma_Q$. This suggests a universal structure applicable to all theories in the context of the large spin expansion. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our results by calculating the leading twist dispersion relation for the correlator $\langle\phi^I\phi^J\phi^I\phi^J\rangle$ up to three-loop order within the $O(N)$ symmetric $\lambda\phi^4$ model. The influence of electron-phonon coupling on valley physics in two-dimensional materials is investigated through first-principles calculations and many-body theory. This study introduces and examines two distinct mechanisms: the first arises from the non-hermity of phonons, leading to lifetime broadening effects that create many-body spectral peaks broadened by phonon decays; the second stems from electron-phonon coupling-induced renormalization of phonon self-energies, resulting in shifts of these spectral peaks. These identified mechanisms are demonstrated to be crucial for interpreting recent experimental findings. The work underscores that many-body effects are essential for a precise understanding of electron-phonon interactions in two-dimensional materials. The research details and analyzes the computational methodologies employed. Furthermore, it offers a unified framework for analyzing experimental data from various groups, specifically regarding electron-phonon induced valley Hall effects in few-layer graphene and moiré graphene. This serves as a foundational step toward developing a unified theory of electron-phonon interactions in two-dimensional materials. Additionally, the study provides a comprehensive list of computational parameters used. Finally, the work functions as a benchmark to validate future computational efforts. For the Visual Domain Adaptation (VisDA) 2022 Challenge, which sought an unsupervised domain adaptation method for image denoising, we won first place with a 33% improvement over the organizer's baseline. Drawing from recent advancements in image-to-image translation, we developed the Unsupervised Noise Reduction for Image Denoising (UNRID) model. This approach employs an autoencoder adapted from the widely used Edge-Enhanced Denoising Autoencoder (EEDA) to learn an effective mapping from noisy to clean images. To enable domain adaptation, we incorporated a self-supervised task that adapts the network for self-reconstruction of synthetic noisy images. Additionally, we utilized Adversarial Training (AT) to facilitate the noise-to-clean transformation. The AT component comprises two sub-networks: one a noisy image-to-clean image translator, and the other a clean image-to-noisy image translator (acting as a decoder for the former). The challenge provided three source domains for training and a single target domain for evaluation. We evaluated all three source domains on the target domain, with UNRID trained on a combination of all three achieving the highest performance. Furthermore, we performed qualitative analysis to interpret the model's success, and our results were highlighted in the challenge report. t-SNE is a widely adopted method for embedding high-dimensional data, yet it relies on a Gaussian distribution in Euclidean space that often fails to capture the intrinsic geometry of non-Euclidean data types, such as spherical or hyperbolic manifolds. To address this limitation, we introduce VMF-SNE, a t-SNE variant that utilizes a spherical visual manifold distribution, offering the flexibility to embed data points onto a spherical visual manifold. Evaluated on various spherical data sets, our results demonstrate that VMF-SNE successfully identifies the spherical nature of the underlying visual manifold, surpassing both standard t-SNE and spherical t-SNE, which either miss this characteristic or become trapped in local minima. The implementation code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishgarg1995/VMF-SNE. Additionally, our code includes an implementation of spherical t-SNE, which was previously unpublished, for the benefit of researchers. We anticipate that VMF-SNE will prove highly beneficial for unsupervised and semi-supervised vision tasks, including clustering, classification, and visualization. The source code will be made publicly available.

This research investigates the two-dimensional Fermi gas in both pure and mixed-particle scenarios using fermionic diagrammatic expansions. We present a diagrammatic Monte Carlo (DMC) approach for fermionic many-body perturbation theory, focusing on the interaction energy of a impurity within a Fermi sea. Our findings align well with existing theoretical data across both weak and strong coupling regimes. Specifically, we examine the diagonal self-energy expansions for perturbation orders up to 16, corresponding to fifth order in the coupling constant. We demonstrate that a simple grand-canonical free energy approximation for resummation yields a comprehensive description of the weak-coupling interaction energy, including the impurity dressed quasiparticle state. Furthermore, we analyze the convergence of the diagrammatic series, observing that while it converges for below-critical interaction strengths, it diverges at the second-order BCS transition. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results regarding the excitation spectrum of the quasiparticle. (This work is partially based on the second author's thesis [1].)

Keywords: Quantum Monte Carlo, Diagrammatic Monte Carlo, Bose-Einstein Condensation, Phase Transitions, Bose gases, Fermi gases, Strongly correlated gases, Bose-Fermi mixtures, Polaron.

We explore a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing framework that enables the execution of any quantum algorithm without relying on conventional two-qubit gates. Instead, this method utilizes universal, tunable interactions inherent to physical qubit arrays. We demonstrate the application of this digital-analog strategy to simulate fermionic systems by adapting the standard time evolution operator emulation technique for bosonic systems and incorporating fermionic Jordan-Wigner (JWT) mapping. We analyze the specific quantum resources needed to execute this simulation on arrays of superconducting qubits, utilizing Jordan-Wigner and Bravyi-Temme-Knill mappings to transform the problem from a Jordan-Wigner basis to a more efficient XZZX basis. Our findings indicate that the digital-analog approach is highly competitive with fully digital strategies for simulating $XZZX$-type fermionic systems using near-term quantum hardware. Furthermore, we extend this analysis to the simulation of interacting spin systems, demonstrating that digital-analog quantum computing can substantially lower the resource demands for these tasks on digital quantum computers by employing the Bravyi-Temme-Knill mapping. Finally, we examine the experimental requirements for digital and digital-analog quantum simulation using an array of superconducting qubits based on flux and charge degrees of freedom. We conclude by outlining potential experimental challenges and avenues for future research. The source code is publicly accessible at \href{https://github.com/quantum-machine-learning-group/qmml-qsd}{QMML-QSD}. Additionally, we have developed a quantum simulation library, \texttt{QMML}, which supports both digital and digital-analog quantum simulation using superconducting qubit arrays; this library is available at \href{https://github.com/quantum-machine-learning-group/qmml}{QMML}. We investigate graph polynomials defined by the sum $G(\xi)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\xi^{f_i(G)}$, in which the coefficients correspond to the counts of graphs exhibiting a specific property $f_i$ and serve as their respective values. Assuming these polynomials exhibit an asymptotic behavior characterized by a dominant term and an error component, we derive an expression for the error as a series of Schur polynomials indexed by strict partitions. This formula relies on the derivatives of the dominant function and the probability distributions of the four possible sign combinations for the error terms across the graph set. We establish a connection between the rate of convergence of $G(\xi)$ to its dominant term and the convergence of the error's magnitude to its asymptotic approximation, thereby validating the "Law of Large Numbers" (LLN) demonstrated in arXiv:2002.01001. Furthermore, we analyze the asymptotic properties of the moments of graph polynomials and their growth rates, while also examining the aspects of almost sure and stochastic continuity for the family of these polynomials. Additionally, we introduce a novel asymptotic behavior for the moments of the Inverse Matching Polynomial (IMP), specifically regarding its mean and variance, and present initial findings on almost sure and stochastic continuity for the IMP within a probabilistic framework. Finally, we outline methods to determine the asymptotic behavior of the impulse response function (IRF) for graph polynomials, along with illustrative examples. These findings are applied to the Inverse Matching Polynomial, a recently identified graph invariant in arXiv:2002.01001, demonstrating that it satisfies the "Law of Large Numbers" with a specific convergence rate for its impulse response function. We also evaluate the accuracy of IRF approximations for the impulse behavior of graph polynomials under various impulse responses. Notably, the IRF of the IMP is found to be independent of the graph size, a property that significantly enhances computational efficiency. The paper concludes with a list of open problems. Our results may hold broader significance, as they could be applicable to the general class of graph polynomials, as conjectured. Additionally, the probabilistic framework for analyzing the impulse behavior of graph polynomials may be extendable to other areas of graph theory. Finally, the concepts of impulse and impulse response functions are also relevant to control theory. This work provides an explicit formula for the pullback of the Hitchin connection from the moduli space of genus two curves to a ten-fold cover of a Teichmüller curve identified by Veech. Furthermore, we derive an expression using iterated integrals for the monodromy representation associated with this connection. As a consequence, we establish quantum representations for infinitely many pseudo-Anosov elements within the genus two mapping class group. Additionally, we offer a conceptual interpretation of a recent formula by Aganagic, Shapira, Shenderov, and Shemesh regarding the pullback of Hitchin's connection on hyperelliptic moduli space, and our findings yield an alternative derivation of their result. Finally, we demonstrate how to generate explicit representations by computing the parallel transport of the Hitchin connection along a specific horizontal path. In this process, we construct a collection of pseudo-differential operators on the curve sheet and compute the pullback of the Hitchin connection through their action. We also calculate eigenvalues for several novel quantum representations in genus two. Notably, we identify a new representation, $\rho_{5b}$, which does not appear in the work of Aganagic et al. and exhibits distinct properties compared to representations of lower degree. Furthermore, we derive an explicit system of differential equations for the pullback of the Hitchin connection and verify that our solution satisfies these equations. Finally, we show that the pullback of the Hitchin system is integrable by verifying the Lax pair equations. Our solution is constructed using the algebra of functions on the pullback of the moduli space of genus two spin curves, which we explicitly describe. This space is isomorphic to the moduli space of genus two curve sheets; we provide an explicit construction of this curve sheet and its pullback. We also detail the pullback of the Hitchin system as a system of pseudo-differential operators on the curve sheet and its two-dimensional pullback. Our construction relies on the Weierstrass $\wp$-function and its associated $\zeta$ and $\eta$ functions. We demonstrate that the pullback of the Hitchin system constitutes a system of pseudo-differential equations on the curve sheet that can be solved via a variational principle. We verify that this system is equivalent to the pullback of the Hitchin system and that its solution corresponds to the pullback of the Hitchin connection. Over the past few years, remote work has become increasingly common, significantly transforming how software development teams operate. This shift has been further accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, which mandated that most teams transition to full-time remote environments. Consequently, many organizations have adopted remote Scrum as their preferred methodology. However, despite the widespread adoption of Scrum, there remains a lack of empirical data regarding its effectiveness in remote settings. To address this gap, this study employs a multi-method approach, combining a survey of 100 teams with case study analyses of both successful and unsuccessful remote Scrum projects. The survey revealed that team members perceive communication, collaboration, and leadership as the primary challenges in remote Scrum environments. The subsequent case studies confirmed that these three factors indeed exert a substantial influence on project outcomes. Ultimately, this research identifies communication, collaboration, and leadership as the most critical issues to manage when applying Scrum in a remote context. Furthermore, the findings suggest that remote Scrum does not necessarily hinder project success; instead, it can enhance the quality of interactions between people and processes. This conclusion is supported by the performance metrics of the teams studied, which show remote Scrum groups often outperform their on-site counterparts. These insights could guide organizations in making remote Scrum decisions and assist teams in overcoming the obstacles associated with fully remote development. Finally, the study offers practical recommendations for improving the remote Scrum environment. Notably, the paper concludes that remote Scrum should not be dismissed as a hindrance to success; rather, it should be recognized as a viable option that can even contribute to project advancement. This conclusion is grounded in the performance data from the examined teams, indicating that remote Scrum can positively impact project success. The paper also examines the various issues encountered and provides practical solutions for remote Scrum environments. The study's primary limitation lies in the fact that the analyzed teams may not be representative of all software development teams, and the issues identified might not encompass the entire spectrum of potential problems. Additionally, the influence of organizational culture on success was not assessed, as the research focused exclusively on team-level dynamics. Future research could explore the intersection of remote Scrum and organizational culture. Finally, this work aims to stimulate further investigation into remote Scrum environments. Specifically, it encourages researchers to investigate how remote Scrum impacts team dynamics, how it influences the emergence of organizational practices, and how it shapes organizational culture. These areas are currently under investigation by the authors. Furthermore, the study seeks to inspire researchers to analyze the effects of remote Scrum

The concept of the Gau–Wu number, originally developed to address the ground state spin of the 1949 gauge-invariant variational approach to the Ising model, has recently been broadened to apply to arrowhead matrices. This generalized version corresponds to the ratio of two specific principal minors of order $n-1$. This paper calculates the Gau–Wu numbers for $4\times 4$ arrowhead matrices and specific subsets of larger arrowhead matrices, noting that these values are frequently irrational. Furthermore, we demonstrate that every positive Gau–Wu $n\times n$ matrix ratio can be represented as a ratio of principal minors of an appropriately constructed arrowhead matrix, thereby offering a new interpretation for these numbers. Our findings also clarify the connection between the original research on the Ising model and these recent advancements regarding arrowhead matrices. Additionally, we present a computational method that yields simple, often exact, approximations for the eigenvalues of these matrices. Our proposed interpretation of the Gau–Wu number may prove valuable for future research in this field. This work serves as a sequel to our earlier study (J. Phys. Conf. Ser. 1309, 012001, 2019), which focused on the $3\times 3$ arrowhead matrix case. Our results indicate that principal minors of the characteristic polynomials of these matrices generate recurrence relations that facilitate the calculation of the Gau–Wu number for $n\times n$ matrices. Specifically, we have identified a class of matrices for which these recurrences produce rational numbers with a relatively short continued fraction representation. We also provide code to compute these ratios and have made it available on GitHub. Finally, we have examined the links between these ratios and the Hurwitz zeta and Riemann zeta functions. These findings underscore the significance of these matrix ratios for the study of number theory. In this paper, we explore the properties of these ratios and their relationship with the Riemann zeta function. Our findings highlight the importance of these ratios in number theory, and the connection established here further emphasizes their relevance to mathematical research. We have utilized these relationships to derive a closed-form expression for the Gau–Wu number associated with a $4\times 4$ arrowhead matrix, which was previously lacking. These findings further emphasize the significance of these matrix ratios for future research in this field. This study examines elliptic flow ($v_2$) within the prompt electron spectrum from semi-leptonic hadron decays, which arises from the anisotropic flow of beauty-hadrons. Data were collected by the ALICE detector at the LHC during Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV, covering transverse momenta ($p_{\rm T}$) from 1 to 80 GeV/c and centralities from 0% to 80%. Measurements span three $p_{\rm T}$ intervals: 1–4 GeV/c, 4–8 GeV/c, and 8–16 GeV/c. The observed $v_2$ values align with expectations derived from NLO pQCD calculations that incorporate beauty-hadron flow, QCD-based hybrid models, and phenomenological parametrizations. Furthermore, the data reveal a trend of increasing $v_2$ as centrality decreases. Notably, in the most peripheral collisions, electron $v_2$ at low $p_{\rm T}$ exceeds photon $v_2$ in the same low-$p_{\rm T}$ range. These findings are compared against various theoretical models. Hybrid model calculations predict a decreasing $v_2$ with rising $p_{\rm T}$, whereas NLO pQCD results indicate an initial increase followed by a decrease. Additionally, the electron $v_2$ is consistently larger than that of pions, with the gap narrowing as $p_{\text{T}}$ increases. In mid-central collisions, the $v_2$ of electrons with $p_{\rm T}$ > 10 GeV/c is also higher than pion $v_2$. Finally, the electron $v_2$ is also compared to light hadron $v_2$ across the full $p_{\rm T}$ spectrum. Finally, a model based on a hadron transport model coupled with NLO pQCD is utilized to determine the $b$-fraction in the data. This analysis indicates that the $b$-fraction rises with increasing centrality. Finally, comparisons with ATLAS and CMS data on prompt electrons in e$e$-spectra are also presented. The results are consistent with the observed $b$-fraction trend. Finally, the $b$-fraction in semi-leptonic decays is estimated to be approximately 10%

Driven by medical science applications, we investigate finite chromatic sets within Euclidean space through a topological lens. Leveraging persistent homology for images, along with kernels and cokernels, we develop provably stable homological metrics that characterize the geometric micro- and macro-structures of how color classes intermingle. These metrics can be efficiently calculated using chromatic Delaunay mosaics, triangulations, and tessellations. Furthermore, we provide an algebraic framework based on persistent Betti numbers, rank invariants, and persistence diagrams. The work includes illustrative examples and extends Alpha complexes to discrete color sets. Many of our results are demonstrated or visualized using synthetic and real images, such as the Cows and Sheep dataset. The corresponding Python code is accessible on our GitHub repository. We view this research as the foundation for a comprehensive theory of geometric invariants, which may eventually aid in solving problems in computer vision, data analysis, and other areas of mathematics. We invite collaboration from experts across mathematics, physics, and engineering. Our preliminary findings are detailed in the following paper: T. Banaschewski, A. Illés, and T. This study examines the General Degrees of Freedom (DoDoF) gap between optimal time-sharing-based linear precoding and binary linear random network coding (NC) at high Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) in Y1-type interference networks, which consist of multiple transmitters and receivers linked by high-capacity bidirectional links. We demonstrate that the gap between optimal precoding and NC is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ in these networks. This finding contrasts sharply with previous research indicating a gap of $\Theta(K)$ between optimal and unoptimized NC. Our results align with earlier observations regarding the gap between optimal precoding and deterministic NC schemes, further supporting the hypothesis that as networks scale, NC strategies will increasingly converge toward time-sharing-based optimal precoding approaches. Additionally, we present a General DoDoF characterization for $K$-user Gaussian interference networks, extending previous work limited to 2-user networks, and prove that achievable sum rates via optimal time-sharing-based linear strategies are $\Theta(K)$ bits/sec/Hz from the transmitters. Finally, we outline several open questions for future research regarding precise bounds on the gap between optimal and unoptimized NC. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how different high-SNR communication strategies interact with network scaling. Furthermore, we provide explicit solutions for specific small-scale networks and numerical results for larger networks to illustrate the applicability of our findings. Finally, we show that deterministic NC schemes achieve the same sum rates as optimal time-sharing-based linear strategies in certain small-scale networks. Our work also contributes to understanding the trade-offs between reliability and spectral efficiency in high-SNR NC schemes, as well as the impact of network topology on optimal time-sharing-based linear strategy achievable sum rates. The findings in this work have potential applications in designing future high-capacity wireless communication systems. We conclude by suggesting several directions for future research inspired by this study. We hope this work will contribute to a broader understanding of how different high-SNR communication strategies interact with network scaling and inspire further research in this area. Finally, we demonstrate the practicality of our findings by providing explicit solutions for specific small-scale networks and numerical results for larger networks to illustrate the applicability of our findings. Our findings also contribute to an understanding of the trade-offs between reliability and spectral efficiency in high-SNR NC schemes, and the impact of network topology on optimal time-sharing-based linear strategy achievable sum rates. The findings in this work have potential applications in designing future high-capacity wireless communication systems. We conclude by suggesting several directions for future research inspired by this study

This paper presents the categorization of audit engagements using Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) and Dempster-Shafer (DS) theory. Categorization serves as a mechanism to group audit engagements into distinct categories based on various attributes. We introduce a method for selecting relevant attributes and integrating FCA with DS theory to enhance the accuracy of audit categorization. The user provides a set of relevant attributes, and FCA is employed to choose a subset that best represents the specific data under consideration. Subsequently, audit categorization is performed by applying DS theory to the selected attributes. DS theory surpasses traditional classification methods because it can express uncertainty regarding an audit engagement's class membership. This advantage is particularly significant in auditing, where uncertainty often arises due to the specialized nature and complexity of specific engagements. Finally, we illustrate the proposed approach using frosinone, an open-source software implementation of FCA. Our experimental results demonstrate that the method achieves a 90% accuracy rate in categorizing audit engagements. Additionally, the source code for this approach is publicly accessible on GitHub. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first application of FCA and DS theory to audit categorization. Furthermore, to our knowledge, no prior research has addressed the combination of these two approaches for categorization purposes. Finally, we outline the method's limitations and suggest potential avenues for future research. These include the need for further investigation and empirical evidence to validate the uncertainty associated with audit engagements, as well as exploring the applicability of FCA and DS theory in other domains. We also recommend further research into the computational complexity of the proposed method. Finally, we propose extending the method to incorporate additional relevant attributes and investigating the use of machine learning to automatically select the most relevant attributes. The STrauss process is a point process defined by an unnormalized density relative to a Poisson point process, where every pair of points must be separated by at least a distance $r$. We demonstrate that samples from this STrauss process can be generated by combining $k$ realizations of a Poisson process with a rate of $\lambda r/(k\rho(r))$, where $k$ is arbitrary and $\rho(r)$ denotes the spherical exclusion volume at radius $r$. Furthermore, we show that samples from the STrauss process with a pair separation limit of $r$ can be obtained by stitching together $k$ such processes, provided that no point falls within distance $kr$ of any other point. Additionally, we introduce methods to evaluate the quality of these samples and determine the optimal value of $k$. Finally, we apply these techniques to a point localisation problem in wireless sensor networks. This approach is valuable for simulations requiring repeated point pattern sampling, such as those assessing coverage probability or outage probability. While exact STrauss sampling methods exist, they are computationally prohibitive for large volumes or high target densities; our method offers a practical solution for approximating these samples. Our approach is straightforward to implement, operates rapidly, and allows for the quantification of result quality. We have made the code available for users to adapt to their specific needs. Additionally, we have provided a quality assessment tool that estimates the optimal $k$ for a given scenario and can be utilized independently of the main code. Through simulations on various scenarios, we demonstrate that our method can achieve an accuracy within 1% of the optimal sample count. Additionally, we have made this tool available for users to adapt to their specific requirements. Finally, we have shown that the chosen value of $k$ can be used to assess the quality of the generated samples. Our approach enables the calculation of coverage and outage probabilities for both isotropic and anisotropic stably paired point patterns, addressing problems previously considered intractable. The Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) is a well-established framework within string theory that incorporates an extra term into the standard uncertainty relation. This study investigates the impact of GUP on both Galilean and Lorentz transformations. We derive modified versions of these principle-based transformations, known as GUP-based Galilean and Lorentz transformations (GPGL and GPL transformations, respectively), and demonstrate that they converge to the classical Galilean and Lorentz transformations when $\epsilon \to 0$. Furthermore, we prove that all $\epsilon$-deformations of the Lorentz transformation can be generated by composing GPGL and GPL transformations. Finally, we demonstrate that both Galilean and Lorentz invariance remain valid under these modified transformations, provided the modified time coordinate is defined as $t' = t$. These findings indicate that the GUP-induced deformation of Lorentz transformations does not alter the fundamental principles of special relativity. Additionally, we examine the gUP-based addition law and show that it retains the special properties of the relativistic addition law established by Weinberg. Our results underscore the robustness of the GUP framework in a post-Newtonian context. Consequently, this suggests that theories extending the Standard Model via GUP can be formulated as either deformed Lorentz symmetric theories (DLST) or generalized Newtonian symmetric theories (GNST), both rooted in principle-based transformations derived from GUP. Notably, these extensions can be developed without relying on specific quantum gravitational models. Finally, we demonstrate the consistency of our approach by deriving the one-parameter Lorentz transformation from both gUP and lUP, recovering the standard Lorentz transformation for $\epsilon = 1$. These findings provide a foundation for developing novel concepts in post-Newtonian physics grounded in the GUP principle. Finally, we outline several significant research avenues stemming from this work, which may facilitate the development of innovative quantum gravitational frameworks. Specifically, our methodology may offer valuable insights for formulating Lorentz deformed theories that stem from principle-based generalizations of the Lorentz transformation. This could potentially advance theories such as Doubly Special Relativity (DSR), Relative Double Length (RDL), and DSR-like Newtonian Symmetry (DSRln). Additionally, this approach may contribute to formulating Newtonian symmetry-based theories with contracted double length (RDL), which also rely on principle-based transformations. Multitasking scheduling has recently gained significant attention due to its ability to enhance system performance. In this model, an advanced mechanism allows a task to transition into an intelligent subtask, capable of executing alongside other tasks. However, this process incurs overhead time, and an unresolved challenge remains in determining optimal subtask generation strategies. This study introduces a novel multitasking model where subtasks are smart components that perform computational work on other subtasks, effectively sharing processing capabilities. The goal is to minimize the maximum completion time across all subtasks for a given task structure. We examine multitasking schedules across various subtask structures, analyzing the optimality of First-Come First-Served (FCFS) and Last-Come First-Served (LCFS) on First-Come First-Served tracks when multitasking is disabled. Furthermore, we address the open problem of multitasking optimization and present an asymptotically optimal algorithm for tasks with unlimited subtask structures. Finally, we address tasks with a single subtask structure, addressing a previously open case, and propose two asymptotically optimal algorithms to minimize makespan. The performance of these optimal algorithms is also evaluated through experimental analysis. Notably, our multitasking strategies generalize to intelligent multitasking, offering new optimal algorithms for intelligent scheduling. The accompanying code repository provides Python implementations of both multitasking schedules and intelligent schedules. This paper introduces a reduced-order model for a monopod machine, an energy-efficient hopping robot designed to navigate uneven and yielding terrains. Unlike many existing robotic systems, this monopod features a single degree of freedom and is constructed from a single, flexible beam. The model characterizes the movement of the front contact point as a function of ground properties, such as stiffness, and the robot's mass and velocity. Additionally, an optimal control strategy is proposed to determine the most efficient input force required to maintain a specified velocity on such terrains, alongside a simple method for selecting that velocity based on the terrain's characteristics. The study also presents a practical method for actuating the monopod using a DC motor and estimates the robot's physical parameters through basic experiments. Finally, the paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the model's predictions regarding uneven and yielding terrains, supported by physical experiments conducted on a concrete floor, a wooden floor, and a carpet. These results demonstrate that the proposed model accurately captures the robot's dynamics under these varying conditions. Furthermore, simulations indicate that velocities on a wooden floor and concrete are comparable to those achievable on soft ground, whereas on a hard concrete surface, the robot can sustain constant velocity for extended periods without requiring any input force. Consequently, the findings suggest that this reduced-order model effectively addresses critical challenges in locomotion robotics, including dynamics modeling, motion prediction, and energy-efficient path planning. The code supporting this work is available at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1992/Yielding-Terrain. Our motivation stems from the work detailed in reference [1]. Given this reduced-order model, we aim to develop an effective method for actuating the beam and derive an optimal control strategy for energy-efficient motion on uneven and yielding terrains. To achieve this, a fundamental understanding of the robot's dynamics is essential. Specifically, the contact point's motion is heavily influenced by the robot's parameters, such as mass and velocity, as well as the terrain's properties, including stiffness. Therefore, the primary objective of this work is to understand the behavior of the contact point across different environments, which is essential for developing an effective actuation method and optimal control strategy. Internet of Things (IoT) networks are becoming increasingly prevalent in both public and private sectors, serving diverse functions from smart home security to critical industrial applications. These systems typically rely on firmware updates to introduce new features, security patches, and bug fixes. However, the widespread adoption of IoT has been hindered by the challenges inherent in developing, deploying, and managing large-scale networks. Although prior research has explored various methods for firmware distribution, no study to date has empirically evaluated the specific requirements and trade-offs necessary to deliver updates reliably. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a high-fidelity, large-scale performance evaluation of IoT firmware updates, grounded in a real-world deployment featuring 1,000+ nodes across 10,000 m². We identify the primary factors influencing update success and reliability, demonstrating that network topology, the frequency of availability windows, and the specific distribution method used are decisive. Ultimately, we offer practical recommendations for reliably executing massive firmware upgrades in real-world scenarios. Specifically, we find that updates should be released during the final installation phase rather than gradually throughout the building process, that multi-threaded updates outperform single-threaded ones, and that topological partitions should ideally be dynamic rather than static. Furthermore, we introduce a novel update method that leverages the peer-to-peer communication capabilities inherent in most IoT networks, proving its superior efficiency over traditional approaches. Our findings from this extensive empirical study provide actionable recommendations for implementing large-scale network upgrades in both real-world and future IoT environments. To ensure reproducibility, we have made our evaluation code publicly available. Finally, this work paves the way for more reliable and secure IoT networks by enabling the rapid deployment of critical patches and facilitating the quick recovery from distributed denial-of-service attacks. We demonstrate that the Fock-space propagator remains robustly multifractal throughout the many-body localization transition, even when the system size becomes excessively large for exact diagonalization and for estimating the spectrum of the random unitary matrix (RUM). We provide several explanations for this phenomenon and attribute the commonly observed scaling of the Fock-space RUM spectrum near the phase boundary to the extensive mixing of basis states within the largest eigenvalue density cluster. Additionally, we offer a novel explanation for the broadest wavefunction scaling cluster in this space, which aids in understanding the broadest wavefunction scaling spectrum both above and below the transition. Finally, we present a new approach to studying the scaling of the Fock-space RUM eigenvalue density cluster, which holds potential for future length-scale clustering analyses. We conclude by discussing how these findings relate to the spectrum of the random unitary matrix and the random matrix model for many-body localization. Our study underscores the critical role of basis-set selection in analyzing localization in interacting many-body systems. We conclude that the spectral signature of many-body localization is most reliably captured by the spectrum of the Floquet operator, rather than by the translation operator or the free fermion evolution operator. Furthermore, we outline several promising future directions for utilizing the RUM model to investigate many-body localization. Specifically, we examine the spectral signature of many-body localization across various system sizes, filling fractions, and disorder strengths. We also explore the relationship between spectral signatures and the spectral statistics of the RUM, alongside the relationship between spectral signatures and the spectral entropy of the RUM. Finally, we discuss the relationship between spectral signatures and eigenstate thermalization in the RUM model, as well as the relationship between spectral signatures and eigenstate complexity in the free-fermion model. These latter aspects are anticipated to yield significant insights into the spectral signature of many-body localization. Future research should similarly examine the system-size, filling fraction, and disorder strength within the free-fermion model, as these parameters were not previously considered. We anticipate that the free-fermion model will also provide valuable insights into many-body localization. We also emphasize the importance of the RUM model as a future tool for studying many-body localization. Optimizing multi-objective problems necessitates engaging with a decision-maker to account for the complexity of multiple goals and to flexibly interact with their preferences. This paper presents the first provably efficient algorithm designed for interactive optimization under uncertainty within a limited budget of evaluations. We develop two algorithmic frameworks: one based on bandits and another utilizing ellipsoidal search, which are specialized for independent and dependent objectives respectively. Our analysis establishes that the expected number of iterations required to identify a point within $\epsilon$ of the ideal Decision Maker's preference is bounded above. Furthermore, we demonstrate the algorithm's ability to converge to a solution within $\epsilon$ of the Decision Maker's preference in the worst-case scenario, requiring $O(\epsilon^{-\frac{1}{1+d}})$ iterations where $d$ represents the number of objectives. Quantum machine learning holds the potential to surpass the limitations of classical approaches, with universal adversarial examples serving as a key proof of concept for models capable of learning from data in the kernel regime. Although recent studies have explored classical adversarial perturbations designed for quantum classifiers, a clean, universal perturbation scheme tailored specifically for this domain has yet to be established. This paper addresses that gap by demonstrating that adversarial perturbations for quantum classifiers must exist within the photonic subspace and possess an amplitude scaled according to the quantity $\sqrt{N_{ph}}/d_{in}$, where $N_{ph}$ represents the number of photons per input qubit and $d_{in}$ denotes the number of input qubits. Leveraging the universal discriminability of Gaussian states, we successfully construct quantum universal adversarial examples that trigger maximum-confidence errors in classifier output predictions. Furthermore, we introduce a universal adversarial classifier and establish a link between the robustness of quantum classifier predictions and the intrinsic robustness of the underlying quantum classifier hypothesis. These findings offer a foundation for developing security protocols that ensure the robustness of both quantum classifier hypotheses and their prediction outcomes. Additionally, our research offers significant insights for the security and reliability of quantum communication systems utilizing quantum key distribution. Finally, we validate the efficacy of these adversarial perturbations across various quantum classifiers, demonstrating that they achieve high success rates in misclassifying test data. This study examines Steklov eigenvalues for three-dimensional domains that are nearly spherical. Building on prior research demonstrating that these eigenvalues are analytic functions of the domain's perturbations when it comes to small deformations, we establish that the eigenvalues are actually real analytic functions of the parameters defining the domain. Furthermore, we uncover a specific structure in their power series expansions, revealing connections to the geometry of the domain as well as its surface area and volume. Finally, we derive lower bounds for analytic functions involving Bessel functions to support our main findings. In the appendix, co-authored by E. Kaxiras, we present numerical computations of Steklov eigenvalues, confirming their analyticity through the convergence of partial derivatives across various orders. These findings align with existing literature on nearly spherical domains in general relativity, where analogous eigenvalue problems arise. Specifically, our results support the analyticity of mode coupling coefficients in perturbed Schwarzschild spacetimes, a critical component in testing the validity of the gravitational wave memory effect. Additionally, we demonstrate the analyticity of analyticity backscattering coefficients within the post-Newtonian expansion of gravitational wave scattering off black holes, thereby addressing an open question in the field. In both scenarios, perturbations are modeled as nearly spherical, necessitating an analytic formulation. Finally, in the appendix, we also prove an analytic identity concerning perturbed mode frequencies, which serves as a consistency check for our work. All definitions and notations regarding frequencies and modes follow those established in the literature. Our work contributes to a broader effort to rigorously derive and test the validity of the gravitational wave memory effect. While previous studies have addressed the mathematical challenges of proving the existence of this effect, this paper serves as a necessary intermediate step toward that goal. By establishing an analytic framework, we ensure that the physical effects associated with gravitational wave memory can be consistently calculated to any desired order. Furthermore, our results regarding Steklov eigenvalues and analyticity provide a foundation for future investigations into two- and four-dimensional nearly spherical domains. In summary, this work offers a rigorous mathematical treatment of Steklov eigenvalues, with applications extending beyond the specific context of gravitational wave memory. Specifically, our findings regarding Steklov eigenvalues and analyticity may prove useful in addressing other physical problems involving nearly spherical domains. Additionally, our work may contribute to advancing the understanding and application of spectral geometry in near-spherical environments. Conformance checking involves comparing the behavior of modeled processes against observed process behavior captured in event logs. In practice, observed process behavior is rarely fully captured by event logs, and log mining and conformance checking techniques must be adapted to extract and utilize intermediate process knowledge. This paper introduces infix and postfix alignments as new conformance checking methods capable of conformance checking with trace fragments. Specifically, we demonstrate how to transform infix and postfix alignments into checklists, flow line diagrams, and cross-walks. Furthermore, we show how to measure the distance between observed process behavior and the model using trace fragments, providing a straightforward and efficient approximation. The paper also addresses the inverse problem of inferring trace fragments from event logs and outlines a method for synthesizing infix alignments from these fragments. Finally, the proposed techniques are evaluated based on their efficiency and utility. To our knowledge, this represents the first work to extend conformance checking techniques to support conformance analysis of trace fragments. The source code for the proposed methods is available at: https://github.com/ProcessMiningGroup/tfa-tl.

Keywords: Process Mining, Conformance Checking, Trace Fragments.

Accurate radio propagation modeling is essential for the planning and optimization of cellular networks. Traditional models rely on empirical formulas, which are typically constructed in two dimensions (2D) for cellular network design or three dimensions (3D) for indoor scenarios. However, 2D models often lack the precision needed for indoor environments, and 3D models suffer from high computational costs. This paper introduces a deep convolutional neural network designed for indoor radio propagation modeling. By utilizing building and room layouts along with room-specific parameters as inputs, the model generates a three-dimensional signal strength map. The approach is validated using both simulated and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in predicting signal strength at any arbitrary point. Furthermore, this model enables the rapid inference of new 2D maps. For rooms with similar architectural designs, the proposed model achieves a prediction accuracy of 99.99%. Additionally, the model demonstrates generalization capabilities across rooms with distinct architectural designs. Given that current 5G networks are being deployed with small form factor base stations and indoor small cells, this model holds significant potential for predicting indoor signal propagation. For a room measuring 10 meters by 10 meters, the model can generate a 256x256x50 three-dimensional map in approximately 0.01 seconds. These results indicate that deep learning-based propagation modeling can achieve both high accuracy and low computation time. Ultimately, this model is applicable to both outdoor and indoor propagation scenarios. In outdoor settings, it can predict propagation based on environmental and base station parameters, whereas in indoor settings, it can predict propagation using room and furniture data. Consequently, this model is particularly valuable for indoor office and home planning. By inputting building and room data, the model can accurately and efficiently generate indoor propagation maps. This capability facilitates the optimal placement of base stations and indoor small cells, thereby enhancing network performance. The model was implemented using PyTorch and made publicly available. It supports room and base station planning and optimization, as well as the prediction of signal strength and interference. The implementation offers pre-trained models trained on both simulated and real-world datasets. For predictions, the model accepts a room layout in SVG format and a base station configuration JSON file as input. Users can then obtain a three-dimensional signal strength map in numpy format. We introduce a straightforward and compact semantics for temporal planning, which extends the established semantics of classical planning. Specifically, our semantics define temporal plans as maximal consistent linearizations of the parametric trace set derived from the parametric disjunctive conjunctive normal form logic program generated by a temporal planning problem. To demonstrate the versatility of our semantics, we develop and verify key properties for temporal plan existence, including a form of monotonicity that extends classical flux. Additionally, we generate and validate a verified coercion theorem for temporal planning, which serves a function analogous to that in classical planning. To achieve this, we explicitly define and formally characterize temporal completion functions. We have implemented all proofs in Dafny, a formal verification tool capable of generating verified code, and have compiled the proofs into verified code. This ensures not only the rigorous validation of our reasoning but also the creation of verified temporal planners. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first time that (a) any reasoning regarding temporal planning, and (b) any temporal planning implementation, has been fully verified. Furthermore, we have experimentally assessed the performance of our verified semantic definitions and completion functions. Our results indicate that, when compared to state-of-the-art implementations, our approach performs competitively on classical planning problems and superiorly on temporal planning problems. Finally, we discuss how our verified semantics and implementation can significantly enhance the validation and coherence of experimental assessments within temporal planning. We demonstrate this by generating verified code that validates the coherence of experimental assessments, a task that has not previously been achieved. This work not only rigorously verifies experimental outcomes but also establishes a framework for more coherent and trustworthy empirical evaluations in temporal planning. We conclude by outlining several directions for future research. Specifically, we propose that (a) many important properties of temporal planning, such as various forms of monotonicity and various forms of temporal coercion, can be derived from our verified semantics using the proof assistant Lean, and (b) various implementations of temporal planning completion functions can be formally verified within Lean. We intend to explore these and other future research avenues in subsequent work. In summary, this work marks a significant advancement in the formalization of temporal planning, driven by the development of verified semantics, verified properties, and verified implementation techniques. These developments substantially strengthen the foundations of temporal planning research. Crucially, our research demonstrates that formal methods can now effectively address complex issues in temporal planning that were previously deemed intractable. This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for both the Vlasov-Poisson and ionic Vlasov-Poisson systems within bounded regions. Regarding boundary conditions, we apply specular reflection to the Vlasov equation, while imposing either homogeneous Dirichlet or Neumann conditions on the Poisson equation. The proof strategy relies on creating multiple extensions of phase space solutions to bypass traditional dimensionality issues, subsequently analyzing the system's solutions through a careful phase space analysis. Furthermore, we demonstrate the global in time existence for global classical solutions. As an application, we derive the existence of solutions in cylindrical domains. Notably, this work represents the first proof of the global existence of classical solutions for Vlasov-Poisson type systems in bounded domains under periodic boundary conditions. Additionally, we provide the first global existence proof with respect to time for ionic Vlasov-Poisson systems in both bounded and unbounded settings under periodic boundary conditions. The proof technique employed extends the classical method typically utilized in whole space settings. We have omitted the detailed derivation of energy estimates to prioritize the primary objective of proving the existence of solutions. However, we explicitly demonstrate the well-posedness of the ionic Vlasov-Poisson system in $\mathbb{R}^3$ by utilizing energy estimates derived herein. Our approach builds upon the work of Pfaffelmoser (1985), who originally established the well-posedness of the ionic Vlasov-Poisson system in $\mathbb{R}^3$. We believe that the results and methodologies presented will find applications in both bounded and unbounded settings. We anticipate that this work will stimulate further research into the existence and nonexistence of solutions in bounded domains. Specifically, we aim to extend these findings to higher dimensions, thereby filling a significant void in the current literature. Finally, we propose that our results will serve as solutions to initial value problems in various applied fields, such as plasma physics and semiconductor physics. Furthermore, the solutions discussed here can be utilized to construct initial data for vortex patch problems in two-dimensional bounded domains under homogeneous Dirichlet conditions for the electric potential. Despite significant advancements in automated code analysis, code-specific search term generation remains a persistent challenge. This paper introduces STRICT, a novel, end-to-end model that leverages information retrieval to identify search terms for code concept location. STRICT represents the initial step toward integrating information retrieval and machine learning to automate the concept location process. We conducted extensive experiments on two public Java bug databases, comparing our approach against baseline methods and related work. The results demonstrate that STRICT outperforms all baselines and existing approaches in accurately generating search terms for concept location. Furthermore, we explore the limitations of STRICT's current design and propose a rigorous framework for evaluating search term identification systems. Ultimately, we argue that STRICT marks a significant step toward fully automating code search. Colloidal gels, characterized by their gel-like structure, exhibit a significant gap between their weak solid-like rheological properties and the ability to process them as fluids. This study presents a new rheo-acoustic technique, utilizing controlled ultrasonic vibrations, to enhance gel processability while preserving their bulk mechanical properties. By applying focused ultrasonic vibrations at frequencies within the 20 to 100 kHz range, we temporarily disrupt the gel's structure, allowing them to flow as viscous liquids with viscosities as low as 100 Pa s. In contrast, removing the ultrasonic vibration restores the original solid-like mechanical properties. These findings are demonstrated using silica and polymer gels. The ability to tune gels between solid and fluid states without altering their bulk mechanical characteristics opens new avenues for the processing, application, and release of materials in smart devices. Furthermore, this rheo-acoustic approach facilitates the creation of complex structures in colloidal gels that are unattainable through slow flow methods. These structures can be formed rapidly (within seconds) by directing ultrasonic vibrations through a piezoelectric speaker or by applying spatially varying patterns of ultrasonic vibrations. Additionally, we demonstrate that structures generated via ultrasonic vibrations can be replicated with high fidelity in purely viscous liquids. This capability is demonstrated by creating letter patterns within silica gels and successfully extracting them by pressing the gel against a liquid surface. This new rheo-acoustic technique is expected to be broadly applicable to various colloidal gel systems. Its potential applications extend beyond material processing to include gel printing, the fabrication of complex structures in smart devices, and controlled material release. For instance, we show that ultrasonic vibrations can induce the release of gelatin capsules from a silica gel within a medical device, a process that is inhibited when a gel barrier with restored mechanical properties is present. This rheo-acoustic processing technique is anticipated to have wide-ranging applications in fields such as microfluidics, drug delivery, and food science. Additionally, it demonstrates that ultrasonic vibrations can induce structural rearrangements in colloidal gels, offering new insights into gel mechanics. Finally, this approach may enable new methods for generating complex structures in colloidal glasses and pastes. Our findings indicate that the ultrasonic frequencies employed in this study are lower than those typically required to induce structural rearrangements in silica gels and polymer pastes via ultrasonic shear rheology. This suggests that future processing methods could leverage ultrasonic vibrations to create new patterns and structures within colloidal gels

This paper examines the proof of the Collatz conjecture. The conjecture asserts that any positive integer $n$, when subjected to the operation $f(n) = \frac{n}{2}$ if $n$ is even and $f(n) = 2n - 1$ if $n$ is odd, will eventually reach 1 after repeated applications. To address this, the author aims to demonstrate the ultimate periodicity of the sequence generated by $f$ to prove the conjecture. The proposed approach utilizes logarithms and binary representations of $n$ to analyze the number of steps required to attain 1. Specifically, the study explores the behavior of even and odd numbers, proving the conjecture for all odd numbers up to 100 and providing numerical verification for even numbers under 100. The core argument involves showing that for an odd number $n$, the sequence reaches 1 in $n + 1$ steps, whereas for an even number, it does so in $2n$ steps. The work concludes by suggesting that verifying the claim for a broader range of numbers could facilitate a general proof of the Collatz conjecture. Specifically, it is proposed to examine the conjecture for even numbers within the interval $[2^{n-1}, 2^n)$. Additionally, to address the case of numbers like $n = 2^p - 1$, the concept of the "height" of a number is introduced, defined as the count of consecutive trailing ones in its binary form. The proof demonstrates that if the claim holds for all numbers with a height less than $p$, it follows that it also holds for numbers with a height equal to $p$. Finally, numerical verification is provided for the conjecture regarding numbers up to $2^6 - 1 = 63$. The paper is written in the LaTeX typesetting system. Keywords include the Collatz conjecture, even numbers, odd numbers, logarithms, binary representation, ultimate periodicity, induction, hyperlogarithm, and proof. Categorizing documents by subject is vital for managing large collections, yet it often fails because a document's subject is ambiguous and dependent on context. This issue is particularly pronounced in STEM fields, where symbols derive meaning only from surrounding text. Although subject classification is typically modeled as a multi-class text classification task, STEM documents cannot be effectively processed as plain text. Consequently, we propose treating them instead as rich annotated text, leveraging surrounding context to resolve ambiguous domain-specific terms. By converting this task into a multi-label classification problem at the entity level, utilizing mathematical entities linked to surrounding context, we aim to explain the document's overall classification decision. This paper outlines the methodology and initial findings from a study involving 2,000 documents from the MATH dataset, demonstrating that the significance of mathematical entities correlates with the degree of subject ambiguity in a document set. Furthermore, we show that a lightweight classifier successfully classifies entities with an F1-score of 0.627, outperforming the baseline F1-score of 0.492. These results indicate that mathematical entities aid in subject classification, thereby enhancing the transparency of classification decisions. The dataset and code utilized in this work are accessible at https://github.com/ra2012/towards-explaining-stem-doc-class. Our primary contributions are twofold: (1) we present a novel approach to decision explanation for text classification that shifts the focus from the document to its annotated mathematical entities, and (2) we introduce a new method utilizing multiple sequential learning stages to improve the transparency of classification decisions. Specifically, (2a) we introduce a new ensemble classifier that leverages the interdependence among labels, and (2b) we demonstrate the first use of a pre-classification stage designed to assign consistent entity links to repeated occurrences of the same entity within a document. Additionally, this work represents the first known attempt to explain subject classification decisions in a large dataset using a rich annotated representation. The paper's main findings include: (1) a multi-label classifier achieving an F1-score of 0.63, outperforming the baseline F1-score of 0.49 achieved by a standard classifier; (2) experimental evidence supporting the use of a pre-classification stage to ensure consistent entity links across documents, thereby improving overall classification quality; and (3) insights into the transparency of subject classification decisions, revealing that the proportion of entities with surrounding text explicitly supporting the assigned label is higher for subjects with less ambiguous representations. Stable marriage and more extensive matching systems find application in various real-world contexts, such as the US National Resident Matching Program, where hospitals and medical residents mutually assess one another. Raghavan and Schrijver demonstrated that if each hospital remains fixed while every resident shifts to making randomly chosen proposals, convergence to a stable matching is guaranteed, though this occurs almost exclusively to the residents' detriment. Addressing this imbalance, we demonstrate that allowing both partners to randomly select proposals yields a matching nearly as beneficial as the optimal one under the "correlated" system, while still ensuring convergence. Furthermore, for small, constant-size hospitals, we prove that consistent student improvements lead to rapid arrival of the stable matching. Finally, even when hospitals are permitted to improve their rankings, their average outcome remains largely unchanged, whereas residents experience a marked decline. These findings are derived from both analytical proofs and simulations. Additionally, we relate our research to the broader field of evolutionary algorithms and offer suggestions for extending these results to more complex matching scenarios. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/alexei77d/SM-Choice. Summary generation models are typically trained using an automatic evaluation metric designed to align with human quality assessments. However, recent research has revealed a significant discrepancy between this metric's evaluations and actual human judgments. This paper presents SummScore, a cross-based scoring approach that demonstrates superior correlation with human feedback compared to existing solutions. Empirical results confirm that SummScore achieves a 10.56% average improvement in correlation with human scores across eight summary extraction datasets, while also exhibiting stronger correlations with other summary quality indicators. Furthermore, SummScore exhibits a Spearman's correlation of 0.612 with human ratings on SummScreen, the largest summary evaluation dataset available. This work investigates the reconstruction of a sparse vector using sparse quadratic measurements, a challenge known as Compressive Sparse Phaseless Recovery. We demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of the solution within a specific ambient dimension range. Furthermore, we present a novel algorithm that combines Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) with amplitude propagation to efficiently recover the target vector. Numerical simulations validate the effectiveness of this proposed method. Additionally, we apply our approach to reconstruct images from intensity data, treating the problem as Sparse Phaseless Image Recovery (SPIR), and compare our results against existing state-of-the-art techniques. Our results indicate that the proposed algorithm achieves superior performance in terms of both recovery quality and computational speed. Finally, we illustrate the utility of our method for phase retrieval in microscopy by recovering simulated microtubule images from simulated experimental data, again outperforming current methods in both recovery accuracy and efficiency. To ensure reproducibility, the code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ehsan-mohammadi/SPAR. Fusion approaches combining camera and LiDAR data have proven to be highly effective for BEV fusion, demonstrating superior performance compared to non-fusion methods. However, these techniques often depend on complex models and advanced strategies, such as fusion at multiple fusion levels (MFL) and fusion time (MTF), which significantly increase computational costs. Additionally, existing methods frequently face challenges from the inherent modality disparities between LiDAR and cameras, including noise, misalignment, and occlusion. To address these issues, we introduce BEVFusion, a straightforward yet robust fusion framework. Our approach combines LiDAR and camera data at the voxel level within a unified coordinate system, utilizing a simple yet effective fusion strategy. This is achieved through: 1) a multi-modal encoder that independently extracts features from both modalities; 2) a fusion module that integrates spatial and semantic information from each modality; and 3) a decoder that facilitates data exchange between modalities. Extensive experiments across CLEVRHAB and n2d datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that our approach outperforms prior art. We also validate the efficacy of each proposed component, showing that the removal of any single component results in a significant performance drop. Finally, we conduct ablation experiments on the KITTI dataset to compare our method against other fusion techniques. We provide an analysis of energy and enstrophy cascades in two-dimensional (2D) incompressible fluid turbulence, incorporating thermal noise through a multiplicative stochastic force. By utilizing the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes parabolic equation and its corresponding Martin-Sirns-Murphy equation, we derive the turbulent diffusion coefficient for noise-affected 2D fluids. This coefficient is determined by the energy and enstrophy cascade rates, eddy viscosity, and the external thermal noise intensity. Our findings indicate that at low noise levels, both direct and inverse cascade asymptotic regimes remain largely unaffected, with direct enstrophy cascades suppressed. However, at sufficiently high noise levels, both energy and enstrophy cascade rates increase proportionally. Consequently, thermal noise can significantly influence the statistical characteristics of 2D incompressible fluid turbulence. Furthermore, our results suggest that noise-induced transitions in 2D fluids may exhibit both first-order and second-order characteristics. Finally, our conclusions provide a partial explanation for the complex statistical behaviors observed in 2D incompressible fluid turbulence. This work addresses a key challenge in plasma physics and laser technology: determining how a laser modifies the thermal profile of a liquid. We achieve this by creating a comprehensive numerical model that accounts for heat transfer, the laser beam's spatial and temporal evolution, and the emergence of phase changes. The resulting profiles are then applied to a phase-contrast self-induced diffraction experiment involving a nanosecond CO$_2$ laser and a micro-drop of water. This approach enables a straightforward yet rigorous explanation of the experimentally observed diffraction patterns and their evolution over time. Furthermore, our numerical results provide a robust foundation for future numerical-experimental comparisons aimed at investigating more complex laser-liquid interactions. The methodology presented herein is broadly applicable to studying thermal phenomena in liquids and solids induced by pulsed lasers. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems can leverage knowledge base (KB) entities to enhance performance, yet the on-the-fly translation of these entities poses significant challenges. Existing approaches, such as encoder-KB and decoder-KB methods, often fail to translate them accurately. This paper introduces a novel "copy mechanism" designed to address the translation of KB elements during decoding. Unlike decoder-KB techniques, our mechanism enables the model to directly copy KB elements from the input sequence while simultaneously allowing other elements to be generated by the decoder based on the input. We integrate this copy mechanism into a decoder-encoder-KB network and evaluate the resulting model on English-French and English-German German News datasets, using both zero-shot and few-shot knowledge transfer settings. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving an average improvement of 4.2 and 3.3 points in Free-form Micro-F1 scores for the English-French and English-German pairs, respectively. Furthermore, we find that NMT systems do not inherently overgenerate KB elements and that incorporating a copy mechanism further reduces such overgeneration. Additionally, analysis reveals that the model tends to copy, rather than generate, KB elements that are frequent within the training data. The code is accessible at https://github.com/taewansong/KnowledgeBaseCopyMechanism.

Although significant advancements have been made recently, verifying neural networks remains a challenging task. Because neural networks are difficult to analyze, they are rarely employed directly; instead, they are typically integrated into a broader system. Verification algorithms for standard neural network architectures are now well-established and can be found in recent literature and their associated papers. However, these methods are often computationally expensive or restricted to small networks. This survey examines recent progress in neural network verification and its application to control systems. It covers various architectures, including feedforward networks and those with recurrent or forward-invariant structures. Furthermore, the paper addresses scenarios where networks serve as components within larger systems, offering an expanded overview of verification techniques for hybrid systems and reinforcement learning. Finally, emerging deep learning control approaches are presented, highlighting limitations and future research directions. Ultimately, this survey aims to elucidate recent developments in the field and inspire further investigation. Keywords: Neural Network Verification, Control, Reinforcement Learning.

This study introduces a novel functorial, order-preserving, non-decreasing hierarchical clustering technique designed to handle data sets containing overlaps. The algorithm generates a complete, finite hierarchy rooted at the data set itself. Being functorial, the process maintains the identity map when applied to isomorphisms. The construction of the resulting diagram is explicit and fully defined, with every intermediate step forming a pull-back diagram. Furthermore, primary distances within the hierarchy are prescribed by a specified function. A key advantage of this method is its ability to capture structural information about data set morphisms by utilizing inverse maps. The proposed approach is demonstrated to be more informative than graph automorphisms for distinguishing data sets and is shown to be highly effective in classifying various types of online social networks. Additionally, a formula is provided to calculate the distance between any two levels of the hierarchy. Finally, the paper concludes by outlining open questions regarding potential extensions of this methodology. Tensor completion leverages low-rank structures to reconstruct missing data in incomplete tensors. While streaming algorithms exist for this purpose, they struggle with large-scale images due to constraints on memory and computational power. This study introduces a novel streaming tensor ring completion algorithm based on patch tracking, designed for efficient visual data recovery in big-data contexts. By decomposing images into patches and treating them as sparse tensors, the method offers significant advantages in memory usage and computational efficiency. Experiments on large-scale image recovery demonstrate that this proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods regarding both recovery accuracy and runtime performance. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchen-Zhang/Patch-Tracking-TR. Furthermore, to enhance interpretability and reproducibility, the experimental code and data are hosted on GitHub under Chenchen-Zhang's account.

This study examines Nichols algebras $\mathcal{B}(V)$ derived from representation modules $V$ of classical orthogonal or symplectic groups. For specific cases of these groups, we determine the dimensions of $\mathcal{B}(V)$, demonstrate the triviality of the coradical of the Nichols algebra $N(\mathcal{B}(V))$, and establish the Lie rank of its restricted enveloping algebra. Additionally, for certain other instances of classical orthogonal and symplectic groups, we prove that $\mathcal{B}(V)$ is infinite-dimensional. Finally, we outline several open questions concerning Nichols algebras and the triviality of the coradical of the Nichols Lie extension $N(\mathcal{B}(V))$. Notably, resolving these issues would necessitate a complete characterization of the primitive elements within classical orthogonal and symplectic groups. Customized neural rendering has recently demonstrated significant potential for creating photorealistic virtual avatars. However, the 3D pose estimation required by these systems often struggles with inaccuracies in real-world scenarios, resulting in distorted or unnatural avatar morphologies. To address this, we introduce a novel articulated neural renderer designed to produce realistic and expressive virtual avatars even when input pose estimates are imperfect. Our method involves learning a 3D articulation model that captures variations in volume and skinning weights across a population, applying this model to out-of-distribution pose estimates. During rendering, we jointly optimize the articulated model and the virtual avatar's neural representation using pose data from training images and the generated articulated model itself. This approach enables the virtual avatar to adapt its volume and skinning weights to accommodate pose variations that differ from the training distribution. Consequently, the synthesized avatar can undergo significant shape deformations without suffering morphological distortions, effectively masking errors in pose estimation. We evaluated our method on challenging real-world pose data, demonstrating that it outperforms state-of-the-art neural renderers by producing more realistic avatars. Additionally, we show that incorporating our method into video super-resolution networks can substantially enhance the realism of virtual avatars. We investigate the impact of extreme image transformations on both human and machine visual perception and cognition. Although certain transformations, like high-contrast adjustments, are familiar and manageable for humans, others—such as severe distortions or motion—can be disorienting. Our results indicate that while algorithms often excel at recognizing visual content even after such extreme modifications, human performance declines more significantly. Furthermore, human responses to these transformations vary based on individual attributes like age and gender, a factor that does not apply to algorithms. We analyze perceptual reactions to a diverse range of transformations, including those affecting color, motion, and spatial layout, and document inter-rater consistency in human judgments. These findings offer valuable insights for digital systems aiming to enhance visual capabilities and underscore the necessity of developing objective metrics to assess the quality of image transformations. This approach establishes a link between the centrality of the Askey-Wilson algebra and the discovery of its $3d$ link invariants.
