Finally, we provide a concise overview of the history behind the Askey-Wilson algebra and present an elementary derivation of the Askey-Wilson $q$-analogue of the Sears' identity. However, these models often struggle to generate high-quality prompts consistently. We introduce D3, a novel framework designed to improve zero-shot learning performance by meta-tuning LLMs on a collection of prompt datasets. Our method constructs an intermediate prompt set by sampling from various existing prompt collections. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that D3 outperforms existing baselines, including fine-tuning on the large ProGprompt dataset. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that our framework is adaptable to different LLMs and is highly scalable across a wide range of zero-shot image classification benchmarks. Cr2Al, a noncentrosymmetric space group 123 antiferromagnet, is recognized for exhibiting a relatively high Néel temperature of 610 K. This study investigates the magnetic structure of Cr2Al using Cr K-edge $\Delta$-resonant elastic x-ray scattering. The results show that the in-plane magnetic moments lie within the (001) plane and adopt a noncollinear spiral configuration. Additionally, the analysis of the magneto-structural factor within the magneto-structural-resonant elastic x-ray scattering term enabled the determination of the phase that breaks inversion symmetry. These findings are interpreted using a phenomenological model. The derived exchange interactions reveal that next-nearest neighbor interactions are responsible for the relatively high transition temperature, while the presence of a magneto-structural term in the resonance-induced scattering amplitude offers a potential explanation for the observed noncollinearity. Furthermore, the resonance-induced scattering amplitude is sensitive to the phase that breaks inversion symmetry, making it a valuable tool for studying related compounds. This technique represents a significant advancement in x-ray scattering, providing a means to investigate magnetic structures in noncentrosymmetric materials. Ultimately, the study aims to enhance the understanding of the relationship between crystal structure and magnetic ordering in this class of materials. This study investigates the potential of training neural parsers on forms-of-english-derived corpora (FoE) by introducing two training objectives: an auxiliary parsing loss and a cross-corpus joint loss. These objectives enable the parser to concurrently learn both synthetic corpora and natural language datasets. Our experiments, conducted on three datasets (PlanB, scriptformer, and Rasa) featuring very few training examples, demonstrate that our proposed CrossCorpus training method can transfer knowledge from FoE to natural language, achieving performance comparable to human annotators even in extreme low-resource scenarios. Additionally, we evaluate how very low-resource parsers generalize to novel FoE instances and natural language sentences not present during training. Overall, this work establishes a foundation for leveraging FoE corpora in very low-resource semantic parsing and significantly enhances performance on existing datasets outside this new regime. The upcoming Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) aims to investigate the internal structure of nucleons and nuclei, as well as particle interactions, with high luminosity and precision. A crucial EIC component will be a forward silicon tracker designed for particle identification and forward hadron physics. This discussion examines the design and technology of the EIC silicon tracker, presenting recent experimental and simulation findings regarding the detector's performance under realistic EIC conditions. Specific attention will be given to developing particle identification methods for pions and protons, enhancing the robustness of track reconstruction algorithms in high-multiplicity events, optimizing detector geometry for forward hadronic physics, and investigating the detector's response to radiation and environmental factors. Furthermore, a sensor and module test campaign for the EIC tracker is underway, with results from the most recent tests to be shared. Ultimately, the EIC silicon tracker will deliver the necessary tracking and pion-proton identification capabilities to advance forward hadronic physics and support the discovery of the physics the collider was built to explore. This talk is based on work by R. S. T. Li and colleagues.

This study examines high-cadence photometric data of the low-luminosity, low-mass active galactic nucleus (AGN) NGC 4103-ULX-1, which exhibits both oscillatory and eruptive variability. We analyze these fluctuations using flux ratio variability, light curve decomposition, and Fourier transform methods. Our findings indicate that the simultaneous detection of multiple frequency components in both the flux ratio and light curve variability, along with their distinct amplitudes, strongly suggests an oscillatory signal. Furthermore, the light curves reveal an eruption occurring between MJD 58470 and 58475, characterized by a flux increase of approximately 1.5 times the baseline level. This eruption is likely caused by a mass transfer event from the companion star to the AGN. Our results highlight the critical role of high-time-resolution observations in uncovering the variability physics of this class of low-mass AGN. Additionally, the flux increase observed in NGC 4103-ULX-1 aligns with the mass accumulation rate required by the Chandrasekhar limit to explain the periodicity found in similar low-mass X-ray binaries. Finally, we demonstrate that these variability characteristics can be effectively modeled using the Disks Around Black Hairs Evolved (DABHE) code. Based on the DABHE model, we estimate a black hole mass of roughly 1.5 solar masses and an orbital period of approximately 10 hours for NGC 4103-ULX-1. These parameters are consistent with those of other low-mass AGNs exhibiting both oscillatory and eruptive variability. The presence of variability in NGC 4103-ULX-1 supports the hypothesis that low-mass AGN and low-mass X-ray binaries may share a common evolutionary path. This hypothesis is further supported by the fact that both systems display flux increases and oscillatory variability, with the variability period in NGC 4103-ULX-1 resembling the orbital periods found in low-mass X-ray binaries. These observations suggest that a binary system with a low-mass black hole and a main-sequence companion could be the final evolutionary stage of a low-mass X-ray binary. The discovery of variability in NGC 4103-ULX-1 provides evidence for this hypothesis and may help explain the nature of some low-mass AGNs. This study presents spectropolarimetry of HD58260, utilizing emission lines of neutral and singly ionized calcium and iron observed with the HARPS-N polarimeter. The spectra, recorded over 17 nights, reveal a significant longitudinal magnetic field variation between $-1500$ G and $+1500$ G. By employing a radiative transfer modeling approach that incorporates a radial magnetic field gradient, we directly observe this radial component and estimate its surface gradient at $\pm 150$ G, consistent with prior spectroscopic findings. Additionally, we identify a magnetic field gradient extending from the stellar surface to the surrounding disk. This gradient suggests a magnetic field strength of $150$ G at the disk's inner edge, which is comparable to other active mid-T dwarfs. Furthermore, the observed polarization aligns with a model featuring a radial magnetic field gradient, thereby confirming the presence of such a gradient within the star-disk system. These results indicate that HD58260 possesses a magnetic architecture distinct from that of the binary system 2M1207. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these observations for understanding magnetic field generation in brown dwarfs. (15 pages, 11 figures, 1 table)

We introduce ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ recombination line in the low-mass, low-metallicity galaxy NGC 5253, revealing a compact, compactly-sourced radio continuum emission region. This detection confirms the presence of a significant population of compact radio sources, such as young massive clusters, previously identified in radio surveys of this galaxy. By analyzing the H30$\alpha$ line, we have derived the gas kinetic temperature, gas density, and ionization parameter. These findings demonstrate that H30$\alpha$ is a sensitive tracer of star-forming regions, exhibiting a strong correlation with the H$\alpha$ recombination line. Consequently, we propose that H30$\alpha$ is a viable tool for studying star formation in nearby galaxies, particularly in low-metallicity environments where the line is expected to be enhanced. Furthermore, we evaluate the H30$\alpha$ line as a potential indicator of the star formation rate surface density ($\Sigma_{SFR}$$)$, comparing it with other recombination lines and the H2 line. Our results indicate that the H30$\alpha$ line is more effective at tracing $\Sigma_{SFR}$ than the H2 line, as it is less sensitive to variations in gas density. Additionally, we show that the H30$\alpha$ line traces $\Sigma_{SFR}$ more robustly than the H$\alpha$ line, as it is less affected by variations in ionization parameter. Overall, the H30$\alpha$ line is most suitable for tracing star formation in low-density, low-ionization regions, such as those found in low-metallicity galaxies. We conclude that H30$\alpha$ serves as a valuable tool for studying star formation in nearby galaxies. Finally, we discuss the utility of H30$\alpha$ as a star formation metric, demonstrating that it is less sensitive to variations in dust attenuation, gas density, and ionization parameters compared to H$\alpha$ and H2, making it a useful method for directly tracing $\Sigma_{SFR}$. However, variations in ionization age can still influence the H30$\alpha$-based $\Sigma_{SFR}$, and we outline future prospects for this technique. Ultimately, H30$\alpha$ is a valuable tool for studying star formation in galaxies with low dust content, low gas density, and low ionization parameters. This study addresses the development of reduced-order observers for a specific state estimator previously proposed in epidemic modeling. The goal of our observer is to generate a dynamically updated estimate of the model's infection rate. The baseline state estimator required full system observability to function correctly, a condition that proved difficult to satisfy in practice. To overcome this, we developed reduced-order observers, which depend on the reduced observability grammar of the system. Our analysis reveals that these observers can be constructed using standard linear reduced-order observer designs, provided certain structural constraints are met. In empirical tests, the reduced-order observers demonstrated robust performance, maintaining a high coefficient of determination ($R^2 > 0.9$) even with noisy data. Furthermore, they remain effective in data-limited scenarios where only latent and recovered state variables are available. These findings hold significant value for epidemiologists, as they enable the accurate estimation of critical state variables like infection counts and transmission rates, facilitating better-informed public health decisions. The mathematical framework and numerical results are implemented in Python and made available on GitHub. Additionally, a Jupyter notebook is provided to illustrate the application of reduced-order observers for infection state estimation. This approach is particularly relevant for epidemiologists working with noisy or partially observed datasets. This represents a substantial improvement over using reduced-order observer-based estimators, which yield $R^2 = 0.45$ under the same noisy conditions. For partially observed data, reduced-order observers achieve an $R^2$ of $0.99$ for latent states and $0.95$ for recovered states, compared to $0.45$ and $0.40$ respectively for the reduced-order observer-based estimator. These results suggest that reduced-order observers are a valuable tool for epidemiologists to estimate state variables from noisy or incomplete data. Integrating temporal information into knowledge graphs has recently attracted significant attention, as it enhances graph expressiveness and enables more effective link prediction. However, many existing methods simply discard temporal data, predicting links solely based on static feature representations. We contend that static models offer distinct advantages for link prediction within temporal knowledge graphs. Our approach utilizes a static framework on a temporal graph while explicitly exploiting static features such as node degree distributions and community structures. We demonstrate that these static characteristics aid in link prediction, often outperforming methods that rely exclusively on temporal features. Evaluated for link prediction on both synthetic and real-world datasets, our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art models, even those that heavily leverage time. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of how leveraging community structure impacts Link PREDiction. To support future research, we have open-sourced our implementation (https://github.com/ashishbhardwaj/TKG-Static). Furthermore, it examines how lens defocusing influences pulse propagation and energy, revealing a critical focal length threshold beyond which pulse propagation becomes impossible. Finally, the proposed framework can be utilized to model the temporal and spatial evolution of ultrafast pulses. These outcomes provide a foundation for future theoretical and experimental investigations into ultrafast nonlinear optics. The current study employs both experimental and theoretical approaches to investigate the magnetic characteristics of antiferromagnetic GdInO$_3$, a material featuring a centered honeycomb lattice in its para-magnetic state. To determine the easy axis within the $ab$-plane, we utilized magnetization measurements, $\mu0-M$ hysteresis loops, neutron diffraction, and first-principles calculations. Our findings indicate that GdInO$_3$ is a quasi-two-dimensional (q2D) antiferromagnet that orders below a Curie-temperature ($T_C$) of 28 K. The observed magnetic structure is a (001) type II antiferromagnetic arrangement, where the magnetic moment lies within the q2D $ab$-plane and is constrained by the hexagonal lattice symmetry to lie either parallel or perpendicular to the body diagonal of the cubic cell. Furthermore, first-principles calculations reveal that the in-plane magnetic moment is stabilized by a single-ion anisotropy of $K$ = -0.0001 eV, with the easy axis oriented along the <110> direction. These results are corroborated by a first-principles spin-spiral calculation. Additionally, magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) measurements demonstrate a pronounced Kerr rotation of approximately 0.01 degrees at 1.06 $\mu$m wavelength. Finally, we discuss the potential of GdInO$_3$ as a candidate for spintronics applications. A supplementary video displaying the magnetic structure of GdInO$_3$ is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5950005. Graph neural networks (GNNs) are widely used for link prediction, yet they struggle with the cold-start issue in novel inference scenarios. To address this, we propose creating a robust and general node representation capable of identifying link targets even when the graph structure is unknown. We introduce Sparse Structure Neuron Embeddings (SSNE), a method that learns representations by integrating local neighborhood information with the global graph topology. SSNE demonstrates superior predictive power across various real-world datasets, outperforming existing node embedding techniques. Additionally, SSNE exhibits robustness against changes in the test graph's network parameters, such as edge density. To further enhance inference, we also develop a linearized version of SSNE. This paper is the first to create a node representation specifically tailored for probabilistic graph models. The code and data will be made available upon request. 1. We introduce Sparse Structure Neuron Embeddings (SSNE), a new and effective node representation designed for link prediction.
2. SSNE is trained using a loss function inspired by the score function of the score function (SF) estimator, which is derived from a score function estimator for general parametric models. This loss function combines a local network term with a global term that models the graph's overall structure.

6. SSNE is the first node representation to demonstrate the effectiveness of structural regularization.

In this study, we present a method for creating a series of silicon atomic vapor cells with depths reaching up to 1.5 mm. These cells were manufactured using a micro-machining process specifically adapted for handling fresh silicon wafers during production. We examined how cell depth influences key parameters, including the number of micro-drops on the inner surfaces, internal stress levels, and final transmission rates. By depositions of $^{87}$Rb and $^{85}$Rb into cells with varied depths and microdrobe conditions, we achieved a maximum transmission of 96% and a steady-state $^{87}$Rb atom density of $1.5\times10^{13}$ cm$^{-3}$. This approach of utilizing deeper cells significantly boosts both transmission and atom density, thereby enhancing the performance of silicon-based optical systems for micro- and meso-cale applications. The ease of creating these deep cells, combined with the inherent advantages of silicon materials, makes them highly suitable for integration within optical systems. Furthermore, the production of these cells is compatible with cleanroom environments, ensuring that no post-production processing is required. This capability is essential for achieving the high levels of integration and compatibility required in optical systems. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of silicon atomic vapor cells with varying depths. Our findings indicate that the optimal cell depth for maximizing transmission and atom density is approximately 0.3 mm. This depth minimizes the number of micro-drops, thereby maximizing transmission, while still allowing for substantial increases in atom density. We attribute the peak performance at this specific depth to the formation of a thin oxide layer on the silicon surface, which acts as a getter to prevent excessive atom loss during cell operation. We also address how to optimize the performance of silicon atomic vapor cells by adjusting the depth of the input and output windows. These results pave the way for further research into deep silicon atomic vapor cells, offering a path toward even higher performance. Such advancements could enhance the performance of various optical systems, such as optical isolators, and improve their resistance to radiation damage. Additionally, these improvements would contribute to greater system stability and reliability, which is crucial for space applications. The creation of these deep silicon atomic vapor cells represents a significant step toward developing more robust and reliable optical systems for meso- and micro-scale applications. This work demonstrates that the proposed method can be readily applied to produce silicon atomic vapor cells with optimized performance, thereby advancing the field of silicon photonics and optical systems. Furthermore, we observe a significant shift in the peak energy of the isoscalar monopole strength when the RPA response is computed using different single-particle potentials. Consequently, our findings indicate that the IGMR in these nuclei is significantly influenced by monopole-quadrupole coupling, leading to a substantial deformation of the RPA strength distribution. These results provide a theoretical basis for understanding the characteristics of the IGMR in nuclei. This work investigates stick-slip phenomena and trajectory convergence in feedback-controlled motion systems featuring Coulomb friction, which manifests as a non-smooth discontinuity. A key challenge in analyzing such systems is the necessity to transform the time domain to handle discontinuous right-hand sides. By employing a smooth parameterization of time, we can apply standard tools from smooth systems theory. In the sliding mode scenario, the resulting closed-loop system becomes autonomous and piecewise smooth, enabling the use of Lyapunov-based methods to prove finite-time convergence to a sliding surface and eventual slip motion convergence. For the stick mode, the system is reduced to an equilibrium point, where conventional Lyapunov techniques assess stability and convergence. Finally, we examine the global behavior of the system, noting that slip motion typically arises from a time-delay hysteresis in the control system. Under a one-sided growth condition, we demonstrate a Zeno phenomenon where the continuous piecewise smooth trajectory reaches a finite sliding mode trajectory in finite time. Additionally, we establish that the stick mode is globally asymptotically stable for a linear time-invariant system. These findings are supported by simulation results. Our approach offers a straightforward methodology for analyzing systems with discontinuous Coulomb friction, avoiding the complexities associated with Filippov convexification. Consequently, this paper serves as both a comprehensive review of the behavior of such systems and a foundation for deriving their analytical properties. Sequential recommender systems are designed to generate personalized suggestions based on a user's historical item interactions. While many sequential algorithms model user states using Markov processes, they frequently overlook user intent, which is crucial for enhancing model performance. To address this, we introduce a novel deep neural network architecture that explicitly incorporates user intent into the make recommendation decision process. Specifically, our proposed Latent User Intent Model (LUIM) employs a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to capture and represent potential user intents from input data. Subsequently, these latent intents guide the selection of the next recommended item. Comprehensive experiments conducted across three large-scale real-world datasets demonstrate that LUIM consistently outperforms both non-intent-based sequential recommender systems and mainstream machine learning models trained on the same datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchen-Liu/LUIM. Furthermore, the project has been featured in a Spotlight demonstration within the RecSys 2021 conference. The reducible double confluent Heun equation (DCHE) stands as the unique DCHE for which the equation reduces to a first-order Cauchy-Euler equation. This study demonstrates that this specific equation embodies the symmetric unfolding of the DCHE. We establish that this unfolding represents a hyperbolic morphism characterized by the exchange of stability between the two fixed points located at $x=\pm1$. Furthermore, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions required for this equation to admit a first integral. Finally, we derive the general integral and double integral single double-confluent Heun equations. Through numerical approximation, we illustrate the exchange of stability occurring at $x=\pm1$ and provide the corresponding integral curves. These results offer a novel perspective on DCHE, which has significant applications in fluid dynamics, quantum mechanics, and electrical engineering. Specifically, they may facilitate the reduction of other DCHE to a first-order form, thereby aiding in the discovery of new, previously unknown Heun equations. Additionally, these findings could prove valuable for numerical approximation methods, such as the finite element method. To achieve this, we have developed a Mathematica package, HeunDCHE, available at: https://github.com/HeunDCHE. The package includes functions to determine the integral of the reduced DCHE, HeunDCEInt, as well as to find the integral and approximate solutions using the finite element method, HeunDCHEIntFEM. We have also provided illustrative examples of solutions obtained through this numerical approach. Ultimately, these results aim to support the solution of Heun-type differential equations across various scientific disciplines. Low-rank matrix estimation is a fundamental challenge in statistics and machine learning. This paper investigates a scenario where a group-structured index set is known, but the underlying group-specific noise variances are unknown. We address the problem of estimating a group-wise heteroskedastic rank-one matrix from noisy observations and derive information-theoretic lower bounds on the minimum achievable groupwise estimation risk for any groupwise estimator. These lower bounds are subsequently compared against the risks of several existing methods, which typically involve either directly fitting group-specific variances or borrowing information across groups through low-rank approximation. Our results indicate that methods fitting group variances perform optimally only when group sizes are balanced, whereas groupwise low-rank fitting achieves near-optimal risk only with sufficient total sample size. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings with a simulation study. Specifically, we propose a penalized groupwise low-rank model that effectively balances model complexity and is proven to be statistically consistent. We further demonstrate that this model can adapt to arbitrary group structures and attain the derived information-theoretic lower bound. Our extensive numerical experiments confirm that the proposed model outperforms competing approaches in terms of risk and computational efficiency. This is particularly advantageous when dealing with a moderate number of groups, each characterized by a small sample size. We investigate the vibrational spectrum of a constrained classical ring, where second-order exceptional points (EPs) emerge at specific locations in the Hamiltonian parameter space. These EPs represent points where eigenvalues and eigenvectors intersect. Although this system lacks the symmetry required for bipartite graphs, it remains stable against weak symmetry-breaking perturbations due to the non-Hermitian nature of the problem. We demonstrate that these second-order EPs possess intrinsic topological characteristics, with a local $Z_2$ index defined by the winding of the local Hamiltonian parameter along a closed loop in parameter space. Furthermore, we highlight that these indices are not conserved across different regions of the parameter space, meaning they cannot predict the presence of EPs unless the Hamiltonian can be factorized. Our findings reveal a novel type of local topological index in weakly non-Hermitian systems and provide a concrete example of an EP system that defies standard symmetry-based predictions. Specifically, our model illustrates how local index theory can identify topologically protected modes within a broader class of systems featuring local invertibility and chiral symmetry. Finally, we explore the potential to encode a $2^{N_p}$-bit memory in a ring containing $N_p$ EPs. This capability arises because perturbations vanishing at each EP allow for large eigenvalues, enabling the storage of one bit per EP through their presence or absence. The memory's stability is ensured by the exponentially small probability of thermal fluctuations. Additionally, we examine the conditions under which this configuration functions as a sensor, showing that the sensor's precision is governed by the sensitivity of the eigenvalues to perturbations. Our results indicate that the sensor achieves maximum sensitivity when EPs are located within the parameter space. To validate our theoretical framework, we conducted experiments using both acoustic waves in a physical ring and microwave setups. The agreement between our theoretical predictions and the observed data confirms the robustness of local index theory in describing vibrational systems with second-order EPs. Overall, our work establishes a new class of systems exhibiting local topological index protection and identifies a distinct category of many-body local integrable systems. These advances expand the scope of local index theory and provide a foundation for developing novel systems with unique topological and dynamical properties. This paper introduces a decentralized control strategy designed for a class of time-varying linear systems implemented across networked agents communicating over a distributed graph. The primary objective is to ensure each agent's output tracks a specific, potentially different, reference signal while utilizing only locally available information from its neighbors. To achieve this, we propose a distributed design method based on distributed model matching that generates a set of distributed controllers for the system. We demonstrate that under certain system conditions, these decentralized controllers can be easily parameterized via a convex optimization problem that can be solved independently by each agent. Furthermore, we establish convergence results showing that the output estimation error over a finite time interval following initial transients can be made arbitrarily small by increasing the order of the proposed distributed controllers. Additionally, we investigate the compatibility of these controllers with switching topologies representing distributed networks, proving that for a broad range of switching signals, a single controller generated at the initial time can be maintained throughout the entire interval. This compatibility is characterized using the concept of average dwell time, which we show is not a necessary condition for stability in the specific case of linear switching systems considered here. Finally, we present a scenario where our approach yields superior performance compared to existing solutions in the literature, demonstrating an 8% reduction in output estimation error relative to switching-based solutions currently available. This confirms that achieving superior performance requires only additional knowledge of the input signal without needing predictions of the switching topology. These findings are supported by an illustrative simulation. Notably, unlike existing solutions, our approach enables each agent to compute its control inputs independently, thereby enhancing the distributed nature of the system. The resulting scheme is termed "plug-and-play" because each agent can design and implement its controller without interacting with other agents. We argue that this capability represents a significant advancement over current literature, which typically assumes inter-agent communication for controller computation. Finally, we address the potential concern that agents might lack the computational resources required for local matrix operations, suggesting that such computations could be delegated to the cloud in a subsequent step. This final step remains distributed, requiring communication only among a subset of agents, such as those with sufficient computational capacity. Thus, our approach achieves the dual benefit of improved performance and algorithmic decentralization, making it broadly applicable to various control problems. This study addresses two binary classification challenges involving COVID-19: detecting its presence in audio and audio/text emotion tagging. We introduce a two-stage approach that utilizes the large language model BERT to extract features, which are subsequently processed by a classifier. These extracted features can also serve as input for a human listener. The method achieved strong performance, yielding F1 scores of 0.916 and 0.915 for the two tasks, with a human AUC of 0.811. Furthermore, our analysis of the test samples offers insights into the relationship between COVID-19 and emotional states. Finally, we demonstrate that our model's outputs generate explanations that enhance human understanding of the link between COVID-19 and emotions. Through a survey, we gathered human feedback on sample classifications, indicating significant agreement between our results and human perception. Consequently, this model may assist clinicians in better comprehending the connection between COVID-19 and emotions. Networks and their underlying structures are fundamental to understanding our world, making the ability to visualize and analyze them essential for anyone involved in their study or analysis. This capability is crucial for researchers, data analysts, and professionals in various fields who utilize network concepts. We present Atlas as an open-source, cross-platform software designed to significantly enhance efficiency in visualizing and analyzing both real-world and synthetic networks. Built upon the open-source libraries NetworkX and Matplotlib, Atlas offers an intuitive, desktop-based graphical user interface that eliminates the need for extensive programming knowledge. This article outlines our motivation for developing the tool, explores its key features through specific examples, and demonstrates how Atlas facilitates visualization and analysis. We hope Atlas will become an indispensable resource for researchers and practitioners in diverse disciplines, enabling them to explore networks and generate insights with greater ease. The field of eco-evolutionary dynamics investigates how ecological and evolutionary processes interact, yet it often fails to account for the time scales on which these interactions occur. While theory and simulations have established the conditions for eco-evolutionary dynamics, there remains a lack of comprehensive experimental evidence. This review examines experimental data spanning from current to deep-time timescales to evaluate the prerequisites for observing such dynamics. Furthermore, it explores the mechanisms that drive these interactions, both collectively and individually, and identifies the factors that regulate their rates. The principles outlined in this review can guide future experimental and observational efforts aimed at uncovering the fundamental conditions necessary for eco-evolutionary dynamics. Additionally, incorporating diverse time scales into the research will facilitate a unified approach to understanding how ecology and evolution interact. This will provide essential insights into the factors responsible for the origins and maintenance of biodiversity, as well as the rates at which biodiversity emerges and shifts in response to environmental changes. These findings are particularly critical for predicting the impacts of global change and the rate at which biodiversity is lost. By integrating timescales and identifying the drivers and modulators of these interactions, we can refine projections regarding the rate of biodiversity loss and the speed at which biodiversity is expected to recover. These insights are vital for making informed decisions regarding global conservation and management strategies. Finally, the review introduces a new classification system for eco-evolutionary interactions, distinguishing between ecological-evolutionary feedbacks, cross-level feedbacks, and cross-level interactions. This framework is based on the spatial and temporal scales at which these processes operate and is aligned with both emerging concepts in ecology and evolution and the emerging field of eco-evolutionary genetics. Furthermore, it offers a potential solution to the "missing heritability" problem in quantitative genetics. By adopting this framework, we aim to inspire a new generation of research focused on unraveling the mechanisms underlying eco-evolutionary dynamics. This initiative will involve collaboration between geneticists, genetic engineers, and ecologists, thereby fostering a new interdisciplinary field known as eco-evolutionary genetics. This approach holds promise for identifying the genetic basis of complex traits and understanding the genetic basis of ecological and evolutionary processes. Additionally, it will enable the manipulation of organisms within ecosystems to achieve specific ecological goals, such as enhancing carbon sequestration or restoring degraded habitats. This initiative is especially pertinent to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, which emphasize the need to conserve and sustainably manage ecosystems, halt biodiversity loss, and reduce inequalities. The Speech Processing and Recognition System based on Self-Supervised Learning (SSSL) has become a cutting-edge approach in speech processing. However, its resilience against adversarial attacks remains an underexplored area. This study investigates the adversarial vulnerabilities of SSSSL systems. Initially, through modified natural gradient perturbation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of targeted attacks on both encoder-based and transformer SSSLS, noting that these attacks remain undetected during fine-tuning for classification. Consequently, we introduce a detection framework utilizing test-time augmented representations. Furthermore, we explore the potential of this framework for black-box attack scenarios. Finally, we analyze the vulnerability of SSSLR systems subjected to such attacks. Our findings indicate that while SSSLR offers higher security than traditional methods, it remains susceptible to simple encoder-based SSSLS. In contrast, transformer SSSLR exhibits superior resistance to adversarial attacks. Additionally, we present evidence suggesting that the robustness of transformer SSSLR is partly attributed to its position embeddings. These results hold significant implications for the development of secure speech processing and recognition systems. Furthermore, our proposed detection mechanism for SSSLR adversarial samples represents a novel approach that extends beyond current white-box attack methods. Finally, this research serves as a foundation for enhancing the security of future speech processing and recognition technologies. Sensitivity analysis serves as a framework for evaluating how uncertainties—such as unverified assumptions or data gaps—impact research conclusions. This is particularly crucial in fields like medicine and social sciences, where critical data, including key covariates or unmeasured confounders, may be absent. We introduce an E-value concept for sensitivity analysis, designed to quantify the minimal effect size of hidden biases required to alter study results. Furthermore, we develop a sensitivity analysis procedure grounded in Bayesian methods to address missing data issues. By utilizing posterior distributions to model uncertainty regarding missing data, we calculate E-posterior distributions to assess how biases influence specific decisions. A simulation study demonstrates the behavior of this Bayesian E-value approach, and the methodology is applied to a medical education dataset to illustrate its practical utility. Additionally, a R package named BayES is provided to facilitate this analysis. This approach offers a straightforward, model-agnostic method for quantifying how missing data affects decision-making while comprehensively accounting for uncertainty. The package is available at https://github.com/kuo-hsuanwang/BayES.

This study presents measurements of the combined $p_\mathrm{T}$ spectra for non-prompt D mesons resulting from bottom and charm quark hadronization in $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, based on data from an integrated luminosity of 2.2 nb$^{-1}$. The analysis covers the $p_\mathrm{T}$ range of 2 to 8 GeV/$c$, with a focus on the D$^0$ meson. This value is compared against predictions from perturbative QCD calculations, which show good agreement with the experimental results. These findings provide insight into the relative contributions of beauty and charm quarks to D meson production in small collision systems. The demand for expanded millikelvin cooling systems stems from the requirement to accommodate an increasing number of cryogenic junctions in quantum processors. Each junction typically requires at least 100 mK to function optimally, serving as a critical parameter for establishing a robust quantum phase space. This paper details the design and performance of a millikelvin platform currently under construction at the Fermilab Center for Computing Science. Designed to support up to 256 qubits, this system serves as a scalable intermediate step toward a 1,024-qubit architecture. The final configuration will provide a base cooling capacity of 10 mK at approximately 1 liter, with an option to integrate a dilution refrigerator for an additional 1.5 mK at 0.25 liter. This work presents a comprehensive analysis of the platform's current status, focusing on the thermal management design and its progress. Furthermore, we introduce a novel thermal test structure intended to facilitate the development of high-density cryogenic junctions. The results demonstrate that a high density of junctions can achieve temperatures as low as 4 mK, thereby validating the system's design. These findings offer valuable insights for researchers designing future large-scale cryogenic cooling platforms for quantum computing. The system is projected to achieve full capabilities by the end of 2022. The thermal test structure will be utilized to evaluate various qubit technologies and to establish a comprehensive understanding of their critical temperature thresholds. Ultimately, this will inform an optimal schedule for the deployment of large-scale quantum processors at the Fermilab Supercomputing Center. This paper introduces a straightforward and robust automatic labelling algorithm designed for large-scale urban datasets. By aggregating individual speaker ascriptions for each word, the method enables the automatic classification of utterances and topics. We demonstrate that this approach is more reliable than annotated data for training data within such contexts. Our results show that, on average, 92% of utterances are correctly labelled using utterance-level tags and 86% using sentence-level tags. Additionally, we present a comprehensive analysis of the automatic tags, comparing them against both human annotations and existing multi-modal resources. The source code for VALUE is accessible at https://github.com/EdinburghNLP/VALUE. The paper itself can be found at https://www.acl-press.org/2021/LREC-K21. The evaluation code is available at https://github.com/rlucas/VALUE-evaluation. Furthermore, all data utilized in this study is released under a Creative Commons Zero v1.0 Universal license.

This study addresses sparse signal recovery problems involving a nonuniform nonconvex loss function $f(x)$, which can be equivalently reformulated as a regularized problem utilizing a nonconvex regularizer $g(x) = -f(x)$. To address the nonconvexity inherent in $g(x)$, we propose employing a proximal average network for its approximation. This technique constructs a convex regularizer by averaging the proximal mappings of all components within a collection, utilizing a learnable weight parameter to control the degree of averaging. We demonstrate that this proxy regularizer aligns more closely with the target nonconvex $g(x)$ compared to previous approaches based on convex matrix- or vector-geometric mean methods for approximation. We integrate this proxy regularizer into a seismic reflectivity inversion framework, where its parameters are optimized via a proximal gradient method to minimize reconstruction error relative to $g(x)$. The effectiveness of our approach is validated through numerical experiments across various sparse recovery scenarios, as well as through comparisons with a seismic inversion method relying on a convex regularizer derived from convex geometric mean averaging and existing methods that directly minimize the nonconvex regularizer using a convex approximation. Numerical results confirm the superior performance of our proposed seismic inversion technique. Furthermore, we illustrate how our proposed proxy regularizer can be applied in deep neural networks for seismic inversion. Finally, we analyze the effect of our proxy regularizer on a deep neural network architecture, showing that it enhances network performance by strengthening the connection between input and output data. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1994/NuSpan. Additional supplementary materials are available at https://nu.span.io/. The NuSPAN package can be installed via pip using the command: pip install NuSPAN. Its source code is also hosted on GitHub at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi1994/NuSPAN. The package name, NuSPAN, is a play on the word Nuclide, a term that may resonate with readers from the geophysics community. NuSPAN stands for Proximal Sparse aPpRoXimation Network, with the 'a' in 'SPAN' emphasized to highlight the averaging operation. The 'Nu' prefix signifies its nonuniform nature, distinguishing it from existing packages that primarily focus on geometric mean methods. This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators acting on the Moceanov BMOA spaces and the associated Hilbert-type spaces $B_{\alpha}$. Our initial focus is on characterizing the semigroups of composition operators within the spaces $BMOA_{\beta}$, which are defined as the "little Moceanov BMOA spaces." Subsequently, we examine semigroups of composition operators in the Hilbert-type spaces $B_{\alpha}$ by leveraging established criteria for bounded composition operators on these spaces. Our results demonstrate that if a non-constant analytic function $\varphi$ satisfies $|\varphi(z)|<1$ for all $z\in\mathbb{D}$, then the semigroup generated by $\varphi$ consists of bounded composition operators on both $B_{\alpha}$ and its "little" counterpart $B_{\alpha-1/2}^0$. We also present an illustrative example of a function that satisfies this condition. Furthermore, we explore semigroups of integral operators on the Moceanov spaces by considering specific integral operators. We establish that for any non-constant analytic function $\varphi$ and $\beta>0$, the semigroup generated by $I_{\varphi,f,\psi,\omega}$, where $I_{I_{\beta}}$, is bounded on the little Moceanov space $B_{\beta}^0$. Additionally, we prove that if $I_{\varphi,f,\psi,\omega}$ is a bounded composition operator on $B_{\alpha}$, then it possesses a compact closure. Finally, we offer several open questions and conjectures regarding semigroups of integral operators on Moceanov spaces. As an application, we show that the integral operator $J_{\varphi,f,\psi,\omega}$ is compact on $B_{\alpha}$. To our knowledge, this represents the first study of semigroups of composition and integral operators on Moceanov spaces. Our findings are distinguished by the broad class of functions $\varphi$ considered and the use of "little Moceanov spaces" as a foundational tool. We have also addressed several open questions within the realm of Moceanov spaces. Notably, our work features the inclusion of illustrative examples, and the theorems presented are often derived directly from the analysis of these examples. We introduce a general framework for computing operator fusion rules by analyzing wavefunction overlaps on the replica torus. This method relies on universal finite-size corrections, specifically universal operator matrix elements, which can be determined through numerical simulations of wavefunction overlaps at early times. To demonstrate the approach, we apply it to the critical Ising model and a previously unexplored quasi-2d. CFT associated with the Haagerup planar algebra. In the case of the Ising model, our findings align closely with established operator algebra predictions. For the Haagerup CFT, we determine the fusion rules for the 1d. primary operator, with results consistent within numerical error margins. Furthermore, we evaluate the reliability of our method by applying it to a reduced set of operators in the Gaussian CFT. Our findings indicate that this technique is highly effective for operators with large scaling dimensions but becomes increasingly unreliable for those with small scaling dimensions. Additionally, we outline a strategy for estimating operator fusion rules across the entire spectrum in the Haagerup CFT. Finally, our results demonstrate the method's high precision by successfully distinguishing between the operator spectra of the Haagerup and Isaacs CFTs. This approach offers a novel technique for characterizing unknown or poorly understood critical phenomena in three-dimensional quantum systems. It is particularly advantageous as it avoids the computational challenges inherent in calculating operator fusion rules via operator growth. Our findings suggest that this technique will prove highly effective for systems governed by extended, low entanglement dynamical circuits. However, systems lacking such simple dynamics, such as those involving Majorana modes, may require refined methods to accurately determine fusion rules. Ultimately, this work establishes a new pathway for extracting fusion rules from few-body dynamics, a fundamental aspect of operator spectrum characterization. These findings are expected to significantly advance current efforts in this field. Part-of-speech (POS) tagging serves as a fundamental prerequisite for linguistic research, yet current state-of-the-art tagging systems often yield unreliable results when applied to historical texts due to vocabulary and style shifts across centuries. These systems typically predict a single most probable label for each word, which can be confidently assigned in many cases but fails to capture the ambiguity inherent in contexts where multiple labels are equally plausible. To enhance the reliability of automatic tagging for historical languages, this paper proposes a robust extension to existing methods by implementing a threshold-based approach during training. This technique enables the model to output a vocabulary of candidate labels for each word, acknowledging that the true label may lie anywhere within this set. Empirical results demonstrate that this method achieves significantly higher reliability on historical data without compromising performance on contemporary texts. Furthermore, the paper utilizes this improved reliability to generate automatically annotated ambiguity scores for every word in historical corpora. These scores are analyzed to investigate the historical consistency of specific grammatical categories and their associated variation patterns. As a case study, the partitive article is examined, revealing that its ambiguity is not only higher in older varieties of the language but also exhibits a more imbalanced distribution of alternatives compared to modern German. This finding suggests that the partitive article's ambiguity profile has evolved over time, shifting from a scenario where one candidate is clearly superior to one that is only marginally more probable than others. The study concludes by discussing the broader implications of these insights for historical linguistics. The code is accessible at https://github.com/philipp-jakob/robust-pos-tagging. This paper aims to investigate reaction-diffusion systems featuring non-smooth reaction terms. Specifically, we establish monotonous Lyapunov functions and boundedness criteria. These findings are applied to analyze the stability and long-term behavior of non-smooth reaction-diffusion systems, including the FitzHugh-Rusakov model, which incorporates a piecewise linear non-smooth reaction component. Furthermore, we demonstrate the stability of equilibrium points, the existence of traveling wave solutions, and the convergence of solutions toward traveling wave solutions within this non-smooth framework. Finally, we provide numerical simulations and computational results for the non-smooth FitzHugh-Rusakov system. This paper outlines the design and implementation of an assistant capable of translating requirements for urban infrastructure projects—such as roads, railways, and waterways—into a formal specification within the specification language RRT. We examine the essential components of such urban projects and their corresponding descriptive requirements, demonstrating how these can be systematically converted into a formal specification. This approach enables project planners to assess whether a proposal satisfies all formal requirements and to identify any discrepancies. The methodology is implemented in a tool that integrates RRT with the proof system Isar, which utilizes an extended version of the Isabelle SML programming language. This integration supports the generation of formal specifications, which are then analyzed to detect inconsistencies and suggest modifications to the initial project plan to address them. Finally, we illustrate how this design facilitates a sustainable development approach to urban infrastructure. Specifically, it allows for the assessment of development outcomes, such as reduced travel times and lower fuel consumption, while ensuring that formal specifications remain aligned with the fundamental principles of sustainable development. We argue that formal specification serves as a practical method for operationalizing the principles of sustainable development. The proposed design and implementation were realized through an interdisciplinary team of computer scientists, mathematicians, and urban planners. We emphasize the value of scientific design teams in computing science, mathematics, and physics, noting that collaborative work across these disciplines has been highly effective. This experience underscores the necessity for academia to foster a more interdisciplinary environment. Consequently, we discuss the challenges associated with recruiting and retaining researchers from diverse fields. Our goal is to inspire a broader adoption of interdisciplinary approaches within the computer science community. To support this, we outline strategies for attracting individuals with diverse backgrounds, including those from mathematics, physics, and urban planning, and we discuss the benefits of such diversity. Furthermore, we address the difficulty of retaining staff from different disciplines, emphasizing the need for a more open and welcoming academic culture. We conclude by discussing solutions to these challenges and providing references to the project's website and publications. A video documenting the development process is also available on our project's YouTube channel. Additionally, we have organized a summer school on formal methods in mathematics and city development, which can be accessed via the project's website. We trust that sharing these resources will be beneficial to the computer science community. Finally, we welcome any inquiries, comments, or suggestions from readers. We look forward to your feedback. This study introduces a quantum error mitigation approach utilizing hidden inverse gates, which substitutes inverse noisy gates with ideal logical gates. Implemented within a deep narrow noisy circuit, the technique demonstrates effective mitigation of non-stochastic noise errors. The research highlights the method's potential for application on superconducting quantum hardware, as evidenced by successful implementation and characterization using native gates on IBM's superconducting quantum processor. Furthermore, this work establishes a foundation for developing alternative error mitigation strategies by incorporating "hidden inverses." These strategies are expected to enhance the scalability of error mitigation in deeper and broader quantum circuits, thereby aiding closer inspection of the quantum advantage threshold. Finally, the paper explores strategies to combine this approach with zero-noise extrapolation to further improve error mitigation performance. These contributions are anticipated to facilitate a new direction in quantum error mitigation research. Within the category of topological spaces, the cocartesian image of a preorder on $X$ that is compatible with a continuous surjection $f\colon X\to Y$ can be constructed via a " $T_1$-reflection." A comparable " $T_0$-reflection" applies to biquasicompact preorders, while a " $T_2$-reflection" applies to Hausdorff preorders. These preorders, along with the associated compatibility conditions for preorders and their characteristic relations under surjections, are also examined in the context of uniform preorders and uniform spaces. Furthermore, the compatibility of equivalence relations with surjections $f\colon X\to Y$ in $\mathbb E$ results in the cocartesian image being a subrelation of an equivalence relation on $Y$ whose kernel pair is the universal regular epimorphic pair for $f$. The kernel pair of the cocartesian image of a biquasicompact Hausdorff preorder is demonstrated to be the transitive closure of the kernel pair of the original preorder. These findings are illustrated through various examples within $\mathbf{Set}$, $\mathbf{Top}$, and $\mathbf{Haus}$. Finally, the concept of preorders and their compatibility with maps is extended to any coreflective subcategory $\mathbb E_0$ of a topological category $\mathbb E$ where the counit of the coreflection is a homeomorphism. This leads to the definition of "abstract preorders" and "abstract topological spaces," which are applied to uniform spaces and uniform Hausdorff spaces. Additionally, preorders are defined on uniform Hausdorff spaces using the uniformity rather than the topology, giving rise to the notion of "uniform preorders." The final section presents the definitions and fundamental properties of preorders on abstract uniform spaces. The joint spatial dependence of extreme wind speeds and significant wave heights is analyzed for the first time at a mesoscale. To achieve this, a spatial Stable GND copula is introduced, serving as a precise asymptotic joint model at both single-site and multi-site locations. This copula is calibrated using single-site extreme value theory (EVT) and spatially dependent vine copula theory. The study also examines how the directional dependence between wind and waves varies with the intensity of the event. Finally, multivariate spatial return levels are derived via EFrE (Empirical Frequentist Estimation), which utilizes the spatially stable GND copula to forecast return levels without relying on asymptotic approximations. Application to the North Sea demonstrates that: (i) spatial dependence among extreme wind speeds is positive and stronger at higher return periods, whereas such dependence is negative or weaker for wave data; (ii) the optimal direction for both variables shifts with the return period, a factor that must be accounted for when forecasting extreme conditions in specific regions; and (iii) return level predictions in the Dogger Bank area are notably higher in multivariate spatial models compared to univariate or "block" models, particularly at longer return periods. These findings indicate that EFrE models provide more accurate predictions of extreme ocean conditions by capturing key physical processes, including spatial and directional dependence. Furthermore, the study confirms that this novel modeling approach is applicable across various spatial scales. These results hold significant implications for coastal engineering, environmental science, and policy-making. Current vision-language models demonstrate strong performance in classifying objects, scenes, and their relationships. However, textual descriptions often lack the visual specificity required to uniquely identify an image. To address this, we introduce VT-CLIP, a method that enhances image representations by integrating visual-guided descriptive text. Our approach employs a novel cross-modal alignment mechanism leveraging a vision-language model, which utilizes a visual-grounding network to detect object regions and a language-processing network to generate semantic text guided by these detected areas. Empirical results confirm that our method effectively improves image representations and yields significant performance gains across image recognition tasks. Additionally, we establish a new benchmark for image captioning, providing a comprehensive dataset and evaluation framework to assess the performance of image-based visual-guided text description networks. The operator shifting technique is a powerful approach for solving noisy linear systems of the form $(T+\delta)z=x$, where $T$ is a known operator, $\delta$ is an unknown but sparse perturbation, and $x$ is a known vector. This method transforms the problem into a root-finding task for the equation $(sI+T+\delta)^{-1}=0$, which can be addressed using Arnoldi iterations. However, the original formulation requires solving multiple unshifted matrix equations, a step that becomes a bottleneck when $T$ is abstract, $T+\delta$ lacks easy invertibility, and $\delta$ is highly sparse. This paper introduces a generalized operator shifting framework that resolves this bottleneck by reducing the required unshifted solves to a single iteration, applicable to a broader class of problems. The method is demonstrated on a model for unknown matrix perturbation, which supports a novel inexact Newton iteration. Numerical experiments confirm the efficiency of the proposed approach. For the full version of this work, which elaborates on the model, see [1].

We establish a criterion using this graded object to determine whether a local ring is $\mathbf{F}$-regular, which requires the polynomial to have a positive constant term. Additionally, we provide a criterion based on this object for the $F$-pure threshold of a local ideal. Finally, we investigate the linked graded rings of $(R,Q)_g$ and demonstrate that if the Hilbert polynomial of $(R,Q)_g$ exhibits a positive constant term, then the Hilbert polynomial of the linked graded ring also maintains a positive constant term. These findings yield new criteria for assessing if a local ring is strongly $F$-regular or if its ideal $Q$ is strongly $F$-regular. Digital pathology and radiology are transforming diagnostic and prognostic workflows, with machine learning (ML) playing a pivotal role. Nevertheless, research in this area often lacks the necessary tools to achieve reproducible and interpretable results. Highdicom is a lightweight, open-source Python library designed to facilitate the creation and consumption of standardized encoding for image annotations and ML outputs within the DICOM format—the de facto standard for digital health data. By enabling the generation of DICOM files from common formats like JSON and CSV, highdicom allows researchers to utilize established tools for storage, exchange, and model evaluation. This capability is demonstrated through examples from the Image Pathology and Radiology (IPR) challenge, which focuses on predicting patient survival based on histopathology slides and CT scans. The library is freely accessible at https://github.com/medicoresearch/highdicom. The accompanying video demonstrating highdicom's functionality can be viewed at https://youtu.be/41111111111. Our findings indicate that highdicom effectively and efficiently standardizes image annotation data for DICOM. We demonstrate this by converting JSON and CSV datasets into DICOM files and subsequently converting them back to their original formats. Additionally, we illustrate how to employ existing DICOM viewers and how to convert existing ML libraries into DICOM exporters. These examples were derived from a ML pipeline developed for the Image Pathology and Radiology (IPR) challenge. The DICOM files produced by highdicom adhere to the same standard as those from established DICOM exporters, ensuring full interoperability. We anticipate that highdicom will serve as a valuable tool for researchers in DICOM encoding, particularly for image annotations and ML-related data. Future versions will incorporate support for additional anatomic contexts, class labels, and private content. This paper derives the Noether current from the surface term of the Einstein-Hilbert action. By selecting a suitable gauge, it establishes the Virasoro algebra for black hole dynamics. Furthermore, applying the method of counting quantum states to a nonrotating black hole yields the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy formula, $S=\frac{A}{4}$. These findings provide essential insights for quantum field theory in curved spacetime and quantum gravity research. Additionally, the study examines thermodynamic properties of black holes within a cavity. It demonstrates that quantum corrections to entropy violate the second law of thermodynamics, suggesting such corrections may not exist. Finally, corrections to the area law of entropy are derived using quantum field theory methods in both Euclidean and Lorentzian spacetimes. The results indicate that these corrections are topological, proportional to a Chern-Simons term, and independent of the specific quantum field theory under consideration. Furthermore, these quantum corrections do not violate the first and second laws of black hole thermodynamics. Consequently, these quantum corrections can be incorporated into the entropy calculation via the Euclidean method. Applying this approach to a nonrotating, uncharged black hole yields the quantum entropy $S_Q=\frac{\pi}{\epsilon}$. In contrast, the entropy of a rotating black hole is $S_Q=\frac{\pi(r_+^2+r_-^2)}{\epsilon}$, where $\epsilon$ represents the cut-off scale. Finally, it is noted that a recent study utilizing the path integral method to derive entropy [arXiv:2101.01101] appears to contradict the conclusions reached in this work. Recent deep learning advancements have leveraged representation learning to extract meaningful, low-dimensional features that enhance the performance of downstream supervised tasks. This study investigates the representation learning of DNA sequences using an unsupervised deep autoencoder, demonstrating that these learned representations retain significant sequence information without requiring pre-defined labels. The representation quality is quantified through the reconstruction error of synthetic sequences generated by an iterative general (IG) algorithm. Furthermore, a statistical test was developed to assess the significance of varying reconstruction errors across sequencies produced by the IG algorithm with different gene inputs. The study also examined the stability of these representations through hold-out validation and explored the interpretability of latent spaces by analyzing how variations in specific nucleotides influence latent states. The findings indicate that the learned representations capture fundamental biological properties of DNA sequences, such as codon usage and nucleosome positioning signals, which are independent of the specific gene used for synthesis. These representations hold potential for representing genomic sequences in a label-agnostic framework, offering a foundation for learning a universal representation of genomic data. Additionally, they can facilitate a supervised downstream task for predicting DNA functional elements in a gene-agnostic manner. The proposed statistical test for reconstruction error significance is also applicable to assessing the significance of specific functional properties within genomic sequences. Finally, the approach can extend to unsupervised variational autoencoders to enable a gene-agnostic generative model of DNA sequences. The metal-insulator transition (MIT) in epitaxial V$_2$O$_3$ films, grown on Al$_2$O$_3$(1-1-02) and CeO$_2$(111) substrates, was examined using X-ray photoemission spectroscopy and low-energy electron diffraction. These techniques enabled the analysis of bulk versus surface termination properties. Results indicate that films exhibiting the MIT display a vanadate termination, whereas those not undergoing the transition feature a vanadium termination. This discovery offers a straightforward method to induce the MIT in ultrathin films and provides the first direct evidence of surface termination influencing the transition. Furthermore, the study confirms that strain does not play a significant role in the MIT for these epitaxial films, contrasting with evidence of strain effects observed in exfoliated V$_2$O$_3$ crystals. These findings enhance our understanding of the MIT mechanism and suggest potential applications for vanadium oxide films in nanoelectronics. Finally, the presence of vanadate terminations in epitaxial films with a (11-02) orientation may help explain the persistent observation of superconductivity in V$_2$O$_3$ thin films. We introduce a systematic method derived from Clebsch variables, which transforms a homogeneous quadratic Poisson system into a collection of uncoupled first-order ordinary differential equations. This approach is demonstrated through an example involving the rigid body's free motion on $\mathfrak{so}(3)^*$. We further demonstrate its application to two $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ examples: a $\lambda$-tensor model with $h=0$ and the body dynamics of an axisymmetric heavy top. Additionally, we examine the Dirac monopole example and discuss a method for achieving the same canonization for any homogeneous quadratic Poisson system. Finally, we highlight applications in control theory, specifically regarding system linearization by state feedback and injection, as well as optimal control problems on Lie groups. Finally, we illustrate the method's use in deriving exact solutions for specific $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ systems. The KMTNet consortium, comprising four prime fields and two sub-fields, has been conducting exoplanet searches through microlensing anomalies. This study details the comprehensive survey of a microlensing planetary event discovered in 2018 at a sub-prime field, utilizing data from all four KMTNet telescopes. By integrating these datasets, we achieved superior astrometric accuracy, which is essential for creating high-quality light curves. We present a thorough analysis of the light curve and model the host star's variability using photometric data from all six fields. Our investigation explores the degeneracies inherent in the anomaly search and the modeling approach, incorporating a Bayesian analysis of the physical parameters. We identify two distinct populations of host stars: one with a mass ratio $q<10^{-3}$ and another where $10^{-3}<q<10^{-2}$. Furthermore, we estimate the fraction of sub-prime fields within the entire KMTNet survey that host planets with $10^{-3}<q<10^{-2}$ to be approximately 0.001. The final section summarizes the constraints on the physical parameters derived from the Bayesian analysis. This research is part of the KMTNet Scientific Consortium initiative. This study examines 3D conservation laws, specifically focusing on the inviscid compressible Navier-Stokes equations. It demonstrates control results that allow these equations to support shock waves while maintaining $L^2$ and $H^1$ norms. The technique involves utilizing a phase function to achieve desired smallness in nonlinear terms, thereby enabling linear growth. By combining this control approach with standard energy estimates, the authors derive global existence theorems for small initial data within the $L^2$ and $H^1$ Sobolev spaces. These findings extend earlier research on incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, notably the work of Klainerman and Shkoller. Furthermore, the study employs a novel, simplified method to globalize control results, which utilizes a phase function to linearize the system and generate a convexity estimate for the linearized model. As a consequence, the proof for small data global existence becomes more streamlined, offering an alternative to the phase function approach used by Klainerman and Shkoller. Additionally, the phase function technique offers an alternative pathway to small data global existence in $H^3$. Finally, a bootstrap argument is employed to reprove the well-posedness of these equations using an $L^2$ energy estimate, building upon Liu's work. Overall, this work provides an alternative, more concise proof of small data global existence for initial data in $L^2 \cap H^3$. The final section of the paper presents a conjecture regarding the construction of control solutions for conservation laws with $L^2$ Sobolev controls, alongside a conjecture concerning the well-posedness of the compressible Navier-Stokes equations within the $L^2$ Sobolev space. These conjectures are supported by recent findings on the Cauchy problem for these equations using $L^2$ energy estimates. Specifically, Huang and Wang have achieved small data global existence in $H^2$, while Liu has reached the same result for initial data in $H^1 \cap L^6$. Furthermore, Liu has proven well-posedness in $H^2$ utilizing a conservation law. These advancements indicate that, through the application of conservation laws, the Sobolev index for small data global existence in compressible Navier-Stokes equations can be lowered from $H^3$ toward $H^2$. The surge in digital transactions has provided Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) with access to extensive customer data, enabling the deployment of advanced data analytics techniques for credit risk assessment. NBFCs face significant challenges in managing credit risk due to potential losses from borrower defaults, which can severely undermine their financial stability. This study evaluates various machine learning models using an NBFC loan applicant dataset to forecast whether applicants will receive approval or rejection. Furthermore, it analyzes the importance of features within these models. The findings indicate that the Gradient Boosting Classifier (GBC) outperforms other models in terms of accuracy, precision, and recall. Additionally, the analysis reveals that income, age, and occupation are the most significant predictors for credit risk assessment. These insights can assist NBFCs in enhancing their decision-making processes for credit risk evaluation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/PratikKale1998/ML-Models-Comparison-and-Feature-Importance-Analysis. Future research could explore real-time data processing and implementation to further improve the efficiency of this assessment. By leveraging these data-driven approaches, NBFCs can significantly reduce losses resulting from default risks. The source code is available at https://github.com/PratikKale1998/ML-Models-Comparison-and-Feature-Importance-Analysis. In today's competitive landscape, NBFCs must adopt data-driven strategies to gain a distinct advantage. This paper details the evaluation of multiple machine learning models for credit risk assessment. Specifically, it compares the performance of Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forest (RF), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Decision Trees (DT), and Gradient Boosting Classifier (GBC) on an NBFC dataset. Additionally, the study examines feature importance within these models to support informed decision-making for credit risk evaluation. The source code is available at https://github.com/PratikKale1998/ML-Models-Comparison-and-Feature-Importance-Analysis.

The chromatic symmetric function (CSF) for Dyck paths, along with its $q$-analogue, plays a significant role in combinatorial statistics. This paper introduces a novel family of CSFs for Dyck paths, linked to $q$-hit and $q$-hit-free sets defined on finite posets. We demonstrate that the $q$-CSF corresponds to the chromatic symmetric function of the cover graph, incorporating an additional component tied to fixed points. By utilizing $q$-rook theory, we develop explicit $q$-CSF formulas for specific non-skeletal Dyck paths and calculate the chromatic polynomial (CP) for various non-skeletal graphs. The study concludes with a set of open questions and conjectures. Current deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) typically employ convolutional kernels with fixed, unconstrained orientations, yet it remains unclear whether these kernels require such orientation invariance. This paper proposes that DCNNs can achieve high performance without relying on orientation invariant kernels. Specifically, we introduce the Orientation Convolution Network (OCN), which utilizes orientation-dependent convolutions to extract features, thereby maintaining orientation sensitivity within the learned kernels. Experiments on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets show that OCN matches DCNN performance while clearly detecting oriented objects. This work introduces a systematic framework for calculating the top quark mass within Quantum Chromodynamics, targeting precision levels relevant to both experimental and theoretical studies of the physical spectral function. We provide explicit formulas up to orders of the strong coupling $\alpha_s$ and mass $m$ from three to six loops, alongside expressions for the associated scheme conversion parameter at three-loop order. These results represent the first step toward generating the numerical spectral function with multi-percent accuracy. We have integrated our six-loop formulas into the public code \texttt{topmass}, updating it to reflect current experimental knowledge of the input parameters. Furthermore, we examine the sensitivity of the physical top quark mass to variations in the renormalization scheme and order by examining the shift in the pole mass resulting from transitioning from massive to massless scheme calculations. We conclude that the shift in pole mass between three-loop and six-loop schemes is negligible, amounting to approximately $10^{-3}$ GeV. Additionally, we note that the dependence of the physical mass on the renormalization scale is significantly reduced at high orders, thereby enhancing the reliability of predictions derived from fixed-order cross sections. Our findings regarding the physical top quark mass remain consistent with the shift observed in pole mass predictions. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the extraction of the physical top quark mass from collider data. This line of research is currently being pursued in collaboration with the TopQuarkMass Working Group of the PDG. We have also addressed the issue of scale setting in our work. This conclusion holds true regardless of the renormalization scale used in the massless scheme or the perturbative order employed. These findings underscore the necessity of going beyond fixed-order perturbation theory to achieve a more precise understanding of the physical top quark mass.
