Let $G$ be a graph where each vertex $v$ has a list $L(v)$ of admissible colors. The problem of finding a proper edge-coloring that uses only these colors is known as list edge-coloring; this is equivalent to determining if $G$ can be mapped to a complete graph $K_{r}$, where $r$ is the maximum degree of $G$, in a way that maps incident edges to distinct vertices of $K_{r}$. This paper establishes a sufficient condition on the maximum degree $r$ that guarantees the existence of such a mapping, provided that for every vertex $v$, the union of the lists of its neighbors, $\bigcup_{u \sim v} L(v)$, contains at most $r-1$ colors. Furthermore, the study examines vertex transitive graphs $G$ where the removal of any vertex results in a $q$-regular graph with $q < r$. For these graphs, it is demonstrated that a mapping exists if $r \geq 2q + 2\log_{q}(n)$, where $n$ denotes the order of $G$. Additionally, the paper presents several examples of graphs that satisfy this bound. Finally, the authors outline several open questions regarding both the original and subsequent problems. Notably, the main result is applied to show that the line graph of any circulant graph $G$ is list-colorable with $\lfloor \frac{5}{3} \omega(L(G)) \rfloor$ colors, where $\omega(L(G))$ represents the clique number of $G$. This bound is tight for vertex transitive graphs and is also tight for the 27-vertex circulant graph mentioned earlier. The increasing number of objects in Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) creates a space environment akin to a crowded room, necessitating methods to quantify sparseness and define the limits of further expansion. This paper addresses these challenges by examining a model that incorporates both attractive gravitational forces and repulsive deconfinement effects to describe the equilibrium state of an expanding system. By deriving an analytical solution that characterizes the distribution of bound objects along with those that are unbound, the study demonstrates how this distribution stabilizes as the system grows, revealing a state defined by universal parameters. These findings offer partial analytical insights that complement recent Monte-Carlo simulations of orbital evolution in LEO. The research quantifies the concepts of territoriality and sparseness within this region, explores factors influencing the capacity for growth, and predicts the bound fraction and critical thresholds for expansion. These theoretical results provide a foundation for developing simplified, non-simulation-based tools to assess future changes in the LEO environment. Specifically, such tools could estimate the bound fraction of cataloged objects, assess collision risks with newly deployed constellations, and determine safe altitudes for new satellite deployments. The model relies on two primary variables: the specific orbital energy of the objects and a dimensionless parameter representing system compactness. Additionally, it considers attractive forces from non-gravitational effects and repulsive forces arising from excluded volume. These concepts are subsequently applied to the current population of Low-Earth Orbit debris and cataloged objects. The results indicate that the bound fraction of LEO objects has reached a limiting state, with most objects clustered in very low Earth orbit. Furthermore, the density of objects in LEO appears to have approached a saturation point. Pearson's correlation coefficient is a standard metric for quantifying linear relationships, yet deriving the moments of its sampling distribution is often complex. While these moments can be calculated via numerical integration, they lack a general analytical expression for sample sizes greater than three. This paper presents analytical formulas for the sampling distribution moments of Pearson's correlation under data permutations, specifically for $n > 3$. These formulas are expressed using sampling and central moment symbols, which can be expanded into their polynomial forms. Although an analytical solution was previously known for $n=3$, our approach generalizes this to any integer $n \geq 3$. Furthermore, we provide an algorithm to convert these formulas into power series expansions around specific points, enabling numerical approximation for any real-valued $n$. We also extend these sampling distribution moments to central moment symbols and demonstrate how to approximate central moments via a Taylor series expansion of the sampling moments. Finally, we employ the symbolic mathematics software Maple to compute the first six sampling moments of the Pearson correlation coefficient for $n=4$ through $n=10$. We conclude by outlining an algorithm for calculating higher-order moments using our derived formulas and Maple. All derivations and algorithms were implemented using Python's SymPy library. This work was motivated by a need to approximate the sampling distribution of the Pearson correlation coefficient. We hope these formulas will serve as a practical tool for researchers. Additionally, we have created a Python script that utilizes SymPy to compute these moments, which is available to assist readers in applying our results. This paper serves as a detailed report on the methods presented in our prior conference abstract [1].

This text outlines the rationale for developing a quantum $S$-matrix framework for classical gravitational two-body scattering and briefly presents the derivation of black-hole metrics across different dimensions as an application. It then details the construction of a classical $S$-matrix from asymptotic data and demonstrates its application to classical scattering using a one-dimensional step potential as an example. Furthermore, it emphasizes the importance of building a quantum $S$-matrix that reduces to the classical $S$-matrix in the classical limit and outlines an efficient method for constructing a quantum $S$-matrix from a classical one. Finally, it presents a beyond-the-Standard-model theory featuring a classical scalar field with conformal coupling to curvature and matter, which is solved exactly and used to construct an exact $S$-matrix. The work concludes by arguing that a complete, exact beyond-the-Standard-model $S$-matrix theory can be constructed without solving the resulting non-linear field equations, and it briefly discusses several open questions. In the corresponding German version, the author intends to elaborate on these points. Additionally, the text will be updated as new material becomes available.

This study addresses the uniform stabilization of the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations, initially defined in bounded domains with Dirichlet boundary conditions within critical $H^2(\Omega)$ spaces. The proposed solution involves implementing finite-dimensional feedback controls located within specific subdomains of $\Omega$. These controls are derived by restricting the projection of the time-integrated conditions required for exponential exponential stabilization within maximal $L^p(\Omega)$ spaces to a specific subdomain. The feedback controls are applied directionally along a single axis. This approach extends the findings of Datko, Li, and Slemrod (SIAM J. Control Optim., 1984), which originally focused on exponential stabilization in critical $H^2(\Omega)$ spaces. Furthermore, the current work demonstrates uniform stabilization in broader functional settings, including Besov spaces, even when initial data in these spaces do not necessarily belong to $L^\infty(\Omega)$. A key component of the methodology is the uniform boundedness of the Navier-Stokes solution's vorticity in $L^r(\Omega)$ over time, leveraging recent results by Fabre, Mazet, and Pazy (J. Funct. Anal., 2009) and Fabre and Mazet (J. Math. Pures Appl., 2011) concerning uniform boundedness in Besov spaces. This paper also presents a novel, direct method for proving the local well-posedness of Navier-Stokes equations in critical $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces, which are equivalent to $H^{2}_{q}(\Omega)$ for $1<q<\infty$. Additionally, the concept of conditions satisfying the Dirichlet condition is extended to these broader spaces. A distinct observation is that the observability of the Navier-Stokes solution remains independent of the domain's dimensionality. Dictionaries serve as essential references for finding word definitions, with contemporary versions also offering synonyms, antonyms, and various usage contexts. Although numerous resources exist where users can query for synonyms and antonyms, the intersection of these three elements—definition, synonym, and antonym—remains uncommon in online dictionaries. This paper introduces the LitMind Dictionary, an open-source platform that integrates all three functions. Designed to be user-friendly and visually appealing, it utilizes a dictionary tree structure to facilitate efficient navigation and comprehensive search results. The growing interest in Explainable Recommendation has led to various local explanation methods, such as RIME, which attribute user-item interactions within a single session. However, this focus is restrictive because it ignores interactions occurring outside that specific context. Consequently, we extend LIME—a global approximation method adapted from natural language processing—to generate attributions for individual interactions. We then evaluate these recommendations against prior work using adherence, constancy,constellation, and sensitivity metrics. Our results show that while LIME-RM achieves high adherence, it suffers from low constancy and sensitivity, performing only slightly better than its base counterpart. These shortcomings stem from the approach's reliance on item representations, leading to explanations that are too interaction-specific and narrowly focused. To address this, we propose a novel method for generating explanations for interactions between a user and multiple items. By utilizing user-history representations instead of item embeddings, our approach produces explanations that are more diverse and consistent. Importantly, these new attributions maintain strong adherence while achieving significantly improved constancy and stability. Code and data are available at https://github.com/fernandogoncalves/LIME-RS. Furthermore, we have developed a web application for visualizing the model's recommendations and explanations, accessible at https://goncalvesf.github.io/LIME-RS/. This tool also demonstrates the impact of different evaluation metrics on LIME-RS evaluations. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the model's predictions and explanations. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to comprehensively assess LIME-RS using multiple evaluation metrics and constancy, consistency, and stability. The tool allows users to interact with the visualization and explore LIME-RS evaluations in detail. We hope this will encourage further research into the limitations of the approach and lead to new advancements. Our findings indicate that the evaluation space for local recommendations requires additional research to define new metrics and heuristics for assessing the quality of recommendations. We believe this will contribute to improved recommendation systems in the future. We look forward to your feedback and collaboration. Thank you.

This study demonstrates that the 2DEG Fermi level in near-surface InAs quantum wells can be raised to coincide with the band edge by substituting InAs barrier and cladding layers with low-band-gap CdInAs$_2$. This material functions as a degenerate n-type semiconductor, where its high electron concentration enables the Fermi level in adjacent 2DEG layers to rise sufficiently to eliminate typical pinning near the surface depletion region. Furthermore, the 2DEG mobility remains unaffected by these degenerate cladding layers; it stays above 20,000 cm$^2$/Vs across all well thicknesses and remains stable up to temperatures of at least 300 K. These degenerate cladding layers offer a novel approach to achieving Fermi level control in semiconductor heterostructures, with potential applications in spintronics and spin qubits. Additionally, the ease of integrating these cladding layers into standard semiconductor fabrication processes makes them a viable solution for widespread adoption. Finally, the influence of degenerate cladding layers on the transport characteristics of InAs quantum wells featuring a quantum dot at their center is also examined. Incorporating degenerate cladding layers results in a significant enhancement of conductance within the quantum dot. This improvement is attributed to the suppression of barrier tunneling, which causes the dot's conductance to rise proportionally to the number of electrons it can hold. Consequently, this methodology may facilitate the realization of high-fidelity spin qubits. To verify this, we plan to investigate the possibility of detecting Coulomb blockades in these degenerate cladding-layer-based InAs quantum dot structures. This investigation will involve measuring the conductance of InAs quantum wells with quantum dots at their centers as a function of gate voltage, thereby uncovering the intricate electron interactions within the quantum dots. This research represents a crucial initial step toward developing semiconductor-based spin qubits. This paper investigates how access to local queries enhances robustness against adversarial perturbations. We establish theoretical results demonstrating that, even when queries provide perfect classification on unperturbed inputs, they may offer no improvement over non-query algorithms. Furthermore, even with queries that yield high predictions, they can fail to boost performance in the face of perturbation attacks. Based on these findings, we propose algorithmic methods for determining whether local queries are beneficial. Our theory indicates that if the target concept is weakly correlated with query outputs, these approaches can efficiently identify the absence of useful queries. We validate these insights through experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world image data. Additionally, we explore potential extensions of this framework to address other data issues beyond adversarial robustness. Finally, we relate our contributions to broader discussions on leveraging auxiliary information in machine learning. Overall, this work advances understanding of when local queries are effective and establishes a foundation for extending their application to other domains. Building on our prior research [arXiv:2006.01808], which introduced the Fast Sinkhorn algorithm operating in $\mathcal{O}(n^p)$ time for an $n \times n \circ n$ submatrix, this paper presents a novel algorithm for the optimal transport problem. This new method achieves $\mathcal{O}(n)$ time complexity by utilizing the collinear structure of a triangular singular $n \times n$ submatrix. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through extensive numerical experiments on synthetic data. These tests reveal orders-of-magnitude improvements in computation time, with a maximum reduction of $99.9\%$ for $n=10^5$ across various data distributions. Furthermore, we establish a worst-case complexity bound of $\mathcal{O}(n)$, representing the fastest known exact algorithm for the optimal transport problem. Finally, we apply the proposed algorithm to the problem of estimating the Hausdorff distance between two curves. Additional implementation details, including parameter selection and data preprocessing requirements, are provided in the supplementary material. This supplementary section encompasses experiments on real-world data, empirical validation of the algorithm's worst-case bounds, and analyses of its limitations. These aspects were previously excluded from the main manuscript to maintain focus on the algorithmic contributions. The accompanying code is available at \url{https://github.com/ahmed-aymanh/FastSinkhornOT/tree/Collinear}. Future work will extend this approach to sublinear time complexity for sparse problems. The AU Microscopii system serves as a critical benchmark for studying exoplanet atmospheres and habitability. This study presents simultaneous far-ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the active T Tauri star AU Mic both during quiescent periods and while capturing extreme flares, utilizing data from the International Ultraviolet Explorer (IUE), the Hubble Space Telescope (HST), and the Swift UVOT. We analyzed these observations to determine the chromospheric temperature structure and to compare AU Mic's activity levels with other active stars. Our findings indicate that the star's temperature structure is governed by chromospheric heating mechanisms driven by magnetic reconnection. Furthermore, we demonstrate that AU Mic's current activity is elevated compared to other stars, and we provide predictions for the radiation environments experienced by exoplanets orbiting this star. Finally, our analysis suggests that both exoplanets AU Mic b and c may have suffered significant atmospheric mass loss. Specifically, we predict that HST-WFC3 observations of AU Mic b will reveal an evaporating atmosphere, whereas no such evaporation is expected for AU Mic c. These results highlight the necessity of incorporating stellar activity into models of exoplanet atmospheric evolution. We examine a point charge experiencing constant acceleration, subjected to radiation reaction forces while moving through a resistive material medium. This scenario is modeled by integrating the radiation reaction equation of motion with the Lorentz force equation, accounting for the electric field generated by the medium's current response to the particle. When this superposition equilibrium is balanced by constant material friction, the charge follows a straight path with two distinct outcomes depending on the velocity relative to the speed of light: if the velocity remains below $c$, the charge stabilizes at constant acceleration governed by the sum of radiation reaction and material friction forces; if the velocity approaches $c$, it tends toward the speed of light, governed solely by material friction as the particle effectively screens the external electric field. Additionally, we analyze the superposition of constant velocity and constant acceleration, noting that the constant velocity component arises exclusively from the material friction field. Finally, we examine the influence of the Minkowski space-time metric on this dynamics. In classification tasks involving significantly imbalanced classes, many statistical approaches treat data points from the smaller classes as noise. This study re-examines the validity of that assumption. We demonstrate that if the noise assumption holds, the conditional distribution of the smaller classes must be singular, meaning it is supported exclusively on the boundary of the ball defined by the majority class's conditional mean given $X$. This theoretical finding offers new insights into the noise assumption and establishes a foundation for developing classifiers for imbalanced data. Leveraging this result, we introduce a classification algorithm that utilizes a modified nearest neighbor rule. We prove that if the error rate of the optimal classifier is strictly less than half, the proposed method's error rate approaches it as the sample size grows. Additionally, we present several real-world examples to validate the method's effectiveness. Specifically, we show that for certain datasets, achieving the optimal error rate requires either increasing the sample size or reducing the dimensionality of the input variable $X$. Finally, we propose a classification approach that reduces the dimension of $X$ to a value close to the estimated number of classes, demonstrating that this reduced-dimension method can attain the optimal error rate on certain real-world datasets. These findings are supported by numerical experiments and real data examples. Through numerical analysis, we illustrate the performance of various modified nearest neighbor rules and establish a lower bound for the reduced dimension. Furthermore, we show that the proposed dimension reduction scheme yields a reduced dimension that is at most proportional to the number of classes. Experimental results indicate that the classification performance of our proposed method is comparable to that of existing approaches. Finally, we introduce a classification method grounded in Support Vector Machines, which serves as a promising alternative for analyzing real-world data. This approach employs a Gaussian kernel and reduces the dimension of $X$ to a value closely matching the estimated number of classes. Extensive numerical experiments confirm that the proposed methods are highly effective for classifying real-world data. For instance, when applied to a well-known real-world dataset, the method achieves an optimal classification error rate of 0.01. Specifically, our follow-up research will address clustering with imbalanced data and regression with partially linear errors, with detailed results to be published. Perpetual view generation, which involves creating new long-range perspectives by virtually flying through a provided image, represents a novel and promising field. We present DiffDreamer, an unsupervised framework designed to produce highly diverse and high-quality images from a single input through continuous, incremental virtual camera movements. Unlike traditional one-step view generation, which often yields inconsistent and limited results, our method employs an iterative diffusion model to ensure consistent and high-quality image synthesis. Furthermore, to enable perpetual camera motion and expand perceptual possibilities, we implement a memory module that facilitates the transmission of visual context from previous images to the current one. This memory module acts as a bridge connecting a sequence of images into a larger visual manifold, with a conditional diffusion model serving as the generator for producing new images based on this sequence. On public datasets, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in both perceptual and fidelity metrics while offering greater result diversity compared to prior methods. **Background:** Ultrasound is increasingly utilized in pediatric scoliosis assessment due to its safety, portability, and cost-effectiveness. While prior research indicates that untrained operators can achieve diagnostic accuracy comparable to radiographs, the reliability of ultrasound by trained operators remains unestablished. Additionally, it is unclear whether manual ultrasound measurements match the reliability of optical methods, such as spinal motion capture, currently used in clinical and laboratory settings.

**Methods:** We conducted a crossover study involving 20 children (ages 6–16) with scoliosis, 10 without scoliosis, and 10 adults. Scoliosis was induced in volunteers via targeted electrical muscle stimulation. Ultrasound scans were performed by both trained and untrained sonographers using two approaches: freehand and structured (similar to spinal motion capture). Trained sonographers also utilized a semi-automated curve measurement software. Scan reliability was evaluated using intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC) and Bland-Altman analysis.

**Results:** Trained sonographers achieved excellent reliability (ICC > 0.8) with freehand scanning using the semi-automated method, yielding ultrasound lateral spine deformity values similar to radiographic results. Untrained sonographers also reached excellent reliability (ICC > 0.8) with freehand scanning but produced lower deformation values than the trained group. Structured scanning by trained sonographers demonstrated good reliability (ICC > 0.7).

**Conclusions:** When performed by trained sonographers, freehand ultrasound scanning by untrained operators yields results similar to radiographs but produces lower deformation values. Future applications should involve training sonographers to achieve freehand ultrasound scans with reliability similar to that of optical spinal motion capture achieved through structured scanning.

This paper introduces a novel method for duration modeling in statistical parametric speech synthesis, utilizing a recurrent statistical model to represent both speech and speech-like audio. By combining a recurrent model with a median-based duration distribution, we achieve speech generation across an extensive volume range. When integrated into the Twittler architectural layer (Shen et al., 2018), this system enables high-quality, multi-utterance speech generation via diffusion modeling. We assess our approach through listening evaluations on the VOS2 dataset (Hsieh et al., 2023) and compare it against both diffusion duration prior methods and conventional solutions. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses other techniques in producing more realistic speech. The code is accessible at https://github.com/SeungwonLee98/RecurrentMedianDuration. Furthermore, the system supports real-time speech generation at 44.1kHz/mono, achieving inference times of approximately 10ms per utterance. This represents a 100-fold speed improvement over state-of-the-art duration modeling and a two-fold speedup over statistical parametric speech synthesis. The method is compatible with any pre-trained diffusion speaker model, facilitating the creation of a new family of synthesis models for any voice. Additionally, we highlight the method's ability to generate speech-like utterances. The complete source code for the proposed method can be found at https://github.com/SeungwonLee98/RecurrentMedianDuration. Finally, we provide a speech generation demo video and a multi-utterance synthesis demo audio sample. The sample audio is available at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/11442141414141414141414141414141?usp=sharing.

This study introduces Multiple State Analysis (MSA), a novel statistical framework designed to handle multiple time-to-event data. MSA offers the analytical flexibility of Cox proportional hazards regression and other conventional methods, while simultaneously accommodating unmeasured latent variables that influence event trajectories. We illustrate this approach using a dataset of 1,012 myocardial infarction patients, which includes three key life course indicators: depression, physical activity, and cardiovascular risk. These indicators were examined as potential mediators influencing transitions between four health states: two adverse outcomes (death, stroke), one favorable outcome (myocardial revascularization), and a reference state. MSA revealed that depression and physical activity, but not cardiovascular risk, drive transitions between health states. Specifically, depression increases the likelihood of stroke and decreases the likelihood of myocardial revascularization, whereas greater physical activity has the opposite effects. MSA represents a new method for investigating how multiple life course factors influence transitions between health states and other significant life course outcomes. The R package msamv, which implements MSA, is accessible at https://github.com/epi-math/R-msemv. Additional code and a user guide are available at https://github.com/epi-math/MSA. The published user guide can be found at https://epi-math.github.io/MSA/. This implementation was developed in collaboration with the EPi-Math research group at the University of Geneva. EPi-Math is a newly established university research group dedicated to advancing statistical methods for epidemiology and public health. The user guide includes examples from both the current study and a second collaborative application involving a cohort of 1,500 individuals with HIV. This group was led by Dr. Laurent Forestier, who passed away in 2019. Dr. Forestier's work on multiple time-to-event data is available at https://epi-math.github.io/. We introduce an explicit quadrature approach for evaluating the molecular continuum of the many-electron Coulomb interaction, which forms the foundation for constructing Kohn-Sham effective single-particle potentials. This computational scheme is applicable to molecules spanning various sizes, including both large and large-to-moderate systems. The resulting Coulomb potential of the Coulomb-Kohn-Sham potential exhibits high accuracy and converges at a rate of O(1/R) in the asymptotic region, independent of the basis set used to represent the Kohn-Sham potential. Furthermore, this potential within the molecular continuum is invariant regarding the molecular frame, whether it is fixed or centered. Our tests demonstrate that the multi-center quadrature scheme for the molecular continuum yields accurate potentials for large, large-to-moderate, and moderately delocalized systems, while also showing that the approach fails for moderately sized and small systems where the electron density is tightly bound. We illustrate the efficacy of the multi-center quadrature scheme for the molecular continuum by applying it to the conformational isomers of n-butane and n-octane. The optimized geometries of these conformational isomers, derived from the Kohn-Sham potentials within the molecular continuum, align with prior quantum chemical calculations. Additionally, we show that the multi-center quadrature scheme for the molecular continuum can be seamlessly integrated into the conventional localized orbital density functional theory framework, thereby facilitating the application of the proposed scheme to the molecular continuum in extended systems. Finally, we confirm the accuracy of the proposed multi-center quadrature scheme for the molecular continuum within the localized density functional theory framework by analyzing the conformational isomers of n-decane. This enables the calculation of the conformational free energy of n-decane, a property that has eluded quantum chemical methods. The conformational free energy of n-decane is computed using the Boltzmann-weighted density functional theory ensemble, where the Boltzmann weights are derived from the density functional theory results within the molecular continuum. We conclude that the proposed multi-center quadrature scheme for the molecular continuum is highly accurate for large-to-moderate and moderately sized systems. This development holds significant promise for advancing the application of quantum theory to nanomaterials, nanoscale materials, nanoscale devices, and nanoscale electronic systems. Ultimately, this work represents a crucial step toward achieving quantum theory at the nanoscale. This study addresses the decisional metric dimension problem, which involves determining whether a graph $G$ possesses a resolving dominating set with size at most $k$. Initially, we examine this question for graphs with a feedback vertex set of size at most $k$, demonstrating that it can be solved in $O(c^k \cdot n)$ time using an extended neighborhood cover approach, where $n$ represents the number of vertices and $c$ is a constant. Subsequently, we analyze the problem parameterized by the radius, showing it is fixed-parameter tractable via a direct method. We also present a fixed-parameter algorithm based on treewidth, which relies on the metric dimension problem's fixed-parameter tractability on graphs with bounded treewidth established by Kratsch et al. [J. Comput. Syst. Sci., 2018]. Finally, we illustrate that all previously proven fixed-parameter results remain valid when resolving dominating sets are substituted with resolving vertex covers. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential extensions. Throughout this work, we utilize graph minors theory, which we believe is a highly effective instrument for addressing deciding parameterized graph problems. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive overview of metric dimension to facilitate its application in parameterized algorithms. Our research is grounded in a novel perspective on resolving neighborhoods, which we present as a useful concept for future investigations. To extend this characterization to total and partial programs separately, the author previously introduced directed powerdomains within prior work. In this paper, that work is refined to establish a full characterization of the statement itself. This refinement necessitates incorporating the distinction between upper and lower powerdomains, aligning with the duality observed in denotational semantics for total versus partial programs. As a direct consequence, the construction of the Higuchi powerdomain is achieved. Furthermore, the relationship between powerdomains and metric spaces is examined in the context of the Gromov–Hausdorff metric, leading to the observation that the Gromov–Hausdorff space of all subsets of a countable, complete metric space is homeomorphic to its subspace of closed subsets. Additionally, the relationship between powerdomains and topological spaces is explored using the concept of quasi-components, revealing that the Gromov–Hausdorff space of all compact closed subsets of a countable complete metric space is homeomorphic to the quasi-component space of its Clopenes. Finally, the paper concludes with an analysis of the relationship between power structures and superschemes, demonstrating that every power structure on the set of all subsets of a countable complete metric space induces a unique superscheme on the associated powerdomain. To facilitate these analyses, a new formalization of power structures is also proposed. A key innovation in this paper is the introduction of quasi-components, defined as the irreducible closed subsets of a topological space, which may be empty. It is noted that non-empty quasi-components encompass various standard topological concepts, including connected components, components, and convex components. The term "quasi-component" is particularly appropriate for subsets of a metric space, as it reflects the metric property of convexity. This formalization was inspired by the need to address the aforementioned observation. The primary contribution of this paper is the extension of power structures to the context of metric spaces. To achieve this, the concept of quasi-components is introduced, alongside a corresponding formalization of superschemes. The paper provides numerous examples of power structures on the set of all subsets of a countable complete metric space, along with their relationships. Additionally, the work examines the relationship between power structures and superschemes, demonstrating that every power structure on the set of all subsets of a countable complete metric space induces a unique superscheme on power substructures.

Earth's history includes numerous extreme weather events, such as deluges, which are expected to occur more frequently under warmer climatic conditions. This study employs a series of one-dimensional models to demonstrate that hydrological cycles operating within "hothouse" scenarios—characterized by high temperatures and abundant atmospheric water vapor—can trigger episodic deluges. These events involve a moist boundary layer drying out, followed by the release of stored vapor from the interior via gravity-driven boundary layer collapse, resulting in massive, periodic precipitation. We show that this instability arises due to the temperature-dependent viscosity of water and can be predicted using simple thermodynamic stability analysis. Although restricted to simulated climates, these findings offer a theoretical basis for the significantly higher precipitation rates observed in warm, wet environments, such as tropical rainforests and alien worlds. Furthermore, the mechanism may help explain extreme weather events recorded in historical and geological data, including biblical floods, extreme rainfall in Shakespeare's era, and global flood layers found in geological strata. Finally, we explore the potential implications of these results for interpreting extreme weather in historical and geological records. **Objective:** This study aims to address label noise in medical image classification, a critical issue that significantly impacts model performance.
**Methods:** We introduce a novel Bayesian statistics-guided label refurbishment mechanism that enhances deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) classifiers by iteratively refurbishing noisy labels. The process begins with a prior DCNN classification, followed by the calculation of posterior DCNN classification probabilities and their divergence from the pre-trained prior. Classification results are then refurbished by selecting the mode of the posterior probabilities, which maximizes the posterior probability of correctness. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this mechanism by integrating it into two popular DCNN architectures: ResNet-50 and the attention-guided DCNN (AGDCNN).
**Results:** Extensive experiments were conducted on the MICCAI 2021 2D Label Noise Challenge Dataset (LN2D) and the 3D Label Noise Challenge Dataset (LN3D). Our Bayesian-guided AGDCNN achieved 2nd place in the LN2D competition and 1st place in the LN3D competition. These results confirm the efficacy of our approach in mitigating the adverse effects of label noise.
**Conclusion:** The success of our method stems from the AGDCNN's superior performance on noisy data and the efficacy of the Bayesian label refurbishment mechanism. Additionally, AGDCNN is computationally efficient and easy to implement. We introduce a correlated random walk on a graph to model the activity within a community on a social network. This correlated walk is defined such that the transition probability matrix represents a graph's activity matrix, where each element indicates the likelihood of moving from one node to another. By utilizing the eigenvalues of this matrix, we can identify community nodes. Specifically, if an eigenvalue is greater than 1, the corresponding eigenvector partitions the community nodes; eigenvalues less than 1 indicate that the node belongs to the other community. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the transition probability matrix of a correlated random walk on a graph is the transition matrix of a Markov chain, which functions as a probability distribution. The stationary distribution of this Markov chain corresponds to the eigenvector associated with the eigenvalue 1. Consequently, the eigenvalue 1 of the transition probability matrix is essential for determining the center node of a community. Finally, we apply the correlated random walk to identify communities in the DBLP and Citeseer datasets, validating the proposed method. The computational complexity of this approach is O(n^2), where n is the number of nodes in the graph. Our method functions as a clustering algorithm, achieving results comparable to those of the Spectral Clustering algorithm, which also utilizes the eigenvalues of a transition probability matrix as its objective function. However, the computational complexity of our approach is lower than that of Spectral Clustering, which typically operates in O(n^3). The source code is available at: https://github.com/ehsan-nejati/CorrelatedRandomWalk. The transition probability matrix can be generated using the GCD algorithm, as detailed in our prior work.

Many functions that may not terminate cannot be directly expressed in logics of total functions like HOL. However, if $\tau$ represents a measure of progress guaranteeing that any execution of function $f$ starting from $\tau$ terminates within a bounded number of $\tau$-decrements, then the $\tau$-clocked version of $f$ (denoted as $f_\tau$) can be defined. The behavior of $f_\tau$ mirrors that of $f$ as long as $f$ executes within a limit of $\tau$-decrements; otherwise, it $\beta\eta$-reduces to bottom. We present a general method for clocked definitions, which are straightforward to input into HOL. This approach is demonstrated with a $\text{nat} \to \text{bool}$ function introduced by Berry and the more complex case of a list reversal function. Additionally, we illustrate how various tools can be naturally defined using this methodology. Our approach has been implemented in a prototype system known as $\mu\text{HOL}$.

This study examines face-centered cubic particle-laden flow within a spatially developing turbulent channel. Initially, we analyze coherent structures within the fluid and identify both coherent structures and elastic coherent structures in the particle phase. These elastic structures are characterized by high potential energy, low kinetic energy, and high dipole strength. We demonstrate that integrating machine learning with conventional coherent structure-based interaction models enhances the prediction of particle wall impact events and instantaneous wall shear stress anisotropy in particle-turbulence systems. This predictive boost stems from the machine learning model's capacity to establish a robust correlation between elastic structures and historical turbulent coherent structures, thereby significantly improving the accuracy of the traditional physics-based interaction model. These findings offer a pathway for developing hybrid physics-informed machine learning models to predict particle-wall and particle-fluid interactions in particle-turbulence systems. Such predictions are crucial for understanding particle-based transport mechanisms in geophysical flows and for optimizing particle performance in fluid processing applications. We investigate the topological characteristics of a lattice model featuring Weyl nodes situated away from the Brillouin zone center, which interacts with a strong magnetic field applied perpendicular to it. This system is promising for experimental realization due to its relatively simple structure and minimal number of bands. Specifically, each Weyl node is accompanied by a pair of Berry curvature monopoles located near the Brillouin zone center. Our findings indicate that monopoles do not restrict Chern numbers to integers; instead, they contribute an oscillatory component within Hofstadter's butterfly's intricate structure. Consequently, experimentally measurable signatures, such as the Chern gap and Hall conductivity, exhibit a frequency determined by the ratio of the magnetic field to the lattice spacing. Furthermore, these signatures display significant dependence on Hofstadter's ratio, defined as the ratio of magnetic field strength to hopping amplitude. This sensitivity is advantageous for experimental detection but necessitates high-precision measurements. Finally, we explore the system's potential for magnetically controlled lattice surgery. Our results are corroborated by numerical computations. We anticipate that Hofstadter's butterfly could be highly effective in demonstrating novel Hofstadter physics, including the lattice model's intrinsic sensitivity to magnetic field position. This sensitivity could serve as a powerful tool for manipulating lattice structures in Hofstadter-based lattice surgery. Finally, we propose that Hofstadter's butterfly could offer a unique platform for lattice control, complementing existing experimental methods. We conclude by discussing the practical implications of these results. We have created and analyzed a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic system featuring a single quantum dot (QD) positioned within a dielectric nanopillar situated on a gold surface. By employing full-wave simulations, we demonstrated that this configuration supports two distinct dipolar modes: one primarily in the dielectric component (out-of-plane field) and another mainly in the plasmonic component (in-plane field). The presence of the QD in the nanopillar facilitates the hybridization of these two modes. We established that the emitted light from a dipole placed at the center of the QD is predominantly directed into the out-of-plane field mode. This dielectrically confined emission mode is characterized by a superior hybridization factor, a high brightness, and a large effective oscillator strength, all while maintaining a relatively long radiative lifetime. The influence of the noise spectrum on the screening process is analyzed, and the theory is demonstrated to hold for both uniaxial and multidimensional agitation. Sgr A East, situated near the Galactic center, exhibits characteristics of a supernova remnant (SNR), yet its origin remains uncertain. Previous research has attempted to reconstruct the event by analyzing its current morphology, but these efforts have yielded conflicting conclusions. This study proposes a novel methodology to address the ambiguity: reconstructing the supernova by examining its recent temporal evolution. By applying a model-based approach, we determined that the progenitor was a 12 solar mass star that exploded with an energy of 10^{51} ergs approximately 600 years ago. Based on the object's past morphology and a specific region of high stellar density identified within Sgr A, we reconstructed the explosion site roughly 0.25" (200 AU) from the Galactic center. We also evaluated various supernova models, finding that a core-collapse scenario offers a more natural explanation than a Type Ia event. Finally, we examined the temporal evolution of X-ray and radio sources within Sgr A, concluding that X-ray flares are likely caused by low-mass stellar interactions rather than a supernova. The proposed reconstruction method is anticipated to be applicable to other ambiguous SNRs. A video documenting our research process is accessible at https://youtu.be/4211111111. Although deep learning methods are highly effective for single-class text classification tasks, they often struggle in real-world multi-class scenarios because of class imbalance. This study evaluates five over-sampling techniques—SMOTE, two-level SMOTE, RSMOTE, the hard to fall algorithm, and the minority class over-sampling algorithm—using a Swedish news dataset. The findings indicate that the SMOTE algorithm yields the most consistent results. Furthermore, the experiment demonstrates that simply applying these over-sampling methods is insufficient; instead, their iterative use combined with retraining leads to significantly enhanced classification performance. Finally, the research confirms that multi-class text classification achieves optimal outcomes when conducted within a supervised learning framework. Future work will explore advanced retraining strategies, including alternating between over-sampling and under-sampling methods. Finally, the authors plan to release the code and dataset used in this study as open-source contributions to the research community. This study examines the connections between COVID-19 news exposure, case rates, fatalities, and regional factors within the United States. Analyzing content from 110 local news websites over a six-month period from April to September 2020, we found no consistent evidence that news coverage was driven by case or death data. However, we did observe an inverse relationship between exposure to COVID news and higher COVID case rates. These findings suggest that local news organizations did not simply reflect existing health trends but rather adapted their reporting to the unique demands and constraints of the pandemic. The paper discusses the implications of these results for both local news consumers and producers. Additionally, the data supports a well-established economic principle: as an economy grows more advanced, it attracts a larger share of news consumption to its more prosperous local outlets. Specifically, advanced economies benefit from the presence of a greater number of skilled journalists. This number is determined by the ratio of journalists to residents, which in turn relies on the relative costs of news production versus the cost of consumer attention. The research is grounded in a model of local news production tailored to the pandemic context. Finally, the article explores the broader significance of these results for understanding the dynamics of local news production and consumption. A dataset containing COVID-19 news articles from 110 U.S. local news outlets is available for future research. Furthermore, the findings contribute to the ongoing debate regarding the impact of media on society, a debate that has taken on heightened urgency during the COVID pandemic. Finally, the study offers insights into the relationship between local economies and local news.

Keywords: local news, COVID-19, attention economy.

The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is a widely utilized technique for accelerating Coulomb-based solvers by accelerating the evaluation of force contributions from particles within dense clusters. This paper examines the rotational invariance of the FMM operator specifically for point particles with zero spin. We demonstrate that, at machine precision, the FMM method strictly conserves the total angular momentum of a particle cluster provided it is isolated. Our analysis reveals a previously unaccounted source of error in rotational invariance caused by the arbitrary truncation of Bessel series. Furthermore, we explore potential strategies to enhance rotational accuracy within acceptable limits by adjusting the order of the Bessel series. To our knowledge, the issue of FMM's rotational invariance has not been addressed in prior literature. Our investigation is supported by the JuliaFMM package, which is available at https://github.com/JuliaFMM/JuliaFMM. This package utilizes extended precision arithmetic for all FMM operations; although this results in slower execution compared to standard single or double precision, it guarantees strict conservation of total angular momentum. We validate these findings with several numerical experiments. First, we test two-body interactions in the laboratory frame using different initial conditions to verify angular momentum conservation. Second, we simulate a three-body system where we compute the change in total angular momentum per step across various resolutions and initial configurations. Finally, we analyze a four-body system exhibiting chaotic dynamics, calculating the conservation of total angular momentum over various time intervals. These numerical experiments confirm that the four-body system maintains its total angular momentum within machine precision when computed using JuliaFMM with extended precision. Additionally, the extended precision variant of JuliaFMM is integrated into the D3M molecular dynamics package, demonstrating its utility for scientific computing applications. Our findings indicate that while the current fmm() implementation in JuliaFMM offers sufficient accuracy for most users, future improvements to the algorithm are anticipated to further optimize performance. These enhancements will be developed through collaborative efforts with the community, as initiated by our recent proposal to the JuliaFMM organization to establish a review board for scrutinizing all future modifications to the package. We encourage users to contribute to these rotational improvements by submitting pull requests to the JuliaFMM organization repository at https://github.com/JuliaFMM/JuliaFMM. Contributions from the community are essential to the ongoing development of this package. This approach models both Dirac and Pauli form factors through a convolution of distribution amplitudes, while vector meson dominance is employed to determine the beam and target spin non-flip amplitudes. Furthermore, the potential transfer of polarization from the incident to the scattered electron is calculated for the first time, followed by an analysis of the spin structure of the proton. We introduce a straightforward yet potent technique for enhancing sample efficiency in models trained on large datasets of structured data. Our method involves generating synthetic training samples by utilizing the current parameter estimates. This approach offers several distinct benefits: it necessitates no architectural changes to existing models, requires no prior knowledge of the underlying data generation process, and involves no additional computational cost during training. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness through applications to structured text, code, and tree-structured biological data, where it substantially boosts the training efficiency of both classification and tree-structured classification tasks. Furthermore, we show that the method can be leveraged to establish tighter upper bounds on the generalization error of our estimators, offering insights into their ability to handle out-of-sample data. Finally, we provide theoretical guarantees for the method under simple assumptions, specifically regarding consistency and its performance in high-dimensional settings. This note examines K3 surfaces featuring Siegel disks and investigates how the characteristic degrees of the monodromy groups for the action on $H^2(K3, \mathbb{Z})$ constrain the possible Picard numbers. We demonstrate that for any even integer $s$ satisfying $2 \leq s \leq 20$, there exists an analytic type of such a K3 surface where the Picard rank is exactly $s$, achieved by identifying suitable $L$-polynomials. In contrast, we also establish that certain characteristic degrees cannot arise from these monodromy groups; specifically, the value $s=22$ is excluded, and the feasibility of $s=8$ remains an open question. Finally, drawing on recent work by Lian, Liu, and Luo regarding K3 fibrations, we provide additional examples of Siegel disk types alongside their corresponding Picard numbers and characteristic degrees. Additionally, we present a computational approach utilizing the `sage` package to calculate the characteristic degrees and $L$-polynomials for specific cases. The computations required to prove that $s=22$ is impossible are executed via a provided python script. Finally, the appendices list all 56 reduced primitive polynomials of degree up to 24, along with their associated characteristic degrees, which are referenced throughout the text. This work is based on a talk delivered at the Seoul National University seminar titled "K3 Surfaces, Picard Numbers and Siegel Disks." Our gratitude extends to Prof. Yoonhee Kim for the invitation and to Prof. Junyi Xie for the insightful discussion. Any errors remaining are our own. If supersymmetry exists at the TeV scale, the neutral lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) naturally serves as a viable dark matter candidate. However, in the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM), the gamma-ray spectrum produced by annihilating LSPs typically exhibits a flat shape, making it difficult to detect. To address this, we propose that beyond standard supersymmetry, an additional $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry exists. In this framework, neutralinos acquire a non-zero charge, while all other particles remain uncharged. The LSP can then decay into a dark photon and other lighter particles; subsequently, the dark photon decays into a gamma ray. This decaying neutralino scenario, characterized by a dark photon lifetime of approximately $10^{19}$ seconds, predicts gamma rays with an exponential decay profile. This distinct signature could be observed by future space-based gamma-ray telescopes with high sensitivity. We demonstrate this mechanism within a TeV-scale supersymmetric framework and illustrate the resulting gamma-ray spectrum. This approach offers a novel perspective on dark matter detection through gamma rays and suggests a potential pathway to resolve the recent galactic center gamma-ray excess anomaly. Our findings indicate that the gamma-ray spectrum from decaying neutralinos is highly sensitive to the dark photon lifetime, with shorter lifetimes producing higher gamma-ray fluxes. Consequently, the most promising detection strategy involves searching for gamma rays with exponentially decaying spectra over a timescale of roughly $10^{19}$ seconds. The dark photon lifetime is determined by the mixing between the $U(1)_Y$ and $U(1)_X$ gauge bosons, which in turn fixes the gamma-ray time scale. This represents a unique feature of the neutralino decay scenario, providing a distinctive signature for dark matter searches. Furthermore, we show that the gamma-ray time scale can be precisely determined by analyzing the gamma-ray spectrum. Our study highlights the potential of gamma-ray observations to detect neutralino decay, thereby advancing our understanding of the nature of dark matter. The proposed scenario provides a new avenue for neutralino decay detection, with the primary challenge being the development of sufficiently sensitive gamma-ray instruments. Our findings suggest that future space-based telescopes with the necessary sensitivity could confirm neutralino decay and investigate its underlying mechanism. The exponential gamma-ray spectrum offers a unique signature that could potentially resolve the galactic center gamma-ray excess anomaly. This paper establishes an efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPTS) for the genus of dense graphs, implying that the genus of any dense graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges can be determined in $\tilde O(nm)$ time. This result enhances the current $O(nm)$ approximation algorithm proposed by M\"uckenheim and Sch\"afer [Dig.J.Comput.Geom. 39 (2016), 203--222]. Furthermore, the proposed method is straightforward and enables straightforward approximations for various dense graph invariants, such as the number of edges absent from all $K_\ell$ subgraphs. Specifically, counts related to these invocations can be computed in $\tilde O(nm)$ time. This result refines the recent findings by M\"uckenheim and Sch\"afer [arXiv:1801.00160], who demonstrated that any dense graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $K_\ell$ deficiency $def_G[K_\ell]$ can be approximately analyzed in $\tilde O(nm)$ time. Additionally, the algorithm identifies an embedding of $G$ in an orientable surface of genus $\tilde O(n + def_G[K_\ell])$, thereby offering an efficient approximation for the genus of dense graphs. Finally, the final section provides an open problem. Keywords: Graph genus, polynomial-time approximation scheme. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 05C10, 05C38, 05C35.

This paper introduces and analyzes a stochastic Newton approach for convex optimization, which is both robust and computationally efficient, making it particularly suitable for large-scale problems. The proposed method operates in two stages: initially, it estimates the inverse Hessian using Mohimani et al.'s method, utilizing a subset of all gradients; subsequently, it executes a standard Newton step. We demonstrate that this algorithm converges to the optimal solution at a rate of $O(1/k^2)$ in expectation, where $k$ represents the iteration number. Furthermore, we extend this approach to a distributed setting, proving that it retains the same convergence performance. Numerical experiments conducted on both small and large-scale benchmark datasets confirm the method's effectiveness and computational advantage. Additionally, we present an experimental comparison against other state-of-the-art algorithms to highlight its superior performance. Finally, we offer a comprehensive discussion on the algorithm's implementation and convergence behavior under various sampling strategies. Notably, we demonstrate that even with a single gradient, the proposed method outperforms traditional stochastic gradient descent. Our implementation is available at: \url{https://github.com/ehsan-mohimani/Distributed-Stochastic-Newton}. The accompanying video can be found at: \url{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4242222222}. Building upon this foundation, we are currently developing a paper that explores applications in convex clustering and dictionary learning. We are also extending this framework to non-convex optimization and have released a implementation available at \url{https://github.com/ehsan-mohimani/Distributed-Stochastic-Newton}. This study presents the first detailed investigation into training neural networks for detecting hate speech in the Hindi and Bengali languages. We developed the inaugural datasets for both languages by scraping and categorizing comments from Twitter and Facebook as either hateful or non-hateful. Following preprocessing and the construction of training and validation sets, we conducted experiments using both single and multi-task neural network architectures. Our findings indicate that a Bi-directional LSTM (BiLSTM) serving as both a feature extractor and classifier achieved the highest performance, reaching 91.5% accuracy for Hindi and 89.2% for Bengali on the test sets. Additionally, we explored transfer learning strategies by pre-training the BiLSTM on large English corpora, which yielded further improvements: 94.3% accuracy for Hindi and 91.2% for Bengali. These results demonstrate significant advancements over the current state-of-the-art. Finally, we examine the ethical challenges inherent in applying machine learning to hate speech detection and discuss the associated implications. The proposed methods and datasets are anticipated to be valuable for future research in this domain. Our code is accessible at: https://github.com/ashishkumar1234567890/Hindi-And-Bengali-Hate-Speech-Detection. The paper is available at arXiv:2001.06062 [cs.CL]. Detecting the direction of nuclear recoil is crucial for high-sensitivity dark matter direct detection experiments, as it could reveal the linear trajectories expected from WIMP interactions. To achieve this, researchers must analyze high-resolution, three-dimensional nuclear recoil tracks within a gas detector. However, the specific signal-to-no and other observables needed to distinguish WIMP recoils from background neutron events remain uncertain. This study utilizes Monte Carlo simulations of the complete experimental setup to investigate these observables for identifying the directional direction of recoiling nuclei in a gas time projection chamber. Our results demonstrate that the 3D spatial positions of recoil sites offer significant potential for identifying WIMP directions, though optimizing this requires combining them with other measured quantities. We introduce a novel set of observables designed for directional identification and show that existing datasets could support their evaluation. Furthermore, we examine the impact of detector resolution on reconstruction accuracy for these new observables. Finally, we assess the feasibility of determining WIMP directionality with future detectors, suggesting that even modest improvements in spatial resolution could substantially enhance the ability to detect the directional signature of WIMP recoils. These findings are directly applicable to the detection strategies of the upcoming DUNE-TPC and LIBRA experiments. Additionally, we introduce a new open-source Python toolkit, RecoilTrackID, to facilitate these analyses. This tool is publicly accessible at https://github.com/berkeleylab/RecoilTrackID. We conclude by outlining the anticipated performance of DUNE-TPC and LIBRA in reconstructing WIMP directions and estimating the resulting constraints on the local halo velocity distribution. Commercial driving represents a complex and hazardous activity influenced by numerous factors, such as weather, traffic, and road conditions. While automated vehicles are advancing, they still face challenges in replicating the performance of human drivers, particularly regarding safety and efficiency. Understanding the specific inputs that drive decisions is essential for automating vehicles and effectively interpreting their output. This paper introduces the concept of a Contextual Intelligent Decision (CID) system, a novel framework designed to automate complex vehicles by moderating automated decisions within the context of human expert knowledge. The system is a hybrid architecture featuring an expert moderation layer where human experts analyze the context of a decision and guide the automated system when its output diverges from human judgment. To address the specific needs of CID systems, we developed a new formal method for modeling context and contextual decisions using abstract input and output spaces. Furthermore, we created the first method for learning the learning process, enabling the moderation layer to dynamically adjust the weight of expert knowledge based on contextual conditions. The framework and learning methodology were validated through a simulation study involving 1,000 miles of commercial driving, which demonstrated that the CID system significantly outperforms an expert moderation layer with a static weighting scheme. These findings indicate that CID systems are a promising approach for enhancing the performance of contextual intelligent decisions in automated vehicles. The code and data required to replicate our results are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar2002/cid_systems. This paper addresses a challenge that split a corpus of 100,000 words, with 90,000 used for training and testing 10,000. Approximately 40% of the test vocabulary was out-of-vocabulary relative to the training set. The task required predicting the part-of-speech class for each word. The authors evaluated the performance of various machine learning algorithms, including CNN, RNN, and LSTM, as well as part-of-speech tagging tools like spaCy and the Brown tagging script. The study's primary finding is that predicting POS classes for LSTM-trained word embeddings yields superior results compared to using raw words. We conduct Rayleigh-Taylor Instability experiments by employing magnetic levitation to induce a controlled initial perturbation. We observe that the resulting exponential growth growth rate depends on the thickness of the fluid layers. Our findings indicate that this growth rate matches known literature values only when the layer thickness is small and varies significantly with increasing thickness, ultimately converging to the standard analytical limit at sufficiently large scales. We provide a partial explanation for these results by analyzing the two dominant length scales: the perturbation wavelength and the fluid layer thickness. Furthermore, we believe our experiments offer unique potential for developing machine learning models aimed at inferring literature-based growth rates, or conversely, training machine learning models to predict growth rates based on layer thickness and initial perturbation data for use in simulations. This latter capability offers distinct scientific value, as it addresses a long-standing challenge in plasma physics. We conclude by outlining our future research directions. A graph with $n$ vertices is defined as pancyclic if it includes cycles of every length $l$ where $3 \leq l \leq n$. This paper establishes a threshold $\alpha_0$ such that for any integer $\alpha$ satisfying $3 \leq \alpha \leq n-1$, a Hamiltonian, pancyclic graph $G$ possesses an independent set of size $\alpha$ provided that $n > \alpha_0$. Specifically, when $\alpha$ is even, $\alpha_0 = \frac{5\alpha^2}{16} + \alpha + 1$; when $\alpha$ is odd, $\alpha_0 = \frac{5\alpha^2}{16} + \frac{11\alpha}{8} + 3$. The bound is determined by the Petersen graph, which is the only pancyclic graph on 10 vertices with an independence number of 4. Additionally, the result demonstrates that the upper bound of $\alpha_0$ is tight. Finally, the findings are extended to biconvex graphs, yielding analogous results with distinct bounds. The analysis of biconvex graphs yields distinct upper bounds for $\alpha_0$ because these graphs cannot contain odd holes of length greater than 8. The adaptive spectral Koopman (ASK) method is introduced as a lightweight framework for real-time state estimation and prediction within nonlinear dynamical systems. Designed for high-dimensional continuous-state scenarios, the approach leverages sparse grid search to enhance computational efficiency. A new algorithm for determining the basis function order is also proposed to further optimize performance. Theoretical analysis confirms the asymptotic convergence of the estimated eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenfunctions. Through numerical simulations and experiments on a magnetic levitation system, the method's effectiveness is demonstrated. Results indicate that the ASK approach outperforms traditional Prony methods in convergence speed and achieves superior accuracy compared to extended Kalman filter-based predictive controllers under measurement noise. Furthermore, it is concluded that this technique is computationally efficient and well-suited for practical applications. Additionally, the study addresses potential limitations regarding model order selection and parameter identification under noisy conditions, offering guidance for future research. Finally, the anticipated advantages of the ASK method are highlighted for future developments in nonlinear dynamical systems, including real-time prediction, state estimation, and predictive control. The exterior complex scaling (ECS) method within the time-dependent Schrödinger (TDSE) framework has been employed to investigate the ionization dynamics of atoms and molecules subjected to intense direct current (DC) fields. Utilizing ECS, the model potentials are transformed into the complex plane, yielding wavefunctions that are square-integrable and extend beyond the real domain. This approach enables the accurate calculation of ionization probabilities and energy spectra. As an application, we examine the ionization of atomic hydrogen and helium as well as molecular hydrogen under DC fields. The computed ionization rates align well with analytical predictions derived from the tunneling probability formula. Furthermore, the spectra generated via ECS match those obtained from the split-operator method. Additionally, the ECS approach facilitates the study of DC-field-induced bound state shifts toward the complex energy plane. These findings demonstrate that ECS serves as a highly effective tool for analyzing ionization processes in strong DC fields for both atomic and molecular systems. Ultimately, this methodology offers a valuable alternative to conventional time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) techniques typically applied to periodic systems under similar conditions. Consequently, ECS holds significant promise for a broad spectrum of applications in atomic, molecular, and solid-state physics. The Sinkhorn algorithm is the leading approach for addressing the Schrödinger problem; however, this problem is not guaranteed to possess a solution in every instance. This paper demonstrates that, despite the absence of a solution, the Sinkhorn algorithm may still converge to a limit, and we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for this convergence. These findings generalize earlier work by \cite{Carlier2010} and advance recent research by \cite{Chen2020} and Liu, Wang, and Zhou \cite{Liu2020}. The study is grounded in a novel methodology for analyzing the evolution of entropic regularized optimal transport plans via coupled Otto-Varentsov calculus. Furthermore, we investigate what occurs when a solution exists, revealing novel and significant properties of Sinkhorn trajectories in this scenario. Specifically, we demonstrate that Sinkhorn iterates converge weakly to a limiting optimal transport plan, and for the first time, we prove the uniqueness of this limit. These results represent a substantial advancement over prior findings by \cite{Santambrogio2020}. Additionally, our framework enables a new perspective on the relationship between the Schrödinger problem and classical optimal transport. Notably, when the two marginal measures differ, we show that the Sinkhorn algorithm converges to a limit that coincides with an optimal plan for the classical optimal transport problem between these marginals. This result aligns with recent numerical observations by Carlier, Genovese, and Maurel-Segala \cite{Carlier2021}. Finally, we present a counterexample illustrating that, even in classical optimal transport, the iterates of the Sinkhorn algorithm may fail to converge weakly to a unique limit. To address this, we propose an alternative algorithm that converges weakly to a limit and, under an extra condition, ensures strong convergence to a unique limit. This alternative method is closely related to the Sinkhorn algorithm. The proofs utilize a combination of techniques from both probability and harmonic analysis. Urban interactions are vital for social, cultural, and economic activities, yet it remains unclear whether the pandemic-induced shifts in human behavior altered the income diversity of urban encounters. This study addresses the question of how behavioral changes during the pandemic impacted the income diversity of urban meetings. By analyzing the movement patterns of 500,000 individuals across .USA using mobile device data from 2018 to 2021, we examined meeting income diversity across various urban areas in the United States. Our findings indicate that pre-pandemic, diverse income encounters were more frequent in areas with high meeting density, a relationship that weakened during the pandemic. Additionally, we observed that the correlation between diverse income encounters and meeting density was stronger in outdoor settings than in indoor ones. These results suggest that the pandemic's impact on income diversity was more pronounced indoors. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the diversity of income encountered was greater in evening meetings than in those held during the day. Finally, we determined that the correlation between meeting density and income diversity was higher in late-night encounters. Overall, these observations imply that the pandemic's effect on income diversity was more significant in the late night. These insights highlight the extent to which behavioral changes during the pandemic influenced income diversity in urban encounters. Finally, we conclude that the pandemic's impact on income diversity was more pronounced among late-night encounters.

This study introduces two nonlinear field-split preconditioners designed for two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media, alongside their linear counterparts previously developed by the authors. The assessment considered performance metrics such as iteration counts, computational time, and robustness regarding model parameters like wettability, capillary pressure, and relative permeability. Results indicate that the classical fully implicit preconditioner and its linear variant perform best under strong heterogeneity and favorable parameter configurations. However, when strong heterogeneity is combined with unfavorable conditions, the nonlinear field-split preconditioner demonstrates superior robustness and efficiency compared to the other three approaches. Finally, the convergence and efficiency of all four preconditioners were analyzed in relation to these model parameters. These findings are supported by extensive numerical experiments. Ultimately, the study concludes that the field-split preconditioner—whether linear or saturation-based—outperforms the classical fully implicit approach for two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media when capillary pressure and/or wettability are unfavorable. Furthermore, the comparison between linear and classical fully implicit methods highlights that the linear version is more sensitive to parameters like permeability contrast, residual saturations, and the number of time steps. The Alcubierre metric defines a spacetime geometry enabling superluminal travel via a "warp drive," simulated as a compact region of spacetime contracting ahead of and expanding behind a specific trajectory known as the "warp bubble." This study demonstrates that the Alcubierre metric constitutes a valid solution to the Einstein equations when coupled with the cosmological constant. Building on this foundation, we introduce a novel metric that extends the Alcubierre concept to include spherically symmetric warp bubbles. For both general and spherical variants, we show that the cosmological constant is the sole term capable of generating the necessary spacetime geometry without requiring the energy-condition-violating negative energy densities typically deemed essential for warp drive mechanisms. Notably, the spherical warp bubble produces a stationary spacetime, whereas the Alcubierre metric yields a non-stationary configuration. Furthermore, we provide explicit calculations of the energy required for warp bubbles of various sizes and translation or rotation velocities using the Alcubierre metric. Finally, we offer insights into the link between spherical warp bubbles and the formation of black holes. Collectively, these findings suggest that achieving warp drive is potentially more feasible than previously believed. These results also hold significant implications for cosmology, as spherical warp bubbles could represent a viable mechanism for dark matter and dark energy phenomena. Additionally, the paper includes an extensive appendix detailing the derivation of the extended Alcubierre metric and its associated source terms. These contributions pave the way for groundbreaking advancements in theoretical physics, mathematics, and engineering, ultimately advancing humanity's pursuit of interstellar space travel.

We introduce GUIDES, a novel open-source framework designed to generate, manage, and access digital representations of urban infrastructure systems. This tool is especially valuable for large-scale, city-wide systems such as water, sewer, and road networks. Currently, most open-source geospatial processing tools are limited to processing only subsets of these systems. GUIDES overcomes this limitation by enabling the automated, bulk creation, management, and querying of extensive urban infrastructure datasets. The software is structured into three primary components: (1) a data preparation module for the automated bulk creation and import of infrastructure features, (2) a data management module for maintaining and updating datasets, and (3) a data query module for executing large-scale spatial and attribute-based queries. To demonstrate its capabilities, we applied GUIDES to a real-world case study involving the integration, processing, and querying of the entire road network of the city of Turin, Italy. GUIDES is freely accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/GUIDES-software/GUIDES. Further details can be found in our publication in ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information, 2021. https://doi.org/10.3390/jgi6010008. Our demonstration video is available on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=41411411140. The source code for this software is licensed under the GNU General Public License v3.0. This tool is intended for scientific and educational purposes. While GUIDES is not yet a production-ready solution, it is highly promising for integration into future geospatial data processing and access platforms. We aim for the community to leverage GUIDES to facilitate the processing and analysis of large-scale urban infrastructure data. We anticipate that this will significantly enhance the capabilities of existing geospatial software and support various applications, including urban mobility and transportation planning, flood risk assessment, and the analysis of urban mobility mobility patterns. Finally, we believe this will contribute to achieving the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goal 11, which focuses on making cities and human settlements more sustainable. Furthermore, this method serves as a diagnostic tool to monitor the evolution of motional state distributions in large ion chains over extended periods, facilitating an analysis of energy transfer between neighboring ions.
