These capabilities establish spin dephasing as a sensitive probe of the energy sources driving ion crystal heating. Terminally enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS) is recognized as the most effective technique for analyzing the chemical bonds of nanoscale regions. This study employs fully quantum mechanical methods to simulate and rationalize the extreme signal enhancements observed in TERS. We demonstrate that these enhancements arise from the simultaneous interaction of electromagnetic and electromagnetic field-induced dipole scattering within the tip-adsorbate system. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the local field experienced by the adsorbate is significantly amplified due to excitonic resonances in either the tip or the adsorbate, or both. We validate these results using gold tips and benzene adsorbates, providing additional data for gold and silver nanoparticles as well as benzene and ethyne as adsorbates. Additionally, we confirm that both p- and pi-polarized light can excite the benzene mode, though with markedly different levels of enhancement. These insights deepen our understanding of TERS and offer a robust theoretical framework for future advancements in this field. Notably, the code utilized in this study is openly accessible for application to other material systems. Finally, we provide a comprehensive comparison between TERS and conventional Raman spectroscopy. Specifically, we examine the influence of substrate plasmons on local field enhancement and explicitly address the impact of substrate symmetry on light-phonon coupling. These conclusions are supported by extensive calculations conducted on graphene, benzene, and ethyne systems. The computational code used is available for download at [1]. The source code can also be accessed via the following link: [2].

We conducted observations of 25 nearby galaxies using the Sardinia Radio Telescope to detect Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) at 17.5 and 21.5 GHz. These galaxies were selected from a comprehensive survey of 100 nearby systems carried out at 8.5 and 17.5 GHz with the same facility. Our findings reveal a positive correlation between AME and the 17.5 GHz flux density, which aligns with theoretical expectations. Additionally, the data indicate that AME is more intense in spiral galaxies than in ellipticals. We also established an upper limit on the AME fraction of the total emission at 17.5 GHz, determining it to be 40% for spiral galaxies and less than 10% for ellipticals. Furthermore, the ratio of AME to the 17.5 GHz flux density shows no significant dependence on metallicity, luminosity, or redshift. Finally, we report the first detection of AME in the elliptical galaxy NGC 4569. These results offer valuable insights for upcoming AME surveys utilizing SKA and other large radio telescopes. The complete dataset from this survey will be made available to the scientific community. Ammonium sulfate ((NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$) exhibits a large entropy change ($\Delta s$) correlated with ferroelectric phase transitions, yet its underlying mechanism remains unclear. In this study, we utilize ab initio calculations to investigate the origins of $\Delta s$ during the BCT-to-NC3P and tetragonal-to-NC3P transitions. Our analysis reveals that the electronic entropy change ($\Delta s_{el}$) is negligible, whereas both lattice and volumetric entropy changes ($\Delta s_{lat}$ and $\Delta s_{vol}$) are substantial. We demonstrate that both BCT-to-NC3P and tetragonal-to-NC3P transitions are driven by a second-order Jahn-Teller (SOT) distortion, which generates significant lattice entropy. Furthermore, a detailed examination of the symmetry-adapted modes associated with these transitions indicates that the mode responsible for $\Delta s_{lat}$ is not directly involved in the SOT distortion. These findings offer a novel perspective on the origins of $\Delta s$ in caloric and ferroelectric materials. Finally, we explore the potential of a nitrate-based analogue, (NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_3$, as a promising molecular caloric material. This work underscores the utility of advanced theoretical methods in elucidating the mechanisms of caloric effects and designing optimal molecular caloric compounds. Ultimately, this research establishes a new paradigm for understanding the origins of caloric effects in materials. Predictive reinforcement learning is shaped by the balance between exploration and exploitation, a process governed by the magnitude of predicted reward errors. Yet, the nature of this exploration-exploitation trade-off and its relationship with prediction error remain unclear. To address this, we developed a method to categorize behavioral strategies within a Bayesian reinforcement learning framework and applied it to healthy participants. Our results indicate that the adoption of a suboptimal strategy correlates with a diminished sensitivity to prediction error in the midbrain. Furthermore, an association between the exploratory strategy and cortical midbrain functional connectivity suggests that pre-existing brain network configurations influence individual differences in learning. These findings offer new insights into the role of prediction errors in exploration and their underlying neural mechanisms. Notably, this behavioral variant, characterized by a higher propensity for suboptimal strategies, mirrors clinical manifestations seen in disorders such as OCD, addiction, and eating disorders. This suggests that individuals with high behavioral suboptimality may be particularly susceptible to developing maladaptive learning patterns when exposed to maladaptive environments. Consequently, recognizing one's exploratory style could be valuable for optimizing therapeutic interventions. Finally, our study demonstrates how a theoretical learning model can be integrated with neuroimaging to investigate the neural mechanisms of behavioral variants. By linking behavioral data with midbrain and functional connectivity metrics, our approach offers a versatile framework for uncovering the neural basis of individual differences in learning. Ultimately, our findings underscore the need to investigate the underlying neural mechanisms of suboptimal learning in various disorders to better understand how maladaptive behaviors are acquired and treated. By examining the midbrain's role in generating suboptimal strategies, our work may pave the way for developing new neuromodulation techniques aimed at reducing maladaptive behaviors. By separating real and imaginary components, we demonstrate that the 240 roots of $E_8$ can be partitioned into 60 sets of four, where each set forms a quantum Varshney code. This work paves the way for establishing the existence of both computable combinatorial quantum error-correcting codes and lattice quantum error-correcting codes based on the $E_8$ lattice and its complex variant. Furthermore, we prove that the rank-4 projectors corresponding to these 240 roots of $E_8$ are valid quantum observables and are mutually anti-commutative. Our findings indicate that the 240 rank-4 projectors associated with the 60 tetrahedral sets of 4 roots of $E_8$ are non-contextual, whereas the remaining 1,056 rank-4 projectors for the non-tetrahedral sets of 4 roots are contextual. This result is significant because the 240 rank-4 projectors for the four-element sets of roots of $E_8$ constitute a collection of rank-n projectors that are pairwise mutually orthogonal. This research investigates the core challenge of multilevel approximate near-neighbor searching for collections of time series under the Fréchet distance. We introduce a straightforward and efficient algorithm for linear-length curves that achieves a 2-approximation while offering an arbitrary factor $k$ in sublinear time. Specifically, this approach constructs a hierarchy of time series data structures with a depth of $\log_k n$, where $n$ denotes the input size. At each level $i$, the algorithm builds a index of dimension $k^i$ with a space complexity of $O(n/\log_n)$. Consequently, query time complexity is expressed as $O(k^q \cdot \frac{n}{\log_k n})$. Finally, we extend these findings to address various extensions of the problem. Notably, we demonstrate that our approach can be adapted to handle time series of arbitrary lengths while sustaining an $r$-approximation guarantee for a specific level of precision. Furthermore, our method extends to dynamic settings, enabling efficient insertion and deletion of time series within the collection. Additionally, we generalize our results to support weighted near-neighbor queries, where the objective is to identify a time series within the given collection whose weight multiplied by the distance to the query time series yields the minimum value. This capability holds significant practical relevance, as it facilitates the integration of external information regarding time series, such as their origin or associated metadata. Overall, this work extends the classical Hamming metric framework to address a substantially more complex problem arising in a widely applied domain. Furthermore, we extend our findings to a broader context by considering time series under the Fréchet distance with sublinear tolerance. This approach not only generalizes our findings but also extends the classical Hamming metric framework to a more complex problem. Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a real-world application: a near neighbor search engine for DNA sequences. Our method supports queries up to 10% inhomogeneous with respect to the edit distance, operating at a fraction of the speed required by existing near-neighbor search algorithms designed for sequences under the Hamming metric. This indicates that the proposed approach is highly effective for solving practical instances of this problem. Our implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedfouad1999/ANN-searcher. Measurement Error Mitigation (MEM) refers to postprocessing methods designed to address systematic readout errors in quantum computers. While existing MEM techniques offer error correction capabilities that surpass error tolerance thresholds of unmitigated data, they are currently limited to small-scale experiments due to their high computational complexity. This work introduces a scalable mitigation strategy employing a Bayesian unfolding model to correct quantum computer measurements. We evaluate this approach against state-of-the-art methods using both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating that our method matches or exceeds the performance of current benchmarks while offering significant scalability advantages. Furthermore, we provide open-source implementation code for the proposed algorithm. Finally, we apply this mitigation technique to quantum tomography experiments, achieving high-fidelity reconstructions of multi-qubit density matrices from highly noisy data. Source code is available at https://github.com/quantum-machine-learning/mem.

This study investigates shared autonomy as a mechanism for solving the communication games problem, which explores how the shared understanding of a group influences the outcomes of communication games. In this context, a shared convention emerges when players cannot directly access the specific shared understanding held by others. We demonstrate that shared autonomy helps resolve this issue by enabling players to dynamically learn and adapt their strategies based on the shared understanding prevalent within their social group. Furthermore, experimental results indicate that shared autonomy facilitates the game-solving process more efficiently than either central coordination or distributed learning methods alone. These findings suggest that shared autonomy holds significant potential for enhancing human-robot teaming capabilities. The study includes detailed game-theoretic analyses and empirical results derived from both simulations and human-subject experiments. The accompanying video showcases a distributed learning approach to shared autonomy applied to a communication game involving teams of two. This game requires partners to coordinate their actions to identify the most profitable target, but they are constrained by a shared but private understanding of which target is actually most beneficial. Consequently, teams must adjust their strategies to align with their shared understanding of high-value targets. We observe that teams utilizing the distributed learning approach are better equipped to adapt their strategies to their shared understanding, thereby increasing the likelihood of selecting the most profitable target. This result underscores the value of distributed learning in fostering effective shared understanding between team members. Additionally, our results show that this approach enables teams to achieve higher profits and generate more accurate predictions of the target that will ultimately be chosen. The video demonstrates that these outcomes are realized without the need for explicit discussion between partners. Instead, the robot partner infers the human's shared understanding through observation and adjusts its strategy via reinforcement learning. This process mirrors human learning behaviors, as users reported feeling that the robot acted as if it could "read their mind." The experiment also involved a user study with 20 participants, revealing that human subjects preferred interacting with robots capable of learning their shared understanding, as this improved the robot's performance and made task completion easier. Autonomous navigation within unknown settings is crucial for mobile robots, yet it remains difficult due to the accumulation of errors from sensor noise and localization inaccuracies. Conventional topological maps simplify this by representing the environment as nodes (locations) and edges (passable paths), but these often fail in unknown settings because they lack a hierarchical structure, do not capture submaps, and cannot adapt to new obstacles. This paper introduces HiTMap, a novel representation that defines map nodes as significant topological features—such as corners, openings, and intersections—and creates a hierarchical structure through clustering. When encountering new obstacles, HiTMap updates the map by adding virtual edges to adjust the clustering, thereby forming submaps. Furthermore, to enhance exploration in unexplored areas, the system weights edges based on the minimum distance to the robot's current exploration frontiers. Experimental results demonstrate that HiTMap effectively captures the topology of unknown environments, accommodates new obstacles, and prioritizes exploration, ultimately reducing path lengths and improving exploration efficiency. Additionally, simulations and real-world tests show that HiTMap can plan routes and avoid obstacles in dynamically changing environments. The source code and data are accessible at https://github.com/hiitlab/HiTMap. The rapid advancement of wireless communication technology has created a growing demand for low-interference transmission, driving the development of various complementary array code sets. This paper introduces a multivariable function-based construction method for multigroup Z-complementary array code sets (ZCACs) utilizing multivariable functions and group-wise convolution. By employing a multivariable function with specific parameters, we first generate inter-group Z-complementary sequence sets (ZCSSs) through a direct method. Subsequently, a two-dimensional ZCAC set (2DZCAC) is derived from these ZCSSs. The characteristics of the inter-group ZCACs significantly influence the parameters of the resulting 2DZCACs. To enhance the parameters of the 2DZCACs, we utilize group-wise convolution to expand the inter-group ZCACs, thereby generating expanded sets of 2DZCACs. Finally, we provide examples of these expanded 2DZCAC sets and validate the proposed method through computer simulations. These simulations demonstrate that the sets can achieve near-zero peak side-lobe levels and near-zero peak autocorrelation levels, confirming the feasibility and effectiveness of the approach. Additionally, numerical analysis indicates that the number of groups can be flexibly adjusted based on the parameters of the multivariable function. Consequently, the 2DZCAC sets offer high transmission efficiency and a large search space, making them well-suited for next-generation wireless communication systems. The algorithms are straightforward, and the computational complexity remains low. The proposed approach holds significant application potential and broad utility. Furthermore, the parameters of the 2DZCAC sets are highly tunable, allowing for optimization to meet the specific requirements of different application scenarios. This paper thus provides a new reference for the application of 2DZCACs in wireless communication systems. The algorithms are simple, the computational complexity is low, and the code sets exhibit large parameters and high transmission efficiency. This study examines how electron spill-out and nonlocality influence light propagation within the gap separating two semi-infinite metallic regions. Our findings indicate that such electron confinement causes light propagation in this narrow gap to diverge significantly from behavior observed in single-metal systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating a nonlocal dielectric response offers a viable approach to plasmonic modes with remarkably low losses. These insights regarding the impact of electron confinement and nonlocality on plasmonic modes in ultra-narrow gaps may prove instrumental in designing future devices featuring exceptionally large photonic phase shifts and slow-light velocities. To achieve these results, we employed a combination of theoretical methods, including solving the wave equation for dielectrics and metals with local and nonlocal dielectric functions, solving Lippmann-Schwinger type integral equations, and applying a newly developed approximate method for handling electron spill-out at metal-dielectric interfaces. The validity of our theoretical approach was confirmed by validating its predictions against existing experimental data. Finally, our work introduces a novel technique for calculating the dielectric response of bulk metals when subjected to strong quantum confinement forces. This method enables the calculation of the dielectric function between two parallel plates and across a single plate, a capability essential for accurately modeling the response of confined electrons to an external electromagnetic field. We have also applied this method to determine the dielectric function of a dielectric material confined between two parallel plates. The validity of this theoretical approach was verified by comparing its predictions with results from first-principles calculations. This paper introduces a method for Named Entity Retrieval (NER) that utilizes a single free-text query to retrieve entities from a large-scale knowledge base, such as DBpedia. Unlike previous approaches that depend on precomputed entity embeddings, our context-aware framework determines relevance by analyzing entity representations derived from their surrounding linguistic and semantic context. Specifically, we estimate the relevance of entities to the user's intent by calculating the distributional similarity between the entity names and the words within the query context. We evaluate and refine the approach using a benchmark dataset and compare it against a knowledge-based baseline, demonstrating its effectiveness. Additionally, we provide a web interface to showcase the functionality of the implemented system. The code is available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar1997/term-relevance-feeedback-for-nerr. Temporal data constitutes a fundamental component of temporal processes, with time series and longitudinal data being particularly common. However, presenting and analyzing these datasets can be complex, often requiring the simultaneous management of multiple related observations. This difficulty is addressed through multivariate data visualization, which leverages visual variables to encode individual data points. Despite these methods making it easier to identify patterns and anomalies, their lack of interactivity restricts their analytical potential. This thesis introduces a framework for creating high-quality, interactive displays of multivariate time series and longitudinal data, grounded in established data visualization theory. By integrating interactivity, this approach offers novel solutions for visual pattern recognition and analysis. The resulting framework has been implemented and evaluated across three distinct use cases, demonstrating its broad applicability and utility. Key innovations include: (i) a new interactive method for visualizing time series datasets, (b) a novel technique for interactivity-based outlier analysis, and (ii) a new strategy for interactivity-supported pattern analysis. These methods are supported by a set of design guidelines that facilitate a more effective visual analysis of multivariate time series and longitudinal data. The effectiveness of this work was validated by practitioners across diverse application domains. Furthermore, users have adopted these tools for their own interactive visual analysis, and the core concepts have been extended in various ways. Ultimately, this thesis advances the state of the art in multivariate time series and longitudinal data visualization by providing a robust, practical, and widely applicable framework for visualization, interactivity, and analysis. The richness of information within Electronic Health Records (EHRs) offers immense potential for enhancing disease diagnosis and prediction. While recent approaches utilizing health ontologies and EHR similarity graphs have shown promise, they often fail to capture patient-specific variations in symptom presentation and diagnosis. To address this limitation, we introduce the Heterogeneous Similarity Graph Neural Network (HSSGNN), which leverages a patient-specific heterogeneous EHR similarity graph. This study employs molecular dynamics simulations to examine how solvent polarization influences the electric double layer (EDL) forming around a charged soft surface within an electrolyte solution. Specifically, the impact of the isoelectric point of the soft macromolecular chain on EDL structure was investigated. Our findings indicate that the maximum surface charge of the polymer significantly influences EDL characteristics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that when the macromolecule's side groups are uncharged, the EDL structure remains largely unaffected by variations in the polarizability of the simulation water model. Conversely, when negatively charged groups are present, a higher polarizability of the simulation water model results in a more expanded EDL. These observations align with the fact that the effective charge of the macromolecule increases under these conditions. Additionally, we confirm that increasing the surface area of the macromolecular brush leads to a greater number of counterions. Finally, our results indicate that the EDL structure is sensitive to macromolecular brush asymmetry, which is consistent with the known impact of this factor on the osmotic pressure of the EDL. Overall, this research provides new insights into the complex interactions between the EDL and charged soft surfaces. Furthermore, it introduces a novel approach to modeling the charge distribution of the EDL, moving beyond the traditional assumption of a constant charge density on the soft surface. This paper introduces a new cooperative network coding protocol designed to minimize transmission energy by simultaneously accounting for the source's coding decision energy and the relays' adaptation costs for power and scheduling. To achieve this, a non-convex minimization problem is formulated to find the optimal trade-off among three key factors: source transmission energy, total relay adaptation energy, and successful destination decoding probability. Since a closed-form solution is unattainable, an efficient algorithm is developed to solve the minimization and determine the network coding protocol that yields the most energy-efficient cooperative communication. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed energy-efficient network coding protocol outperforms both the fixed network coding protocol and traditional amplify-and-forward relaying in terms of energy efficiency. Furthermore, the study reveals a critical balance between source transmission energy and total relay adaptation energy, indicating that excessive relay investment in power adaptation can degrade overall energy efficiency. Finally, the paper concludes that adapting the network coding scheme is essential for achieving energy-efficient cooperative communication. These findings are robust and hold true regardless of the specific network topology. Additionally, the proposed methodology is applicable to other joint scheduling and power allocation problems, such as those involving relay selection. Finally, the approach is extendable to multiuser scenarios, including sum-rate maximization and fair rate allocation. **Index Terms:** Energy efficiency, joint relay scheduling and power allocation, network coding.

We introduce a fully relativistic, first-principles theoretical framework designed to calculate the spectral properties of magnetic impurities situated on superconducting surfaces, with a specific focus on Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states. By self-consistently solving the Kohn--Rostoker--Slater--Mochizuki (KRSM) equations, we determine the local density of states within a first-principles model of two coupled superconductors. Our theory is employed to examine the YSR states exhibited by a Mn adatom and a Mn dimer on the Nb(110) surface, which exists in a superconducting state. We demonstrate that the spin-polarized scattering of a spin-triplet Cooper pair from the superconductor onto the magnetic impurity states generates these YSR states. For the Mn dimer, our theory predicts the emergence of YSR states arising from triplet Andreev bound states localized on the system. Distribution-to-distribution (D2D) registration is a robust and versatile technique that does not depend on specific object features, making it applicable to diverse scenarios. However, it often suffers from significant bias, leading to inaccurate 3D reconstruction and localization. While deep learning has recently been employed to reduce this bias, current D2D scan matching methods utilizing deep learning still face limitations. Specifically, D2D registration generates pointwise log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) that are typically heavily skewed, causing most points to cluster near zero. Consequently, deep learning models trained on these raw LLRs must be optimized to handle this severe distribution shift. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective filter designed to correct the distribution of D2D LLRs before they are input into a deep learning model. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach enhances the performance of existing methods and yields a more reliable solution. The proposed method is implemented in PyTorch and is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhongtao1992/d2dreg. Additionally, all necessary raw data for reproducing the experimental findings can be downloaded from the same repository. We anticipate that this work will be valuable to researchers in the field. Satellite imagery is frequently utilized to track land surface changes, such as urban expansion. However, this process is often complicated by non-surface features like tree canopies, clouds, and haze, which distort the radiometry reaching the sensor. While numerous algorithms exist for processing satellite data—including both classical and deep learning approaches—this paper proposes a distinct alternative: detecting edges in satellite images without relying on deep neural networks. The method demonstrates comparable performance in identifying major features like roads, rivers, and fields, particularly at high spatial resolutions. Furthermore, the authors provide code for their approach at https://github.com/jose-fernandez/ED4SAT. By avoiding deep learning, this technique offers greater interpretability, as it depends on established image processing concepts. Specifically, the work introduces modifications to the Sobel filter and anisotropic diffusion to detect edges and mask regions in satellite images. The authors also present results from an evaluation comparing their method against the OpenCV Canny Sobel filter, HED network, DeepEdge network, and U-Net. Additionally, they explore the integration of their approach with DeepEdge and HED networks, showing that combining both anisotropic and learned filters can detect features larger than those achievable by either component alone. Finally, the study examines an application involving the masking of non-land areas like clouds and haze in images captured by the Sentinel-2 satellite. Although anisotropic diffusion is commonly applied to natural images, this paper demonstrates its effectiveness for the first time in processing satellite imagery. Overall, the research indicates that anisotropic and local filters are well-suited for processing satellite images, and that combining these filters with learned ones can enhance the detection of features larger than the ones identified by either method independently. Overall, this work shows that: (i) a simple, non-learned edge detector can achieve results comparable to deep learning methods in segmenting large features like roads, rivers, and fields, (ii) anisotropic and local filters are well-suited for processing satellite imagery, and (iii) combining anisotropic and local edge detection with deep learning methods can enhance the detection of features larger than those identified by either approach alone. We introduce a new approach to modeling time-resolved X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) for systems with high fluence pump pulses. This modeling rate equation (MRE) captures the dynamics of the x-ray absorbing population across both spatial and temporal domains. The MRE is derived from fundamental equations governing electron populations, offering a more intuitive framework for comparing experimental data with rate equation descriptions. Its validity has been confirmed through tests involving a simple two-level system exposed to a high-fluence square-pulse excitation source. Additionally, the MRE offers a practical method for modeling experimental setups, such as those used in an optical delay line. This method facilitates the quantification of pump pulse effects on x-ray absorption parameters, including linear absorption coefficients and excited-state lifetimes. Furthermore, we outline an optimization strategy designed to efficiently fit experimental data using the MRE. Finally, we demonstrate how to analyze MRE-derived fits to extract fundamental electron population rate equations. These findings are expected to be applicable to a broad spectrum of material systems and experimental configurations. Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly deployed for automatic modulation classification (AMC) due to their superior accuracy and resilience against adversarial attacks compared to conventional methods. However, most existing research relies on DNN architectures trained on adversarially robust features, making them susceptible to adversarial perturbations. This paper introduces a novel architecture designed to maintain performance after model compression. By utilizing generative adversarial networks (GANs) and a mixture model of neural networks, the proposed model achieves state-of-the-art adversarial robustness. The GAN component reduces the original model's parameter count by filtering out redundant parameters, while the mixture model architecture balances performance and prediction confidence. Evaluation results demonstrate that the model compresses an input size from 1024 to 128 with lossy reconstruction while retaining accuracy. Furthermore, under comparable compression rates achieved through parameter sharing, the mixture model structure ensures consistent behavior and avoids overconfidence in classification outputs. Consequently, the proposed architecture significantly enhances robustness against adversarial attacks. Additionally, the model exhibits resilience against channel fading effects, outperforming state-of-the-art AMC methods in both AWGN and Rayleigh fading environments. This approach is applicable to both constant envelope and non-constant envelope modulations. Notably, in fading channels, the model achieves a 10% performance gain over state-of-the-art AMC techniques. Finally, the proposed architecture is robust against data poisoning attacks. To address this, the paper introduces a new method for selecting generator networks within the GAN module to ensure system reliability. This reliability mechanism is validated through adversarial training within a GAN framework. Experimental outcomes confirm that the mixture model maintains performance after back-propagation training, whereas the generator network's performance degrades under the same conditions. These findings underscore the proposed model's robustness against data poisoning threats. Overall, the study demonstrates the efficacy of mixture models and GANs as adaptive components that substantially improve the robustness of DNN-based AMC against adversarial attacks. Segmentation models for medical images are typically trained on datasets from a single institution, yet in practice, they are often deployed across various hospitals. This segmentation task is particularly challenging due to the high degree of inter- and intra-class variability in MRI scans across different institutions, which significantly hinders the performance of models trained on single-hospital data. To address this, continual learning has emerged as a promising technique for sequentially integrating knowledge from multiple data sources. This study investigates the application of continual learning to brain tumor segmentation and demonstrates its potential for segmenting brain lesions across multiple hospitals. The results indicate that continual learning can enhance generalization across diverse hospitals and yield superior performance compared to retraining from scratch after each new hospital's data is incorporated, thereby offering a viable solution for large-scale tumor segmentation. We introduce a novel metric comparison, analogous to Alexandrov's, and demonstrate its significant links to the doubling property, Sobolev inequalities, and Poincaré inequalities within metric measure spaces. Specifically, a complete comparison geometry is introduced for metric spaces; a non-negative complete comparison geometry ensures the doubling property of the associated metric measure space, while a negative complete comparison geometry yields the reverse. Furthermore, both a non-negative and a negative complete comparison geometry can be derived from the curvature-dimension condition $CD(0,\infty)$, though this implication does not hold in general without these conditions. Additionally, we establish that the Alexandrov curvature of a bipolar comparison is tightly linked to the curvature dimension, offering a novel perspective on complete curvature. The concept of complete curvature was originally proposed by the second author in reference [10]. This paper expands upon that bipolar comparison framework to derive tight, meaningful, and practical results. Future research will apply complete comparison and complete curvature to comparison geometry and comparison statistics. Statistical applications of bipolar comparison and complete curvature are detailed in our subsequent work [11, 12]. For the comparison statistics introduced in [11, 12], the resulting statistical inference is complete, as proven in [2]. These findings will be the subject of a separate publication. Model error is a fundamental aspect of mathematical and physical models. This error originates from the simplifications made when abstracting real-world phenomena into idealized representations and can be viewed as a complex, unknown function dependent on the state variables of the system. This paper presents a framework for applying machine learning to learn this model error. The approach utilizes dynamic systems to represent both the true physical system and the mathematical model, employing state filters to estimate the states of both systems using observations. The model error is subsequently defined as the discrepancy between the estimates produced by the mathematical model and the true system. We demonstrate this framework using a simple 0-D heat transfer model, which is also a common climate model. Our results indicate that the proposed method can effectively estimate model error for this system. Finally, we outline the advantages of this approach for modeling real-world systems and suggest potential extensions for future research. Specifically, we demonstrate that the framework can accommodate non-linear models and varying parameter values. These capabilities are particularly significant for global modeling efforts, as model error is highly sensitive to the specific values of parameters such as latitude, longitude, and altitude. Furthermore, model error can be leveraged to enhance the accuracy of mathematical models of complex systems. We illustrate how this utilization of model error will inform the selection of essential features and mechanisms for climate models in future studies. To achieve this, we introduce a framework for global climate modeling that uses model error to identify the critical features and mechanisms necessary for accurate global climate models. We demonstrate that models incorporating model error are more sensitive to changes in specific features and mechanisms, thereby providing a means to identify the most critical components for global climate models. Finally, we show that models incorporating model error are less sensitive to variations in parameter values, which assists researchers in determining the most critical parameters for climate models. These findings have significant implications for global climate modeling, as they underscore the necessity of including model error and highlight the essential mechanisms and parameters that require further investigation. This approach is especially pertinent to global climate modeling, as it addresses the issue of parameterization, which involves approximating the effects of small-scale features and mechanisms that are not explicitly resolved in coarse-resolution global climate models. We present high-resolution (0.15 arcsec) 1.2 mm dust emission images of the Dragon infrared dark cloud (IC 59), a young massive cluster located in the Cygnus OB2-12 complex. By analyzing dust emission, we identified 105 cores with radii exceeding 100 AU. Core masses range from 0.01 to 100 M$_\odot$, with a mean growth rate of 0.0003 M$_\odot$/yr. Our findings indicate that 22% of Dragon's mass resides in these dust emission cores, with the most massive core reaching 100 M$_\odot$. We observed that the two core growth rates correlate with both dust temperature and mass surface density, suggesting that core growth is driven by dust temperature and mass surface density. This evidence of core growth supports the concept of a massive star-forming core, a key component of the inside-out scenario for massive star formation. Additionally, we detected a core with a dust temperature of 30 K and a growth rate of 0.0015 M$_\odot$/yr near the 1.2 mm dust emission center; this core is likely the primary driver of gas accretion onto the center. These results suggest that the gas accretion onto the center of the Cygnus OB2/12 massive star-forming region is driven by the gravitational collapse of a massive core. This study represents the first detailed analysis of dust emission cores in a young massive cluster. Our findings support the inside-out scenario, indicating that the Cygnus OB2/12 young massive cluster may have formed via the gravitational collapse of a massive star-forming core. This aligns with the growing body of evidence that young massive clusters are the product of the gravitational collapse of a massive star-forming core. Future research should focus on the physical processes driving core growth in young massive clusters. Furthermore, we recommend that similar detailed studies of young massive clusters be conducted using the ALMA and the NGVLT. This will enhance our understanding of the core growth phase in young massive clusters and the physical processes driving core growth. Finally, we propose that the Cygnus OB2/12 young massive cluster may have formed via the gravitational collapse of a massive star-forming core, a hypothesis that should be tested in future studies. This will provide additional evidence for the inside-out scenario and a better understanding of the core growth phase

We introduce a novel simulation exploring the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs) as a potential dark matter candidate. This simulation utilizes PopSyCLE, a code package designed to model early universe structure formation and the resulting PBH mass distribution. By integrating a simulation with the Planck data, we constrain parameters such as the inflaton field and the reheating temperature. Furthermore, we examine the limitations of the resulting PBH mass spectrum and its implications for dark matter. Our PBH mass distribution spans from $10^{-16}M_{\odot}$ to $10^{5}M_{\odot}$, with peaks at $10^{-16}M_{\odot}$ and $10^{3}M_{\odot}$. Additionally, the spectrum between $10^{2}M_{\odot}$ and $10^{5}M_{\odot}$ aligns with recent observations from the OJ 287 binary system. Finally, we assess the PBH density required to account for all dark matter, noting that the density of PBHs occupying the space between $10^{-16}M_{\odot}$ and $10^{-15}M_{\odot}$ is insufficient to constitute the entirety of dark matter. The density distribution between $10^{2}M_{\odot}$ and $10^{5}M_{\odot}$ remains consistent with observations of OJ 287. Furthermore, the PBH density within the range of $10^{3}M_{\odot}$ to $10^{5}M_{\odot}$ could potentially explain all dark matter. This research demonstrates that PopSyCLE is a highly effective tool for simulating PBH formation. A key advantage of our method is that it relies on standard astrophysical formation processes rather than relying on the inflation model. Future work will investigate the ability of PBH density to explain all dark matter. PopSyCLE holds significant potential for simulating various dark matter candidates, including axions, supersymmetric particles, and dark matter fermions. We employed hard-particle Monte Carlo simulations to investigate equilibrium systems formed by monodisperse, wedge-shaped molecules. Each molecule is constructed from six tangent spheres arranged radially and grouped into two or three pairs. These molecular units interact via steric repulsion and are immersed in a solvent. Our analysis focused on the isotropic-to-nematic phase transition, examining systems with both two- and three-pair structures. For each unit, we calculated the end-to-center of mass correlation function, denoted as $C(r)$, which quantifies the modulation of the local density along the molecular axis. This function was found to exhibit a decay pattern characteristic of the smectic liquid crystal phase, specifically showing splay deformation. Furthermore, we analyzed the nematic order parameter, $S$, to identify a critical threshold below which the Monte Carlo simulations indicate the system remains in an isotropic phase. We determined that for all examined two-pair structures, the crossover value of $S$ lies between 0.4 and 0.5, aligning with our earlier findings for hard ellipsoids. Additionally, we determined that none of the three-pair structures investigated can stabilize a nematic liquid crystal phase. These results indicate that the crossover value for two-pair structures is structure-dependent and is lower than that observed in hard ellipsoids. Finally, we determined that no nonequilibrium structures were detected in any of the simulation boxes. These findings collectively demonstrate that liquid crystals cannot be accurately modeled as packings of convex polyhedra with facets of varying sizes. Instead, they must be represented as assemblies of nonconvex, closed convex-like shells. We conclude that our research provides a novel and potentially more precise framework for investigating liquid crystals. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation (grant no. Parameter-efficient tuning focuses on adjusting only a small subset of parameters within a pre-trained model. Notably, many existing methods utilize embedded tokens to represent these adjustable parameters. This studyForts: 1) demonstrates that these embedded token representations constitute a substantial portion of the transformable embedded space in transformer-based language models; 2) reveals that despite their effectiveness, current representations lack expressive richness and exhibit redundancy; and 3) proposes a strategy to mitigate redundancy and enhance expressiveness, thereby facilitating better optimization and superior performance. Specifically, we initially conduct an analysis of the spectral properties of the feature matrix generated by trainable parameters across training epochs. Based on this analysis, we develop an approach to eliminate redundancy and enrich expressiveness by projecting parameters onto a lower-dimensional subspace. This technique allows for the redistribution of information from redundant parameters to non-redundant ones, resulting in more effective utilization of the transformable parameter space. We demonstrate the substantial impact of this method on the RedSHELL and SHELL benchmarks, achieving significant performance gains across various tasks and models. Our findings confirm that this approach enables models to attain performance levels previously unattainable without fine-tuning all parameters. This research investigates the challenge of assessing preferences over subsets of a finite set, where elements represent attributes of a target object. Preference relations are established based on how well each set satisfies the decision-maker's implicit preferences. The core challenge involves identifying an unknown attribute vector by posing set addition problems, asking the user to rank the results of applying different attribute improvements. The objective is to minimize the count of these queries while ensuring the entire Pareto frontier can be distinguished, thereby enabling the identification of all attribute levels. We introduce a new "contextual" approach to active preference ranking, drawing an analogy to contextual bandits, which significantly reduces the required number of questions. Specifically, for $m$ attributes and $L$ levels, our method needs $L^{m}(\log L+1)$ queries, representing a substantial drop from the previous best bound of $L^{m+1}$. This total cost encompasses both experimental (set addition) and cognitive (ranking) costs. Additionally, we examine a non-contextual variant of set addition, demonstrating that it requires $L^{m}(\log L+1)^2$ queries, highlighting a more moderate efficiency gain. We also present a lower bound of $L^{m}(\log L+1)$, indicating that both methods perform nearly optimally. Finally, we illustrate the algorithm's application in determining human preferences regarding synthetic food products with genetic modifications. A web-based interface is available at https://geneticfood.org for users to explore this application. Our computational results indicate that m = 10 attributes with L = 3 levels per attribute can be evaluated in approximately 10 minutes on a standard laptop. The complete code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/DeepakSahoo1995/ActiveSetAddition. This work is grounded in a collaboration with geneticists and food scientists, and we acknowledge that current limitations in genetic food production restrict the number of achievable attribute levels, making m = 10 a practical upper limit. Furthermore, we posit that users are unlikely to express transitive preferences, meaning the most demanding cases involve expressing only weak preferences rather than strict ones. We also note that our analysis currently assumes no significant interactions between attributes, and we demonstrate that detecting interactions would require exponentially more queries. However, we argue that interactions are less likely to vary in a manner discernible through weak preferences, and thus, we do not account for them in our analysis. This study employs extensive molecular dynamics simulations of bead-spring polymers to investigate the connection between thermodynamic and dynamic fluctuations in supercooled fluids and their adjacent glass states. We demonstrate a substantial increase in the correlation between the enthalpic fluctuations of structural units (monomers) and their mobility as the system temperature decreases below the polymer's dynamic crossover temperature ($T_{\rm DX}$). This phenomenon is quantified using the concept of "total $\gamma$-factor," which integrates the product of thermodynamic fluctuations with the well-established Pratchett-Jones-Yip structural $\gamma$-factor. Our findings indicate that the total $\gamma$-factor rises exponentially as temperature drops from the $T_{\rm DX}$ region down to the glass transition temperature ($T_{\rm g}$). Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the total $\gamma$-factor and the ideal entropy of mixing, which diminishes as mobility decreases. Finally, we examine a thermodynamic version of the Pratchett-Jones-Yip scaling law, which links the total $\gamma$-factor to the heat capacity at constant pressure ($C_{p}$) in these supercooled fluids. This relation proves robust for molecular dynamics polymer models that exhibit only a two-state heat capacity singularity, but fails to hold for models featuring a heat capacity divergence. These outcomes align with recent experimental findings. Finally, we explore the implications of our results for both the thermodynamic theory of glass formation and the longstanding debate regarding the nature of the glass transition. Specifically, the rapid exponential growth of the total $\gamma$-factor below $T_{\rm DX}$ may signal a thermodynamic crossover from the structural relaxation dynamics of a supercooled liquid to those of a glass. Consequently, the Pratchett-Jones-Yip scaling of the total $\gamma$-factor below $T_{\rm DX}$ could serve as a precise, experimentally accessible metric for distinguishing between enthalpic and configurational entropy driving the relaxation of supercooled liquids. This approach may also help differentiate between the glass transitions of molecular fluids and chain-forming polymers. Ultimately, the strong scaling of the total $\gamma$-factor below $T_{\rm DX}$ supports the hypothesis that the dynamic crossover in supercooled liquids is closely tied to the crossover from a liquid to a glass, a glassy state characterized by a thermodynamic instability toward crystallization. Transformer language models excel at nongrammatical inputs like negation, yet it remains unclear which linguistic capabilities they actually possess. By integrating linguistic insights on negation from the Developmental Psycholinguistics (DPL) community into automated negation manipulation methods, we introduce a novel evaluation metric. We demonstrate that Transformer models vary significantly in their performance on this task, with levels of performance aligning more closely with DPL than with traditional Natural Language Processing metrics. Furthermore, we find that models lacking negation handling abilities still achieve strong performance on "masked negation" tasks. These findings suggest that Transformers may be exploiting spurious patterns to complete negation tasks. Finally, we show that ablation studies on development layers can offer a more granular assessment of negation processing than evaluating full models. Collectively, our findings may enhance NLP task definitions and facilitate a more nuanced understanding of how Transformer models process language. Attention mechanisms have become a cornerstone of Neural Machine Translation (NMT), yet they often struggle to fully capture long-range dependencies during token generation. This limitation can result in the incorrect ordering of words in the target sentence. This paper introduces a novel look-ahead attention approach that utilizes future target tokens to inform attention distribution across source tokens. By incorporating future target information, this method enhances the model's capacity to model long-range dependencies. Experimental results on German-English machine translation demonstrate that the proposed look-ahead attention model significantly improves single sentence perplexity and bleu4 scores by 1.3% and 2.3%, respectively, relative to an baseline NMT model without look-ahead attention. Furthermore, the model's effectiveness is validated through a human evaluation of 100 sentences, which confirms the quality gains indicated by the automated metrics. We present an explicit, detailed calculation of the weights for Kontsevich graphs generated by connection and curvature terms in the globalization framework, specifically for symplectic manifolds. We demonstrate how the weights associated with these curvature graph terms can be derived from the weights of non-equivariant Kontsevich graphs that describe the associativity of the product on smooth functions. We illustrate the resulting formulae using low-dimensional examples and provide a detailed computation for a 21-edge manifold. These findings support a conjecture, which extends the classical classification of low-dimensional weights for orientable surfaces to graphs and edges representing higher-dimensional spheres. Additionally, we outline several applications, including the calculation of quantum cohomology classes for symplectic manifolds and the construction of symplectic field theories. This work serves as a sequel to arXiv:1802.02204, where we explicitly defined the symmetry-based graphs and described their connections to manifold topology, cubical structures, and thickened manifolds with symplectic boundaries. The current paper focuses on the explicit formulae for graph weights, while our subsequent paper will detail the application of these formulae to specific symplectic categories. Throughout, we emphasize the computational and combinatorial aspects of our approach. Finally, we note that our methods may have applications in other contexts involving a classical symplectic field theory, such as the explicit construction of symplectic field theories or Floer cohomology. This is the third installment in a series of papers stemming from our foundational work, arXiv:1509.03359, which introduced an explicit, constructive approach to the classical globalization programme. In that first paper, we developed a combinatorial, equational method applicable to broad classes of symplectic manifolds. Here, we provide the explicit formulae and detailed calculations for symplectic spheres that complete the programme initiated in the first paper. Our approach offers a new, constructive, and explicit formula for the equivariant extension of manifolds with corners based on their combinatorial data, alongside a combinatorial formula for the weights of the equivariant manifold of polygons. We also present an explicit formula for the weights of the equivariant extension of a manifold of polygons given its non-equivariant counterpart, and we demonstrate the explicit construction of symplectic fields based on combinatorial data. This study examines large $N$, single-trace interacting conformal field theories (CFTs) constructed via the $O(N)$ model augmented by an $O(N)$-invariant deformation $\lambda \int d^dX\, F[\phi^I]F[\phi^I]$, employing methods rooted in large $N$ analysis and holography. A prior extensive numerical investigation of the dual $AdS_ {d+2}$ solution near its critical point suggested that such models remain conformal across the entire range of coupling constants $\lambda$. In this work, we provide a rigorous analytical proof confirming the validity of this conjecture for all values of $\lambda$. Furthermore, we establish that these models adhere to the large $N$ limit of the generalized entropy formula. Finally, we compute the large $N$ limit of thermal entropy for $O(N)$-invariant single-trace CFTs derived from $AdS_ {d+2}$ solutions formed by gluing two backgrounds along their ($AdS_ {d+1}$) boundaries. Our findings indicate that for solutions possessing non-trivial hair, the thermal entropy approaches the free theory entropy as $\lambda \to \infty$. Additionally, we observe a divergence between thermal and entanglement entropies that grows with $\lambda$, a behavior that intensifies for higher dimensions $d$. This divergence is attributed to the fact that, unlike thermal entropy, the large $N$ limit of entanglement entropy does not receive contributions from the solutions' "hairs." Consequently, in the limit $\lambda \to \infty$, the entanglement entropy of free theories emerges as an upper bound for all interacting CFTs within this class. This result is conjectured to extend to the general case involving arbitrary single-trace deformations in the dual CFTs. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for understanding the relationship between entanglement entropy and energy. Specifically, we explore a potential link between the entanglement entropy of the ground state and thermal entropy, which becomes exact in the large $N$ limit when $T\to 0$ for free theories but fails in interacting CFTs as $\lambda$ increases. This insight may be relevant for investigating the relationship between the two entropies in quantum field theories in general dimensions $d$. We conclude by proposing that the relationship between these entropies could aid in investigating the relationship between the two types of states in quantum systems that maximize these entropies

Cai and Kou (2assistant_2013) proposed pricing Asian options by underpricing call options, treating them as a special case. However, their numerical Algorithm 1 yields highly inaccurate results for short-maturity American Asian options. This study re-examines their framework, specifically addressing the strong convergence and error estimation of their two finite difference schemes. Furthermore, we enhance their finite difference approach for the American Asian option pricing problem. Through numerical experiments, the superior performance of the revised algorithm over Cai and Kou (2013) is demonstrated. These computational findings are supported by an analysis of mesh generation and step size selection within the Cai and Kou (2013) framework. Additionally, the paper concludes with a detailed derivation of the weak error estimate for Equation (15) on Page 15 of Cai and Kou (2013). Finally, the appendix presents a corrected version of Theorem 2 (Page 25) and the subsequent discussion, which contained significant errors. These mistakes, which affect both theoretical and numerical outcomes, are highlighted in bold. The core issue lies in the inability of a polynomial approximation to accurately model the state variable's time average. We illustrate this failure using a simple finite difference scheme to solve a basic Asian option problem. Given that the original framework relies on a strong convergence method with a significant error constant, the computational results indicate that finite difference schemes yield highly inaccurate prices for short-maturity American Asian options. Consequently, the primary contribution of this paper is a scheme that enhances the finite difference results of Cai and Kou (2013). This improvement is achieved by introducing a specialized finite difference scheme for Asian options, developing corresponding error estimates, and refining the mesh generation and time step size strategies for option maturity.

Keywords: Asian options; Asian options; Asian options.

The gamma-ray flux observed from clusters of galaxies is primarily attributed to inverse Compton scattering, which occurs when relativistic electrons within the cluster interact with the cosmic microwave background radiation. This study presents a novel method for calculating the diffuse gamma-ray flux from clusters by utilizing the relativistic electron population and cluster dimensions derived from X-ray observations of the intracluster medium. Our approach employs a Monte Carlo simulation that incorporates a radial dependence for the cluster's relativistic electron population. By comparing simulation outcomes with available observational data, we can estimate the probability of detecting gamma-ray signals from clusters at distances up to $z=1$. We further apply this methodology to predict the potential for future detections using the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA) and the Cherenkov Telescope Array Large Medium-Sized Instrument (CTA-LMIG). Finally, we outline a strategy to include cluster counts as a component of the cosmological gamma-ray background at these distances. This work is published in *Astroparticle Physics*. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Sebastian-Beckmann/ICSC. The computational notebook utilized in this study can be found at https://github.com/Sebastian-Beckmann/ICSC/tree/master/ICSC_notebook. This work demonstrates that such data allows for the identification and characterization of specific features in the primordial power spectrum, effectively acting as an early-universe feature detector. Notably, we reveal a link to a well-known classical scattering result: the precession of spinning test particles moving along geodesics in the Kerr metric. Consequently, primordial gravitational waves (PGWs) with time-variable amplitude generated by pre-reheating cosmology preceding inflation can induce angular momentum modes in outgoing scalar perturbations, thereby triggering "cosmological precession." This offers a new perspective on PGW signatures and establishes a novel connection between high-energy scattering and PGW physics. Furthermore, we illustrate that PGW features detectable through this precession mechanism include both local features, such as sharp transitions, and non-local ones like oscillations. In both scenarios, traditional cosmological collider signals are overshadowed by these gravitational features, which can alter the tensor spectrum before inflation begins. Finally, we discuss the observational implications of these findings. **Significance Statement:** While cosmological collider physics has traditionally sought to detect short-range gravity effects during inflation by observing a B-mode quadrupole in polarization data, this study shows that PGWs can imprint angular information on both scalar and tensor perturbations prior to the inflationary epoch. This enables the development of new observational techniques to characterize non-local features in the primordial power spectrum and gravitational wave power spectra. Crucially, this research introduces a new class of observable gravitational wave features that differ significantly from scalar features, thereby advancing our ability to understand non-local early universe phenomena. Ultimately, these findings deepen our comprehension of physical processes occurring before and during inflation, as well as those occurring after it. This includes analyzing how sharp transitions in the power spectrum of primordial gravitational waves can serve as cosmological detectors, offering a novel approach to observational cosmology. Additionally, we explore how these gravitational wave features can help distinguish between different high-energy scattering models and identify specific forms of non-Gaussianity. By providing a new window into the early universe, this study enhances our ability to trace the evolution of the cosmos and uncover its fundamental secrets. Ultimately, this work represents a significant step toward understanding the origins and evolution of our universe. Although explaining black-box deep neural networks is essential, current methods struggle because they often concentrate on high-level abstracts while neglecting visual details. This study proposes leveraging external semantic knowledge to bridge the gap between visual and semantic representations. We introduce a deep visual-semantic (VS) filter attention (FA) network that integrates deep CNN features with external semantic tags or class-specific neural network (NN) embeddings. By computing the attention weights for deep feature maps using class-wise shallow VS embeddings, we can filter and highlight salient visual regions. These attention weight maps are then fused with deep features to enhance classification performance. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach yields significant improvements in both explanation quality and classification accuracy. Furthermore, we show that a key advantage of these models is their ability to detect visual anomalies during inference, such as image cuts and adversarial attacks. These findings indicate that our method produces more robust and trustworthy explanations and predictions. In addition to empirical results, we also provide theoretical insights into why combining visual and semantic knowledge is highly effective. Our findings indicate that while the effective phonon interaction is weak at high energies, it transitions into a strong form at low energies. This low-energy attraction drives strong pairing of charge excitations, resulting in a composite bosonic gas. Specifically, electrons coupled to phonons are modeled as polaronic quasiparticles; consequently, they engage in intense phonon exchange interactions via their virtual phonon clouds. This mechanism generates a significant attractive interaction at both single-particle and single-boson energy levels. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the energy gap of these composite bosons exhibits dependence on the electron-phonon coupling constant $\lambda$ and the bare phonon frequency $\omega_0$. Finally, we propose that experimental values of $\lambda$ and $\omega_0$ in 1D cuprates fall within the strong-attraction regime. Our approach is applicable to analyzing electron pairing behaviors across multiple dimensions in cuprates. Additionally, we show that within the composite boson gas framework, the superconducting gap is smaller than the pairing energy scale, consistent with recent ARPES data from 1D cuprates. We contend that these results offer a comprehensive explanation for the superconducting gap and pairing energy scale observed in cuprate systems. This study advances our understanding of electron-phonon mediated pairing mechanisms and establishes a foundation for further investigating phonon-mediated interactions in cuprates. Specifically, we demonstrate that both composite boson formation and pairing are governed by $\lambda$ and $\omega_0$, with the pairing regime being the most critical. Our approach enables a systematic analysis of how these parameters influence composite boson formation and superconductivity. This provides a unified theoretical framework for interpreting the physics of electron-phonon mediated pairing in cuprates. Finally, we outline prospects for future research aimed at experimentally verifying our theoretical predictions. In conclusion, this work advances our fundamental understanding of electron-phonon mediated pairing mechanisms and lays the groundwork for future investigations into phonon-mediated interactions in cuprates. Identifying causal relationships is essential for making evidence-based decisions in fields such as medicine and public policy. While large-scale surveys offer an efficient means to study population health, the absence of randomization and reliance on self-reported data often result in datasets plagued by missing values, outliers, and unmeasured confounders. The Multi-Domain Health Perception Survey (MPHIA) serves as a prominent example of such a dataset. This study introduces a novel Structural Equation Model (SEM)-based approach designed to learn causal graphs under these specific constraints. The method employs penalized estimation using either the L1 or L1/L2 penalty, with the ability to add specific edges when prior knowledge exists. Furthermore, the framework supports confounder selection via semi-parametric marginal regression, a critical step for addressing unmeasured confounding. We assessed this approach using the U.S. MPHIA Individual dataset, a large-scale survey that details individuals' perceptions of their health, lifestyle, and working conditions. The analysis yielded a causal graph that offers new insights into health determinants, including the discovery of an unexpected connection between life satisfaction and physical activity. Additionally, the study confirms that this SEM-based methodology can successfully uncover a broad spectrum of causal relationships. The proposed approach is accessible on GitHub. We present findings from a study on the magnetic structure of the Heusler alloy Co$_{9}$Zn$_{9}$Mn$_{2}$, which undergoes a topological phase transition from a skyrmion lattice to an antiferromagnetic state. Employing in situ neutron reflectometry, we examined a thin film along the easy-axis direction across a temperature range from 5 to 100 K. Our results indicate that within the metastable skyrmion lattice regime, increasing thermal treatment leads to magnetic "smearing" of both the skyrmion lattice and the second-order magnetic transition. This phenomenon is interpreted as the topological melting of the skyrmion lattice, a process driven by the reduction of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction strength resulting from accumulated topological defects. These observations are corroborated by Monte-Carlo simulations. Our work demonstrates the topological melting of a long-range ordered skyrmion lattice in a simple system, offering insights into the stability of magnetic skyrmions and their potential manipulation for memory and spintronic technologies. Furthermore, the detected magnetic smearing in Co$_{9}$Zn$_{9}$Mn_{2}$ may have significant implications for spintronic devices, where skyrmions are manipulated via magnetic field gradients or electric currents. We also address the broader context of similar magnetic smearing effects observed in other systems, such as thin ferromagnetic films and multilayers, and their potential topological interpretations. Finally, our neutral stance on the viability of topological melting in non-Heusler alloys is grounded in the historical observation that this concept was initially proposed nearly a decade ago. We conclude by outlining future research directions. This study was conducted at the I. M. This paper offers a detailed examination of high-dimensional dynamic factor models, emphasizing their representation, consistency, and asymptotic normality. Our analysis focuses on a specific framework where latent factors evolve according to a local-to-unity random walk, while observed variables react to both these factors and unobserved transitory shocks. Our findings rely on specific structural assumptions regarding the response functions and the convergence properties of certain sample analogues. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive overview of current estimation techniques and dominant forecasting strategies in factor models, supplemented by a substantial empirical section that includes over 100 exercises and experiments. We also highlight several promising avenues for future research. Ultimately, this study aims to deepen understanding of dynamic factor models and expand the standard forecasting benchmark that compares existing methods against each other. Furthermore, the paper serves as a detailed extension of our previous work (Arellano and Galvao 2017). Finally, the estimation and forecasting techniques presented here are implemented in the R package `dynfm`, which is accessible at https://github.com/rgalvaob/dynfm. This repository also hosts a collection of R scripts designed to address the exercises outlined in the paper. We believe these teaching materials, including the exercises and supporting code, will be valuable to graduate students and early-career researchers entering the field of macroeconomics. We also demonstrate the application of the `dynfm` package to the dynamic factor model of Galvao and Lin (2019). Furthermore, we show that `dynfm` can be employed to estimate and forecast the factor model proposed in our earlier work (Arellano and Galvao 2014). Our empirical analysis reveals that `dynfm` models perform robustly, often surpassing the performance of other approaches found in the literature. Finally, we demonstrate the flexibility of `dynfm` by implementing a factor augmented vector autoregression (FAVAR) model that successfully predicts U.S. GDP growth. This implementation utilizes the `dynfm` class and functions to estimate factors and forecast using factor-augmented models, features that can also be utilized for teaching purposes. The `dynfm` package is continuously updated, and new features are regularly incorporated. We welcome collaboration from the research community to further expand the package's capabilities. Our objective is to make `dynfm` a valuable and versatile tool for macroeconomists, financial analysts, and other professionals utilizing dynamic factor models. The Nikaidō-Isoda-Fan inequality defines an equilibrium problem that encompasses several well-known problems—including optimization, variational inequalities, Kakutani fixed points, and Nash equilibria—as specific instances. This paper illustrates the connection between the fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and the solutions to the equilibrium problem, under certain monotonicity and Lipschitz-type conditions. It also introduces an iterative algorithm for nonsmooth optimization and establishes both weak and strong convergence theorems within Hilbert spaces. Finally, the study examines the stability of this iterative process. Notably, this research marks the first application of the Moreau proximal mapping to address the equilibrium problem. Additionally, an illustrative example is provided to demonstrate the equivalence between the fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and the solutions of the equilibrium problem. **Keywords:** Equilibrium problem; Nash equilibrium; Variational inequality; Moreau proximal mapping; Optimization; Proximal point algorithm; Monotonicity; Lipschitz condition; Stability.

Recent advancements in reversible steganography have focused on utilizing deep neural networks, yet existing methods are either vulnerable to noise or depend on specific characteristics of the input data. To address these limitations, this work introduces a fully Bayesian approach employing Bayesian neural networks, which are capable of quantifying uncertainty. By performing inference on low-precision hardware, we demonstrate that Bayesian inference can be accelerated through techniques such as tensorization, factorization, and pruning, thereby reducing both memory usage and computational demands. Our experimental results indicate that Bayesian-based fully reversible steganography outperforms the current state-of-the-art in terms of bit-rate while maintaining robustness against noise. Furthermore, we validate the method's fully reversible nature by confirming its compatibility with low-precision hardware. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/DeepSecLab/bayesian-steganography. We investigate the impact of turbulent effects on the stability of global convective dynamos, modeled through $\alpha-\Omega$ mean-field theory equations derived from numerical simulations. Our findings indicate that these turbulent effects significantly influence both the threshold and frequency of convective dynamos. Consequently, both laboratory and astrophysical observations of these systems must address the influence of turbulent dynamics to accurately interpret their behavior. This conclusion is based on a model where the $\alpha$-effect is defined as a function of the local convective Rossby number. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the observed turbulence effects stem from the nonlinearity inherent in the Rossby number definition and suggest that similar influences are expected to manifest in other turbulence-dependent formulations. Finally, our results underscore the critical role of the Rossby number in determining the onset of global convective dynamos. This sensitivity arises because the $\alpha$-effect is intrinsically linked to the Rossby number, which is a function of the Rayleigh number. Given that the Rayleigh number scales quadratically with the Rayleigh number, variations in it lead to substantial fluctuations in the Rossby number. This mechanism explains the pronounced sensitivity of the onset to the Rossby number. Our model is applicable to astrophysical contexts, including the Sun, where the Rossby number is estimated to be approximately 1. Our results suggest that the global convective flow in the Sun is highly sensitive to turbulent effects, as the Rossby number is expected to vary by an order of magnitude across different regions of the Sun. This sensitivity may help explain the observed discrepancies between the depth of the tachocline and predictions from mean differential rotation models. Additionally, we highlight the necessity of incorporating turbulent effects into mean-field models to comprehensively describe convective dynamics. We conclude that future research should employ $\alpha$-effect prescriptions that account for turbulence. Ultimately, future models should rely on the Rossby number as a function of local turbulent properties, which can be estimated using the Rossby number derived from numerical simulations. This approach is essential for accurately predicting the onset of convective dynamos. Our conclusions are broadly applicable to astrophysical objects, as the Rossby number is known to correlate with turbulence. For instance, in Jupiter, the Rossby number is approximately 0.1, whereas in the interstellar medium, it is roughly 10. These relationships further support the necessity of including turbulent effects in mean-field models.
