We present ALMA observations of a molecular outflow in the nearby starburst galaxy NGC 4945, utilizing a 1.5" x 1.5" field of view at a spatial resolution of 0.12". The data reveal a massive outflow extending over 100 pc, characterized by a high-velocity jet and two prominent bow-shocks located at a distance of 1.5 kpc from the galaxy's center. This structure indicates that the outflow is driven by a central compact region roughly 100 pc across, which is dominated by a supermassive black hole with a mass of approximately 10^7 solar masses. The outflow's total mass is estimated at 10^4 solar masses, and its momentum generation rate is calculated to be 10^-2 (M_sun/yr)(km/s). The momentum flux of the outflow closely matches the radiative momentum flux derived from the galaxy's luminous starburst, suggesting that massive stars are the primary drivers of NGC 4945's outflows. This starburst appears to be the most massive outflow driver identified to date. Our findings suggest that outflows from starbursts, whether individual or clustered, can significantly impact the evolution of massive galaxies. Furthermore, we propose that the compact starburst in NGC 4945 serves as an ideal laboratory for studying the feedback mechanisms of both massive stars and supermassive black holes. This research is part of the NGC 4945 Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS-ALMA). The COSMOS-ALMA project aims to investigate the connection between outflows and star formation in galaxies by observing a wide variety of outflow drivers with a uniform, high spatial resolution. The COSMOS-ALMA survey targets 17 outflow drivers, including starbursts, AGNs, and star clusters, across a wide range of redshifts. These observations are expected to provide crucial insights into the nature of outflow drivers and their feedback effects on cosmic cosmic evolution. The COSMOS-ALMA survey was initiated in 2017 and is scheduled to conclude in 2019. This paper reports on the first observations of the survey. The COSMOS-ALMA survey is a major initiative of the COSMOS Legacy Survey, a comprehensive effort to study the cosmic star formation history and the evolution of galaxies and clusters over the past 13 billion years.

This study introduces the first conservative Galerkin solver, utilizing an entropy-satisfying discretization, for the diffusion equation across both positive and negative diffusion coefficients. Conservative and entropy-satisfying methods are essential for simulating magnetized plasmas, where ion kinetic energy must be rigorously preserved regardless of magnetic field strength. These solvers are also critical for modeling shock dynamics in astrophysics and inertial confinement fusion. The proposed algorithm employs a fully implicit scheme based on the fractional stepping method and is extended to three dimensions. Validation is provided using test cases with known analytical solutions and by coupling the solver with a gyrokinetic code to simulate plasmas with both constant and quasilinear diffusion coefficients. A performance benchmark was established by comparing computational costs on up to 320 GPU cores. This work paves the way for high-performance, quasilinear diffusion simulations aimed at supporting high-resolution inertial confinement fusion research. Additionally, it establishes a foundation for conservative Galerkin discretizations of diffusion equations in general geometries, offering valuable insights for numerical simulations involving magnetohydrodynamic turbulence and shock waves. The solver is available at https://github.com/afg2002/DCGalerkin. Future research will extend the algorithm to include momentum equations. The current implementation is designed for high-performance computing environments featuring large-scale GPU clusters. Specifically, the code is optimized for NVIDIA A100 GPUs and the Summit supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The computational cost for a 3D diffusion problem with quasilinear diffusion coefficients is approximately 1.5 hours for 128$^3$ grids and 1.5 days for a 512$^3$ grid, utilizing 128 and 768 GPU cores, respectively. These durations correspond to 1.2 hours and 32 hours on equivalent CPU cores. For the 3D grids with quasilinear diffusion coefficients, the problem involves 1.5$\times$10$^6$ unknowns solved via a linear system featuring a 7-point stencil on each GPU. The code was developed using CUDA and cuSOLVER libraries, leveraging the Hopper and Ampere architectures found on the Summit GPU cluster. Furthermore, the implementation includes a conservative finite difference scheme, which serves as a valuable alternative for users preferring finite difference methods over the presented finite element approach. This code was developed by Alejandro F. Garcia, who acknowledges the support of the US Department of Energy's National Nuclear Security Administration under Award Number DE-NA000

Variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods (SGLMs) have previously been realized using the Nordsieck technique; however, this paper presents variable stepsize SGLMs formulated directly on nonuniform grids. We derive the order conditions for these methods, specifically targeting order $p$ containing $s$ variable steps, and provide explicit examples where the count of variable steps matches the number of stages. For evaluating derivatives, we utilize the Runge-Kutta pair $(5,9)$ as the base scheme, which yields at least order 5 for fixed steps and is capable of up to 9 variable steps. By integrating this approach with the order $s$ SGLMs, we construct overall methods that achieve a minimum of $s+5$ stages. The efficiency of our proposed methods is assessed using the Efficiency Index (EI), defined as the ratio of stage order to total index sum. Numerical experiments involving both initial value problems and benchmark benchmarks demonstrate the accuracy and stability of the methods across both fixed and variable stepsize scenarios. Notably, the results indicate that the order of accuracy remains consistent regardless of whether the steps are fixed or variable. These findings are supported by both theoretical analysis and numerical evidence. Furthermore, the study confirms the benefit of employing high-order SGLMs under variable steps, achieving a reduction in stage count by up to 40%. Finally, the paper concludes by comparing the number of stages, order of accuracy, and order of stability for variable stepsize Runge-Kutta methods, SGLMs, and GLMs. The efficiency of the methods presented in this work is comparable to that of existing variable stepsize RK and GLM approaches found in the literature. Additionally, the computational cost of the methods is substantially lower than that of variable stepsize RK methods. To our knowledge, the variable stepsize schemes introduced here represent the first of their kind derived from the $\mathrm{VDP}_5(9)$ Runge-Kutta method. This article introduces MuMuPy, a computational library and cloud-based tool designed to calculate cross sections for dimuonium (true muonium) interactions with matter. The muonium component within true dimuonium is assumed to interact as if it were a proton. These calculations rely on the true muonium wave function and the probability of it fluctuating into a muon-antimuon pair. The primary mechanism under consideration is the true muonium's passage through a foil, accompanied by one or more annihilation events involving the muon pair. True muonium is theorized to form in collider experiments when a muon and an antimuon briefly bind, even if they eventually scatter. MuMuPy currently supports true muonium interaction calculations for $e^+e^-$ and $\mu^+\mu^-$ collisions. The generated outputs facilitate the inclusion of true muonium effects in simulations for the KEDR and BESIII experiments. Portfolio selection under relative performance criteria has recently garnered significant attention. This study examines the infinite-horizon investment problem involving logarithmic utility over a combination of absolute and relative wealth, where relative wealth is defined as the ratio of the investor's portfolio value to that of a benchmark. We address the problem using both self-financing strategies and trading strategies. First, we derive the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation and its corresponding adjoint Fokker-Planck equation for the trading strategy approach, providing a model reduction for the resulting integro-differential equation. Subsequently, we introduce a state-variable transformation for the trading portfolio value that converts the HJB equation into a form equivalent to that derived under the trading strategy assumption, thereby establishing a relationship between the two value functions. Finally, we construct an explicit optimal strategy by solving the reduced HJB equation, demonstrating its relationship to the value function obtained under the trading strategy method. Throughout the analysis, we employ the Feynman-Kac representation to provide a probabilistic interpretation of the solution. Our findings are valid in both complete and incomplete financial markets. Dwarf galaxies are the most abundant type of galaxy in the universe and are crucial for understanding the formation and evolution of larger systems. This review examines the physical and chemical properties of the interstellar medium (ISM) within these dwarfs, based on observational data from the last decade. We analyze the ISM's thermodynamic state, focusing on the relative proportions of cold and warm phases, and explore the relationship between galactic mass and star formation efficiency. Additionally, we address cosmic rays, the ionization structure, and the chemical evolution of the ISM in dwarf galaxies. Finally, we highlight current challenges and outline future directions for research in this field. Key findings indicate that dwarfs possess a wide range of ISM characteristics, including gas temperatures spanning over three orders of magnitude, densities ranging from $10^{-4}$ to $10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$, and metallicity variations up to two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the relative volumes of cold and warm gas phases in dwarfs differ significantly from those seen in larger galaxies. In the star-forming regime, thermally unstable gas dominates in more massive dwarfs ($M_{\rm vir}>10^8$ M$_\odot$), whereas in lower-mass systems, the cold phase is more significant. Conversely, during star formation suppression, the cold phase is more prominent in higher-mass dwarfs, while the warm phase dominates in lower-mass ones. Finally, we find that cosmic rays and ionizing photons are essential for driving the chemical evolution of the ISM in these systems. In conclusion, future research must combine observations with theoretical models to better understand the ISM in dwarf galaxies. This can be achieved by developing more efficient and sensitive instruments, such as the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope, and by incorporating detailed theoretical models that account for the complex physical and chemical processes occurring within these galaxies. Furthermore, a deeper understanding of the ISM in dwarfs will require a combination of multi-wavelength observations and a thorough analysis of the observational data. In addition, we emphasize the importance of developing new methods for analyzing and interpreting observational data, such as machine learning and Bayesian inference, to better understand the ISM in dwarf galaxies. This research investigates the stability of fermionic quasiparticles within a fermion-boson model defined on a Bethe lattice, where fermions interact with local bosons via a coupling strength $\lambda$. As $\lambda$ increases, the system transitions into an incompressible state characterized by a gap in the quasiparticle density of states. We demonstrate that for any fixed $\lambda$, a secondary, rare event occurs in the thermodynamic limit: the emergence of an isolated resonance within the quasiparticle spectrum. This phenomenon is most probable when the self-energy can be expressed as the ratio of two real-valued polynomials of the self-energy. Furthermore, we establish that this event is significantly more frequent than the standard zero-bias emergence observed in superconductivity or insulating gap formation, which typically requires tuning model parameters. The resulting rare system collapse is supported by the emergence of a finite dc conductivity in the thermodynamic limit. This mechanism offers a framework for understanding the breakdown of fermionic quasiparticles in strongly correlated systems, such as the normal phase of high-$T_c$ cuprates, where quasiparticle stability is maintained by specific fine-tunings. Finally, we outline potential extensions of this model to higher dimensions and systems with greater connectivity. These extensions may explain fine-tuning requirements in quasiparticle-based theories of high-temperature superconductivity, as well as the non-universal rare-locus behavior seen in quantum criticality and deconfined quantum criticality. Additionally, it could account for the non-universal finite temperature observed in experiments. This work is conducted in collaboration with A. M. Tsvelik. A preliminary report was previously published in *Phys. Rev. B* (2019). For a comprehensive overview, see our accompanying paper in *Phys. Rev. B* (2021). Our prior publication, *Phys. Rev. B* (2019), serves as a proof of concept, while this current study provides a detailed proof and discussion. The earlier paper is included here for completeness. In that context, we demonstrated that quasiparticle collapse is more common than the emergence of zero-bias resonances or the opening of the Higgs gap in a simplified model. This current work presents a detailed proof and discussion of those findings. In the prior study, we illustrated that fine-tuning is unnecessary and that the collapse frequency is higher; this is evident in the broader discussion of the text. This current paper offers a detailed proof and discussion of those conclusions.

Golan and Goursat recently introduced a graph model to generate braided-Thompson groups, denoted as V and W, which serve as braided extensions of the Thompson groups F and W, respectively. Furthermore, the author recently demonstrated that V shares key properties with the Thompson group F, including amenability, a finite first Lipschitz cohomology group, and a divergence growth rate of n log n. This paper extends the divergence result to V by utilizing a random walk model based on the graph formulation. Additionally, this study examines the divergence of the Thompson-like groups U and Z, introduced by Golan and Goursast as groups analogous to F and W but constructed via braided boundary diagrams instead of standard boundary diagrams. It is proven that U is amenable and possesses a first Lipschitz cohomology group of dimension 1, while its divergence grows at a rate of n log n. In contrast, Z exhibits amenable divergence growth of n log n + cn, though its first Lipschitz cohomology group has a dimension of at least 2. Finally, the author establishes that U is a normal subgroup of V with a Z factor group, thereby confirming that U is also a braided boundary group, while demonstrating that such a property does not hold for U when constructed from "twisted" boundary diagrams. Notably, U and Z are not braided Thompson groups, distinguishing them from other groups with polynomial divergence growth, such as the generalized braided Thompson group $\tilde{W}$, which exhibits a divergence growth rate of n log n + cn. Ultimately, this work elucidates the connection between divergence growth and the boundary diagram formulation of braided Thompson groups, thereby distinguishing between the cases of "inverted" and "outward" boundary diagrams. Specifically, it shows that only inward diagrams yield groups with at most polynomial divergence growth, whereas outward diagrams can produce polynomial divergence growth, thereby refuting a conjecture by Golan and Goursat. Additionally, the study addresses a question posed by Golan and Goursat regarding whether a braided boundary group with polynomial divergence growth must necessarily be a braided Thompson group, providing a positive answer. Finally, the work provides a proof of a conjecture by Golan and Goursat regarding the conditions under which a braided boundary group exhibits polynomial divergence growth. Specifically, the proof demonstrates that a braided boundary group has polynomial divergence growth if and only if it is formed by a collection of boundary diagrams that are not "twisted." This paper determines the asymptotic behavior of recurrence coefficients for polynomials orthogonal against the logarithmic weight $w(x) = \log \frac{1}{|x|}$ on the interval $[-1,1]$. Employing the method of steepest descents applied to the Riemann-Hilbert problem associated with these polynomials, we establish the asymptotic formulas for the recurrence coefficients. Notably, our findings align with the 1961 conjecture regarding the coefficients' growth order and converge with the most recent numerical data. Furthermore, we derive a corresponding asymptotic relation for the Jacobi matrix linked to this specific weight. Finally, we compare these results with those obtained for constant weights on $[-1,1]$ and discuss the distinctions between the two scenarios. Additionally, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of the recurrence coefficients when the weight is shifted to the interval $[a,b]$ where $a,b \in \mathbb{R}$. In this case, we confirm the 1970 conjecture by Golinskii and Simons concerning the growth order of the coefficients. Finally, we establish a strong asymptotic relation for the monic orthogonal polynomials:
$$\frac{P_n(x)}{\prod_{j=1}^n (x-x_{j,n})} = 1 + O(n^{-1}), \quad n \to \infty,$$
where $x_{j,n}$ denote the zeros of the $n$th orthogonal polynomial, and $j=1,2,\ldots,n$. This conclusion holds for any interval $[a,b]$ with $a,b \in (-\infty, \infty)$, provided $a \leq -1 < 0 \leq 1 \leq b$. In this context, we also examine the asymptotic behavior of the recurrence coefficients. Specifically, the first recurrence coefficient $a_n$ satisfies $a_n = \frac{b-a}{12n} + O(n^{-2})$ as $n \to \infty$, whereas all higher-order coefficients remain bounded. These conclusions apply to the case where the weight is $w(x) = \log \frac{1}{|x-a|} + \log \frac{1}{|x-b|}$. This paper presents a new method for assessing automatic summarization models by evaluating their outputs with human readers. We begin by investigating the quality of summaries produced on Amazon Mechanical Turk, where results were inconsistent, likely due to the inclusion of poorly performing models or human workers lacking the necessary qualifications. To address this, we introduced a filtering strategy to isolate high-quality responses from qualified workers. Using this approach, we conducted a detailed quality analysis on the 2020 ACM Summary Writing Competition data, examining human responses based on worker qualifications. Our findings indicate that, contrary to general assumptions, workers with lower English writing skills often outperformed those with higher skills. We demonstrated that our method can identify summaries that automatically labeled as incoherent by a model were actually coherent to humans, offering a superior labeling technique for evaluating summarization performance. The source code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/needle-in-a-haystack. This research is being made open-source to assist researchers in efficiently identify and mitigate low-quality workers, thereby enhancing the quality of results obtained from Amazon Mechanical Turk. By improving the reliability of crowdsourced data, this process can ultimately enhance the performance of summary generation models. Furthermore, identifying qualified workers enables researchers to design better models and refine their evaluation metrics. We anticipate that this line of research will significantly contribute to the field of automatic summarization. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work, Section 3 outlines the methodology, Section 4 presents the results, and Section 5 provides the discussion. The authors gratefully acknowledge the participants of the 2020 ACM Summary Writing Competition for their valuable contributions. We also extend our thanks to our lab members for their insightful feedback and support. Finally, we are deeply grateful to the reviewers for their thorough and insightful reviews of our work. Text-video retrieval (TVR) has garnered significant interest due to its critical role in real-world video comprehension and analysis. However, existing TVR approaches often struggle with suboptimal performance because they fail to effectively model intra-modal relationships or align multi-modal tokens during retrieval. To address these limitations, we introduce the Token Shift and Selection Network (TS2-Net), an end-to-end trainable framework that iteratively iterates and selects modal tokens based on cross-modal attention. TS2-Net comprises a modal shift module that permutes modal tokens to enhance their internal modeling, and a cross-modal selection module that filters out the most informative tokens from both modalities using a similarity matrix. We assessed the model's performance across three large-scale benchmark datasets: MSRVTT, ActivityNet, and DiDeMo. Experimental results demonstrate that TS2-Net achieves superior performance, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by 1.5% to 10.6%. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the model's effectiveness and highlight the essential contributions of the modal shift and cross-modal selection mechanisms. Additionally, empirical analysis reveals that TS2-Net exhibits stronger robustness against noise compared to other models. This study examines hybrid undirected random networks formed by combining the preferential attachment and uniform attachment mechanisms. Networks generated from such processes are termed hybrid attachment networks. We demonstrate that the degree distribution of these networks follows a power law and derive formulas for the shape parameter and cutoff, grounded in a general condition ensuring the stability of the degree distribution. Subsequently, we analyze two models of directed networks, which we call preferential/uniform networks, where the probability a node connects to a component of size $s$ is a nondecreasing function of $s$. We prove the emergence of a giant weak component and a giant strong component within these networks, contingent on the specific undirected sub-combination upon which they are built. Furthermore, we show that power law degree distributions are asymptotically attainable in these directed networks provided the growth function satisfies a specific condition. Finally, we calculate the probability that a node belongs to the giant strong component. Our findings regarding the existence of a giant strong component in the directed network are novel, even when the underlying undirected network exhibits a power law degree distribution. We illustrate the applicability of our results to various directed network models, including the directed barabasi-albert model, the diestel-leitner model, and the pappalardi model. Additionally, we clarify the relationship between our work and that of Bhamidi et al. and establish the stability of the degree distribution for all three aforementioned directed network models. In the initial section, we also provide an example of a valid power law growth function that fails to ensure a power law degree distribution in the corresponding preferential/uniform network. Finally, we introduce a model for networks with inhomogeneous attachment probabilities, extending the current paper's results to this broader context. This extension is achieved through a coupling of our model with one developed by Bhamidi et al., thereby enabling the calculation of the degree distribution for the extended model. All proofs are supported by differential equation methods. We also provide a comprehensive introduction to these mathematical methods within the paper. Our results are applicable to a wide spectrum of network growth models, including barabasi-albert models, diestel-leitner models, and various hybrid network models. Moreover, this work serves as a foundation for a broader research program aimed at understanding networks with inhomogeneous attachment probabilities. This paper serves as a sequel to the work of Bhamidi et al. and is the first to establish the stability of power law degree distributions in networks with inhomogeneous attachment probabilities. In modern wireless environments, multiple devices compete for limited spectrum, creating complex interference patterns that degrade communication quality and reduce efficiency. While traditional analytic and machine learning approaches have been used to identify and mitigate interference, they often struggle with the high dimensionality and non-linearity of real-world problems. Recent advancements in deep learning offer a promising solution to these challenges. This paper introduces a new deep learning framework designed for interference identification, which enhances the generalization capability of conventional methods. We also present a novel approach for identifying multiple types of interference simultaneously within a signal, leveraging the ability of deep neural networks to learn from the inherent correlations among interference classes. Our approach is validated using a synthetic dataset generated from a specific model. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses traditional techniques, achieving superior accuracy and reduced computational complexity. Furthermore, an extensive empirical study reveals that our approach can identify all interference classes in a mixture with a detection rate exceeding 90%. Finally, we outline the current limitations of the proposed scheme and suggest potential avenues for future research. Countable locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair consisting of a Steinitz number and a real number that is not equal to one. This result serves as an analogue to the theorems established by J. Dixmier and A. A. Kurosh regarding countable abstract groups. Generalized parton distributions (GPDs) characterize the interplay between a nucleon's quarks and gluons in terms of their longitudinal momentum and transverse spatial location. While recent experiments have significantly advanced our understanding of the unpolarized distribution of quark helicity within the nucleon, transverse spatial information remains unmeasured. Dual-Virtual-Compton-Scattering (DVCS) offers a potential pathway to constrain transverse spatial distributions of quark spins in both the proton and neutron. However, DVCS observables are often limited by background noise from meson production, which complicates interpretation. This study demonstrates that the recoil proton polarization during DVCS interactions acts as a strong observable for distinguishing DVCS from background processes. This finding relies on the specific behavior of the hard coefficient in DVCS versus meson production at high invariant masses. Consequently, the analysis recommends that future experiments prioritize the measurement of this recoil proton polarization. Although the investigation utilized proton targets, the proposed observable is applicable to other nucleon types, such as protons, neutrons, and pions. Furthermore, this observable could facilitate future extractions of the neutron, provided the necessary polarized neutron targets become available. Finally, this observable holds promise for enhancing the precision of future DVCS analyses. Supporting code is accessible at https://github.com/kevinmuller/GPDVariations. This paper introduces a conceptual and methodological framework for a new paradigm in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and Artificial Intelligence (AI), termed Augmented Artificial Intelligence (Augmented AI). We argue that ongoing advancements in human cognition and digital technologies will converge to create a new era of augmented human intelligence. Drawing on the historical evolution of artificial intelligence, we contend that augmented AI represents a vital and necessary paradigm. Furthermore, we explore how this concept could be extended to other disciplines, detailing both its potential benefits and challenges. Finally, we conclude by emphasizing the critical importance of Augmented AI as a foundational and ethical framework for HCI and AI. Specifically, we stress the need to prioritize human agency, meaningful engagement, and the dynamic interplay between human and machine capabilities. Additionally, we stress that ethical principles must be embedded within the very foundations of Augmented AI rather than applied as superficial afterthoughts. Overall, we advocate for the immediate adoption of the Augmented AI paradigm to foster more human-centric, ethical, and sustainable interactions between humans and intelligent systems. Muon Colliders face a beam-induced background problem that may exceed the detector's radiation tolerance. A potential solution involves dechirping the beam in the beam dump to lower the beam energy before the collider. This study examines the resulting beam spectrum and background implications. The analysis focuses on two scenarios: one where the spectrum significantly affects the innermost detector components, and another where it primarily influences the outermost components. In both cases, the focus is on $t\bar{t}$ pair production, which serves as a benchmark for beam-induced backgrounds. The research highlights two critical design decisions: the magnitude of beam energy reduction and the method for removing energy, specifically comparing magnet ramping and dechirp cavities. Furthermore, the impact of the reduced beam spot size on innermost components is explored. Finally, a simple analytical model is presented to describe the background, and strategies for mitigating this issue are outlined. Ultimately, reducing the beam energy by a factor of ten or more is recommended to prevent the beam-induced background from overwhelming the detector. Additionally, employing a dechirp cavity to eliminate the beam energy is identified as a viable mitigation strategy. These findings will inform the design of the beam dump and the overall detector for a Muon Collider. The simulations were conducted using the Muon Collider Design Toolkit (MC-DT), a framework developed by the Muon Accelerator Program. A detailed design study of the beam dump and detector will be presented in a future paper. The source code for this study is available on GitHub. The Pauli principle is essential for the emergence of superfluidity in both Bose and Fermi gases. Typically, it is believed that superfluidity arises in Bose gases due to Pauli blocking of low-momentum fermions involved in two-particle scattering, whereas it is suggested that superfluidity in Fermi gases stems from the formation of a degenerate Fermi sea even at very low densities. Here, we show that Pauli blocking can drive superfluidity within a Bose gas even when the degenerate density of the contributing fermions is significantly lower than the molecular density. Specifically, we demonstrate that rigorous exact diagonalization of a Bose gas, even with a minimal number of particles and including all momentum states up to the Fermi momentum of the corresponding Fermi gas, can accurately predict superfluidity. This finding underscores the ability of a very small Bose gas system to emulate key aspects of fermionality. Moreover, we show that similar findings hold for a larger number of particles, thereby validating exact finite-size scaling approaches that utilize the momentum distribution of the corresponding Fermi gas. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for experiments involving ultracold atoms in optical lattices. In particular, we propose an experiment using a Bose-Hubbard model to directly observe the emergence of Pauli blocking. In this setup, we demonstrate that superfluidity can occur at temperatures well above the phase-transition temperature predicted by mean-field theory, provided that states below a certain momentum cutoff are filled in the corresponding Fermi gas. We also show that this superfluid transition can be rigorously confirmed using exact finite-size scaling methods. Our findings highlight that finite Bose gas systems can be used to investigate fundamental many-body quantum phenomena, such as superfluidity, that are inherently fermionic in nature. This capability can be achieved by carefully selecting the number of particles, the system volume, and the temperature. Consequently, this underscores the potential of finite-size systems, including those in lattices, for both fundamental and applied investigations. Unit testing serves as a critical element of the software development lifecycle, yet writing effective tests is challenging for many developers due to various test smells. While prior research has established thresholds to flag these smells, there is a lack of consensus on their relative severity. This study empirically investigates developer perceptions on the severity of eight test smells using an online survey. The participants, drawn from a global pool of 104 software developers with experience in software and testing, were asked to imagine a scenario where a test method exhibits one of the eight common test code smells. They then rated the severity of testing faults on a scale from 0 to 100 for each scenario. The findings indicate that developers perceive "Test Spies" as the most severe issue, while "Deceptive Markup" is viewed as the least severe. Additionally, the research identifies significant differences in perceived severity across the different test smell categories. These results can guide researchers in setting appropriate code limits to minimize the occurrence of test smells. Finally, we offer practical recommendations for developers to assist in avoiding these common pitfalls.

Measuring the inter-beat interval (IBI) is a fundamental technique for estimating heart rate, a process that requires continuous data collection. While many algorithms have been developed to derive IBIs from raw data, most depend on reconstructing the signal using a model to generate proxy data. This study introduces the Tiramisu model, a novel approach designed to minimize IBI estimation errors. The method involves stacking multiple stacked autoencoder (SAE) layers and incorporating the outputs of the final layer into a fully connected (FC) layer. Experimental results on MIT-BSTA and ValidHeart datasets confirm that the proposed method achieves the lowest root mean square error (RMSE) and standard deviation compared to existing approaches. This success is attributed to the Tiramisu model's heightened sensitivity in capturing local signal features and its ability to mitigate estimation errors from previous iterations. Furthermore, the model's efficacy is demonstrated by its superior performance relative to other established algorithms. Given that heart rate estimation is widely used in various applications, reducing IBI estimation errors is essential for accurate outcomes. Consequently, this model is particularly suitable for scenarios where IBI estimation is critical. The source code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/abdullahduran/tiramisu}. Embedding static graphs has been extensively investigated and has effectively addressed key challenges in network analysis. In contrast, embedding dynamic graphs has received far less attention. The primary distinction between static and dynamic graphs lies in the presence of temporal edges in dynamic graphs, which are often overlooked in traditional methods. Furthermore, emerging applications in network science increasingly demand dynamic graph embedding to model scenarios involving multiple networks over time. Consequently, developing methods for dynamic graph embedding has become crucial. This paper begins by embedding temporal edges into dynamic graphs to retain critical temporal information. It then applies and extends existing static graph embedding techniques, adjusting them to account for temporal edges. Additionally, the paper introduces dynamic graph embedding via online embedding and graph state machine approaches. Finally, the study compares dynamic and static graph embedding methods, emphasizing that dynamic graph embedding offers both greater complexity and wider applicability. The paper concludes by discussing open issues and potential future research directions. This work serves as a comprehensive overview of dynamic graph embedding. We establish the existence of global smooth solutions for radial problems featuring prescribed even scalar functions that approach infinity at the equator. This finding complements our main theorem, which addresses the existence of smooth solutions for even prescribed scalar functions satisfying a growth condition near the equator. Both results rely on global a priori $C^k$ estimates derived from recent work by the last two authors and S.R. Adimarkhi. Specifically, for the case $k=2$, we provide a detailed proof of a global $C^2$ estimate for radial even functions, which directly supports Adamchik's result regarding logarithmic divergence. We subsequently outline how this estimate extends to higher-order orders with logarithmic factors. The core of our proof for the higher-order estimate is built upon a metric construction by S.R. Adamchik and S.T. Yau, which describes the conformal geometry near infinity of manifolds with constant negative curvature. By demonstrating that this metric satisfies the prescribed scalar curvature equation with even functions, we validate its utility as a blow-up alternative. While recent approaches utilizing optimal transport (OT) have demonstrated efficacy, embedding the OT objective directly into a neural network presents convergence challenges. This study proposes learning the optimal embedding function through a sequence of Sinkhorn divergences, which approximate OT divergences and facilitate more stable gradient calculations. We demonstrate that the limit of these Sinkhorn divergences recovers the original OT divergences, ensuring the well-posedness of the learning objective. Furthermore, experiments on several image-to-image translation tasks highlight the advantages of this proposed OT-divergence minimization strategy. To evaluate how partnerships between local tracing teams and health visitors influence COVID-19 contact tracing in England, a simulation-based approach was employed. The study utilized a stochastic epidemic model, where an R0 value of 1.3 indicated future growth, and an agent-based tracing model incorporated both human and computational behaviors. The results demonstrated that partnerships reduced the total number of transmissions by 21% and decreased human-day transmission counts by 24%. Furthermore, partnerships with notification and tracing rates set at 70% and 50% respectively achieved a 21% transmission reduction, while those including hospitalization of contacts with high transmission history (HCHTH) achieved the same reduction level. However, when tracing and notification rates were lowered to 20% and 10%, hospitalizing highly exposed HCHTH individuals resulted in only a 1% transmission reduction. Consequently, the study concludes that partnerships between local tracing services and health visitors are highly effective for contact tracing, though hospitalizing HCHTH individuals is not recommended. The model further highlighted that increasing tracing and notification rates from 50% to 70% or from 20% to 70% would result in only a 1% and 4% reduction in transmissions, respectively. Finally, with an R0 of 1.3, partnerships with hospitalization of HCHTH individuals would be unnecessary, as the entire tracing service could be discontinued, resulting in no significant increase in transmissions. The research also noted that partnerships with higher tracing rates and hospitalization of HCHTH individuals would yield greater reductions in transmissions. The model's ability to simulate partnerships with hospitalization of HCHTH individuals and to quantify the impact of varying tracing and notification rates on transmission outcomes further demonstrates its utility. This study investigates the kinematics and physical characteristics of Melotte 72 using Gaia DR2 data. By analyzing the position-velocity diagram, we confirm the cluster's membership and identify a group of stars exhibiting uniform motion. Utilizing the Bayesian method, we determine the cluster's three-dimensional position, spatial dispersion, and age to be $(-1.5 \pm 0.2)$ deg, $(-1.1 \pm 0.1)$ mas, and $1.2 \pm 0.2$ Gyr, respectively. Additionally, by combining Gaia DR2 data with photometric data from the V-band, we construct the cluster's color-magnitude diagram. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the cluster's nature and contribute to a more complete picture of the stellar population in this region. This research examines the Bayesian Logical Inference model (BLI) within a Gaussian field characterized by a linearly decaying covariance function. Logical inference, defined as the incidence of significant field cells along specific directions, is established as a fundamental property of self-organized criticality. The focus is on "sparse" BLI configurations, where the fractal dimension of the incidence set is determined by inflection points in the decay of the Gaussian probability function along that direction. A direction-dependent topological Betti number is derived for the sparse regime and validated using numerical simulations. These numerical results confirm that inflection points in the Gaussian function govern the transition from non-trivial to trivial BLI regimes across the entire parameter space. Furthermore, the implications of these findings regarding inference efficiency, measured by the average distance between significant cells, are analyzed. It is demonstrated that sparsity maximizes topological efficiency by maintaining a constant inflection-point distance across all directions. Finally, the concept of "directional sparsity" is explored, revealing that sparsity is a field property rather than a directional one. Additionally, the paper addresses "non-unique sparsity," a phenomenon arising from the non-uniqueness of inflection points in the Gaussian probability function under certain parameter conditions. This leads to the identification of a critical exponent linked to sparsity, exhibiting universal behavior across all directions, and provides a theoretical framework to predict the average distance between significant cells in both sparse and non-sparse regimes. The resulting theoretical framework is supported by numerical validation. Finally, the study investigates the relationship between sparsity and robustness, showing that sparsity is a necessary condition for robustness, though it is not sufficient in the absence of a linear covariance function. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions. **Keywords:** Bayesian Logical Inference; Gaussian Field; Self-Organized Criticality; Robustness; Critical Exponent. *Corresponding Author: Dr. Youssef Morsi (Email: youssef.morsi@uqam.ca)*. *Affiliation: Universite QAM, Montreal, Canada.*. *Funding: This work was partially funded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC).*. *Reference: [1] Morsi, Youssef; Karami, Mohammad; Morsi, Yousef. Eye-in-hand camera calibration remains a critical challenge in robotics. While numerous algorithms have been developed to address this, they predominantly depend on precise knowledge of the robot's joint angles. This reliance creates vulnerabilities when the robot's controller is compromised or malfunctioning. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a learning-based method capable of determining eye-in-hand camera calibration using only a single image, without requiring any robot joint angle data. Additionally, our algorithm can operate without pre-training by leveraging synthetic training data generated through simulation. We evaluated this approach on two malfunctioning V5 RobotiQ V5 Robotiq Grippers. The algorithm successfully estimated the gripper's pose from the captured images, enabling correct operation despite the robot's joint angles being unknown. This demonstrates that our learning-based solution is robust against a broad spectrum of camera distortions and gripper pose variations. The source code and data required to replicate this work can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishkumar123456789/Single-Image-Calibration. A detailed video description of the experiments is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=14422222222. Future research will focus on expanding and diversifying the training dataset to enhance performance across a wider range of cameras and grippers. Furthermore, we aim to refine the algorithm to reduce the extensive pre-training period currently required and to minimize the substantial memory consumption of the trained model. Finally, we plan to implement these solutions on a greater number of gripper types and to deploy the system in real-world scenarios. Our ultimate goal is to enable correct pose estimation for unknown grippers without necessitating any pre-training. This paper was submitted to the IEEE Robotics and Automation Magazine. Recently, researchers have employed linear reward functions for Reinforcement Learning, yet these functions often suffer from reward hacking and lack interpretability. To address these issues, this work introduces a framework for learning inverse weights under constraints to achieve specific desirable outcomes. We establish convergence guarantees for both discrete and continuous action spaces and demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through numerical experiments in gridworld and continuous control settings. Additionally, we highlight its utility in solving reverse challenges, such as identifying rewards that result in desired behaviors. The code is available at https://github.com/ashishgarg1992/ICRL. Furthermore, numerical results can be accessed at https://drive.google.

Gaia, the European Space Agency's mission, serves as a cornerstone global effort for Milky Way astronomy. It is designed to create a comprehensive 3D map of our galaxy by surveying nearly every star within its luminosity limits and a significant fraction of the extragalactic sky. This survey will characterize over one trillion objects by measuring their positions, distances, and motions with high precision, while simultaneously providing a multi-wavelength view of the sky. Additionally, the mission will detect and map variable and non-variable sources, such as asteroids, using the same data. The primary GAIA Data Release (GDR1) is scheduled for late 2022 and will include the first batch of Gaia's most significant datasets, offering unprecedented detail on stellar and substellar sources, including stars with planets, white dwarfs, and brown dwarfs. This presentation will outline the GAIA mission and its data products, highlighting their relevance to substellar sources and exoplanets. Furthermore, it will detail the GAIA Data Release and Publication (GD7P) process, which ensures that GAIA's data products remain current and continuously expand. The ultimate vision is to enable the GAIA community to utilize and contribute to the ever-growing GAIA database. The GAIA community itself is a diverse group of scientists from various disciplines, including those specializing in substellar objects and exoplanets. The talk will conclude by inviting all interested individuals to join the GAIA community. We introduce a word-RAM algorithm capable of finding an efficient vertex separator for any graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and treewidth $w$. This approach utilizes $O(m + nw \log \Delta / \varepsilon_n)$ bits of memory, where $\Delta$ represents the maximum degree and $\varepsilon_n$ denotes a dynamically computable $O(\log n)$-approximation of the minimum vertex removals needed to divide $G$ into two components each with at most $2/3n$ vertices. Our method runs in $O(m + nw \log \Delta / \varepsilon_n)$ time, ensuring that no vertex is removed more than $O(2/3n)$ times. To the best of our knowledge, the space and time complexities for this specific vertex separator problem have previously been analyzed only under the assumption of $O(n)$ available memory. Leveraging this space-efficient algorithm, we develop a dynamic $O(1)$-approximation for the graph minor problem, which operates within the same memory framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our implementation of the Four-Color Theorem, also based on this algorithm, can be adapted to run in external memory. This advancement improves the existing external-memory algorithm for planar graph coloring, reducing its time complexity from $O(m + n \log^* n)$ to $O(m + n \log \Delta / \varepsilon_n)$. Finally, we establish that any algorithm solving the vertex separator problem in $T(n,m,\varepsilon_n)$ time and using $S(n,m,\varepsilon_n)$ space must satisfy the lower bound $T(n,m,\varepsilon_n) + S(n,m,\varepsilon_n) = \Omega(m + nw \log \Delta / \varepsilon_n)$. This lower bound is tight given that all our algorithms run in $O(m + nw \log \Delta / \varepsilon_n)$ time and space. Additionally, we prove that any algorithm solving dynamic four-coloring for $PW$-graphs must require $\Omega(m + nW \log \Delta / \varepsilon_n)$ time, demonstrating that our dynamic four-coloring algorithm is also optimal. Overall, these findings highlight the inherent trade-off between time and space complexity in solving graph problems. The analysis of high-dimensional networks is a central theme in the complex systems field. Traditional clustering techniques are typically adapted for networks by adding a diagonal to the adjacency matrix, converting it into an adjacency-plus-I (A+) matrix, and applying standard methods. However, this approach is often ill-suited for diverse network types, particularly those derived from experiments, computations, or measurements, which may include heterogeneous node degrees and be either directed or undirected. In these contexts, the standard method can yield misleading results. We propose four distinct clustering interpretations for the Laplacian (L = I - A+) of a directed, possibly non-normal network (where "normal" refers to spectral properties), with normalized versions serving as a special case. These interpretations include: (i) a natural generalization of the standard graph interpretation for symmetric, 0-1, network-plus-self-loops; (ii) a formulation of the least-squares orthogonal projection of vectors onto the column space of L; (iii) an interpretation of the least-squares error in reconstructing L given only the network's degree sequences; and (iv) an interpretation of the least-squares error in reconstructing L given only a network's cluster assignments. We also present a non-orthogonal projection interpretation for the generalized inverse of L. Furthermore, we develop weighted directed clustering frameworks for scenarios where networks are inferred from noisy data or partially measured, alongside methods for combining such inferred networks with a subset of known, ground-truth networks. For each interpretation, we provide numerical examples across various network types to demonstrate the significance of these formulations. We argue that the specific interpretation of clustering adopted should be tailored to the specific context of the network in question. Finally, we note that our approach is also applicable to other matrix-based clustering problems. Supplemental material is available at: https://github.com/alexmahaffy/weighted_directed_clustering. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a prominent method for integrating prior physical knowledge into machine learning models. Nevertheless, the black-box nature of PINNs hinders the derivation of rigorous error bounds. This study presents the initial framework for a rigorous, component-wise a posteriori error estimation for PINNs. The proposed method is grounded in a deep splitting approach, where a finite element discretization of the underlying partial differential equation (PDE) serves as an intermediate step to derive error estimates for the final PDE solution. We establish sharp error bounds that rely on the discretization resolution and model approximation capabilities, alongside the convergence rates of the neural network approximations for both the error residual and the data mismatch. Crucially, these error bounds can be computed without requiring knowledge of the true solution. Furthermore, we integrate these bounds into a framework for the certified minimization of a PINN-based quantity of interest, enabling the reliable machine learning of PDE solutions with quantifiable, computable uncertainty estimates. The theoretical findings are demonstrated through a case study involving the one-dimensional heat equation. Additionally, our proofs underscore the significance of a recently developed convexity property for PDE-based quantities of interest, a property that is not universally satisfied by all such quantities. Finally, we argue that our proposed error estimation framework is extendable to a broader class of PDEs and physics-informed statistical models. In this context, our method yields computable upper and lower error bounds, thereby facilitating the creation of a robust meta-algorithm for the certified training of such models. This approach ensures that the training process is accompanied by trustworthy uncertainty quantification. To our knowledge, this marks the first instance where a black-box model can achieve certified training with provably reliable uncertainty assessment. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/philipp-gillhaus/pinn-certified-optimization. Keywords: certified optimization, a posteriori error estimation, physics-informed neural networks, uncertainty quantification. Air pollution epidemiology faces the dual challenge of analyzing observational data while accounting for spatial and temporal correlations. Consequently, researchers employ various statistical methods, including geostatistics and machine learning, within air pollution models to address these issues. Geostatistics offers benefits such as kriging for spatial interpolation, variance estimation, and kriging-based smoothing. In contrast, machine learning facilitates the non-linear integration of multiple air pollutants, enabling the assessment of joint health effects. This review examines recent advancements in air pollution models, with a specific focus on geostatistics and machine learning applications. It evaluates the strengths and limitations of these approaches and outlines potential future directions. To illustrate these concepts, the authors present a series of case studies. The first involves an integrated analysis of two large-scale studies investigating short-term air pollution effects on mortality in the Netherlands. The second case study explores an integrated analysis of long-term air pollution associations with dementia using a unified framework that combines kriging, Bayesian hierarchical modeling, and random forests. Finally, the authors address an emerging research topic concerning the spatial variability of ultrafine particles. By integrating a physical particle coagulation model with Bayesian kriging, they develop a statistical model for estimating the number concentration of ultrafine particles. Throughout this review, the authors advocate for a more integrated analysis of air pollution data. They argue that this integration is essential for jointly estimating the effects of multiple pollutants, characterizing their spatial and temporal variability, and ultimately elucidating the underlying mechanisms of human exposure and health impacts. To facilitate this, they introduce a new software package for integrated air pollution analysis. This package implements Bayesian kriging, Bayesian kriging within a random effects framework, and kriging alongside random forests. It is designed to be easily extensible to incorporate other statistical methods. The package is freely available on GitHub. This article and the associated software were developed through a close collaboration between statisticians and epidemiologists. Therefore, the authors conclude that statisticians and epidemiologists must collaborate closely to advance air pollution research. They believe that bridging the gap between these disciplines is crucial for elucidating the spatial and temporal variability of air pollutants and their impacts on human health. Ultimately, such a collaboration is indispensable for understanding the mechanisms of exposure and health effects, which remains a primary challenge in air pollution epidemiology. In support of this conclusion, a case study is provided that analyzes joint exposure to physical and chemical factors using a Bayesian approach combining kriging, Bayesian hierarchical modeling, and random forests. We introduce a method to distinguish between zero-mode peaks and other ordinary Andreev peaks at zero bias within chiral Majorana modes under inhomogeneous environments. This approach involves applying an Ohmic current to the normal lead, which induces temperature-dependent broadening for zero modes but leaves other Andreev peaks at zero bias unaffected. This Ohmic current can be controlled via a gate voltage, producing a characteristic "bell-shaped" conductance signature unique to the presence of chiral Majorana modes. Furthermore, we highlight a previously overlooked issue regarding the stability of Andreev peaks against environmental noise in tunneling spectroscopy setups with normal electrodes. While a bosonized treatment of electromagnetic coupling suggests that Andreev peaks are resilient to environment-induced dissipation, we demonstrate through path-integral numerical simulations that this is incorrect. We observe that the breakdown of Andreev peaks occurs at zero bias when even a minimal coupling is present, with the lifetime of these peaks exhibiting extreme sensitivity to system parameters. Consequently, practical implementation of tunneling spectroscopy using normal electrodes remains challenging. Finally, we explore the connection between the persistence of Andreev peaks at zero bias and the KMS condition. Our findings suggest that bosonization results are more reliable at finite temperatures, leading to a systematic analysis of conductance peaks at zero bias both above and below the chemical potential difference between the superconductor and normal metal. This analysis reveals a crossover behavior driven by the tunneling amplitude and provides a comprehensive understanding of Andreev conductance signatures. Ultimately, our work establishes a framework for interpreting experimental data and aids in the identification of topological qubits based on chiral Majorana modes. Additionally, our findings regarding the instability of Andreev peaks at zero bias may offer new perspectives for interpreting experimental results. In summary, this proposal advances the understanding of topological qubits and highlights the necessity of developing innovative experimental techniques to achieve high-resolution spectroscopy for investigating Andreev conductance. Such resolutions are crucial for accurately probing the fundamental properties of qubits and their constituent Majorana modes. Specifically, the proposed scheme necessitates achieving a temperature lower than the previously estimated minimum using Ohmic electrodes. Furthermore, it suggests that future experimental efforts should explore tunneling spectroscopy using superconducting electrodes, as this configuration is less sensitive to Andreev peak instability and may facilitate the observation of fundamental phenomena in chiral Majorana modes. We establish a non-asymptotic lower bound for the expected regret of any exploration-based linear bandit algorithm, applicable to problem instances with a large number of arms. This bound is derived using a novel product of divergences, which is strictly greater than the sum of divergences, thereby explaining why certain algorithms struggle to explore all arms within finite slates. This finding offers a more granular understanding of exploration dynamics and suggests that lower bounds based on the sum of divergences may be insufficient for validating inference validity in certain settings. To support robust inference, we propose a novel linear bandit algorithm that achieves an exploration-based regret guarantee matching the lower bound (up to a constant factor) when the number of arms is polynomial in the problem's information-theoretic parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our algorithm supports valid inference by providing a rigorous lower bound on the gap between the estimated success probability for any arm and its true value, regardless of that arm's selection frequency. This advancement enables reliable, provable inference for all arms within a polynomial-time framework. Finally, we support our theoretical findings with an empirical study that highlights the limitations of existing methods and confirms the effectiveness of our proposed approach. To our knowledge, this work represents the first exploration-based linear bandit algorithm that provides a tight regret bound while also supporting a tight inference bound that remains effective even when exploration is imperfect. Our implementation is available at \url{https://github.com/ashwinbhat/RL-Inference}. Gapped graphene has been suggested as an ideal system for observing the valley Hall effect, a transport phenomenon involving electron flow characterized by distinct valley indices. However, this study demonstrates that the effect is more accurately understood as a manifestation of the orbital Hall effect. In this framework, the "valley" index signifies opposite phases of the orbital current, while the Hill identity links the valley Hall conductance to the derivative of the orbital relaxation time. The orbital (and spin) Hall effects are intrinsic phenomena in charge-neutral systems, with their primary distinction from charge-carrier based effects lying in their opposite signs. These effects are significant because they enable magnetoelectric coupling, facilitating the conversion between electrical and magnetic responses. This research explicitly details how orbital and valley Hall effects manifest in various types of graphene. Furthermore, we propose a method for generating a magnetic field within a current-carrying system and examine a time-reversal symmetry-breaking mechanism driven by an in-plane electric field acting on curvature-induced out-of-plane electron displacement. Finally, our findings regarding magnetic field generation in magnetic graphene may have implications for thermoelectric devices and the design of unconventional spintronics components. Notably, our analysis of orbital Hall effect in graphene is also applicable to other semiconductors, such as GaAs. All theoretical results are supported by numerical computations. Furthermore, this work offers a pathway to decouple orbital relaxation from momentum scattering, thereby enabling the observation of orbital Hall effect in topological semimetals. The proposed framework is also applicable to designing unconventional spintronic devices that couple orbital and magnetic states. Data poisoning represents a critical security risk in machine learning, where attackers compromise training data to degrade model performance post-deployment. Although graph classification tasks are highly susceptible to such attacks, current research predominantly relies on manual construction of poisoning templates, often guided by domain expertise. This study introduces a data-driven methodology utilizing data augmentation and reinforcement learning to automatically generate effective templates and targeting labels specifically designed to exploit graph neural networks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that targeting labels significantly enhance learning efficiency. Our findings indicate that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches, requiring fewer poisoned nodes with targeting labels to achieve the same attack success rate. Additionally, we present an efficient algorithm based on data augmentation and reinforcement learning to automatically search for optimal poisoning templates. Extensive experiments confirm that these targeting labels not only accelerate the attack process but also improve the attack success rate. The code for this method is available at: https://github.com/zhenghao1212/D4GP.

Matching sources across multiple sky catalogues is a critical component of source separation, which is essential for the 42-inch SALT telescope. This process is vital for planning observations and analyzing data by providing source positions, magnitudes, and redshifts. This study compares two methods for 2MASS and UCAC3 catalogue matching: UCALIS and a newly developed algorithm referred to as MagMatch. Both methods were tested on SALT imaging data from the 2MASS and UCAC3 catalogues. The analysis involved evaluating over 1.5 million sources, examining source density variations, and comparing the two methods. The study found that MagMatch outperforms UCALIS by correctly identifying sources that UCALIS misses and by reducing false source identification. Additionally, incorporating two more filter bands into MagMatch further enhances its performance. This improvement was tested using synthetic sources with three and four filter bands against catalogues that have and do not include a Z-band. The results indicate that adding a fourth filter band increases correct source identification by approximately 10% compared to using only three bands. This finding suggests that future catalogues with four filter bands will enable more accurate source separation. Overall, MagMatch demonstrates potential for matching sources in multi-band catalogues, and further enhancements are possible through the integration of extra filter bands. The code for MagMatch is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1989/MagMatch. We introduce a method for enhancing speech recognition accuracy in automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems by leveraging a limited labeled dataset through the cycle-GAN framework. This approach enables our ASR model to extract features robust against both accent and language variations within the cycle-loss constraint. Furthermore, we implement three loss functions and one metric-based loss to enforce speech invariance across our generative model. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses the baseline ASR system by 3.15 WER points on the test set using 20% of the training data. Active inference (AFI) is a unified theoretical framework originating in neuroscience and cognitive science that addresses perception, action, and decision-making for autonomous agents by minimizing variational free energy. However, its reliance on density factorization renders it computationally prohibitive for real-time control in complex environments. To address this, we propose a deep active inference model (DAFI) inspired by the hierarchical architecture of the mammalian brain. DAFI decomposes the world model into parallel predictive networks operating at distinct spatial resolutions, while a decision network selects actions to minimize free energy at the appropriate resolution. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that DAFI can approximate free energy minimization more accurately than AFI. We validate this through robot navigation simulations, comparing AFI and DAFI across two scenarios: a simple grid world requiring few states, and a complex grid world demanding many states. In the simple environment, both systems successfully complete tasks. However, in the complex scenario, AFI fails to identify key states and remains trapped in local minima, whereas DAFI efficiently navigates the environment and completes the mission. These results confirm the superior performance of DAI inference in challenging navigation tasks. Additionally, we illustrate how both models can be implemented using the PyAFI Python library. The experimental code is accessible at https://github.com/PyAFI-team/PyAFI/tree/main/examples/robot_navigation. Our findings suggest that DAFI holds promise for developing intelligent autonomous agents capable of navigating intricate environments. The Python library serves as a versatile tool for applying free energy principles to problems in perception, decision-making, and control. Furthermore, the library's design supports the autonomous construction of intelligent agents, thereby facilitating scientific progress. This paper aims to inspire further research into autonomous systems grounded in neuroscience principles. We anticipate that enhanced computational capabilities will enable free energy-based intelligent agents to achieve superior performance in complex real-world settings. Ultimately, this may contribute to solving the fundamental problem of autonomy, which remains a significant challenge for humanity. Our ultimate aspiration is to foster the emergence of intelligent life on Earth. Using non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations, we examined the Soret effect in binary mixtures of dimers and monomers, specifically targeting the contribution of internal degrees of freedom in flexible molecules to this phenomenon. Our results indicate that under typical experimental conditions, this contribution amounts to only a few percent. Additionally, we demonstrate that both the thermal diffusion coefficient and the Soret coefficient can assume either positive or negative values, remaining highly sensitive to the internal structure of the molecules and to adjustments in intermolecular potentials. These findings offer a clear explanation for why literature reports on the Soret effect for soft molecules are highly variable. Finally, we propose that systems exhibiting large internal degrees of freedom, such as polymers, may be unsuitable candidates for selecting materials for solar cell applications. This conclusion is supported by a simple mean-field model that utilizes our previously reported parameters for dimers. Our analysis of literature regarding polymers in salt solutions confirms that this conclusion is consistent with existing experimental data. We conclude that our insights are essential for the rational design of materials for solar cells. Finally, we outline potential future research directions aimed at clarifying the underlying mechanisms of the Soret effect. Specifically, we outline the need to investigate whether a single, universal mechanism explains the effect, or whether there are distinct mechanisms for hard and soft molecules. Furthermore, it is crucial to examine whether the mechanism for soft molecules aligns with that of charged species. To address these questions, we must conduct simulations on a broader range of model systems, including polymers, ions, and both polar and apolar molecules. Our work will serve as a foundation for such future investigations. Finally, we have made our input potentials available to facilitate these upcoming research endeavors. This decision was driven by our conviction that the mechanisms responsible for the Soret effect in soft molecules remain an open and unresolved question. We firmly believe that resolving this issue is a significant scientific challenge that demands a concerted future research effort. We hope that our findings will contribute to a better understanding of the internal mechanisms driving the Soret effect. We believe that our conclusions regarding polymers will aid in the selection of appropriate materials for solar cell applications. We are confident that our findings will stimulate further research into the various internal mechanisms of the Soret effect. We hope our conclusions will encourage a more thorough investigation of the internal mechanisms driving the Soret effect. We believe that our conclusions regarding polymers will assist in the selection of suitable materials for solar cell applications. Following the generation of a latent vector through ideal scoring, the model predicts a score for each paragraph. False positives remain a critical challenge in domain-adaptive pedestrian detection, where models trained on clean indoor datasets often perform poorly in complex, real-world outdoor environments. The performance gain from additional outdoor training data is frequently outweighed by domain shifts. Conventional approaches address this through box re-ranking or pooling techniques to eliminate false positives; however, these methods suffer from limited improvement because most relevant detections are suppressed at low confidence thresholds. To address this limitation, we introduce Box Re-Ranking, an unsupervised domain-adaptive approach for pedestrian detection. Our method employs a curated, high-quality subset of outdoor images as an oracle to unsupervisedly refine an initial detection set. Specifically, we employ an unsupervised outlier detection model to refine confidence scores and filter out most false positives. Furthermore, an expert model is trained on the initial set augmented by the high-quality outlier set to further enhance performance. We demonstrate that our approach significantly reduces false positives while maintaining recall rates. Extensive evaluations on outdoor datasets confirm that our method outperforms existing domain-adaptive pedestrian detection techniques. The source code is available at https://github.com/1000x1000/Box-Re-Ranking. This paper introduces a motional editing technique designed to simulate a throw originating from an erroneous point of release. Simulating this error is crucial for researching the motor control aspects of throwing. Our approach leverages the underlying structure of motion capture data, which exhibits strong correlations between adjacent frames due to the continuous nature of human movement. We construct a Gaussian process model to predict frame values based on these local correlations from the motion buffer. This model enables us to generate a simulated release error by altering only a small subset of frames, thereby minimizing the amount of synthetic data required. We assess the fidelity of our method through visual comparisons, quantitative error metrics, and a study involving healthy participants. Our results demonstrate that subjects can identify a throwing motion even with a simulated point of release error, suggesting that our approach captures the essential characteristics of throwing action. Consequently, this method is valuable for investigating the motor control mechanisms of throwing. To facilitate this, we have made the code and a sample motion capture clip available at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/fauxthrow. Additionally, we provide the complete motion capture dataset upon request. The term "FauxThrow" is a play on words combining "faux pas" and "throw." Although Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models have demonstrated strong translation capabilities, they often lack explicit grammatical structure. While recent efforts attempt to incorporate syntax, these approaches differ fundamentally from our proposed method which generates output step-by-step via an autonomous tree-structured decoder. This decoder is integrated into a standard encoder-decoder framework and leverages grammatical connections to direct the search for the most grammatical tree structure. Our primary contributions include the top-down tree-structured decoding process, the development of syntactic connections, and the resulting model's ability to produce grammatical structures that outperform state-of-the-art results in both machine translation and dependency parsing. Additionally, our model exhibits an robust error-correction mechanism that significantly enhances performance on low-resource languages and minimizes extrinsic grammar loss. Experiments across six NMT datasets and two parsing benchmarks highlight the efficacy and practical utility of our approach. To our knowledge, this is the first decoder designed to explicitly target the generation of tree structures. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/taehyungkim/TSD. We demonstrate that our method can accurately estimate non-trivial multi-local observables, such as string order parameters and energy, satisfying the precision requirements of the quantum phase estimation algorithm. Additionally, we assess our method's efficacy on error-mitigated simulated noisy data, showing that it achieves a sufficient accuracy level for variational quantum algorithms comparable to exhaustive measurement strategies. The research presented in \cite{Kam} and \cite{Kam2} examines two integrable non-linear partial differential equations linked to the Davey-Stewartson system. The first equation is $q_{tt}-q_{xxxx}+\frac{1}{2}(k^2(q\overline{q}_x-q_x\overline{q}))^2=0$, while the second is $q_{tt}-q_{xxxx}+\frac{1}{2}(k^2(\overline{q}q_t-\overline{q}_t\overline{q}))^2=0$. In both scenarios, solutions are defined via $2\times 2$ matrix Riemann-Hilbert problems featuring reflection coefficients that become polynomial in the large $k$ limit. This paper derives explicit bounds for the reflection coefficient in both cases as $|k|$ approaches infinity. These results are instrumental in establishing rigorous error estimates for the large $k$ asymptotics of the stationary phase method applied to the Fourier transform of the initial data. Such estimates are required to demonstrate that the KdV equation emerges as the $k\to\infty$ limit of the integrable DS-II equations described above. Specifically, this work supports the argument presented in \cite{BGKKT2}. Consequently, this approach may be essential for rigorously deriving the Camassa-Holm equation as the $k\to\infty$ limit of the second DS-II equation, a derivation currently under development. Sibylvariant transformations (SVT) are recently introduced, model-agnostic data transformations designed to enhance the robustness of text classification models. By operating at the token level, SVT introduces greater diversity compared to other existing transformations, while effectively preserving both semantic and syntactic data integrity. Experimental results across ten standard text classification datasets demonstrate that integrating multiple SVTs boosts model AUC scores by an average of 3.5%. Furthermore, an ablation study on large language models indicates that even smaller SVT ensembles yield significant improvements in robustness against in-distribution data. Finally, applying SVT ensembles to out-of-distribution data reveals that the transformations help models distinguish between in-distribution and out-of-distribution samples more effectively than a single model. The code for implementing SVT ensembles is available at https://github.com/DeepSibyl/Sibyl-Transformations.
